Series title: bod kyi gtsug lag gces btus vol. 14 Volume title: dus ´khor ´grel chen dri med ´od kyi rgyan Author: mkhas grub nor bzang rgya mtsho (1423-1513) Translator: Gavin Kilty
1. Indo-Tibetan Buddhism; Vajrayana; Kalachakra Tantra. 2. mkhas grub nor bzang rgya mtsho; Pundarika. Printed in New Delhi, India
mchod brjod/
Homage
rgyal ba kun gyi mkhyen brtse gcig tu bsdus pa'i ngo bo rje btsun 'jam pa'i dbyangs la phyag 'tshal lo/ /
Homage to noble Mañjuśrī, composite of the knowledge and wisdom of every buddha.

mi 'gyur g.yo ba dang bral zla ba bdud rtsi d+hU tI'i mkha' la gyen du 'dzegs pa las/ / mi 'gyur mchog gi bde ba dam pas rnam med shes rab dbyer med 'khyud pa'i rnam 'gyur gang / / in+d+ra nI la'i ri bo mchog gang 'tshams [1] sprin gzhon nus 'khyud pa dang mtshungs mchog gi sku/ / rnam kun mchog ldan stong pa'i gzugs la rnam bcas shes rab dga' mas 'khyud pa de la 'dud/ /

Manifestation of unchanging and ultimate great bliss in indivisible union with nonaspected wisdom, arising from unchanging, immovable moon nectar stacked in the skies of the central channel, a supreme form, a mighty indranīla mountain embraced by a few young clouds, in empty-form aspect endowed with every attribute supreme, embraced by the wisdom consort Viśvamātā: to you I bow.

d.div: [1] ma dper 'tshams zhes skabs du mar 'as 'phul byung na'ang mtshams zhes yin nam snyam pas 'dir de bzhin du bcos yod/

f.d: blo gros gting mtha' mi mngon zab mo'i dbyings las g.yo ba mi mnga' yang / / skal ldan skye bo smin grol lam la 'god mdzad bzang po'i 'phrin las kyi/ / rnam dkar grags pa phyogs kyi bu mo'i rna lung dag la gar byed pa/ / rgyal ba'i dbang po blo bzang sras bcas zhabs sen pad+mor spyi bos 'dud/ /

Not moving from realms of profound, unfathomable wisdom, yet the untainted renown of your enlightened activity in bringing the fortunate to the paths of ripening and freedom dances before the ladies of the ten directions; mighty conqueror, Losang Drakpa and your disciples, I bow my head to your lotus feet.
blo gros chu 'dzin che las lung rigs char gyis phan bde'i lo tog skyong / / shes rab pir gyis gang thugs ngos la mkhyen gnyis rin chen ri mo gsal/ /

From the great clouds of their knowledge fall the rains of scripture and reasoning to nourish the harvest of happiness. Pens of wisdom have drawn in clarity upon their minds precious pictures of the two types of knowledge.
chos kyi rgyal po'i ring lugs gsal mdzad rnam dkar grags pa'i ba dan 'dzin/ / bka' drin mtshungs med yongs 'dzin mchog rnams bdag gi gtsug na rtag bzhuT 'tshal/ /
By expounding the doctrine of the mighty dharma king, you hold aloft a banner of stainless renown; sublime masters, kindness without parallel, remain forever upon the crown of my head. /4/
[gleng brjod ]
Introduction
brtsams chos kyi spyi bshad/
1. Compilation of the Root and Condensed Tantra

'dir dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i brjod par bya ba phyi nang gzhan gsum gyi don cung zad brjod par bya ste/ 'di la bzhi/ ston pas rtsa ba'i rgyud gsungs tshul sogs bshad pa'i gleng bslang ba dang / bla med kyi rgyud kun gyi brjod bya'i gtso bo gnyug ma'i sems bshad pa dang / bla med kyi rgyud rnams kyi dgongs pa'i 'grel tshul bshad pa dang / skabs su bab pa dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i brjod bya phyi nang gzhan gsum bshad pa'o/ /

Here I will write a little on the Outer, Inner, and Other, which make up the three main themes of the glorious Kālacakra. There are four main outlines: 1. Introduction: How the Buddha taught the Kālacakra Root Tantra 2. The primordial mind and body: Principal themes of the highest yoga class of tantra 3. Explanations of the intentions of the highest yoga tantras 4. An exposition of the Outer, Inner, and Other: The three themes of Kālacakra
ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs tshul sogs bshad pa'i gleng bslang ba/
1. Introduction: How the Buddha taught the Kālacakra Root Tantra

dang po la gsum/ ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa'i tshul dang / sdud pa pos ji ltar bsdus pa'i tshul dang / bsdus pa'i rtsa rgyud dang bsdus rgyud chos rgyal dang rigs ldan rnams kyis bstan pa'i tshul lo/ /

The first has three outlines: 1. How the Buddha taught the Kālacakra Root Tantra 2. Compilation of the Tantra 3. How the Root Tantra and the Condensed Tantra were taught by the dharma kings and the Kalkī[1] kings of Shambhala

d.div: [1] rigs ldan. Lineage bearer, the lineage being that of the vajra caste.

f.d: dang po [ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa'i tshul ]ni

d.i: How the Buddha taught the Kālacakra Root Tantra

f.d: ston pa shAkya thub pas rgya gar 'phags pa'i yul gyi rdo rje gdan byang chub kyi shing drung du mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas te pha rol tu phyin pa spyi dang / bya rgod phung po'i rir shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i chos kyi 'khor lo bskor/ de nas rgya gar lho phyogs dpal gyi ri dang nye ba dpal ldan 'bras spungs kyi mchod rten chen por byon nas mchod rten gyi nang gi 'og tu chos dbyings gsung gi dbang phyug gi dkyil 'khor dang / steng du dpal ldan rgyu skar gyi dkyil 'khor chen po spros te/

Our teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, actualized complete enlightenment in the noble country of India under the Bodhi tree in Bodhgaya and turned the wheels of dharma by teaching the perfections, particularly the perfection of wisdom, upon Vulture’s Peak. He traveled to the great stupa of Dhānyakaṭaka near Śrīparvata in southern India. Inside the stupa he emanated the mighty dharmadhātu speech mandala below and the glorious constellation mandala above.

gnas phun sum tshogs pa bde ba chen po'i gnas rdo rje dbyings kyi dkyil 'khor chen por rdo rje seng+ge'i khri la bzhugs pa/ ston pa phun sum tshogs pa shAkya seng+ge dus kyi 'khor lo'i ting nge 'dzin la snyoms par zhugs nas dkyil 'khor bdag po'i rnam par gnas pas/ 'khor phun sum tshogs pa dkyil 'khor la bkod pa'i 'khor sangs rgyas dang byang chub sems dpa' dang khro bo dang lha dang klu dang lha mo'i tshogs kyi rnam par gnas pa rnams dang / zhu ba po'i 'khor phyag na rdo rje'i sprul pa'i sku rgyal po zla ba bzang pos sham+b+ha la'i yul nas rdzu 'phrul gyis byon te gsol ba btab pa la brten nas nyan pa po'i 'khor byang chub sems dpa' du ma dang sham+b+ha la'i yul chen po dgu bcu rtsa drug gi rgyal po dgu bcu rtsa drug dang skal ba dang ldan pa'i lha dang lha ma yin la sogs pa'i tshogs dpag tu med pa dang / chos phun sum tshogs pa 'jig rten dang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i dbang bskur ba byin nas sangs rgyas nyid du lung bstan te dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsa ba'i rgyud stong phrag bcu gnyis pa gsungs pa yin no/ /

In this perfect place, a place of great bliss, he sat upon a vajra lion throne in the great Vajradhatu mandala. There this perfect teacher, the lion of the Śākya, entered the meditative concentration upon Kālacakra and became the master of the mandala. Surrounding him was the perfect mandala entourage of buddhas, /5/ bodhisattvas, wrathful protectors, gods, nāgas, and goddesses, as well as the entourage of the tantra requestor, King Sucandra, an emanation of Vajrapāṇi, who had traveled by miraculous powers from the kingdom of Shambhala. By requesting the tantra an audience gathered, consisting of the ninety-six kings of the ninety-six lands of Shambhala, many bodhisattvas, and countless fortunate gods and asura. There the perfect dharma of worldly and nonworldly initiations, followed by prophecies of enlightenment and the Twelve Thousand Kālacakra Root Tantra was taught.

stong phrag bcu gnyis ni sh+lau ka'i grangs yin te/ mdor bsdus gnyis pa'i 'grel chen las/
stong phrag bcu gnyis zhes pa ni stong phrag brgyad cu rtsa bzhi lhag pa'i 'bum gsum gyi yi ge'i tshogs te/ yi ge sum cu rtsa gnyis pa rjes su bsngags pa stong phrag bcu gnyis yod pa ni stong phrag bcu gnyis pa'o/[2] / zhes gsungs pa ltar tsheg bar brgyad ma la tshig rkang du byas pa'i tshigs bcad ni rjes sngags kyi sdeb sbyor ro/ /

Here “twelve thousand” refers to the number of verses. In the Realms chapter of the Great Commentary, in the second summary it says:
“Twelve thousand” refers to a collection of 384,000 syllables, which comprise 12,000 thirty-two-syllable anuṣtubh verses, and this is the Twelve Thousand Tantra.[2] As this quote explains, a verse in anuṣtubh meter consists of lines of eight syllables.

d.div: [2] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 15_na3_sde dge'i nang 'bum gsum gyi thad du 'bum phrag ces gsal/
[2] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 15a3.

f.d:
'bras spungs kyi mchod rten du dus 'khor rtsa rgyud gsungs pa bzhin du bla med kyi rgyud thams cad gsungs par bzhed pa dus 'khor gyi rgyud rtsa 'grel gyi dgongs pa yin te/ dus 'khor gyi rgyud phyi ma las/
dpal ldan 'bras spungs chos kyi dbyings su stobs bcu pa yis sangs rgyas pa yi rgyud rnams mtha' dag bstan/[3] / ces dang /

Although the tantra taught in the Dhānyakaṭaka stupa was the Kālacakra Root Tantra, it is the assertion of the Kālacakra and its commentaries that every highest yoga tantra was being taught. The Later Kālacakra Tantra says:
By the teaching of the Twelve Thousand in the dharmadhātu of Dhānyakaṭaka, all tantras of the Buddha were taught.[3]

d.div: [3] sde dge_363_bka'/ rgyud/ ka141_na6_le'u/ 5_ye shes le'u/ dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud phyi ma rgyud kyi snying po zhes bya ba/
[3] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, ka, 141a6.

f.d:
nyi ma dpal gyi mtshan brjod 'grel par/
'dir nges par dpal ldan 'bras spungs rgyal ba'i mchod rten chen por sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das shA_kya seng+ge zhes bya ba la rgyud sna tshogs pa nyan par 'dod pa rnams kyis gsol ba btab pas dpyid zla 'bring po'i nya la chos kyi dbyings gsung gi dbang phyug gi dkyil 'khor dang / de'i steng du dpal ldan rgyu skar gyi dkyil 'khor dang po'i sangs rgyas rnam par spros nas der nyi ma de nyid la lha la sogs pa rnams la sangs rgyas kyi dbang bskur nas rgyas pa dang bsdus pa'i dbye bas gsang sngags kyi tshul thams cad bstan to/[4] / zhes bshad pa'i shes par byed pa las so/ /

This can also be known from the Sūryaśrī’s Drops of Nectar:
In the great and regal stupa of Dhānyakaṭaka, the conquering Buddha, the lion of the Śākya, was supplicated by those who wished to hear various tantras. There on the full moon of the middle spring month, in the form of the primordial buddha, he emanated the dharmadhātu speech mandala and the glorious constellation mandala above. There on that very day gods and others were initiated by the Buddha and taught extensively and in condensed form all the systems of secret mantra.[4]

d.div: [4] sde dge_1395_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ pha_'phags pa mtshan yang dag par brjod pa'i mdor bshad bdud rtsi'i thigs pa/ 36_na7_'gyur cung mi mthun/
[4] Toh 1395 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, pha, 36a7.

f.d: 'o na ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa'i dus ni gang zhig yin/ ston pa sangs rgyas pa'i dus ni ci zhig yin snyam na/
But when did our teacher teach the Root Tantra, and what are the dates of the Buddha? /6/

de yang zhib tu bshad par bya ste/ lo 'di nas ni drug brgya'i lo yis zhes sogs kyi mdor bsdus dgu pa'i 'grel chen las/
de bzhin gshegs pas chos bstan pa'i lo ste lo de nas lo drug brgya na chu bo shI ta'i byang sham+b+ha la zhes bya ba'i yul du grags pa zhes bya ba ni lung gi brjod pa ste 'jam dpal grags pa chen po gsal bar 'byung /[5] zhes ston pas rtsa rgyud bstan pa'i lo de nas rags pa lo drug brgya 'das pa'i 'tshams su rigs ldan 'jam dpal grags pa 'byung zhing /

This should be explained in detail. The words of the Root Tantra, “Six hundred years from this year” are explained by the Great Commentary in the ninth summary from the Realms chapter:
This is the year the Tathāgata taught the dharma. It was prophesized that six hundred years after that year the great Mañjuśrī Yaśas would surely appear in the land known as Shambhala, north of the Sīta River.[5] Therefore, approximately six hundred years after the Buddha taught the Root Tantra, the Kalkī king Mañjuśrī Yaśas appeared.

d.div: [5] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_bsdus pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po dus kyi 'khor lo'i 'grel bshad rtsa ba'i rgyud kyi rjes su 'jug pa stong phrag bcu gnyis pa dri ma med pa'i 'od ces bya ba/('grel chen dri med 'od/) 68_ba6
[5] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 68b6.

f.d:
khams le'i mdor bsdus gsum pa las/
'jam dpal rgyal po grags par gyur te byang chub sems dpa'i seng+ge'i khri de las lo brgya'i bar du chos bstan to/[6] zhes pas 'jam dpal grags pa'i lo brgya ste bdun brgya/

The Great Commentary in the third summary from the Realms chapter says:
Mañjuśrī became King Yaśas and from the bodhisattva lion throne he taught the dharma for a hundred years.[6] Therefore, adding the hundred years of Mañjuśrī Yaśas to the previous six hundred since the time of the Buddha totals seven hundred years.

d.div: [6] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 23_na2
[6] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 23a2.

f.d:
yang khams le'i mdor bsdus dgu pa'i 'grel chen las/
de nas klu yi lo brgya rnams kyis zhes pa ni grags pa mya ngan las 'das pa de nas klu zhes pa lo brgyad brgya nas nges par zhes pa ni gdon mi za bar ma kha'i yul du kla klo'i chos dag rab tu 'jug par 'gyur te/[7] zhes pa ltar bdun brgya'i steng du grags pa 'das nas kla klo 'jug pa'i bar gyi brgyad brgya bsnan pas stong lnga brgya/

The Great Commentary in the ninth summary from the Realms chapter states:
“Naga hundred years from then” means that “naga, or eight, hundred years from the time of Yaśas’s” passing, “definitely,” meaning without doubt, the dharma of the barbarians will enter the land of Makha.[7] Adding the above seven hundred years to these eight hundred years between death of Mañjuśrī Yaśas and the coming of the barbarians totals one thousand five hundred years.

d.div: [7] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 68_ba7
[7] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 68b7.

f.d: de'i steng du me mkha' rgya mtsho'i lo bzhi brgya dang gsum bsnan pas lo stong dgu brgya dang gsum ste/ ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa nas rtsis lo nyis brgya nyer gcig 'das pa phan chad la lo stong dgu brgya dang gsum 'ong /

Adding fire, sky, and ocean[8] years to the above makes 1,903 years. Therefore, from the time of the Buddha teaching the Root Tantra, up to the end of the 221 years of astronomy,[9] 1,903 years elapsed.

d.div: [8] Fire (3) Sky (0) Ocean (4) — the 403 years from the arising of the barbarians (624 c.e.) to the first sixty-year cycle, (rab byung, prabhava) purported to be on the arrival of the Kālacakra Tantra in India in 1027 c.e. See Shawo Tsering, chap. 1, p. 48.
[9] These begin with the rule of Shambhala king Aja, the eleventh Kalkī (806 c.e.), who reformed karaṇa astronomy. See Shawo Tsering, chap. 1, p. 48.

f.d: de la rab byung la sogs 'das pa rnams bsres zhes gsungs pas lo stong dgu brgya dang gsum pa de'i mtha' 'am rtsis la nyis brgya nyer gcig gi tha ma'i lo de zad pa me stag yin par grub/

The Condensed Tantra states, “The past years of prabhava[10] and so forth are to be added.” The last of the 1,903 years, or the last year of the 221 years of astronomy, is established as the kṣaya Fire Tiger year.[11]

d.div: [10] First year of the sixty-year cycle.
[11] The last year of a sixty-year cycle.

f.d: de 'dra'i lo stong dgu brgya dang gsum po de drug cus bgos te me stag nas de'i gong rol tu 'das pa'i drug cu skor du longs pa rnams dor bas lhag zhe gsum 'ong / zhe gsum po de'i thog ma de me stag nas yar bgrangs pa'i nyi sgrol byed shing pho spre'u la phog pas shing spre de'i rtsis lo nyis brgya nyer gcig gi mjug nas yar bgrangs pa'i stong dgu brgya dang gsum po'i thog ma dang /

Dividing 1,903 by sixty and working backward from Fire Tiger year in sixty-year cycles leaves a partial cycle of forty-three years. The first year of that forty-three, counting backward from the Fire Tiger year is the tāraṇa male Wood Monkey year. Therefore, that year is the first year of the 1,903, working backward from the last year /7/ of the two 221 years of astronomy.

lo drug brgya nas 'jam dpal grags pa 'byung bar lung bstan pa'i lo drug brgya'i thog ma'ang yin no/ / de yang drug brgya nas 'jam dbyangs grags pa 'byung zhes pa'i drug brgya yang rags pa'i dbang du byas pa yin te/ ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa'i lo dang lo drug brgya'i thog ma shing spre'i bar der rgyal po zla bzang gis rtsa rgyud bsdus te 'grel pa mdzad pa sogs kyi lo 'ga' zung gzhug dgos so/ /

It is also the first year of the six hundred years mentioned in the prophecy, “After six hundred years Mañjuśrī Yaśas will appear.” Six hundred years is an approximation because between the teaching of the Root Tantra and the beginning of the six hundred years, King Sucandra compiled the Root Tantra and composed a commentary. This would have involved one or two years.

de yang lo grangs ji tsam zhig gzhug dgos na/ mdor bsdus gsum pa las/
de bzhin gshegs pa'i nges pa de'i phyir rtsa ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po stong phrag bcu gnyis pa dang rgyas 'grel stong phrag drug cu pa yang sham+b+ha la la sogs pa'i yul gyi skad gzhan gyis glegs bam la bris nas rgyal po zla ba bzang pos grong bye ba phrag dgu bcu rtsa drug na gnas pa rnams la rab tu bstan to/ / de nyid de la mos pa rnams kyis mnyan zhing bklags te rang gi sems la bzung nas gzhan dag la yang rgya cher rab tu bstan to/ / rgyud bstan pa'i dus de nas lo gnyis pa la sems can rnams kyi dngos grub kyi rgyu'i slad du dkyil 'khor gyi 'khor lo dang rdzu 'phrul bstan nas sprul pa'i sku gang nas byon pa longs spyod rdzogs pa'i sku de nyid du gshegs so/[8] / zhes gsungs pas zla bzang nyid kyis rtsa rgyud dang rgyas 'grel bstan pa'i lo gnyis pa la zla bzang gshegs par gsungs pa'i zla bzang gshegs pa'i lo gcig /

How many years exactly? The Great Commentary, in the third summary, says:
With the ascertainment of the tathāgata, the twelve-thousand-verse king of tantras and the extensive commentary of sixty thousand verses were written down in the languages of Shambhala and other lands and were taught by King Sucandra to those who lived in the many towns of the ninety-six lands. This teaching was heard and read by those with faith. They committed it to memory and taught it extensively to others. In the second year of teaching of the tantra, in order to create the causes for powerful attainments in others, he displayed the mandalas and magical creations, then entered the saṃbhogakāya enjoyment body, source of the nirmāṇakāya emanated body.[12] This quote explains that in the second year of his teaching the Root Tantra and the extensive commentary Sucandra passed away. This year counts as the year of his passing.

d.div: [8] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 22_ba6_tshig sna cung mi mthun/
[12] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 22b6.

f.d: de'i gong gi rtsa rgyud sdud pa dang rgyas 'grel stong phrag drug cu pa mdzad pa sogs la lo gnyis te zla ba bzang pos rtsa rgyud rgyas 'grel dang bcas pa thog mar bstan pa nas gshegs pa'i bar la lo gsum du byed dgos pa ni

Before that, compiling the Root Tantra, composing the sixty-thousand-verse Extensive Commentary, and so forth took two years. Therefore, from the time of Sucandra first teaching the Root Tantra and commentary until he passed away, three years must have elapsed.

rgyud kyi khams le'i go sla las/
sham+b+ha la zhes rab tu grags pa'i ka lA par ni dpal ldan rgyal po nyi ma 'ga' zhig gis/ / lha yi dbang po rab mchog mi yi bdag por bzhag nas khyod ni rang gi gnas su 'gro bar gyis/[9] / zhes pa'i nyi ma 'ga' zhig ces pa ni skabs mang por lo gsum phyogs gsum la nyi ma 'ga' zhig ces bshad pa dang phyogs mthun pa yin no/ /

In the “easy to understand” verses from the Realms chapter, it says:
In Kalāpa, of the land known as Shambhala, glorious king, for some days you were the lord of men, supreme among gods, before returning to your abode.[13] “Some days” is often explained as meaning three years and three fortnights,[14] and the phrase “some days” in this quote is no exception.

d.div: [9] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka156_38_ba5_'gyur cung mi mthun/
[13] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, ka, v. 156, 38b5.
[14] A “part” (Tib. phyogs) refers to the waxing or waning part of a month. Three parts therefore, is one and a half months.

f.d:
zla bzang gi lo gsum po lo drug brgya'i khongs su gtogs pa yang ma yin te/ zla bzang longs spyod rdzogs pa'i sku de nyid du gshegs so zhes gsungs pa'i de ma thag pa'i 'grel chen las/
de nas lha dbang gis lo brgya'i bar du rgyud ston par mdzad de/ de bzhin du gzi brjid can dang zla bas byin dang lha'i dbang phyug dang sna tshogs gzugs dang lha'i dbang ldan gyis kyang ngo /[10] / zhes rgyal po drug po de lo brgya brgya par bshad pas so/ /

The three years of Sucandra are not included in the six hundred years because in the Great Commentary, immediately after the words “he entered into the saṃbhogakāya enjoyment body, source of the nirmāṇakāya emanated body,” it says:
Then Sureśvara taught the tantra for a hundred years, as did Tejī, Somadatta, /8/ Sureśvara, Viśvamūrti, and Sureśāna.[15] Thus, the six kings each taught for a hundred years.

d.div: [10] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 23_na1
[15] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 23a1.

f.d: rgyu mtshan de bas na zla ba bzang po la lo gsum dang / ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa'i lo gcig ste lo bzhi po de drug brgya'i nang du mi gtogs pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa nas lo drug brgya na 'jam dpal grags pa 'byung zhes pa'i drug brgya rags pa'i dbang du byas pa yin no/ /

Therefore, the three years of Sucandra and the year the Buddha taught the Root Tantra account for four years not included in the six hundred, and so in the quote that states that Mañjuśrī Yaśas will appear six hundred years after the teaching of the Tantra, the six hundred years are an approximation.

de ltar na rgyal po grags pa 'byung bar lung bstan pa'i lo drug brgya'i thog ma shing spre'i gong gi lo bzhi pa lcags 'brug gi nag pa'i nya la ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa yin te/ mchog mi 'gyur gyi mdor bsdus las/
'jam pa'i dbyangs kyang nga mya ngan las 'das nas lo drug brgya na sham+b+ha la'i yul du shAkya'i rigs la lha mo rnam par rgyal ma'i mngal nas lha'i dbang ldan gyi sras rigs ldan grags pa zhes bya ba 'byung bar 'gyur ro [11] zhes gsungs shing ston pas rtsa rgyud bstan nas lo drug brgya na 'jam dbyangs grags pa 'byung bar yang gsungs pas so/ /

Therefore, the actual first year of the six hundred years mentioned in the prophecy of King Mañjuśrī Yaśas would be four years before Wood Monkey year.[16] This is Iron Dragon year and in this year on the full moon of the Caitra month the Buddha taught the Root Tantra. In the Gnosis chapter of the Great Commentary, in the Supreme Unchanging Gnosis summary, it says:
Six hundred years after I have passed away, in the land of Shambhala, from the womb of Vijayadevī of Śākya lineage, Mañjuśrī as Kalkī Mañjuśrī Yaśas, son of Sureśāna will appear.[17] The passage also states that Mañjuśrī Yaśas will appear six hundred years after our teacher taught the Root Tantra.

d.div: [11] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 431_ba3
[16] The first of the 1,903 years as calculated previously.
[17] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 431b3.

f.d: de ltar na mya ngan las 'da' ba'i lo de la rtsa rgyud gsungs pa yin pas dpa' bo lcags 'brug gi lo ni ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa'i lo dang ston pa mya ngan las 'das pa'i lo yang yin no/ /

Therefore, the Root Tantra was taught in the year of Buddha’s passing.[18] This means that the vikrama Iron Dragon year was the year in which our teacher taught the Root Tantra and was also the year in which he passed away.

d.div: [18] Because the Tantra prophecy says, “six hundred years from this year,” which means, according to the Great Commentary, “This is the year the Tathāgata taught the dharma,” referring to the Kālacakra Root Tantra. The same six hundred years is mentioned in the line “six hundred years after I have passed away.” Therefore the year of passing and the year of teaching the Root Tantra are the same.

f.d: des na ston pa 'khrungs nas lo brgyad cu bzhugs shing gya gcig pa'i sa ga'i nya la mya ngan las 'das pa yin pas ston pa 'khrungs nas lo brgyad cu pa myos ldan sa yos nas yar bgrangs pa'i zhe drug pa rgyal ba shing rta la ston pa mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas pa yin no/ /

From his birth our teacher stayed for eighty years and in his eighty-first year on the full moon of Vaiśākha, he passed away. His eightieth year was pramathi Earth Rabbit year and, counting backward from that year, the forty-sixth year is jaya Wood Horse year, and that is the year of our teacher’s enlightenment.

de'i rgyu mtshan yang myos ldan sa yos nas yar bgrangs pa'i lo brgyad cu pa drug po lcags spre ni ston pa'i 'khrungs lor grub la/ mngon par 'byung ba'i mdo las/
byang chub sems dpa' la nyi shu rtsa dgu bzhes nas khab nas byung ste lo drug tu dka' ba spyod par 'gyur/ de nas bdud rtsis rtogs par 'gyur bar mthong ngo /[12] / zhes gsungs pas lcags spre nas mar bgrangs pa'i lo nyer dgu pa kun 'dzin sa pho byi ba la khab nas byung /

Using the same method, counting back from pramathi Earth Rabbit year, the eightieth year is rudra Iron Monkey year, which establishes it as the year of our teacher’s birth. Moreover, in the Abhiniṣkramaṇasūtra it says:
The bodhisattva turned twenty-nine, left the palace, and for six years practiced austerity. After that, it is known that he came to actualize the nectar of immortality.[19] Counting forward from Iron Monkey year, the twenty-ninth year is sarvadhara male Earth Rat and that is the year of leaving the palace.

d.div: [12] sde dge_301_bka'/ mdo sde/ samangon par 'byung ba'i mdo/ 52_ba7
[19] Toh 301 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 42b7.

f.d: sa byi dang por byas pa'i lo drug 'das pa'i rgyal ba shing rta ni sa yos nas yar bgrangs pa'i lo zhe drug pa yin pas rgyal ba shing rta de'i sa ga zla ba dpyid zla tha chung gi nya'i mtshan mo'i thun tha ma'i cha skya rengs 'char ba'i 'tshams rnga rdung ba la nye ba na mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas pa yin te/

Six years on from that year is jaya Wood Horse year, and that year is the forty-sixth year counting back from pramathi Earth Rabbit year. Therefore, in the Vaiśākha of Wood Horse year, the last of the spring months, on the full moon, in the last period of the night, at the onset of dawn, close to the beating of the drum, he became a complete and perfect buddha. /9/

rgya che rol pa las/
dge slong dag de ltar byang chub sems dpa' nam gyi cha smad skya rengs 'char ba'i dus kyi tshe rnga rdung ba'i nam tshod tsam na [13] zhes dang /

The Lalitavistarasūtra says:
Monks, in that way, the bodhisattva in the third part of the night, as dawn approached, close to the time of the beating of the drum…[20]

d.div: [13] sde dge_95_bka'/ mdo sde/ khargya cher rol pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ 168_ba1
[20] Toh 95 Kangyur, mdo sde, kha, 168b1.

f.d:
dbang le'i mdor bsdus dang po las/
sa ga'i nya'i skya rengs 'char ka'i tshe bcom ldan 'das shAkya thub pa mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas te de nas chos kyi 'khor lo bskor zhing theg pa gsum bstan pa mdzad nas zla ba bcu gnyis pa nag pa'i _nya la shrId+hAn+ya ka Ta ka ra/[14] zhes sa ga'i nya'i skya reng_sa 'char ba'i dus su sangs rgyas par bshad pas so/ /

In the first summary of the Initiation chapter from the Great Commentary it also explains that he became a buddha during Vaiśākha at the approach of dawn:
As dawn approached on the full moon of the vaiśākha month, the conqueror, the mighty one of the Śākya, became a complete buddha. He turned the wheels of dharma and taught the three vehicles. Then in the twelfth month on the Caitra full moon in Śrī Dhānyakaṭaka…[21]

d.div: [14] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 264_ba3
[21] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 264b3.

f.d: de yang lo drug brgya'i thog ma shing spre'i gong ma chu lug nas bgrangs pa'i lo lnga bcu pa rgyal ba shing rta'i sa ga zla ba'i nya dang shin tu 'byor ba yin te/ zhal lung [15] dang 'khrul sel ba ma gtogs rtsis pa thams cad kyis skyon cung zad kyang med par 'dod pa rtsis lo nyis brgya nyer gcig gi mjug tu shar ba'i byed rtsis kyi rtsis 'phro gzhir bzhag ste rnam par dag pa'i yar log gi rtsi ba byas pas shing rta de'i sa ga'i nya'i gza' tshes la gza' gcig chu tshod bzhi bcu/ tshes 'khyud zla skar la skar ma bcu drug chu tshod gcig /sgra gcan gdong la skar ma bcu drug chu tshod nyer dgu 'ong ba dang / zhal lung gi grub mtha'i rtsis 'phro gzhir bzhag ste sngar bzhin brtsis pa na gza' gcig chu tshod so brgyad/ tshes 'khyud zla skar la skar ma bcu drug chu tshod stong pa/ sgra gcan gdong la skar ma bcu drug chu tshod nyer dgu 'ong bas bcom ldan 'das tho rangs sangs rgyas pa'i zhag ngo de la zla ba sgra gcan gyis bzung bar bshad pa dang yang 'grig pa yin no/ /

This Vaiśākha full moon corresponds perfectly to the Vaiśākha full moon of the jaya Wood Horse year, fifty years[22] before the Water Sheep year, which is the year preceding the Wood Monkey year, the first year of the prophesied six hundred years, because of the following reasons. On the basis of the karaṇa[23] epoch data[24] that appeared at the end of the 221 years of astronomy and accepted as correct by all astrologers except for those of the Puṇḍarīka Transmission and the Elimination of Error Tradition,[25] calculating backward shows that on the full moon of that Vaiśākha, the planetary day was day one[26] and was forty hours old. The moon’s lunar mansion was sixteen and one hour.[27] The lunar mansion position of the face of Rāhu was sixteen and twenty-nine hours. Using siddhānta astronomy epoch data from the Puṇḍarīka Transmission, the planetary day was day one and thirty-eight hours. The moon’s lunar mansion was sixteen exactly, and the face of Rāhu was also sixteen and twenty-nine hours. Therefore, the claim that on the day the conqueror became a Buddha, at dawn the moon was held by Rāhu[28] is confirmed.

d.div: [15] 'dir zhal lung zhes pa phug pa lhun grub rgya mtshos mdzad pa'i rtsis kyi bstan bcos legs par bshad pa pad dkar zhal lung zhes pa de yin la/ 'khrul sel ba zhes pa deb ther sngon po mdzad pa po 'gos lo gzhon nu dpal gyis brtsams pa'i rtsis kyi bstan bcos 'khrul sel zhes pa de yin nges/
[22] Forty-six years plus four years: from the time of enlightenment to the first of the (approximately) six hundred years.
[23] See glossary.
[24] The data obtained or left over at the end of an astronomical period and used for future calculation. I am grateful to Edward Henning for his assitance in this area.
[25] Two influential works on astronomical calculation. See bibliography.
[26] Beginning with Saturn at zero, seven planets rule the days in turn. The planet ruling this particular day was the sun.

[27] According to Edward Henning, normally this means that sixteen mansions have been traversed and the moon is one hour into the seventeenth. The month is usually named after the lunar mansion in which the full moon falls but this is often approximate. The sixteenth lunar mansion is Vaiśākha and the seventeenth is Anurādha. Therefore either the author is using a system of numbering in which “sixteen” means “in the sixteenth mansion” or that the month was named after the sixteenth mansion even though it was actually (although only one hour) into the seventeenth. The hours are hours of “distance” or degrees.
[28] A lunar eclipse.

f.d:
zhag de la zla ba sgra gcan gyis bzung bar bshad tshul ni 'dul ba lung las/
bcom ldan 'das kyis bla na med pa'i ye shes brnyes pa na grags 'dzin ma la yang khye'u zhig btsas so/ /zla ba yang sgra gcan gis zin to zhes dang /
'di btsas pa na zla ba yang sgra gcan gyis zin pa de bas na khye'u'i ming yang sgra gcan zin zhes btags so [16] zhes pa dang /

How is such a claim made? A Vinaya passage states:
When the Conqueror attained the highest wisdom, Yaśodhara gave birth to a son, and the moon was held by Rāhu. Also:
When he was born the moon was held by Rāhu. Therefore, the child’s name was also Rāhula.[29]

d.div: [16] sde dge_1_bka'/ 'dul ba/ nga 'dul ba gzhi/ 33_ba7_'gyur cung mi mthun/
[29] Toh 1 Kangyur, ’dul ba, nga, 33b7.

f.d:
mngon par 'byung ba'i mdo las/
de nas rgyal po zas gtsang la rang gi skyes bu rnams kyis/ lha dgyes pa skyed du gsol/ gzhon nus bla na med pa'i ye shes brnyes so/ / de thos pa dang nyi ma de nyid la grags 'dzin ma la yang khye'u zhig btsas so/ / bdud rtsi zas la yang khye'u zhig btsas so/ / de nyid kyi nyin mo zla ba yang sgra gcan gyis zin te [17] zhes gsungs pa rnams so/ /

In the Abhiniṣkramaṇasūtra it says:
To King Śuddhodana, his people said, “Please the gods! The prince has attained the highest wisdom!” When that was heard, and on that very day, a son was born to Yaśodhara and a son was born to Amṛtodana. On that day also, the moon was held by Rāhu.[30] /10/

d.div: [17] sde dge_301_bka'/ mdo sde/ samangon par 'byung ba'i mdo/ 51_na5
[30] Toh 301 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 41a4.

f.d: 'o na ston pa mya ngan las 'da' khar rtsa rgyud gsungs pa yin na/ zla ba bcu gnyis pa nag pa'i nya la zhes gsungs pa dang 'gal te/ 'grel tshig 'dis ston pa sa ga'i nya la sangs rgyas pa'i lo phyi ma de'i nag pa'i nya la rtsa rgyud gsungs par bstan pas so zhe na/ 'di'i 'gal spong la thams cad mkhyen pa chos rje bu rjes 'brang dang bcas pa rnams ni/ zla ba bcu gnyis pa nag pa'i nya la zhes pa dang / mya ngan las 'das nas lo drug brgya na 'jam dpal grags pa 'byung ba gnyis ka tshad mar mdzad cing / ston pa sangs rgyas pa'i lo ngo gnyis pa de la rtsa rgyud gsungs par yang mdzad nas 'grel tshig gnyis mi 'gal ba'i 'chad tshul mang du mdzad la/ chos rje phyogs rgyal ba [18] rjes 'brang dang bcas pa/ nga mya ngan las 'das nas zhes pa ni rgya dpe la mchan bu dkyus la shor bas ma dag gsung ste jo zhal rjes 'brang dang bcas pa rnams ston pa sangs rgyas pa'i lo ngo gnyis pa de nyid la rtsa rgyud gsungs par bzhed do/ /

If our teacher taught the Root Tantra when he was close to passing away, doesn’t this contradict the quote “Then in the twelfth month on the Caitra full moon…?” Doesn’t this line from the commentary explain that our teacher attained complete enlightenment on the Vaiśākha full moon and on the Caitra full moon of the following year he taught the Root Tantra? To avoid any contradiction that might arise on this point, the omniscient dharma master Butön and his followers hold that the quote “Then in the twelfth month on the Caitra full moon” and the prophecy that six hundred years after the Buddha passed away Mañjuśrī Yaśas would appear are both valid, and assert that our teacher taught the Root Tantra in the second year of his enlightenment. They present many reasons why the two commentary quotes are not contradictory. The Jonang dharma master Choglé Namgyal[31] and his followers say that the quote beginning “Six hundred years after I have passed away… ” is merely a note in the margins of the Indian text and therefore is invalid. The Jonang followers assert that our teacher taught the Root Tantra in the second year of his enlightenment.

d.div: [18] chos rje phyogs rgyal ba zhes pa jo nang phyogs las rnam rgyal yin nges la/ jo zhal zhes pa jo nang dol bu ba shes rab rgyal mtshan dang / zhwa lu lo tsA ba chos skyong bzang po la go dgos par snang ste phyi nas dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsis kyi man ngag zhes brtsams 'dug pas dpe ma rnyed/ yang na zhal zhes pa bu ston la'ang go srid pas dpyad/
[31] Jonang Choglé Namgyal, 1306–86.

f.d: de ltar bzhed pa ni mi 'thad par go ste/ de ltar yin na ston pa mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas pa'i dus kyi sa ga'i nya'i mtshan mo zla ba sgra gcan gyis bzung bar mdo las gsungs tshul gong du bshad pa ltar lo drug brgya na 'jam dpal grags pa 'byung bar gsungs pa'i drug brgya'i thog ma'i lo de nyi sgrol byed shing pho spre'u yin pas shing spre de dang de'i snga ma chu lug chu rta lcags sprul lcags 'brug sa yos sa stag rnams dang / shing spre de'i phyi ma shing bya rnams gang yang rung ba zhig gi sa ga'i nya la zla ba gza' 'dzin yod dgos pa la de rnams gang gi yang sa ga'i nya la gza' 'dzin med par ri mos 'grub pa'i phyir te/ rtsis pa thams cad [*] byed rtsis nyid kyi gnas skabs su dag par 'dod pa'i rtsis lo nyis brgya nyer gcig gi mjug tu shar ba'i rtsis 'phro rnams gzhir bzhag ste rnam dag gi yar log gi rtsi ba byas pa na lo de rnams gang gi yang sa ga'i nya'i mtshan mo la zla ba la sgra gcan zhugs pa'i ri mo 'char ba mi srid pa'i phyir ro/ /

Such claims can be understood as being wrong. If they were correct, then consider this. When our Teacher attained complete enlightenment it was the full moon night of Vaiśākha, and the moon was held by Rāhu, the sutra reference of which has been explained previously. According to the above claims, the first year of the six hundred years mentioned in the prophecy concerning the coming of Mañjuśrī Yaśas would have been the male tāraṇa Wood Monkey year.[32] Therefore, the preceding years would have been Water Sheep, Water Horse, Iron Snake, Iron Dragon, Earth Rabbit, and Earth Tiger. The following years would have been Wood Bird and so forth. If the above assertions were correct, then in one of those years, on the full moon of Vaiśākha there would have been an eclipse. However, the charts establish that there was no eclipse on the full moon of Vaiśākha of any of those years. This is because if a reverse calculation is made using karaṇa epoch data that arose after the 221 years of astronomy and accepted as being authentic during the time of karaṇa astronomy by all astrologers[*] , then for none of those years is it possible to construct a chart in which Rāhu eclipses the full moon night of Vaiśākha.

d.div: [*] 'khrul sel ba ma gtogs
[32] Because, according to Butön Rinpoché and others, the six hundred years must begin from the year of the enlightenment, which is the Wood Monkey year.
[*] (except the Elimination of Error Tradition)

f.d:
'o na 'grel chen las/
sa ga'i nya'i skya rengs 'char ba'i tshe bcom ldan 'das shAkya thub pa mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas te de nas chos kyi 'khor lo bskor zhing theg pa gsum bstan pa mdzad nas zla ba bcu gnyis pa nag pa'i nya la shrId+hAnya ka Ta ka ra [19] zhes gsungs pa 'dis sangs rgyas pa'i lo ngo gnyis pa'i nag pa'i nya la rtsa rgyud gsungs par bstan pa ma yin nam snyam na/

However, the Great Commentary says:
As dawn approached on the full moon of Vaiśākha, the Conqueror, the mighty one of the Śākya, became a complete buddha. He turned the wheels of dharma and /11/ taught the three vehicles. Then in the twelfth month on the Caitra full moon in Śrī Dhānyakaṭaka…[33] Doesn’t this indicate that the Root Tantra was taught in the second complete year of his enlightenment on the full moon of Caitra?

d.div: [19] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 264_ba3
[33] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 264b3.

f.d: de ltar du go ba ni dus kyi 'khor lo'i lugs kyi zla ba dang po nag zla kho na dang / bcu gnyis pa dbo zla kho nar bzung ba las byung ba yin la/ don la gnas pa ni dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i dgongs pa la yang zla ba rnams yar ngo sngon 'gro'i dbang du byas pa dang mar ngo sngon 'gro'i dbang du byas pa gnyis las dang po'i dbang du byas pa'i tshe nag zla zla ba rnams kyi dang po dang dbo zla zla ba bcu gnyis pa dang / gnyis pa mar ngo sngon 'gro'i dbang du byas pa'i tshe sa ga zla ba zla ba rnams kyi dang po dang nag zla zla ba bcu gnyis par mdzad do/ /

Such a conclusion arises from holding Caitra always to be the first month in the Kālacakra tradition and Phālguna as always being the twelfth. The reality is that, in Kālacakra thinking, months are formed by being either “waxing-led” or “waning-led.”[34] On the basis of being waxing-led, Caitra is the first of the months and Phālguna is the twelfth. On the basis of being waning-led, Vaiśākha is the first of the months and Caitra is the twelfth.

d.div: [34] Edward Henning says that months are either waxing-led or waning-led depending on which half of Caitra month the sun enters Aries. Entering Aries in the waxing half designates Caitra as a waxing-led month beginning from the first lunar day of the waxing or “bright side.” That month becomes the first month of the new year. When the sun enters Aries during the waning or “dark side” of Caitra, Vaiśākha is posited as beginning from that full moon and becomes the first month of the new year. See Lochen, p. 43.

f.d:
de ltar mdzad pa'i rgyu mtshan yang dus kyi 'khor lo'i dgongs pas dus kyi thog ma ni dpyid mnyam lug khyim du nyi ma zhugs pa'i dkar nag gi phyogs gnyis gang yang rung ba la 'jog la/ nyi ma lug khyim du zhugs pa'i nyi bar 'char ba'i dus ni yar ngo sngon 'gro'i nag zla'i tshes gcig nas gnam gang gi bar gang yang rung bar nges la/ de'i yang tshes gcig nas bco lnga'i bar la nyi ma lug khyim du zhugs pa'i nyi bar shar ba'i tshe dus kyi dang po lug khyim yar ngo sngon 'gro nag zla dang sbyor/ tshes bcu drug nas gnam gang bar la nyi ma lug khyim du zhugs pa'i nyi bar shar ba'i tshe dus kyi dang po lug khyim mar ngo sngon 'gro'i sa ga zla ba dang sbyar nas sa ga zla ba zla ba dang po dang nag zla zla ba bcu gnyis par mdzad pa yin te/ khams le'i mdor bsdus dgu pa las/
lhun po'i lho'i dum bu 'dir lug la nyi ma gnas pas dpyid kyi dus su sa ga'i zla ba byed do/[20] / zhes gsungs pas so/ /

The reasons for designating months in this way is as follows. In Kālacakra thinking the beginning of the seasons is established by the sun entering Aries at the spring equinox during either the waxing or waning phases of the moon. The mean sun entering Aries will appear between the first lunar day and the empty-sky lunar day[35] of a waxing-led Caitra. When this mean sun appears between the first and the fifteenth of the month, Aries, as the beginning of the seasons, is assigned to waxing-led Caitra. When the mean sun entering Aries appears between the sixteenth lunar day and the empty-sky lunar day, Aries as the beginning of the season is assigned to a waning-led Vaiśākha month. In this case Vaiśākha is the first month and Caitra is the twelfth. In the Realms chapter, in the ninth summary, it says:
In this continent, south of Meru, when the sun dwells in Aries, it is Vaiśākha in the season of spring.[36]

d.div: [20] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 88_ba2
[35] The thirtieth lunar day.
[36] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 88b2.

f.d:
spyir zla ba'i 'jog tshul de ltar du mdzad pa bzhin du/ zla ba bcu gnyis pa nag pa'i nya la zhes pa yang mar ngo sngon 'gro'i sa ga zla ba zla ba rnams kyi dang po dang / nag zla zla ba bcu gnyis par byas pa'i dbang du byas pa yin par nges te/ bcu gnyis pa nag pa'i nya la zhes sogs ni/ nag pa'i mthar ni dkar po'i tshes la zhes sogs kyi 'grel pa yin zhing / nag pa'i mthar ni zhes sogs des nag zla'i nya nag zla'i mtha' ru bshad pa dang / zla ba bcu gnyis pa nag pa'i nya la zhes pa'i gong de nyid du/
'phags pa'i yul 'dir dkar po'i tshes gcig la sogs pa cha bco lnga'i mthar nag po'i tshes gcig 'jug pa sa ga'i nya'i skya rengs 'char ba'i tshe/[bcom ldan 'das shAkya thub pa mngon par rdzogs pa sangs rgyas te/] zhes nag nya'i mthar nag po'i tshes gcig 'jug pa sa ga zla ba dang zla ba'i thog mar bshad pas so/ /

Generally, months were designated this way. Therefore, “Then in the twelfth month on the Caitra full moon,” from the quote above, is made on the basis of a waning-led Vaiśākha as the first month and Caitra as the twelfth month. The line “Then in the twelfth month on the Caitra full moon” and so on is commentary to “The end of Caitra is at the time of waxing,” and so forth. “The end of Caitra” and so forth explains the full moon of Caitra as being the end of the Caitra month. Immediately before the quote “Then in the twelfth month on the Caitra full moon” is the passage: /12/
Here in India after the last of the fifteen days of the bright side begins the first day of the dark side. Therefore, as dawn approached on the full moon of Vaiśākha, the Conqueror, the mighty one of the Śākya, became a complete buddha.” This indicates that the end of the full moon of Caitra, which begins the days of waning, is the beginning of Vaiśākha and is the first month of the year.

de ltar na 'jam pa'i dbyangs kyang nga mya ngan las 'das nas lo drug brgya na zhes sogs sgra sor bzhag cing / 'grel tshig rnams 'gal med du 'chad tshul de ltar byas te rwa 'bro snga ma [21] rnams dang dpal ldan bla ma dam pa dang pad dkar zhal lung las bshad pa ltar bcom ldan 'das mya ngan las 'da' kha'i nag zla'i nya la dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsa rgyud gsungs pa nyid 'thad par mthong ngo / /

The quote beginning “Mañjuśrī also, six hundred years after I have passed away” can therefore be left as it is, and the above commentary quotes are freed of contradiction.[37] Therefore, as asserted by those of the earlier traditions of Ra and Dro, by Palden Lama Dampa,[38] and as explained by the Puṇḍarīka Transmission, the explanation that the Conqueror taught the Root Tantra on the full moon of Caitra as he approached his passing away can be seen to be correct.

d.div: [21] rwa 'bro zhes pa rwa lo tswa ba'i dpon po rwa chos rab dang 'bro lo tsA ba ste de gnyis kyi lugs la go dgos shing / dpal ldan bla ma dam pa zhes pa ngos 'dzin ma thub kyang 'gos los deb sngon du gsungs pa ltar na bu ston gyi slob ma zhig yin par snang /

[37] The twelfth month in the line “Then in the twelfth month on the Caitra full moon” is not twelve months after enlightenment but refers to the twelfth or last month of the year. This could not be accepted if it is asserted that Caitra is always the first month of a Kālacakra year.

[38] Dro Lotsāwa Sherab Drak (eleventh century) and Ra Lotsāwa Dorjé Drak (1016–1198), two translators of the Kālacakra through whom the two main lineages passed. Palden Lama Dampa Sönam Gyaltsen (1312–75).

f.d: mdor bsdus na ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa'i dus la dogs pa skye ba'i gnas ni mya ngan 'da' kha'i dus kyi lo dang sangs rgyas pa'i dus kyi lo phyi ma de gnyis su nges la/ sangs rgyas pa'i lo ngo gnyis pa de yin par byas na sangs rgyas pa'i dus kyi sa ga'i nya'i mtshan mo zla ba gza' 'dzin ji ltar byas kyang sa ris la mi 'char ba'i phyir ro/ /

To summarize, the focus of the doubts is whether our teacher taught the Root Tantra in the year in which he passed away or in the year following his enlightenment. If the second year of his enlightenment is posited as the year he taught the Root Tantra, an eclipse of the moon on the night of the full moon of Vaiśākha at the time of his enlightenment cannot in any way be constructed in the charts.

kha cig ('jam dbyangs chos mgon/) gis lo drug brgya'i gong gi chu rta sna tshogs kyi sa ga'i nya la gza' 'dzin gyi ri mo 'char bar byas pa ni byed rtsis kyi yar log byas pa yin la/ de lta bu'i sgrub tshul 'di la stong drug brgya gya gnyis kyi bar gyi nyi ma dang gza' la mang nyung gi nyes pa chen po yod pas mi 'thad/

Some (such as Jamyang Chögön)[39] have constructed a chart showing an eclipse on the full moon of Vaiśākha of the viśva Water Horse year just before the beginning of the prophesied six hundred years. This is a reverse calculation using karaṇa astronomy, but within this particular method of calculation there are many quantitative faults regarding the sun and the planets in the 1,682 years,[40] and so it is not valid.

d.div: [39] Jamyang Chökyi Gönpo: fourteenth-century Sakya lama.

[40] These are the 1,682 years up to the 806 c.e. epoch when the 221 years of astronomy began. These years are: the six hundred years of the Yaśas prophecy, the hundred years of his reign, the eight hundred years of the barbarian prophecy, and the 182-year reign of Samudravijaya. Thanks to Edward Henning for his help on this.

f.d:
kha cig /(chos rgyal byang pa/) [22] lcags sbrul khyu mchog gi sa ga'i nya la gza' 'dzin nyin mo 'ong ba'i tshul du bkod pa sa ris sgrub tshul dag kyang zla ba la sgra gcan zhugs pa'i dus nyin mo yin pa la zla ba gza' 'dzin gyi tha snyad med cing / mngon par 'byung ba'i mdo las/
de nas rgyal po zas gtsang la rang gi skyes bu rnams kyis/ lha dgyes pa skyed du gsol zhes pa nas/ de nyid kyi nyin mo zla ba yang sgra gcan gyis zin to/[23] / zhes zla ba sgra gcan gyis bzung ba rgyal po zas gtsang gi 'khor gyi skye bo rnams kyis mig gis mthong ba lta bur gsungs shing / de nyid kyi nyin mo zhes pa'ang zhag gcig gi rtsis la nyin rtsis zhes brjod [24] pa dang 'dra bar gza' 'dzin byung ba'i nyin zhag de la de nyid kyi nyi mo zhes smras pa yin no/ /

Some (such as Chögyal Jangpa)[41] have formulated an eclipse of the full moon in Vaiśākha of the vyaya Iron Snake year occurring in daytime. The way the chart was constructed is correct, but there is no terminology for Rāhu grasping the moon in the daytime. Moreover, the quote from the Abhiniṣkramaṇasūtra says:
To King Śuddhodana, his people said, “Please the gods! The prince has attained the highest wisdom!” When that was heard, and on that very day, a son was born to Yaśodhara and a son was born to Amṛtodana. On that day also, the moon was held by Rāhu.[42] This passage speaks as if the moon being held by Rāhu was actually seen by those around King Śuddhodana. Concerning the phrase “on that day,” the calculation of one complete day is referred to as the “calculation of a day.” Similarly, it is the complete day within which the eclipse occurred that is spoken of in the phrase “on that day.” /13/

d.div: [22] 'dir yig chung du bzhed pa snga ma 'jam dbyangs chos dgon dang / phyi ma 'di chos rgyal byang pa'i yin par gsungs la/ 'jam dbyangs chos dgon ni kun mkhyen dol bu pa dang / bu ston rin po che/ g.yag sde paN chen dang / jo nang phyogs rgyal ba sogs kyi slob ma yin tshul deng rabs rtsis kyi mkhas dbang tshul khrims rgyal mtshan gyis skar nag rtsis kyi lo rgyus skor shog grangs 158_nang bshad pa ltar na dus rabs 14_nang byung ba'i rtsis kyi bstan bcos brtsams mkhan gyi bod kyi mkhas pa zhig yin/ chos rgyal byang pa zhes pa su yin ngos 'dzin ma thub kyang gcig byas na byang pa rnam rgyal grags bzang yin nam snyam/
[23] sde dge_301_bka'/ mdo sde/ samangon par 'byung ba'i mdo/ 51_na5
[24] ma dper skabs du mar rjod ces snang na'ang brjod yin nam snyam mod/ 'on kyang ma dpe ltar rang sor bzhag
[41] Chögyal Jangpa Namgyal Drakpa Sangpo (1395–1475).
[42] Toh 301 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 41a4.

f.d: de ltar na gong du bshad pa ltar ston pa mya ngan las 'da' kha'i nag nya la rtsa rgyud gsungs pa dang / mya ngan las 'da' ba'i dus ni dpa' bo lcags 'brug gi sa ga zla ba'i nya'i thun tha ma'i cha yin par grub pas lcags 'brug de nas yar bgrangs pa'i lo gya gcig pa lcags spre ni ston pa'i 'khrungs lo yin par grub cing / de'i zla ba dang tshes dang gza' skar sogs ji ltar yin pa ni zhib par pad dkar zhal lung las shes par bya'o/ /

Therefore, our teacher taught the Root Tantra on the full moon of Caitra just before he passed away. The time of his passing is established as being the final part of the Vaiśākha full moon of vikrama Iron Dragon year. Eighty-one years back from that year is the Iron Monkey year and is established as the year of our teacher’s birth. The month, the date, and planetary positions can be known by a thorough study of the Puṇḍarīka Transmission.
gnyis pa sdud pa pos ji ltar bsdus pa'i tshul
['di ]la gnyis/ rtsa rgyud ji ltar bsdus pa'i tshul dang / bsdus rgyud ji ltar bsdus pa'i tshul lo/ /
This has two outlines: 1. Compilation of the Root Tantra 2. Compilation of the Condensed Tantra
dang po [rtsa rgyud ji ltar bsdus pa'i tshul ]ni

mdor bsdus gsum pa las/
de bzhin gshegs pa'i nges pa de'i phyir rtsa ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po stong phrag cu gnyis pa dang rgyas 'grel stong phrag drug cu pa yang sham+b+ha la la sogs pa'i yul gyi skad gzhan gyis glegs bam la bris nas rgyal po zla ba bzang pos grong bye ba phrag dgu bcu rtsa drug na gnas pa rnams la rab tu bstan to|[25] | zhes gsungs pa ltar ston pas lcags 'brug gi nag nya la rtsa rgyud gsungs pa rgyal po zla ba bzang pos thugs la bzung ste sham+b+ha lar byon nas ston pa mya ngan las 'das pa'i rjes su sham+b+ha la'i yul gyi skad kyis rtsa rgyud dang rang nyid kyis mdzad pa'i rgyas 'grel stong phrag drug bcu pa yang glegs bam la bris te grong bye ba phrag dgu bcu rtsa drug na gnas pa'i rgyal po dgu bcu rtsa drug sog_sa skal ba dang ldan pa'i gang zag rnams la lcags 'brug nas chu rta'i bar gyi lo gsum gyi bar du bstan cing / rgyud bstan zin pa'i dus chu rta de nas lo gnyis pa chu lug la sems can rnams kyi dngos grub kyi rgyu'i slad du dus kyi 'khor lo'i dkyil 'khor bzhengs te rdzu 'phrul bstan nas gshegs so/ /

In the Realms chapter, in the third summary it says:
Because of the ascertainment of the Tathāgata, the twelve-thousand-verse King of Tantras and the Extensive Commentary of sixty thousand verses were written down in the languages of Shambhala and other lands and were taught by King Sucandra to those who lived in the many towns of the ninety-six lands.[43] Our teacher taught the Root Tantra on the full moon of Caitra in the Iron Dragon year. King Sucandra memorized the text and returned to Shambhala. After our teacher passed away, he wrote down the Root Tantra as well as his own composition, the sixty-thousand-verse Extensive Commentary, in the language of Shambhala. These he taught to the ninety-six kings of the nine hundred and sixty million towns and to other fortunate beings for three years from the Iron Dragon year to the Water Horse year. Having completed his teachings in the Water Horse year, in the following Water Sheep year he created the Kālacakra mandala in order to bring about the causes of siddhi in others. There he displayed magical powers and passed away.

d.div: [25] sde deg_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 22_ba6
[43] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 22b6.

f.d: 'o na dkyil 'khor gnas gang du ji ltar du bzhengs snyam na/ ka lA pa'i grong gi lho phyogs na ma la ya'i skyed mos tshal rgyar dpag tshad bcu gnyis pa ka lA pa'i grong gi tshad dang mnyam pa yod pa de'i dbus su rin po che sna lnga'i rang bzhin can lha dang lha mo'i bdag nyid yongs su grub pa gru bzhi sgo bzhi pa/ sku'i dkyil 'khor gyi rtsa thig tshun gyi tshad gru bzhi brgya yod pa rta babs bzhi dang dur khrod brgyad kyis brgyan pa rwa ba lngas bskor ba phyi rol tu sa la sogs pa'i khor yug bzhi dang rdo rje'i 'phreng bas bskor ba ste/

Where was this mandala created, and how was it created? South of the city of Kalāpa is the park of Malaya, twelve yojana across and of the same size as Kalāpa. There in its the center, built entirely of the five precious stones whose nature was that of gods and goddesses, stood the body mandala with four sides and four entrances. It was four hundred cubits wide, adorned by four portals and the eight cemeteries, enclosed by five walls, surrounded by the four mandala environments of earth and so forth and encircled by the vajra garland. /14/

sku'i dkyil 'khor gyi phyed kyi tshad kyi dbus su gsung gi dkyil 'khor gru bzhi sgo bzhi pa rta babs bzhis brgyan pa rwa ba lngas bskor ba/ gsung gi dkyil 'khor gyi phyed kyi tshad kyi dbus su thugs kyi dkyil 'khor gru bzhi sgo bzhi rta babs bzhis brgyan pa rwa ba gsum gyis bskor ba/ thugs kyi dkyil 'khor gyi phyed kyi tshad kyi dbus su ye shes kyi 'khor lo ka ba bcu drug gis mdzes pa'o/ / de'i phyed kyi tshad kyi dbus su pad+ma 'dab ma brgyad pa ste dkyil 'khor gyi mtshan nyid thams cad yongs su rdzogs pa'i blos bslang bzhengs pa'o/ /

Within the body mandala and of half its size was the speech mandala with four sides and four entrances, adorned by four portals and enclosed by five walls. In the center of the speech mandala and of half its size again was the mind mandala with four sides and four entrances, adorned by four portals and enclosed by three walls. In the center of the mind mandala and of half its size was the mandala of gnosis, beautified by sixteen pillars. In its center and of half its size was a lotus of eight petals. This mandala, with every feature complete, was created by the power of mind.

de ltar na ston pa mya ngan las 'das pa'i rjes su zla ba bzang pos dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsa rgyud bsdus pa ni 'grel chen las/
de bzhin gshegs pa mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas pa'i 'phags pa'i yul 'dir bcom ldan 'das yongs su mya ngan las 'das par gyur pa na sdud par byed pa po rnams kyis theg pa gsum glegs bam la bris te/[26] zhes gsungs pa dang shin tu 'byor ba yin no/ /

That Sucandra compiled the Kālacakra Root Tantra after our teacher had passed away is verified by the Great Commentary:
In this noble country the Tathāgata attained complete enlightenment. When the Conqueror passed away, the compilers wrote down the three vehicles.[44]

d.div: [26] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 37_na6
[44] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 32a6.

f.d: gnyis pa bsdus rgyud ji ltar bsdus pa'i tshul ni/

rgyal po zla bzang gshegs pa'i rjes su lo drug brgya'i thog ma shing spre de nas bzung ste lo drug brgya'i bar la lha dbang sogs chos rgyal drug gis rtsa rgyud bstan/ de nas mdor bsdus gsum pa las/
'jam dpal rgyal po grags par gyur te byang chub sems dpa'i seng+ge'i khri de las lo brgya'i bar du chos bstan to/[27] /de nas lo brgya rdzogs pa'i rjes la zhes gsungs pa ltar rgyal po 'jam dbyangs grags pas rtsa rgyud lo brgya'i bar du bstan nas de'i lo brgya pa khrag skyug chu phag gi dbo zla'i nya la/ rgyu de bzhin gshegs pa'i lung bstan pa'i byin gyis brlabs pa'i stobs dang / nyi ma'i shing rta sogs drang srong rnams rgyud yongs su smin te/ yang dag pa'i lam 'thob par mngon par shes pa lngas mkhyen pa'i rgyu yis/ gnas rgyal po zla ba bzang pos bzhengs pa'i dus kyi 'khor lo'i dkyil 'khor gyi khang pa der/ ched du bya ba'i gdul bya nyi ma'i shing rta sogs tshangs pa'i drang srong bye ba phrag phyed dang bzhi po bos par gyur te/ de ltar bos nas nges pa byin pa ni/

After King Sucandra passed away, Sureśvara and the other five dharma kings taught the Root Tantra for the next six hundred years beginning from the Wood Monkey year, the first of the prophesied six hundred years. Then, as it says in the Realms chapter, in the third summary:
Mañjuśrī became King Yaśas and from the bodhisattva lion throne taught the dharma for a hundred years. When the hundred years ended…[45] King Mañjuśrī Yaśas taught the Root Tantra for a hundred years. Then, with the power of the blessings of the Tathāgata’s prophecy as a cause, and knowing with his five kinds of clairvoyance that the minds of Sūryaratha and the other ṛṣi were fully ripened and would move to the perfect path, on the Phālguna full moon of the hundredth year, the rudhirodgārin Water Pig year, he gathered his intended disciples, Sūryaratha and the other thirty-five million Brahmin ṛṣi, in the mansion of the Kālacakra mandala created by King Sucandra. There he announced:

d.div: [27] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 23_na2
[45] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 23a2.

f.d: kye nyi ma'i shing rta la sogs pa tshangs pa'i drang srong rnams bdag gi tshig thams cad mkhyen pa'i phun sum tshogs pa byed pa nyon cig/zla ba phyi ma'i nag pa'i nya 'di la khyed rnams la rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa sbyin par bya'o/ / zhes gsungs pa dang drang srong rnams skrag nas 'gyel bar gyur to/ /

Sūryaratha and you other Brahmin ṛṣi, my words will produce the perfection of omniscience. Listen! Next month on the full moon of Caitra I will give you the teachings of the Vajra Vehicle. /15/ As soon as he had spoken these words, the ṛṣi fainted from fear.

de nas chos de dang drang srong rnams kyi bsam pa 'gal bar gzigs nas rgyal po grags pas gsungs pa/
bdag gis bcom ldan 'das dus kyi 'khor lo'i dkyil 'khor gyi khang pa 'dir gzhug par bya zhing 'jig rten dang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i dbang sbyin par bya'o/ / gzhan yang bdag gi bkas khyed kyis rdo rje'i rigs dang lhan cig bza' ba dang btung ba dang / bag ma blang ba'i 'brel pa rnams kyang bya'o/ / de ltar mi byed pa lta na bdag gi grong bye ba phrag dgu bcu rtsa drug por [28] gang dang gang du mos pa der khyed rnams song zhig/ rnam pa gzhan du na lo brgyad brgya 'das pa'i rjes la khyed kyi rigs kyi bu dang tsha bo la sogs pas kla klo'i chos dar bar byas nas zhes pa nas
de bas na khyed rnams kyis bdag gi bka' bzhin bya'o/ / zhes gsungs pa dang

Seeing that this teaching and the thoughts of the ṛṣi were in conflict, King Mañjuśrī Yaśas said:
I will lead you into this mansion of the conqueror Kālacakra and give both worldly and nonworldly initiations. Furthermore, by my command, you should eat, drink, and create relationships through marriage in accord with the vajra caste. If you choose not to do this, then leave my nine hundred and sixty million towns and go where you will. Otherwise, after eight hundred years the descendants of your castes will spread the barbarian dharma… And so on until:
Therefore, do as I say.

d.div: [28] ma dper dgu bcu rtsa drug por la zhes byung /

f.d:
de nas rgyal po grags pa'i gsung chad pa dang bcas pa'i bka' 'di mgo bor thog lhung ba bzhin gyur nas tshangs pa'i drang srong rnams kyis nyi ma'i shing rta la smras pa/ kye nyi ma'i shing rta zhes bos nas/
rgyal po grags pa la/ bdag cag rnams ni rdo rje'i rigs kyi dbang bskur ba'i chos la mi 'jug ste/ de bas na khyod kyi bkas 'phags pa'i yul du 'gro ba mchog go/ /zhes zhus mdzod cig ces smras pa dang

These words of King Mañjuśrī Yaśas with his admonishment struck the Brahmin ṛṣi like thunderbolts, and they called to Sūryaratha:
Sūryaratha, tell King Mañjuśrī Yaśas that we will not enter the initiation of the vajra caste and that therefore, by his command, it would be better to go to the noble land of India.

nyi ma'i shing rtas mi dbang grags pa la zhus pa/ kye rgyal po chen po mchog gi rgyal po zhes sogs yon tan brjod nas
rang rang gi rigs kyi chos la zhugs pa rnams la thugs rje mdzod cig/ ci ste bdag cag gis gdon mi za bar khyod kyi bka' bzhin bya ba yin pa de lta na bdag cag rdo rje'i rigs kyi dbang bskur ba la 'jug par mi bgyi ste/ khyod kyi bkas chu bo shIta'i lho kha ba can dang lang ka'i gling gi bar 'phags pa'i yul du 'gro ba mchog go/ /zhes nyi ma'i shing rtas zhus pa las/

Sūryaratha addressed the mighty Mañjuśrī Yaśas with words of praise for his qualities, beginning “O great king, supreme king,” and so on. He continued :
Show kindness to those who live within their own castes. If we must do as you say without question, we will not enter the initiation of the vajra caste, but by your command, it would be best for us to go south of the Śīta River to the noble land of India, which lies between the snow mountains and the island of Lanka.

rgyal po grags pas bka' stsal ba/
khyed rnams sham+b+ha la'i yul nas myur du song zhigces so/ /

King Mañjuśrī Yaśas replied:
Then quickly leave the land of Shambhala.

de nas rgyal po grags pa'i bka' des tshangs pa'i drang srong de dag thams cad ka lA pa'i grong nas byung ste nyi ma bcu pa la nags tshal gyi nang du zhugs par gyur to/ / de ltar du gyur par rgyal po grags pa'i mngon par shes pa'i stobs kyis mkhyen te/ dgos pa khyad par can du ma gzigs nas drang srong rnams dgug pa'i don du re zhig drang srong rnams rmongs par bya ba'i phyir rgyal po grags pas khyab 'jug dang tshangs pa dang drag po'i rigs rnams rmongs par byed pa zhes bya ba'i ting nge 'dzin la snyoms par zhugs so/ /

On the command of King Mañjuśrī Yaśas, the Brahmin ṛṣi all rose and left the city of Kalapa. On the tenth day they entered a forest. With his clairvoyant powers King Mañjuśrī Yaśas was aware of this, and with many reasons in mind he entered the /16/ meditative concentration known as deluding the castes of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra to temporarily bewitch the ṛṣi and to bring them back.

ting nge 'dzin de dang lha'i byin gyis rlabs kyi stobs kyis drang srong de rnams nags tshal de nyid du rmongs par gyur ba dang de na gnas pa'i ri khrod pa la sogs pa rnams kyis drang srong thams cad bcings nas khyer te dkyil 'khor gyi khang pa de nyid du mi'i dbang po grags pa'i zhabs drung du dor ba dang rmongs pa las sad de rgyal po dang dkyil 'khor gyi khang pa dang ma la ya'i skyed mos tshal rnams mthong bar gyur to/ / de mthong ba na ya mtshan thob ste ngo mtshar du gyur pa'i tshig dag smras pa na sprul pa'i sku blon po rgya mtsho'i blo gros kyis rgyal po grags pa'i bsngags pa brjod de drang srong rnams la dus kyi 'khor lo'i dbang zhu bar gsol ba thob cig ces bskul ba'i tshig de dang sangs rgyas kyi byin gyis rlabs kyis nyi ma'i shing rta la sogs pa'i drang srong rnams kyi chos kyi blo rab tu sad de/ de nas drang srong rnams kyis nyi ma'i shing rta la gsol ba 'debs par bskul to/ /

By the power of that meditative concentration and the blessings of the gods, the ṛṣi were so spellbound that local hunters and others were able to capture them and carry them back to place them at the feet of mighty Mañjuśrī Yaśas. Once the ṛṣi were freed from the spell and saw the king, the mandala, and Malaya Park, they were amazed, and as they uttered words of astonishment, Sāgaramati, the king’s minister and an emanation, praised King Mañjuśrī Yaśas and urged the ṛṣi to petition the king for initiation into Kālacakra. By the power of these words and by the blessings of the buddhas, the dharma minds of Sūryaratha and the other ṛṣi were truly awakened. The ṛṣi urged Sūryaratha to make the request.

de ltar bskul ba la brten nas drang srong rnams dang thabs cig tu rgyal po grags pa'i zhabs la phyag 'tshal nas rin po che dang gser gyi me tog rnams kyi maN+Dal byas nas phul te gsol ba btab bo/ /
ji ltar na 'jig rten dang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i dbang bskur ba dang / de bzhin gshegs pas rgyal po zla ba bzang po la bstan pa'i dang po'i sangs rgyas stong phrag bcu gnyis pa de nyid gzhung nyung ngus mchog gi dang po'i sangs rgyas las btus pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po yang dag par sdu ba mdzad nas tshangs pa'i drang srong rnams la bstan du gsol/ zhes gsol ba btab bo/ /

In response, and together with all the ṛṣi, he prostrated to the feet of King Mañjuśrī Yaśas, offered a mandala made of jewels and gold flowers, and made his petition:
Bestow the worldly and nonworldly initiations, abridge the king of tantras within the Supreme Original Buddha[46] with a shorter version of the twelve thousand verses of the Original Buddha as taught to King Sucandra by the Tathāgata, and teach it to the ṛṣi.[47]

d.div: [46] An epithet of the Root Tantra.
[47] This is the end of the account beginning at 23a2, in which Khedrup Norsang Gyatso paraphrases between citations.

f.d: de nas nyi ma'i shing rtas gsol ba btab pa de gsan nas tshangs pa'i drang srong rnams kyi mos pa'i bsam pa dang de bzhin gshegs pa'i byin gyi rlabs kyi stobs kyis rgyal po grags pas bsdus rgyud sdud par mdzad do/ /
Mañjuśrī Yaśas listened to Sūryaratha’s plea, and because of the inclination of the Brahmin ṛṣi and the power of the Tathāgata’s blessings, he compiled the Condensed Tantra.

de yang ji ltar mdzad na/ sgra bzang po smra ba nyi ma'i shing rta sogs de rnams sgra bzang po la zhen pa spang ba'i slad du don la ston pa nyid la brten te tshigs su bcad pa kha cig tu sgra nyams dang / kha cig tu gcod 'tshams nyams pa dang/ _kha cig tu rnam dbye med pa dang / kha cig tu dbyangs dang gsal byed phyis pa dang / kha cig tu ring po thob pa la thung ngu dang thung ngu thob pa la ring po dang / kha cig tu rnam dbye lnga pa'i don la rnam dbye bdun pa dang / rnam dbye bzhi pa'i don la drug pa sbyin pa sogs su byas te

In what style was that accomplished? Sūryaratha and the others were adherents to good grammar, and to wean them away from their attachment to that the king employed “reliance upon meanings,”[48] whereupon some verses had bad grammar, some had poor line and word separation, some had no grammatical cases, while in others vowels and consonants were omitted. In some verses short vowels were long while /17/ long vowels were short. Some that should have been in the fifth case were in the seventh, and some of the fourth case were in the sixth.

d.div: [48] The four types of reliance: not on the person but on the dharma, not on words but on meanings, not on ordinary consciousness but on gnosis, not on interpretable meanings but on definitive meanings. See The Great Lexicon, p. 1080.

f.d: phreng ba 'dzin pa'i sdeb sbyor gyis bcings pa'i yi ge brgyad khri drug stong lnga brgya nyi shu'i bdag nyid can tshigs su bcad pa re la yi ge brgyad cu rtsa bzhi'i bdag nyid can gyi tshigs bcad stong dang sum cu'i bdag nyid can dang po'i sangs rgyas rtsa rgyud stong phrag bcu gnyis pa las bsdus te drang srong rnams la bstan to/ /

Therefore, encased in the sragdhara meter and consisting of 86,520 syllables, with each verse possessing eighty-four syllables, the twelve thousand verses of the Original Buddha were condensed into 1,030 verses and taught to the ṛṣi.

de ltar yang rtsa rgyud mdor bsdus gsum par drangs pa las/
des na snying po'i don bsdus 'di/ / thams cad mkhyen sogs bdag 'dod do/ / 'phreng 'dzin tshigs bcad sum cu ni/ / lhag pa'i phyogs brgya le'u lngas/ / dpal ldan rgyud dag rdzogs par ni/ / smra ba'i rgyal pos ston 'gyur te/ / sdud par byed pa po yang 'di/[29] / zhes gsungs so/ /

This is mentioned in the Root Tantra, quoted in the Realms chapter, in the third summary:
Therefore this condensed essential meaning is asserted by myself the omniscient one. In sragdhara verses of thirty more than ten hundred, in five chapters, the glorious tantra complete, will be taught by the king of orators. He too will be the compiler.[49]

d.div: [29] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 22_na4
[49] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 22a4.

f.d: 'o na da ltar gyi jo nang 'gyur gsar sogs la tshigs bcad stong zhe gnyis dang / gyi jo dang sma'i 'gyur la stong zhe gsum dang / de'i steng du rtsa ba'i 'gyur rnams la ma chud pa'i mchog mi 'gyur du drangs pa'i ye shes le'u'i tshigs bcad/ las ni nyon mongs las te de las sdug bsngal du 'gyur nyon mongs nyid ni rang gi sdug bsngal las/ / zhes sogs tshigs bcad brgya bdun cu pa dang / dpal mo 'thor thos lha yi ljon pa glang po'i bdag dang / / zhes sogs tshigs bcad brgya gya gnyis pa dang gnyis te tshigs bcad stong zhe lnga 'ong ba ji ltar yin snyam na/ dpal ldan dpal gyi zhes sogs ye shes le'u'i tshigs bcad nyis brgya nga gnyis pa man chad kyi tshigs bcad bcu dang / khyod ni ma dang khyod ni pha ste zhes sogs nang le'i tshigs bcad tha ma dang / dpal ldan dus kyi 'khor lo zhes sogs khams le'i tshigs bcad go bzhi pa dang / rab mchog sa gzhi dag la zhes sogs khams le'i tshigs bcad brgya zhe dgu pa dang bcas pa'i tshigs bcad bcu gsum rgyal po grags pa dang nyi ma'i shing rta'i gsung yin gyi rtsa rgyud las btus pa ma yin par nges shing / ye shes le'u'i tshigs bcad dgu bcu rtsa bzhi pa yang rtsa rgyud las btus pa min zhes zer ba dang bcas pa'i bcu bzhi dang / da dung rtsa rgyud nas ma btus pa'i tshigs bcad gcig yod par mngon te brtag par bya

However, in the current Jonang translations there are 1,042 verses, while in the Gyijo[50] and Ma[51] translations there are 1,043. On top of that, there are two verses from the Gnosis chapter, quoted in the Great Commentary in the Supreme and Unchanging Gnosis summary, that are not found in these root translations.[52] These are the 170th verse that begins, “Karma arises from disturbed states of minds, and from that comes suffering. Disturbed states of mind arise from one’s suffering,” and verse 182. Together these make up 1,045 verses. How is this to be explained? Thirteen verses, comprising ten verses beginning with verse 252 of the Gnosis chapter that begins, “The glorious dharma,” plus the last verse of the Inner chapter beginning, “You are the mother, you are the father,” as well as the ninety-fourth verse of the Realms chapter beginning, “Glorious Kālacakra,” and verse 149 of the Realms chapter beginning, “On the pure supreme foundation,” are the words of King Mañjuśrī Yaśas and Sūryaratha, and are not compiled from the Root Tantra. Also it is said that the ninety-fourth verse of the Gnosis chapter is not compiled from the Root Tantra. This clearly leaves one verse not compiled from the Root Tantra, and that is something to examine. /18/

d.div: [50] Gyijo Dawa Öser (eleventh century), probably the first translator of the Kālacakra into Tibetan.
[51] Ma Lotsāwa Gewai Lodrö. Translator of the Kālacakra (eleventh century).
[52] Verses quoted in the Great Commentary but not found in the Condensed Tantra.

f.d: zhing de dang bcas pa'i bco lnga ma gtogs pa'i de dag gi lhag ma stong sum cu rtsa rgyud las btus pa'i grangs yin no/ /
Apart from those fifteen, the remaining 1,030 verses have been compiled from the Root Tantra.
gsum pa bsdus pa'i rtsa rgyud dang bsdus rgyud chos rgyal dang rigs ldan rnams kyis bstan pa'i tshul

d.i: How the Root Tantra and the condensed Tantra were taught by the dharma kings and the Kalkī kings of Shambhala

f.d: ['di ]la dngos dang / de ltar bstan pa'i bstan pa'i gnas tshad dang bstan pa spyi'i gnas tshad sbyar te bshad par bya'o/ /
This section is divided into two: 1. The main explanation 2. The duration of these teachings and the duration of the Buddha’s teachings in general
dang po [dngos] ni
[1. The main explanation]

chos rgyal zla ba bzang pos lo gsum rtsa rgyud bstan/ de mya ngan las 'das pa'i rjes su chos rgyal drug gis lo brgya brgyar rtsa rgyud bstan pa'i chos rgyal drug ni rtsa rgyud mdor bsdus gsum par drangs pa las/
zla ba lha dbang gzi brjid can/ / zla bas byin dang lha dbang phyug / sna tshogs gzugs dang lha dbang ldan/[30] / zhes gsungs pa rnams so/ /

The dharma king Sucandra taught the Root Tantra for three years. After he passed away, six dharma kings each taught the Root Tantra for a hundred years. These six kings are spoken of in the Root Tantra, which is quoted in the Realms chapter in third summary:
Sucandra, Sureśvara, Tejī, Somatta, Sureśvara, Viśvamūrti, and Sureśāna[53]

d.div: [30] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 22_na6
[53] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 22a6.

f.d:
de rnams gang gi sprul pa yin pa ni de'i 'phro nyid las/
chos rgyal bdun po dang rim pa bzhin sbyor bar gsungs pa ni/ phyag na rdo rje zla bzang khyod/ / sa snying gshin rje mthar byed dang / / sgrib pa thams cad rnam sel dang / / rmugs byed khengs byed rim pas te/ / nam mkha'i snying po/[31] zhes sogs so/ /

The text continues to explain who these kings were emanations of:
Vajrapāṇi is you Sucandra, then Kṣitigarbha, Yamāntaka, Viṣkambhī, Jambhaka, Mānaka, Khagarbha.[54]

d.div: [31] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 22_na6
[54] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 22a6.

f.d: lha'i dbang ldan gyis lo brgyar rtsa rgyud bstan pa'i rjes su lha'i dbang ldan gyi sras rig_sa ldan 'jam dbyangs grags pas lo brgyar rtsa rgyud bstan cing / lo brgya rdzogs pa'i rjes kyi mig dmar shing pho byi ba de'i nag pa'i nya la nyi ma'i shing rta sogs drang srong rnams la dbang bskur byin te bsdus rgyud sdu ba mdzad nas mya ngan las 'das so/ /

Sureśāna taught the Root Tantra for a hundred years. After him his son, Kalkī Mañjuśrī Yaśas, taught the Root Tantra for a hundred years. In the hundredth year in the male Wood Rat year on the Caitra full moon, he gave initiation to Sūryaratha and the other ṛṣi, compiled the Condensed Tantra, and passed away.

de nas shing pho byi ba de la pad dkar gyis 'grel chen dri med 'od mdzad/ de nas bzung ste lo brgyad brgya'i bar la pad+ma dkar po sogs rigs ldan brgyad kyis bsdus rgyud 'grel pa dang bcas pa lo brgya brgyar bstan pa yin te/ mdor bsdus dgu pa las/
de nas klu yi lo brgya rnams kyis zhes pa ni grags pa mya ngan las 'das pa de nas klu zhes pa lo brgyad brgya nas nges par zhes pa ni gdon mi za bar ma kha'i yul du kla klo'i chos dag rab tu 'jug par 'gyur te/[32] zhes rgyal po grags pa mya ngan las 'das nas lo brgyad brgya na ma kha'i yul du kla klo 'jug par bshad cing

In that male Wood Rat year, his son Puṇḍarīka composed the Vimalaprabhā or Great Commentary. From then on, for eight hundred years, Puṇḍarīka and seven other Kalkīs taught the Condensed Tantra together with its commentary, each teaching for a hundred years. In the Realms chapter of the Great Commentary, in the ninth summary, it says:
“Naga hundred years from then”: naga (meaning eight) hundred years from the time of Yaśas’s passing, definitely (meaning without doubt) the dharma of the barbarians will enter the land of Makha.[55] This teaches that eight hundred years after the passing of King Mañjuśrī Yaśas, the barbarians would enter the land of Makha.

d.div: [32] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 68_ba7
[55] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 68b7.

f.d:
khams le'i go slar/
rigs ldan rigs kyi nang nas lag pas bsgyur ba'i dus kyi bu dang tsha bo dag ni 'das gyur pa/ / de yi dus su nges par ma kha'i yul du kla klo'i chos ni rab tu 'jug pa dag tu 'gyur/[33] / zhes rigs ldan gyi rigs su gyur pa rnams kyi nang nas lag pa ste gnyis kyis dus te bzhi bsgyur pa'i rigs ldan grags pa'i bu pad dkar dang tsha bo bzang po sogs brgyad 'das pa'i mtha' der ma kha'i yul du kla klo 'jug par bshad pas so/ /

In the “easy to understand” verses of the Realms chapter it says:
Among the Kalkīs, sons and grandsons of time multiplied by hands, will have passed away, and at that time and without doubt, /19/ the barbarian dharma will enter the land of Makha.[56] “Hands” here means two and “time” means four. After eight Kalkīs comprising Mañjuśrī Yaśas, his son Puṇḍarīka, his grandson Bhadra, and the others have passed away, the barbarians will enter the land of Makha.

d.div: [33] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka159_39_na2
[56] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 159, 39a2.

f.d: des na grags pa 'das nas lo brgyad brgya na kla klo ma kha'i yul du 'jug par bshad cing / grags pa 'das nas kla klo 'jug pa'i bar la pad dkar sogs rigs ldan brgyad 'byung bar bshad pa pad dkar nas shin tu bzang gi bar rigs ldan brgyad po des lo brgya brgyar chos bstan par grub bo/ /

Therefore, eight hundred years after the passing of Mañjuśrī Yaśas, the barbarians entered the land of Makha, and from his passing until that time, Puṇḍarīka and seven others appeared. This establishes that the eight Kalkīs from Puṇḍarīka to Subhadra each taught the dharma for a hundred years.

de ltar na grags pa nas shin bzang gi bar rigs ldan dgu ste/ rtsa rgyud mdor bsdus gsum par drangs pa las/
grags pa rigs ldan rigs kyang ste/ / de nas rigs ldan pad+ma dkar/ / bzang po rigs ldan gsum pa ste/ / de bzhin bzhi pa rnam rgyal lo/ / bshes gnyen bzang po rin chen phyag / bdun pa khyab 'jug sbas pa'o/ / nyi ma grags dang shin tu bzang / /[34] zhes gsungs pa rnams so/ /

The nine Kalkīs from Mañjuśrī Yaśas to Subhadra are spoken of in the Root Tantra quoted in the third summary of the Realms chapter:
Yaśas of Kalkī line, then Kalkī Puṇḍarīka, and Kalkī Bhadra, these three. Likewise, the fourth, Vijaya, then Sumitrabhadra, Ratnapāṇi, the seventh, Viṣṇugupta, Sūryakīrti, and Subhadra.[57]

d.div: [34] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 22_ba1
[57] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, 22b1.

f.d: shin bzang 'das ma thag gi rjes der kla klo zhugs pa dang rigs ldan rgya mtsho rnam rgyal khri thog tu byon pa dus mnyam zhing rgya mtsho rnam rgyal gyis lo brgya brgyad cu rtsa gnyis kyi bar du chos bstan/ de'i mjug tu rigs ldan rgyal dkas lo nyis brgya nyer gcig gi bar du chos bstan pa yin pas chos rgyal drug dang rigs ldan nyer gsum po gzhan rnams lo brgya bar mtshungs kyang / rgya mtsho rnam rgyal dang rgyal dka' gnyis lo brgya pa las ches mang ba yin no/ /

As soon as Subhadra passed away, the barbarians arrived, and Kalkī Samudravijaya ascended to the throne. Samudravijaya taught the dharma for 182 years. After him came Kalkī Aja, who taught the dharma for 221 years. Therefore, the six dharma kings and twenty-three Kalkīs are similar in that they each taught for a hundred years. The reigns of Samudra vijaya and Aja, however, lasted more than a hundred years.

de ltar yin pa'i rgyu mtshan yang mdor bsdus dgu pa las/
'dir byed pa la nges pa ni de bzhin gshegs pa'i dus nas lo drug brgya na 'jam dpal gyi dus so/[35] / zhes pa ni rgyal po grags pa byung ma thag pa'i dus bstan pa dang /
de bzhin du de nas lo brgyad brgya na kla klo'i dus so/ / zhes pa 'dis kla klo zhugs ma thag pa'i dus bstan pa de bzhin du/
