kla klo'i dus de las brgyad cu rtsa gnyis lhag pa'i brgyas dman pa ni rgyal dka' gang gis nyung ngu'i byed pa rnam par sbyong ba rigs ldan rgyal dka'i dus so/ / zhes gsungs pa 'dis kla klo ma khar zhugs nas rtsis lo nyis brgya nyer gcig gi mjug yan chad la lo me mkha' rgya mtsho 'das pa'i lo me mkha' rgya mtsho la lo brgya brgyad cu rtsa gnyis dman pa rtsis lo nyis brgya nyer gcig gi thog ma de rigs ldan rgyal dka' byung ma thag pa'i dus yin par bstan pa dang / lo me mkha' rgya mtsho 'jog pa yang kla klo zhugs nas ji tsam song gi 'das lo'i grangs rtogs pa dgos pa'i gtso bo yin na'ang rgyal po gnyis po de'i lo grangs bye brag tu rtogs pa'i ched kyang yin no/ /

This can be known as follows. In the ninth summary it says:
Six hundred years after the Tathāgata is the time of Mañjuśrī.[58] This establishes the time of King Mañjuśrī Yaśas.
Similarly eight hundred years from then is the time of the barbarians. This establishes the time of the arrival of the barbarians. Similarly:
Less 182 years from the time of the barbarians is the time of Kalkī Aja, who reformed the abridged karaṇa astronomy. The years from the time of the barbarians arriving in Makha until the last of the 221 years of astronomy are the fire, sky, and ocean years. Subtracting 182 years from the fire, sky, and ocean years is to arrive at the first year of the 221 years of astronomy. That year is the time that Kalkī Aja appears. Establishing the fire, sky, and ocean years is primarily for the purpose of knowing the number of years that have passed since the barbarians arrived, but it is also for knowing the dates of these two kings.

d.div: [35] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 69_ba7
[58] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, 69b7

f.d: de ltar ma yin par rigs ldan thams cad lo brgya par snga ma rnams bzhed pa ltar yin no zhe na mi 'thad de/ ma kha'i yul du kla klo thog mar zhugs pa nas rigs ldan drag pos kla klo 'jom_sa pa'i bar gyi kla klo'i chos kyi gnas tshad ni lo stong brgyad brgya yin zhing / kla klo zhugs pa dang khri thog tu phebs pa dus mnyam pa'i rigs ldan rgya mtsho rnam rgyal nas rigs ldan drag po 'khor lo can gyi bar la rigs ldan bcu drug las med pas so/ /

It is incorrect to assert, as those of the past have done, that every Kalkī ruled for a hundred years. This is because from the time the barbarians first arrived in Makha until they are destroyed by Kalkī Rudra, their barbarian dharma will have been in existence for 1,800 years, and from the time of Kalkī Samudravijaya ascending to the throne simultaneous with the arrival of the barbarians until the coming of Kalkī Rudracakrī, the number of Kalkīs does not exceed sixteen.

des na rgya mtsho rnam rgyal dang rgyal dka' la lo bzhi brgya dang gsum du byas na kla klo'i gnas tshad dang shin tu 'grig pa yin te rigs ldan nyi ma nas drag po'i bar rigs ldan bcu bzhis lo brgya brgya dang / rgya mtsho rnam rgyal dang rgyal dka'i lo bzhi brgya dang gsum ste stong brgyad brgya dang gsum 'ong bas so/ /

Therefore, positing the reigns of Samudra vijaya and Aja as totaling 403 years accords perfectly with the duration of the barbarians, because each of the hundred years of the fourteen Kalkīs from Sūrya to Rudra, added to the 403 years of Samudravijaya and Durjaya totals 1,803 years.

kla klo'i gnas tshad kyang lo stong brgyad brgya yin te/ dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud phyi ma las/
de la bco brgyad lo yis brgya phrag bsgyur te brgya yis 'phags pa'i yul gyi ma kha la sogs par/ / kla klo rnams kyi grags pa gang dang gang zhig mun can gyur pa de rnams bdag gis drungs phyung ste/[36] / zhes dang /

The Later Kālacakra Tantra establishes the barbarian duration as eighteen hundred years:
For eighteen years times a hundred in Makha, and elsewhere in noble lands, are those renowned as barbarians, those of the darkness. These I will destroy.[59]

d.div: [36] sde dge_363_bka'/ rgyud/ kadapal dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud phyi ma rgyud kyi snying po/ 142_na6
[59] Toh 363 Kangyur, rgyud, ka, 142a6

f.d:
khams le'i go sla'i jo nang 'gyur gsar las/
de ltar dum bu thams cad du yang dus bzhi'i _dus su kla klo'i chos ni rab tu 'jug pa ste/ / lo ni brgyad dang gcig gi brgyad ni nges par gnas te de nas kla klo'i chos ni nyams pa'o/ /[37] zhes gsungs te

In the “easy to understand” verses of the Realms chapter from the new Jonang translations it says:
In every continent, during the four ages, the barbarians will enter, remaining there for a hundred of eight and one years. Then their dharma will decline.[60]

d.div: [37] jo nang 'gyur gsar gyi gzhung 'di brnyed son ma byung /
[60] Reference not found.

f.d: brgyad dang bcu gcig gi brgyar ni zhes pa'i don ni rtsis kyi gnas gzhan 'god pa'i rim pa ste/ de yang mjug tu brgyad bkod/ de'i gong du gcig bkod de brgyas bsgyur bas stong brgyad brgya 'ong ba'o/ / de ltar na rgya mtsho rnam rgyal man chad kyi rigs ldan gyi rgyal po rnams kyi sku tshe'i tshad bsdoms pa'i lo grangs dang kla klo'i gnas tshad sgrig dgos pa dang / rgya mtsho rnam rgyal dang rgyal dka'i lo grangs khyad par bar bshad pa 'dis rigs ldan nyi ma sogs lhag ma bcu bzhi po lo brgya par grub bo/ /

“A hundred of eight and one years” is written using another system of enumeration. Putting eight last and one first and multiplying that by a hundred totals one thousand eight hundred. The sum of the reigns of the Kalkī kings from Samudravijaya onward must tally with the duration of the barbarians, and because of the differences found in the reigns of Samudravijaya and Aja, /21/ it can be established that the remaining fourteen Kalkīs each reigned for a hundred years.

rgya mtsho rnam rgyal sogs bcu drug po ni rtsa rgyud las/ /
rgya mtsho rnam rgyal rgyal dka' dang / / rigs ldan nyi ma bcu gnyis pa/ / sna tshogs gzugs dang zla ba'i 'od/ / mtha' yas dang ni sa skyong dang / / dpal skyong seng+ge rnam par gnon/ / stobs po che dang ma 'gags pa/ / mi yi seng+ge dbang phyug che/ / mtha' yas rnam rgyal rigs ldan dang / / grags pa rigs ldan de nas slar/ / de sras 'khor lo chen po can/ / rigs ldan drag po 'byung 'gyur te/ / smra mkhas rta mchog ting 'dzin gyis/ / kla klo'i chos ni mthar byed pa'o/ / nyi ma'i shing rta la sogs kyi/ / ston pa smra mkhas 'byung 'gyur gang / / zla bzang khyod ni rtsa ba'i rgyud/ / de ni sdud par byed pa ste/ / rgyas 'grel byed pa po yang khyod/ / 'dir ni sems can yongs smin byed/ / 'jam pa'i rdo rje'i bsdus rgyud la/ / rgyas 'grel byed pa pad 'dzin dang /[38] / zhes pa ltar ro/ /

The sixteen Kalkīs beginning from Samudravijaya are stated in the Root Tantra:
Samudravijaya, Aja, Kalkī Sūrya is the twelfth, Viśvarūpa, Śaśiprabha, Ananta, and Mahīpala, Śrīpala, Hari, Vikrama, Mahābala, and Aniruddha, Narasiṃha, Maheśvara, Kalkī Anantavijaya, then his son, again the Kalkī Yaśas, as Kalkī Rudra, possessed of the great wheel, who by skillful speech, the best of horses samādhi,[61] will put an end to the barbarian dharma. For the skillful teacher of Sūryaratha and the others, Sucandra, you will compile the Root Tantra and be the composer of an extensive commentary, and here sentient beings will be ripened. For the condensed tantra of Vajra Mañjuśrī, Padmapāṇi[62] will compose the commentary.[63]

d.div: [38] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 22_ba2

div.i: rta mchog ting nge ’dzin, paramāśva samādhi.

d.div: [62] Puṇḍarīka.
[63] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 22b2.

f.d:
de ltar na rgyal po zla ba bzang po nas rigs ldan drag po 'khor lo can gyi bar la rgyal po sum cu rtsa gnyis dang / 'khor lo can de yang tshe lo brgya pa yin te/ de ltar yang khams le'i go sla las/
sum cu rtsa gnyis gdan gyi mthar ni lha min dgra bo tshe lo brgya pa phyag na 'khor lor 'gyur/[39] / zhes gsungs pa dang /
'di _ni dpal ldan 'jam pa'i _rdo rje lha yi mchog gis btud pa rdo rje'i rigs kyi rigs ldan te/[40] / zhes rgyal po 'jam dbyangs grags pa 'jam dbyangs kyi sprul pa dang / rigs bzhi rdo rje'i rigs su byas pas rigs ldan du gsungs shing /
gdan ni nyi shu rtsa lnga po rnams rim par yongs su bgrangs pa de yi nang nas dus kyi mthar/ / rigs ldan rigs la lha yi dbang po lha yi mchog gis btud pa drag po'i rigs ldan 'byung bar 'gyur/[41] / zhes rig_sa ldan 'jam dbyangs grags pa nas drag po 'khor lo can gyi bar nyer lngar grangs nges pa dang / ston pa'i bstan pa'i dus bzhi'i rtsod dus kyi mthar rigs ldan drag po 'byung bar yang gsungs so/ /

Therefore, from King Sucandra to Kalkī Rudracakrī, thirty-two kings will have reigned. Rudracakrī also reigns for a hundred years. In the “easy to understand” verses in the Realms chapter it says:
For a hundred years on the final throne of the thirty-two will sit the enemy of the asura, possessor of the wheel.[64] Also:
Vajra Mañjuśrī, Kalkī of the vajra caste, bowed to by the king of the gods, the supreme god.[65] This states that Mañjuśrī Yaśas was an emanation of Mañjuśrī. Because he amalgamated the four castes into the vajra lineage, he is spoken of as a Kalkī. The verses continue:
At the end of the ages, from the succession of twenty-five reigns, the caste of Kalkī bowed to by the greatest of gods, the wrathful Kalkī will appear.[66] This teaches that the number of Kalkīs from Mañjuśrī Yaśas to Rudracakrī is ascertained at twenty-five, and that of the four ages of our teacher’s doctrine,[67] /22/ the Kalkī Rudra will appear at the end of the age of troubles.

d.div: [39] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka152_38_na7
[40] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka157_38_ba6
[41] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka158_39_na1
[64] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 152, 38a7.
[65] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 157, 38b6.
[66] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 158, 39a1.

[67] Refers to times during the life span of the Buddha’s doctrine of varying levels of wealth, dharma, pleasures, and well-being. The age of completeness (rdzogs ldan, caturyuga) has all four, the age of three (gsum ldan, tretāyuga) lacks one, the age of two (gnyis ldan, dvāparayuga) lacks two, while the age of troubles (rtsod ldan, kaliyuga) lacks three. See The Great Lexicon.

f.d: de lta bu'i drag po 'khor lo can des ston pa shAkya thub pa'i sngags kyi bstan pa rtsod ldan gyi mthar gyur pa kla klo ma khar zhugs nas lo stong brgyad brgya song ba'i mtha' rigs ldan drag po rang nyid kyis lo go bdun bzhes pa'i dus der lha chen bcu gnyis la sogs pa'i grogs dang bcas pa'i dmag dpung gis bskor te sham+b+ha la'i gnas nas 'thon nas chu bo shI ta'i lho 'phags pa'i yul du byon te kla klo rnams dang de dag gi dpung grogs lha min la sogs pa'i dmag tshogs rnams 'dzam gling chung ngu 'dir g.yul du bcom ste rang gi chos rdo rje theg pa la kla klo dang kla klo de'i chos la zhugs pa'i mi gzhan rnams kyang bkod nas/ de nas 'dzam gling chung ngu 'di nas g.yas bskor gyis dum bu bcu gcig po gzhan rnams su yang rim gyis byon te ston pa shAkya thub pa'i rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa rtsod ldan gyi mthar song ba rnams kyi nyams pa gsos [42] te gling bcu gnyis po thams cad rgyal ba'i rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa rdzogs ldan du byed do/ /

Therefore, Rudracakrī appears when our teacher Śākyamuni’s doctrine of tantra has reached the end of the age of troubles, and eighteen hundred years will have passed since the arrival of the barbarians in Makha. In the ninety-seventh year of his reign, aided by the armies of the twelve great gods and others, Kalkī Rudra will leave Shambhala to journey to the noble land south of the Śīta River, and there, in lesser Jambudvīpa, they will defeat in battle the armies of the barbarians with their asura allies and bring them and others dwelling in the barbarian dharma to the Vajra Vehicle. Then, clockwise from lesser Jambudvīpa, they will enter the other eleven sectors[68] one by one, and where the Vajra Vehicle of our teacher Śākyamuni has declined at the end of the era of troubles, they will restore it. In all twelve sectors, thereby, the teachings of the victorious Vajra Vehicle will bring about an era of completeness.

d.div: [42] ma dper bsos gsal yang gsos zhes bcos/

[68] dum bu. Part, sector. These are the twelve sectors of the outer earth mandala, or Greater Jambuvīpa, which is geometrically divided up into twelve parts. Sometimes called “continents” (gling). See chap. 3.

f.d: de ltar byas nas 'khor lo can rang nyid kyi sku tshe'i tshad lo brgya rdzogs pa'i rjes su rang nyid kyi sras 'jam dpal gyi sprul pa tshangs pa dang spyan ras gzigs kyi sbrul pa lha'i dbang po gnyis rdo rje theg pa'i chos ston pa por bskos nas mya ngan las 'da'o/ / de yang tshangs pa ni chu bo shI ta'i byang sham+b+ha lar lo brgyad brgya'i bar du chos ston pa por 'gyur zhing / lha'i dbang po ni chu bo shI ta'i lho phyogs 'phags pa'i yul la sogs par chos ston pa por 'gyur ro/ /

With such an accomplishment and his hundred-year life at an end, his two sons, Brahmā, an emanation of Mañjuśrī, and Indra, an emanation of Avalokiteśvara, will be appointed teachers of the Vajra Vehicle, and Rudra will pass away. Brahmā will be the dharma teacher in Shambhala north of the Śīta River for eight hundred years, while Indra will be the teacher of dharma in the noble country and other lands.

de ltar 'khor lo can gyis rgyal ba'i rdo rje theg pa rtsod ldan gyi tha mar gyur pa de rdzogs ldan du byas pa'i bstan pa de yang ji tsam du gnas na/ sa dum bu re rer yang lo stong dang brgyad brgya brgyad brgyar gnas pa yin te/ khams le'i go sla las/
rdzogs ldan gsum ldan gnyis ldan rtsod pa'i dus ni nus pa'i tshad kyis sa gzhi dag la nges par rgyu/[43] / zhes gsungs pa ltar drag po 'khor lo can gyis bstan pa gsos [44] pa'i dus bzhi gnas pa gling bcu gnyis po thams cad bsdom_sa pa'i yun tshad nus pa 'og min pa'i zhag re'i tshad mi lo nyis khri chig stong drug brgya yin la/ de la bcu gnyis kyis bgos pas stong brgyad brgya re 'thob pa gling bcu gnyis po re re'i dus bzhi gnas pa'i yun tshad yin pas so/ /

In this way, Rudracakrī brings the Vajra Vehicle of the Conqueror at the end of the age of troubles into an age of completeness. How long will that doctrine last? In each continent it will last for eighteen hundred years. In the “easy to understand” verses in the Realms chapter it says:
The ages of completeness, of three, of two, and of troubles is ascertained by the measurements of None Higher.[69] As this quote states, the total duration of the four ages of the restoration of the doctrine by Rudracakrī in the twelve continents is the length of one day in the realm of None Higher,[70] or in the human realm, 21,600 years. That divided by twelve is eighteen hundred and that is the duration of the four ages in each of the twelve sectors.

d.div: [43] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka168_40_na2
[44] ma dper bsos gsal yang gsos zhes bcos/
[69] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 168, 40a2.
[70] The highest realm of the form realms (’og min, akāniṣṭha).

f.d:
de yang rdzogs ldan gsum ldan gnyis ldan rtsod dus te dus bzhi re re'i yun tshad ni khams le las/
re re dag gi tshad ni dus dang mda' yis bsgyur ba'i mi rnams dag gi lo brgya gang yin pa'o/[45] / zhes gling bcu gnyis po'i rdzogs ldan sogs dus bzhi re re bsdoms pa'i yun tshad lnga stong bzhi brgyar gsungs la/ /de la bcu gnyis kyis bgos pas bzhi brgya lnga bcu re 'thob pa gling bcu gnyis po re re'i dus bzhi so so'i yun tshad yin no/ /

Moreover, concerning the length of each of the /23/ four ages of completeness, three, two and troubles, the tantra says:
As to the length of each, a hundred human years multiplied by time and arrow.[71] Therefore, the sum of each of the ages’ duration in the twelve sectors is 5,400 years. That divided by twelve is 450 and is the duration of each age in each of the twelve sectors.

d.div: [45] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka23_25_na1
[71] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 23, 24a1. The second line uses word numerals: time = 4, arrow = 5; therefore 54 × 100. See appendix 5.

f.d: de ltar na bstan pa'i dus bzhi 'di la tshan pa gnyis te/ rgyal ba'i bstan pa'i dus bzhi dang / drag po 'khor lo can gyis bstan pa bsos [46] pa'i dus bzhi'o/ /
Therefore, the duration of the doctrine known as the four ages is of two kinds: the earlier four ages of the Buddha’s doctrine and the later four ages of Rudracakrī’s restoration of the doctrine.

d.div: [46] ma dper bsos gsal yang gsos zhes bcos/

f.d: rgyal ba nyid kyi bstan pa'i dus bzhi ni ston pa mya ngan las 'das nas drag po 'khor lo can gyis lo ril po go bdun bzhes pa'i bar lo sum stong sum brgya dang bzhi rnams kyi bar te/ de yang ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa nas zla bzang gshegs pa'i bar lo bzhi/ de nas lha dbang nas grags pa gshegs kyi bar lo bdun brgya/ de nas pad dkar nas shin bzang gshegs kyi bar lo brgyad brgya/ de nas rgya mtsho rnam rgyal dang rgyal dka' gnyis kyi lo bzhi brgya dang gsum/ de nas rigs ldan nyi ma nas mtha' yas rnam rgyal gyi bar rigs ldan bcu gsum gyi lo brgya brgya ste stong sum brgya/ de nas drag po 'khor lo can gyi lo go bdun te sum stong sum brgya dang bzhi'o/ /

The four ages of the Conqueror’s doctrine run from his passing until Rudracakrī has completed ninety-seven years. This is a total of 3,304 years. These years are made up of the four years from our Teacher delivering the Root Tantra until the passing of Sucandra, seven hundred years from King Sureśvara until the passing of Mañjuśrī Yaśas, eight hundred years from Puṇḍarīka until the passing of Subhadra, the 403 years of Samudravijaya and Aja, the 1,300 years of the thirteen Kalkīs from Sūrya to Anantavijaya and the ninety-seven years of Rudracakrī.

gal te rigs ldan drag pos lo go bdun bzhes pa'i dus su kla klo bcom pa yin na khams le'i go sla'i rgyud las/
kla klo'i tshogs ni rab tu bcad nas 'khor dang bcas pa'i skye bo mi yi lo ni brgya phyed na/ / rigs ldan grub par 'gyur te lha yis bkod pa'i pho brang mtho ba kai la sha yi rgyab tu'o/[47] / zhes gsungs pa dang 'gal te/ rgyud tshig des drag po 'khor lo can gyis kla klo 'khor dang bcas pa lhag ma med par bcad zin nas lo lnga bcu bzhes pa'i dus su ri bo kai la sha'i rgyab grub pa'i gnas sham+b+ha lar gshegs par 'gyur bar bshad pa'i phyir ro snyam na/

However, if Rudracakrī defeats the barbarians at the age of ninety-seven, in the “easy to understand” verses in the Realms chapter of the Tantra it says:
The barbarian hordes destroyed with allies, at half one hundred human years, the accomplishment of the Kalkī in the great celestially designed palace behind Kailash.[72] Doesn’t this quote say that Rudracakrī will destroy the barbarians and their allies at the age of fifty and then pass away in Shambhala behind the mountain of Kailash?

d.div: [47] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka164_39_ba2_'gyur cung mi mthun/
[72] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 164, 39b2.

f.d: de'i skyon med de/ rgyud tshig des rigs ldan drag pos rang lo go bdun bzhes pa'i lo ngo go brgyad pa'i dus nas brgya pa rdzogs kyi bar la klo klo'i tshogs 'khor gyi skye bo dang bcas pa klo klo'i chos la 'jug pa rab tu bcad cing / gling bcu gnyis po rnams su rtsod dus kyi mtha'i chos ma yin pa nyams par byas te rang lo brgya bzhes pa'i mthar rang gi sras tshangs pa dang lha dbang chos ston pa la bskos nas bde bar gshegs pa'i rjes kyi mi lo brgya phyed lnga bcu'i bar la rang gi gzhom bya kla klo 'khor dang bcas pa de rnams kyis rigs ldan gyi lam grub par 'gyur ro/ / gnas gang du 'grub na lha yis bkod pa'i pho brang mtho ba kai la sha'i rgyab tu ste sham+b+ha lar 'grub bo/ / zhes pa'i don yin pas so/ /

There is no contradiction. This quote explains that Kalkī Rudra, from his ninety-eighth year until the completion of his hundred years, will thoroughly destroy the barbarian hordes and their allies who have accepted /24/ the barbarian dharma. Having weakened the non-dharma flourishing at the end of the age of troubles in the twelve sectors, he will appoint his sons Brahmā and Indra as dharma teachers at the end of his hundred years. Half one hundred, or fifty human years, after his passing into great bliss, the barbarians that he defeated and their allies will accomplish the path of the Kalkī. Where will this occur? In Shambhala, in the great celestially designed palace behind Kailash.
gal te de las gzhan du rigs ldan drag pos lo lnga bcu bzhes pa'i dus su kla klo'i chos bcom pa yin na klo klo'i gnas tshad la stong brgyad brgya la lnga bcu ma tshang ba'i skyon yod pa dang /
If it were otherwise, and Kalkī Rudra defeats the barbarians at the age of fifty, then the barbarian duration of eighteen hundred years would be fifty years short.

gzhan yang
sum cu rtsa gnyis gdan gyi mthar ni lha min dgra'o tshe lo brgya pa phyag na 'khor lor 'gyur/[48] / zhes rigs ldan drag po tshe lo brgya par bshad cing /
rdzogs ldan 'tshams su klo klo'i chos rnams mtha' dag srid pa gsum gyi bla ma dag gis bcad byas te/ / bcad nas lo ni brgyad brgya rnams su tshangs pa bzhag pa mdzad nas bde ba'i gnas su 'gro bar 'gyur/[49] / zhes kla klo'i chos bcad pa'i mjug thogs de nyid du tshangs pa lo brgyad brgya'i bar du chos ston pa por bzhag nas drag po rang nyid bde ba'i gnas su 'gro ba ste mya ngan las 'da' bar bshad pas so/ /

Furthermore, the Tantra says:
For a hundred years on the final throne of the thirty-two, will sit the enemy of the asura, possessor of the wheel.[73] This states that Kalkī Rudra reigns for a hundred years. Also:
In the age of completeness every dharma of the barbarians will be destroyed by the master of the three worlds. Appointing Brahmā for eight hundred years, he will travel to the place of bliss.[74] This explains that immediately after destroying the barbarian dharma, Brahmā will be appointed dharma teacher for eight hundred years, and Rudra will travel to the place of bliss, meaning that he will pass away.

d.div: [48] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka152_38_na7
[49] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ sh+loka165_39_ba3
[73] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 152, 38a7.
[74] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 165, 39b3.

f.d:
de ltar na gong du bshad pa ltar ston pa sa ga'i nya la sangs rgyas pa dang mya ngan las 'das par bshad pa rnams dang / khams le'i mdor bsdus gnyis pa las/
nang du ni ro zhes pa dbugs 'byung ba dang 'jug pa sum stong drug brgyas dman pa'i nyis khri chig stong drug brgya rnams 'gags pas so/[50] / zhes phyag na rdo rje'i sprul pa rgyal po zla ba bzang po rlung stong brgyad brgya pa tshan pa gnyis ma 'gags pa'i sa bcu pa par bshad pa dang / de bzhin du 'jam dpal dang spyan ras gzigs kyi sprul ba rgyal po grags pa dang pad dkar sogs sa bcu pa'i byang sems su bshad pa rnams dang / dus kyi 'khor lo'i zab don chags bral nyan thos kyi spyod yul ma yin par 'chad pa'i skabs su khams le'i mdor bsdus bdun pa'i 'grel chen las/ chags bral ni 'phags pa kun dga' bo la sogs pa dang /[51] zhes zab don 'phags pa kun dga' bo'i spyod yul ma yin pa sogs su bshad pa rnams ni sangs rgyas dang sprul pa'i byang sems nyan thos dang bcas pa rnams kyis mdzad pa'i tshul bstan pa rnams ji bzhin du zhen pa'i gdul bya rnams kyi ngor theg pa thun mong ba dang mthun par gsungs pa yin gyi/

It was previously explained that our teacher became a buddha and passed away on vaiśākha full moons. In the Realms chapter, in the second summary, it says:
Internally, “corpse” refers to the cessation of 21,600 in and out breaths, less 3,600.[75] This passage explains that the Vajrapāṇi emanation King Sucandra was a tenth-level bodhisattva who had not yet negated two sets of 1,800 breaths.[76] There are similar explanations of the Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara emanations, Mañjuśrī Yaśas and Puṇḍarīka, as being tenth-level bodhisattvas. Furthermore, in the Realms chapter of the Great Commentary, in the seventh summary, in the part where it explains how the profound meaning of the Kālacakra is not for the attachment-free listeners,[77] /25/ it begins, “Those free of attachment, the noble Ānanda and others,”[78] and goes on to explain how the profound meaning is not for the noble Ānanda and others. These statements and others are made in accordance with the views of the common vehicle in which disciples take the deeds of the Buddha and the emanations of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as being factually true in the way they were performed.

d.div: [50] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 14_ba7
[51] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 49_na4
[75] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 14b7.
[76] Breaths of karma.
[77] nyan thos, śrāvaka. Non-Mahayana disciples of the Buddha.
[78] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 49a4.

f.d:
rtsa rgyud bsdus rgyud sems 'grel skor gsum dang bcas pa'i dgongs pa mthar thug pa ni 'grel chen las/
sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das ni sangs rgyas kyi zhing stong gsum gyi stong chen po'i 'jig rten gyi khams rnams su sgyu ma'i sprul pa'i sku sgrib pa dang bral ba mtha' yas pa mtha' yas pa rnams kyis sems can mtha' yas pa mtha' yas pa rnams kyi skad mtha' yas pa mtha' yas pa rnams kyis gsol ba 'debs pa po sna tshogs kyis gsol ba btab pa na sems can thams cad kyi skad la rab tu 'jug pa thams cad mkhyen pa'i gsung gis 'jig rten dang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i chos ston par mdzad de thams cad mkhyen pa de du ma ma yin no/ / des na sems can thams cad la 'jig rten dang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i chos bstan pa'i phyir sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das sngon sa bcu gnyis kyi dbang phyug tu gyur pa mkhas pa sgyu 'phrul chen po 'chang ba sgyu 'phrul chen po'i mig 'phrul dang ldan pa 'phags pa'i yul lum bi nir shAkya'i rigs mi'i dbang po zas gtsang ma'i lha mo sgyu 'phrul chen mo'i lhums nas bltams pa ni gzhon nu don grub yin la/[52] zhes gsungs pa ltar

However, the final thinking of the Root Tantra, the Condensed Tantra, and the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries is expressed in the Great Commentary:
The conquering Buddha in countless, countless emanated illusory and nonobscured forms in the great thousand world realms engages in the languages of every sentient being when various supplicants request the Buddha in the limitless tongues of limitless sentient beings. With omniscient speech he teaches worldly and nonworldly dharma. Yet the omniscient one is not more than one. Therefore, in order to teach worldly and nonworldly dharma to all sentient beings, the conquering Buddha first became the powerful one of the twelve levels, then with skilful and great magic, with great visual illusion, he took birth from the womb of Māyādevī, wife of Śuddhodana, king of the Śākya clan, to become the youth Siddārtha.[79] As this quote indicates,

d.div: [52] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 21_na1
[79] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 21a1.

f.d:
shAkya thub pa sngon gyi dus nas sangs rgyas zin sprul pa'i sku mtha' yas pas sems can mtha' yas pa'i don mdzad bzhin pa zhing 'dir sangs rgyas pa dang mya ngan las 'das pa'i tshul bstan pa dang / de bzhin du phyag na rdo rje 'jam dbyangs spyan ras gzigs la sogs pa rnams kyang sngon gyi dus su sangs rgyas zin pa sa bcu pa'i byang sems kyi tshul bstan nas sems can gyi don mdzad pa sogs bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i gnas yin te/ khams le'i mdor bsdus gsum pa'i 'grel chen las/
'jig rten dbang phyug bdag sems can gyi don la dmyal bar zhugs pa'i dus su gshin rje'i pho nya rnams dang gshin rje'i rgyal po rnams kyis bstod pa brjod pa/ gang zhig srid pa'i 'ching ba rnams las grol kyang sems can don du srid pa 'dzin/ / de ni stong pa'i don dag ston mdzad dus las las kyi 'bras bu gtong ma lags/ / sems kyi dri ma yang dag ye shes mes bsregs rtag tu yang dag brtse bas brlan/ / mdzad spyod rtag min sems can don la dgyes pa'i sangs rgyas de la bdag cag 'dud/[53] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

Śākyamuni had already attained complete enlightenment in the past, and in the course of working for the benefit of countless sentient beings with countless emanations, in this world he manifested enlightenment and passing away. Similarly, Vajrapāṇi, Mañjuśrī, Avalo kiteśvara, and others had already attained complete enlightenment when they took the form of tenth-level bodhisattvas and worked for the benefit of others. These and other examples are beyond the scope of thought. In the Realms chapter of the Great Commentary, in the third summary, it says:
The great one of the world dwelt in the hells for the sake of sentient beings. There the messengers of death and the lords of death spoke these words of praise, “Although free from the chains of existence, he holds to existence for the sake of sentient beings. He is here to teach in order to empty hell and not as a result of previous actions. The taints of the mind have been burned off by the fire of wisdom, a mind always moist /26/ with flawless compassion, whose deeds, without conception, are joyfully done for the benefit of sentient beings. To the Buddha we prostrate.[80]

d.div: [53] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 20_ba3_tshig sna cung mi mthun/
[80] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 20b3.

f.d:
khyad par du yang sgron gsal las/
gsol pa/ 'o na btsun pa kun dga' bo la sogs pa sdud par byed par ci'i phyir 'jig rten du grags/ smras pa/ kun dga' bo ni 'dir byang chub sems dpa' sems dpa' chen po kun tu bzang po ste phyag na rdo rje yin la rdo rje 'chang chen po yang de nyid las gzhan ma yin te/ gzhan du na mdo sde la sogs pa'i chos kyi phung po brgyad khri bzhi stong po 'di dag de bzhin gshegs pa las phyag na rdo rjes thos nas lhag chad med par lan gcig gis 'dzin par ga la nus/[54] zhes gsungs nas

More specifically in Bright Lamp it says:
Why in this world are the venerable Ānanda and others renowned as compilers of scripture? Ānanda is the great bodhisattva Samantabhadra. He is Vajrapāṇi, undifferentiated from the great Vajradhara. Otherwise, how could Vajrapāṇi, having heard from the Tathāgata the eighty-four thousand volumes of sutra, memorize them on a single hearing without omission or addition?[81]

d.div: [54] sde dge_1785_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ha_sgron gsal/ 9_na5
[81] Toh 1785 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ha, 9a5.

f.d:
de'i shes byed du thun mong ma yin pa'i gsang ba zhes bya ba'i bla med kyi rgyud las/
de nas gzhan yang thams cad mkhyen pa'i 'khor phun sum tshogs pa bshad par bya'o/ / 'di lta ste 'jam dpal ni rgyal po chen po zas gtsang mar gyur to/[55] / zhes sogs drangs nas bcom ldan 'das kyis bla med kyi rgyud gsungs pa'i dus kyi ston sdud nyan pa'i 'khor dang bcas pa ston pa nyid dang rgyud gcig pa bcom ldan 'das nyid kyi rnam 'phrul dang / thun mong gi 'khor gyi rnam par bstan pa'i kun dga' bo dang rgyal po zas gtsang sogs kyang ston pa nyid kyi rnam 'phrul rgyud sdud pa po sogs dang rgyud gcig tu bshad pa bzhin du dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud 'grel pa dang bcas pa'i mthar thug gi dgongs pa yang rgyal po zla ba bzang po sogs ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs pa'i 'khor thun mong ma yin pa rnams rgyud ston pa po nyid kyi rnam 'phrul du shes par bya ste/

As scriptural support for the above, a passage from a highest yoga tantra called Special Secrets is quoted:
Furthermore, I will explain the perfect entourage of the omniscient one. It is like this: Mañjuśrī was the great king Śuddhodana.[82] Therefore, when the Conqueror taught the highest tantras, the teacher, compilers, and entourage of listeners were emanations of the Buddha and of the same continuum as the Teacher himself. Even those of the commonly accepted entourage such as Ānanda and King Śuddhodana were emanations of the Teacher and of the same continuum as the compilers of the tantras. Similarly, it should be known that it is the final thinking of the Kālacakra Root Tantra and its commentaries that King Sucandra and others, who were at the special gathering for the teaching of the Root Tantra, were also emanations of the Teacher.

d.div: [55] gzhung 'di ngos 'dzin ma thub pas lung 'di brnyed son ma byung /
[82] Quoted in Bright Lamp; probably not translated into Tibetan.

f.d:
brtag gnyis las/
'chad pa po nga chos kyang nga / / rang gi tshogs ldan nyan pa nga / / 'jig rten ston pa bsgrub bya nga / / 'jigs rten [56] 'jig rten 'das pa nga /[57] / zhes pa'i 'grel pa rdo rje snying pos mdzad pa las/
'jig rten 'jig rten 'das pa nga / /zhes bya ba la byis pa'i skye bo gang dag sangs rgyas btsun mo dang dbang po'i bde ba dang 'khor 'dus pa dang chos bstan pa dang ston pa dang nyan pa la sogs pa dang 'dod chags kyis bstan pa nges par yod par sems pa dag bkag pa yin te 'di ltar ma 'ongs pa'i skye bo rnams kyis rtogs par bya ba'i phyir sangs rgyas kyi rol pa bstan pa yin la/ yang dag par na sangs rgyas ni rdo rje lta bu'i sku dang / glang po ltar mi g.yo bar shes par bya'o/[58] / zhes gsungs pas so/ /

The Hevajra Tantra says:
The teacher is me, the dharma too is me. The gathering and the listeners are me. The teacher of the world and the practices are me. The worldly and the nonworldly are me.[83] In the commentary to the above by Vajragarbha it says:
“The worldly and the nonworldly are me” means that all that is held with certainty by infantile beings — the Buddha and his queens, the sensual pleasure, the entourage, the teachings of the dharma, the teacher, the listeners, and teaching by desire[84] — are to be refuted. These are for developing the insights of sentient beings in the future. They are the play of the buddhas. /27/ In reality, the form of a buddha is as a vajra, immovable as an ox.[85]

d.div: [56] ma dper/ 'jigs rten 'jig rten 'das pa nga / / zhes byung /

f.d: gnyis pa de ltar bstan pa'i bstan pa'i gnas tshad dang bstan pa spyi'i gnas tshad sbyar te bshad pa ni/

d.i: The duration of these teachings and the duration of the Buddha’s teachings in general

f.d: mdo phyogs nas gsungs pa'i bstan pa'i gnas tshad la lo stong dang nyis stong sogs mi 'dra ba mang po gsungs pa rnams kyi nang nas mdo bskal bzang gi glegs bam kha cig tu lo lnga stong gnas [59] zhes 'byung ba bzhin du yum gsum gyi gnod 'joms su yang / de bzhin gshegs pa'i bstan pa gnas pa ni lo lnga stong du gsungs te/[60] zhes bshad pa dang / slob dpon 'jam dpal grags pas kyang lo lnga stong du gnas par gsungs pas lo lnga stong du gsungs pa sgra ji bzhin pa dang / mdo las lo stong la sogs pa tshul gzhan du gsungs pa dgongs pa can du rnam bshad chen mo de kho na nyid snang bar byed par gsungs pa [61] bzhin du sa zhal sogs mkhas pa mang dag zhal gyis bzhes shing de dag gis kyang 'di ltar du 'chad de/

In the sutra tradition the duration of the teachings has been variously put at one thousand years, two thousand years, and so on. In some volumes of the Sutra of the Good Eon[86] the duration is said to be five thousand years. In Destroying Harm to the Three Mothers it says, “It is taught that the Tathāgata’s teaching will last for five thousand years.”[87] Āchārya Mañjukīrti also says that the teachings would remain for five thousand years. Therefore, these claims can be taken literally, while other estimates found in the sutras, such as one thousand years, were taught, as the commentary Illuminating Reality says,[88] for specific reasons. This position is accepted by many masters, including those of the Sakya tradition, and therefore the five-thousand-year duration will be explained here.

d.div: [59] sde dge_94_bka'/ mdo sde/ ka_bskal ba bzang po zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ le'u/ 2_103_na2
[60] sde dge_3807_bstan/ sher phyin/ nashes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa 'bum pa rgya cher 'grel pa/ le'u/ 31_81_na5
[61] mkhas grub rje/ gsung 'bum/ khakhams kyi le'u/ 15_ba4
[86] Toh 94 Kangyur, mdo sde, ka, chap. 2, 103a2.
[87] Toh 3807 Tengyur, sher phyin, chap. 31, 81a5.
[88] Khedrup Jé, Collected Works, vol. kha, Realms chapter, 15b4.

f.d: lnga stong po de nyid lnga brgya pa phrag bcur bcad pa'i lnga brgya pa dang po dang gnyis pa dang gsum pa rnams la rim pa bzhin dgra bcom pa dang phyir mi 'ong dang rgyun zhugs thob pa mang du 'byung bas dgra bcom pa'i le'u dang phyir mi 'ong gi le'u dang rgyun du zhugs pa'i le'u zhes bya ste khong du chud pa'i le'u gsum dang / de nas lnga brgya pa phrag gsum la rim pa bzhin lhag mthong dang ting nge 'dzin dang tshul khrims dang ldan pa mang du 'byung bas lhag mthong gi le'u sogs sgrub pa'i le'u gsum dang / de nas lnga brgya pa phrag gsum la rim pa bzhin mngon pa mdo sde 'dul ba ston pa mang du 'byung bas mngon pa'i le'u sogs lung gi le'u gsum/ lnga brgya pa tha ma la lta spyod rnal ma med par rab byung gi rtags tsam 'dzin pas rtags tsam 'dzin pa'i le'u zhes 'chad do/ /

The five thousand years are divided into ten sets of five hundred years. In the first three sets many arhats, nonreturners, and stream-enterers[89] appeared. These first three periods are known, therefore, as the period of the arhat, the period of the nonreturner, and the period of the stream-enterer respectively. Collectively they will be known as the three periods of realization. In the following three sets of five hundred years, many beings endowed with special insight, meditative concentration, and morality appeared. These three periods are known individually as the periods of special insight and so forth and collectively as the three periods of practice. In the next three sets of five hundred years many teachers of Abhidharma, Sutra, and Vinaya will appear. Individually these periods will be known as the periods of Abhidharma and so forth. Collectively they will be called the three periods of transmission. In the last five hundred years there will be no pure views or practice and only the outward signs of monasticism will be adhered to. This period will be known, therefore, as the period of adherence to mere signs.

d.div: [89] Arhats are freed from samsara, nonreturners will not take birth again in samsara, stream-enterers have entered the ārya paths.

f.d: de yang ston pa mya ngan las 'das nas rtags tsam yang 'dzin pa rdzogs pa yan chad kyi lo lnga stong yin te 'di yang pha rol tu phyin pa'i theg pa'i bstan pa'i gnas tshad yin gyi rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa'i gnas tshad kyi dbang du byas pa ma yin no/ /

These are the five thousand years from the passing of the Buddha until the completion of the period of adherence to mere signs. This is the duration of the Perfection Vehicle teachings. However, this is not duration of the teachings based upon the Vajra Vehicle.
phar phyin theg pa la sngags kyi thun mong ma yin pa'i lam gyi rnam gzhag med pa bzhin du phar phyin theg pa'i sde snod du rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa'i gnas tshad 'ong don med do/ /
As there is no presentation of the special path of mantra within the canon of the Perfection Vehicle, /28/ there is no reason for it to state the duration of the teachings of the Vajra Vehicle.

de ltar na rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa'i gnas tshad ni dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud 'grel pa dang bcas pa las dngos su gsungs pa ltar yin te/ de yang ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs shing mya ngan las 'das pa'i lo nas rigs ldan drag pos kla klo thog mar bcom pa'i bar la gong du bshad zin pa ltar gyi rgyal ba shAkya thub pa nyid kyi sngags kyi bstan pa'i dus bzhi'i lo grangs sum stong sum brgya dang bzhi'i steng du rigs ldan drag po'i gling 'di'i dus bzhi'i lo grangs stong brgyad brgya bsnan pas lo lnga stong dang brgya dang bzhi 'ong ngo / /

Therefore, the duration of the teachings of the Vajra Vehicle is as taught in the Kālacakra Tantra and its commentaries. The four ages of Śākyamuni’s mantra teachings begin from the time of his teaching the Root Tantra and his passing until the time Kalkī Rudracakrī first defeats the barbarians. This has been explained as totaling 3,304 years. To this is added the four ages that make up the eighteen hundred years of Rudracakrī’s restoration in Greater Jambudvīpa. This comes to 5,104 years.

de ltar na 'dir bshad pa'i bstan pa'i gnas tshad dang mdo nas bshad pa'i gnas tshad la lo brgya tsam gyi khyad par byung yang skyon yod pa ma yin te/ phar phyin theg pa dang rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa'i gnas tshad mdo sngags so so nas bshad pa'i rnam gzhag so so ba yin pa'i phyir te/ dpal dus kyi 'khor lo rtsa 'grel las byang gi sgra mi snyan du yang bstan pa'i dus bzhi snga phyi gnyis rim can du 'byung bar bshad cing / phar phyin theg pa'i mdo sde rnams las sgra mi snyan pa rgyal ba'i bstan pa'i snod du mi rung bar bshad pas so/ /

Therefore, the duration as explained here and the duration as explained in the sutras differ by about a hundred years. This, however, is no error because the duration of the Perfection Vehicle teachings and of the Vajra Vehicle teachings are separate presentations from separate canons. For example, in the glorious Kālacakra and its commentaries, it is explained that in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, both sets of the four ages of the teachings will arise after each other, whereas in the Perfection Vehicle canon it is stated that the beings of Uttarakuru are unsuitable vessels for the Conqueror’s teachings.

'o na bstan pa'i gnas tshad de dag gi steng nas sngar ji tsam zhig 'das shing da ji tsam zhig lus snyam na/ snga ma rnams kyis ston pa mya ngan las 'das nas mdzes byed chu mo yos 'di yan chad la lo sum stong drug brgya dang bco lnga 'gro ba'i tshul bkod pa sogs mi 'dra ba du ma byung yang dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsa 'grel gzhir bzhag na ston pa mya ngan las 'das nas rgyal po zla bzang 'das kyi bar lo bzhi/

How much time has already passed and how much remains? Those of the past would have calculated, to quote one set of figures, that from the time of the Buddha’s passing to this śobhana female Water Rabbit year,[90] 3,615 years have passed. Many differing calculations exist. Using the Śrī Kālacakra Tantra and commentaries as a basis, four years elapsed from the time of the Buddha’s passing until the passing of King Sucandra.

d.div: [90] 1483/4, the year in which the author was writing.

f.d: de nas 'jam dpal grags pa gshegs kyi bar lo bdun brgya/ de rjes pad dkar nas kla klo zhugs kyi bar lo brgyad brgya/ de nas lo me mkha' rgya mtsho ste ston pa mya ngan las 'das nas rtsis lo nyis brgya nyer gcig gi mtha' yan chad la lo stong dgu brgya dang bdun 'das pa ni rgyud 'grel las mthar chags su gsungs la/

From then until the death of Mañjuśrī Yaśas, seven hundred years passed. After Yaśas came the eight hundred years from Puṇḍarīka to the arrival of the barbarians. Then came the fire, sky, and ocean years. Therefore, from the passing of our teacher up to the last year of the 221 years of astronomy, 1,907 years elapsed. These figures have been sequentially quoted in the Tantra and commentaries.

de'i steng tu paN chen shAkya shrI la sogs pa dus 'khor ba'i mkhas pa snga ma rnams kyi+i gsung ngag gcig nas gcig tu brgyud pa las lo mdzes byed chu yos 'di 'das pa yan chad la 'das lo drug cu skor bdun dang lo rkyang sum cu rtsa bdun rnams 'das par mdzad pa bsnan pas nyis stong sum brgya dang re bzhi 'das pa [*] yin pas phar phyin theg pa'i bstan pa'i dbang du byas na ting nge 'dzin gyi le'u'i dus las lo sum brgya re bzhi 'das shing lhag ma lo nyis stong drug brgya dang so drug lus so/ /

To this total is added the number of years of the teachings of past Kālacakra masters, such as Paṇḍita Śākyaśrī up to the end of this śobhana Water Rabbit year. This comes to seven sixty-year cycles and thirty-seven years.[91] As a total this comes to 2,364 years. Therefore, according to the Perfection Vehicle, /29/ 364 years of the period of meditative concentration have passed, and 2,636 years of the teachings remain.

d.div: [*] de nas da lta'i me bya 'di rdzogs pa'i sa khyi 'di yan la lo brgya dang bdun cu don bzhi song /

f.d: rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa'i dbang du byas na dus bzhi snga ma'i steng nas rdzogs ldan dang gsum ldan 'das shing gnyis ldan gyi steng nas lo bdun brgya dang bcu gnyis 'das la brgya dang bcu bzhi lus/ rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa spyi'i gnas tshad las lo nyis stong bdun brgya dang bzhi bcu lus so/ /
According to the general duration of the teachings of the Vajra Vehicle, 2,740 years are still to pass.

gzhan yang da ltar gyi lo mdzes byed chu mo yos 'di yan chad la rigs ldan gyi rgyal po mtha' yas yan gyi bco lnga 'das nas bcu drug pa rigs ldan sa skyong gis chos bstan nas lo nga bdun song zhing chu yos 'di 'das pa'i rjes nas lo dgu brgya dang bzhi bcu 'das pa'i 'tshams der rigs ldan drag po 'khor lo can 'byung zhing rgyal ba shAkya seng+ge'i rdo rje theg pa'i bstan pa dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i lung rtogs la sogs pa rdzogs ldan du 'byung bar 'gyur ro/ /

Moreover, up until this śobhana Female Water Rabbit year, fifteen Kalkīs up to King Ananta have passed, and since Kalkī Mahīpala began teaching the dharma, fifty-seven years will have passed by the end of the year. Nine hundred and forty years from the end of this Water Rabbit year, Kalkī Rudracakrī will appear, and the Vajra Vehicle teachings of the conquering lion of the Śākya, such as the transmission and practice of the Śrī Kālacakra, will enter the age of completeness.
de ltar na ston pas rtsa rgyud gsungs tshul la sogs pa bshad pa'i gling bslang ba bshad zin to/ /
The introduction on how the Buddha taught the Root Tantra and so forth is complete.
bla med rgyud kyi brjod bya'i gtso bo gnyug ma'i sems dang lus bshad pa/
2. The Primordial Mind and Body
gnyis pa bla med kyi rgyud kun gyi brjod bya'i gtso bo gnyug ma'i rang bzhin bshad pa

d.i: The tantras and Indian scripture: Sources for primordial mind

f.d:
ye shes le'u las/
sems can rnams ni sangs rgyas yin te sangs rgyas chen po gzhan 'dir 'jig rten khams na yod ma yin/[62] / zhes dang / dbang le'i 'grel chen las/
'dir sems can thams cad kyi snying gi nang na gnas pa ni ye shes so/ / de yang gzhom du med pa'i sgra ste rtag tu na de'i mtshan nyid do/[63] / zhes dang /

The Great Commentary, in the Gnosis chapter, says:
Sentient beings are buddhas. Mighty buddhas other than that are not found in the world.[92] In the Initiation chapter of the Great Commentary:
That which abides in the hearts of sentient beings is gnosis. It is the indestructible sound, constantly in the character of the nāda.[93] /30/

[93] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 298a6. In the stacked arrangement of the ten-syllable mantra of Kālacakra, the nāda is the squiggle at the very top.

f.d:
nang le'i mdor bsdus dang po las/
stong pa la ni ye shes rnam par bsres pa zhes pa ni 'dir lus la khyab par bya ba dang khyab par byed pa'i 'brel pa kun rdzob kyi nges par gnas pa sems can thams cad kyi rang gi lus la gnas pa'i ye shes gang yin pa de nyid ni stong pa ste [64] zhes dang /

The Great Commentary in the first summary on the Inner chapter says:
“Gnosis is mixed with emptiness.” That which dwells conventionally in the body in the form of a relationship between that which is pervaded and that which pervades is gnosis dwelling in the bodies of all sentient beings as emptiness.[94]

d.div: [64] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 118_na6_'gyur cung mi mthun/
[94] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 118a6. The passage as quoted here varies somewhat from the Vimalaprabhā passage. Emptiness refers to empty form.

de bzhin du brtag gnyis las/
lus la ye shes chen po gnas/[65] / zhes dang / yang de nyid las/
sems can rnams ni sangs rgyas nyid/ / 'on kyang glo bur dri mas bsgribs/ / de nyid bsal na sangs rgyas nyid/[66] / ces dang /

Similarly in the Hevajra Tantra:
The great gnosis abides in the body.[95] Also:
Sentient beings are buddhas but are obscured by transient impurity. Once removed, there will be buddha.[96]

de'i rdo rje snying 'grel las/
gzod nas sems can thams cad lhan cig skyes pa'i rang bzhin yin pa'i phyir sangs rgyas so/[67] / zhes dang

From the Vajragarbha Commentary:
Since, from the beginning, all sentient beings are of the nature of the innate, they are buddhas.[97]

f.d:
de bzhin du do ha las kyang /
gnyug ma'i rang bzhin byis pas ma mthong bar/ / 'khrul pas byis pa bslus zhes mnga' bsnun smra/[68] / zhes sogs ji snyed pa dag go/

Similarly from the Treasury of Songs:
Not seeing the primordial nature, the foolish are deluded, the foolish are deceived; thus speaks Saraha.[98] There are many other such quotes.

d.div: [68] sde dge_2224_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_sa ra ha'i do ha mdzod kyi glu/ 71_ba3_'gyur cung mi mthun/
[98] Toh 2224 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, wi, 71b3.

f.d: gnyis pa de dag gi don cung zad bshad pa ni/

d.i: A short explanation of the content of these passages

f.d: de yang gnyug ma'i sems 'di rgyud 'grel dang rgya gzhung 'di dag nas bshad pa'i bskyed rdzogs kyi sbyang gzhi mthar thug pa yin la/ 'di'i don 'chad pa la drug/ gnyug ma'i sems kyi ngo bo ngos bzung ba dang / ming gi rnam grangs dang / rang bzhin gyis dag tshul dang / dri ma rnams glo bur ba yin tshul dang / de lam gyis sbyong tshul dang / de mngon du byed pa'i dus so/ /

This primordial mind is the ultimate basis of purification for the generation stage and completion stage taught by these tantras, their commentaries, and other Indian scriptures. Its explanation is under six headings: 1. Identifying primordial mind 2. Synonyms 3. Its natural purity 4. The transience of the impurities 5. Its path of practice 6. Times when clear light manifests
dang po [gnyug ma'i sems kyi ngo bo ngos bzung ba] ni

shin tu phra ba'i sems te/ rang nyid mngon du 'gyur ba'i tshe spros pa'i mtha' thams cad dang bral ba stong nyid mngon sum du rtogs pa lta bu'i yul snang can/ sangs rgyas kyi yon tan thams cad skyed pa'i nus pa dang ldan pa/ sems can thams cad kyi rgyud la thog ma med pa nas skad cig kyang rgyun mi chad [69] du rjes su zhugs pa/ rang gi ngo bo dri mas dag pa na chos kyi skur 'gyur ba'o/ / 'di yang phyogs tsam mtshon pa yin gyi 'di'i gnas tshul ji lta ba ni mngon du byas pa rnams kyis kyang rjod par mi spyod na gzhan dag gis lta ci smos te/ de ltar yang do ha mdzod kyi glu las/
gnyug ma'i rang bzhin sus kyang mtshon du med/[70] / ces dang / yang de nyid las/
gnyug ma'i rang bzhin tshig gis brjod min yang / / slob dpon man ngag mig gis mthong bar 'gyur/[71] / zhes dang /

The primordial mind is a very subtle mind, and when manifest, it takes as its objects phenomena such as the complete absence of any limiting conceptual elaboration,[99] the direct cognition of emptiness. It has the ability to create every quality of a buddha, and it has dwelt in the continuum of every sentient being since beginningless time without interruption. When it is purified it becomes the dharmakāya. However this is just a partial description. When even those who have actualized the primordial mind cannot describe it in words, what need to mention those who have not. In the Treasury of Songs it says:
The nature of the primordial cannot be shown by anyone.[100] Also:
The nature of the primordial cannot be expressed in words, /31/ but with the eyes of the master’s teachings it will be seen.[101]

d.div: [69] ma dper 'chad ces gsal/
[70] sde dge_2224_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_sa ra ha'i do ha mdzod kyi glu/ 72_ba1
[71] sde dge_2224_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_sa ra ha'i do ta mdzod kyi glu/ 72_ba2

div.i: spros pa’i mtha’ dang bral ba.

d.div: [100] Toh 2224 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, wi, 72b1.
[101] Toh 2224 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, wi, 72b2.

f.d:
do ha'i 'grel pa gnyis med rdo rjes mdzad par lung drangs pa las/
'gro ba rnams la rtag 'chang rgyu rkyen bral gyur pa/ / gang zhig gis ni de nyid rjod pa'i dus dag na/ / thams cad mkhyen pa dag kyang tshig gis phongs par gyur/[72] / zhes sogs mang du gsungs so/ /

Advayavajra in his Commentary to the Treasury of Songs says:
That which dwells in sentient beings forever, without cause and condition, when the time came for it to be spoken of, even the omniscient would be lost for words.[102] There are many such quotes.

d.div: [72] sde dge_2256_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_gnyis med rnam rgyal gyi do ha mdzod kyi glu'i dka' 'grel/ 191_ba3
[102] Toh 2256 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, wi, 191b3.

f.d: gnyis pa ming gi rnam grangs ni

rang bzhin lhan skyes dang / 'od gsal gyi sems dang / chos kyi dbyings kyi sems dang / rang bzhin 'od gsal dang / gnyug ma'i sems dang / mi shigs pa'i sems dang / gzhi'i chos sku dang / sems kyi rdo rje zhes sogs rnam grangs du ma'i sgo nas rgyud dang rgya gzhung rnams las bsnyad do/ /

It is taught in the tantras and Indian texts under many names. These include, the innate, the mind of clear light, the dharmadhātu mind, natural clear light, primordial mind, the indestructible mind, foundation dharmakāya, and the vajra of the mind.
gsum pa rang bzhin gyis dag tshul
['di ]la gnyis te/ rkyen gzhan gyis bzang ngan du mi 'gyur ba dang / rang gi ngo bo dri ma'i rang bzhin du ma skyes pa'o/ /
This is under two headings:
dang po [rkyen gzhan gyis bzang ngan du mi 'gyur ba] ni
1. It does not become good or bad by the force of circumstance.

dper na nyi ma'i 'od zer ni rin po che la sogs pa dngos po bzang po dang mi gtsang ba la sogs pa'i dngos po ngan pa rnams la yang khyab byed du 'bab kyang de dag gi rkyen gis bzang ngan du mi 'gyur ba ltar 'od gsal gyi sems shin tu phra ba yang lha la sogs pa'i skye gnas bzang po dang dmyal ba la sogs pa'i skye gnas ngan pa rnams su 'jug mod kyang de dag gi dbang gis bzang ngan du 'gyur ba med de/ nyi ma'i 'od zer ltar rang bzhin gyis rnam par dag pa'i phyir ro/ /

The rays of the sun spread themselves equally upon the beautiful, such as jewels, and upon the ugly, such as filth, and yet it remains unaffected, either adversely or beneficially. Likewise, the mind of clear light is very subtle, and though it enters good states of existence such as those of the gods or bad such as those of hell, it remains unaffected by them, either adversely or beneficially. This is because, like the sun, it is pure by nature.
gnyis pa rang gi ngo bo dri ma'i rang bzhin du ma skyes pa ni
2. As an entity it never develops into the impurities of the mind.

gser g.ya' dang bcas pa'i gnas skabs na yang g.ya'i ngo bor ma skyes la/ chu rnyog ma dang bcas pa'i gnas skabs na yang rnyog ma'i ngo bor ma skyes pa ltar 'od gsal gyi sems shin tu phra ba yang nyon mongs dang rnam rtog sogs kyi dri ma dang bcas pa'i gnas skabs na yang nyon mongs dang rnam rtog sogs dri ma'i ngo bor ma skyes pa yin te/ de las gzhan du na 'od gsal gyi sems de la nyon mongs dang rnam rtog gnyen pos sbyang du mi rung ba'am/ yang na nyon mongs sogs kyi dri ma rnams spangs pa'i tshe 'od gsal gyi sems kyang rgyun chad par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / de nyid kyi phyir na 'od gsal gyi sems ni rang bzhin gyis rnam par dag pa yin no/ /

Gold even when tarnished never becomes the tarnish. Water when dirtied never becomes the dirt. Likewise, the mind of clear light is very subtle, yet when dwelling with the impurities of deluded states of mind, conceptuality, and so forth, it never develops into the actual entities of these states of mind. If it did, it would not be possible to eradicate, with appropriate opponent forces, the conceptuality and deluded states of mind within the clear-light mind. Alternatively, if these impurities were eradicated, the continuum of the clear-light mind would also come to an end. The mind of clear light therefore is pure by nature. /32/
bzhi pa dri ma rnams glo bur ba yin tshul ni/

dper na chu dang rnyog ma lhan cig tu byung ba'i tshe'ang chu ni rang gi nyer len las shin tu dwangs pa'i ngo bor skyes la/ rnyog ma ni chu'i nye bar len pa las gzhan sa rdul la sogs pa'i rkyen las byung bas chu'i ngo bo las 'bral du rung zhing glo bur ba yin pa de bzhin du 'od gsal gyi sems dang sgrib gnyis kyi dri ma rnams thog ma med pa'i dus nas lhan cig tu grub kyang 'od gsal gyi sems ni rang gi rigs 'dra snga ma'i nyer len las rnam par dag pa'i ngo bor skyes la/ dri ma rnams ni 'od gsal las chu las nya ldang ba'i tshul gyis tshul bzhin ma yin pa yid la byed pa'i rkyen las byung bas rang bzhin 'od gsal gyi sems las 'bral rung gi glo bur ba yin no/ /

In a mixture of water and dirt, the water has been created from its own substantial cause into its own clear and transparent nature, and its dirtiness has come about from its own causes, such as dust and so forth, which are distinct from the water’s substantial cause. The dirt therefore can be separated from the water and is a temporary phenomenon. Similarly, the mind of clear light and the impurities of the two kinds of obscuration have been linked since time without beginning. Nevertheless, the mind of clear light is developed from its own substantial similar-type cause into its own entity of purity. The impurities, on the other hand, develop from their causes of improper mental activity and arise from the clear-light mind like fish jumping from water. They are therefore temporary phenomena, capable of being removed from a mind whose nature is clear light.

de yang chu ni sa rdul gyi rkyen dang ma 'brel na shin tu dngas pa'i ngo bor dmigs pa bzhin du rang bzhin 'od gsal gyi sems kyang dri ma rnams 'byung ba'i rgyu rkyen dang ma 'brel na gnyis snang gi spros pas dben pa'i gsal la dwangs pa'i rnam pa can du skye ba yin no/ / de lta na yang 'od gsal gyi sems de tshul min yid byed la sogs pa'i rkyen gyis chags sogs dri ma rnams dang lhan cig tu 'byung ba'i tshe yod bzhin du byis pa rnams la mngon du mi 'gyur pa ni chags sogs kyi dri mas bsgribs nas mi mthong ba yin no/ /

Furthermore, when water is not in contact with conditions such as dirt and dust, it is clear and transparent. Similarly, if the natural mind of clear light were separated from the causes and conditions that bring about the impurities, it would reveal its clarity in its separation from the entanglements of duality. As long as the mind of clear light dwells with impurities, such as desire generated by improper mental activity, it will not become manifest to ordinary beings even though it is everpresent. This is because it is obscured by these impurities and remains unseen.
lnga pa de lam gyis sbyong tshul ni/

dang po gzugs sgrub kyi yan lag sor bsam gnyis kyis rtsa dbu ma sbyang zhing stong gzugs kyi snang ba bsgrubs te de nas srog sgrub kyi yan lag srog 'dzin gnyis kyis ro rkyang gi rlung dbu mar thim pa las byung ba'i 'od gsal gyi sems mngon du byas pa'i sgo nas sems de'i rang snang gi stong gzugs je dag tu byas te yas babs mas brten gyi dga' ba bzhi drangs pa'i sgo nas 'od gsal gyi sems de lhan skyes kyi bde ba'i ngo bor song ba stong nyid dang sbyor ba'i ye shes bskyed par bya'o/ /

Firstly, the central channel is purified and empty forms appear to the meditator. These forms are created by the practices of the yogas of withdrawal and meditative absorption which make up the branch of form accomplishment. Then the winds from the left and right channels are brought into the central channel by the yogas of prāṇāyāma and retention, which make up the branch of wind accomplishment. This manifests the mind of clear light, and the appearance of that mind as empty form becomes progressively purer. The generation of the four joys of descent and ascent develops the mind of clear light into innate bliss, which is applied to emptiness, and the gnosis of bliss and emptiness is developed.

de ltar 'dzin pa'i yan lag mthar thug pa'i rjes su yab yum zhal sbyor gyi rnam pa can gyi stong gzugs dngos gnas la grub pa'i rjes dran bsgrubs te de 'dra ba'i rjes dran gyi gnas skabs su yang 'od gsal gyi sems bde ba'i ngo bor skyes pa de nyid stong pa nyid dang yul yul can du sbyar ba'i bde stong gi ye shes lan mang du bsgom/ de ltar bsgoms pas stong gzugs phyag rgya chen mo nyid la brten nas mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba 'dren nus pa'i 'tshams nas 'od gsal gyi sems de nyid ting nge 'dzin gyi yan lag gi 'gyur ba'i bde ba nyi khri chig stong drug brgya'i ngo bor song ba'i mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba rnams stong pa nyid dang sbyor ba'i bde stong gi ye shes bsgoms pa las sa bcu gnyis rim gyis rdzogs te las rlung nyi khri chig stong drug brgya rim gyis 'gags/ 'pho ba'i bag chags sogs dri ma rnams rim gyis bsal te 'od gsal gyi sems mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba'i ngo bor skyes pa de bde ba chen po'i skur 'gyur ba yin no/ /

After the completion of the yoga of retention comes the yoga of recollection, in which an actual empty form in the aspect of father-mother union is meditated upon. Also, during recollection, the mind of clear light develops into bliss and, as a consciousness, is applied to its object of emptiness. /33/ The resulting bliss-and-emptiness gnosis is meditated upon many times, which will eventually produce the mahāmudrā consort. Reliance on this consort will develop the ability to induce unchanging bliss. From that point onward the clear-light mind develops into the 21,600 instances of unchanging bliss on the yoga of meditative concentration. This unchanging bliss is applied to emptiness, and the resulting bliss-and-emptiness gnosis is meditated upon. One by one the twelve levels are attained, and the 21,600 karmic winds are halted. Impurities, such as the predispositions for emission,[103] are gradually eradicated, and the mind of clear light in the form of unchanging bliss becomes the body of great bliss.

d.div: [103] The author points out later that in the Kālacakra tantra, one of the main causes of samsara is the loss of semen. Therefore eradication of the predispositions for loss of semen is a particular goal of Kālacakra.

f.d: drug pa de mngon du byed pa'i dus ni
['di la ]gnyis te/ 'bad med lhun grub kyi tshul gyis mngon du byed pa dang / ting nge 'dzin gyi stobs kyis mngon du byed pa'i tshul lo/ /
There are two kinds of manifestation: natural or effortless manifestation and manifestation through the power of meditative concentration.
dang po ni
The first [natural or effortless manifestation]

lus can rnams 'chi ba'i tshe ste/ de yang dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud 'grel ba dang bcas pa'i dgongs pa gzhir bzhag na khams drug ldan gyi mi lta bu 'chi ba'i tshe thog mar chu'i khams kyis me'i khams nyams par byed cing / de nas sa'i khams kyang chu la zhugs te mi snang bar 'gyur la/ de nas chu'i khams kyang rlung gis skem par byed/ de nas rlung yang nam mkha' la rim gyis thim ste mi snang bar gyur pa de'i tshe rtsa dbu ma'i mdud pa rang grol byas nas ro rkyang gi rlung gi rgyu ba 'gags te rlung dbu mar zhugs shing thim pa na glo bur yul snang gi rtog pa ma lus par 'gags pas rang bzhin 'od gsal gyi sems spros pa'i mtha' thams cad dang bral ba stong pa nam mkha' lta bu'i rnam pa can la pra bab pa lta bu'i stong gzugs sna tshogs kyi snang ba rang gi ngang gis 'char zhing 'di la 'chi ba 'od gsal mngon du byas pa zhes zer ro/ /

occurs when sentient beings die. On the basis of the Kālacakratantra and its commentaries, when someone possessed of the six elements dies, first the water element weakens the fire element, then the earth element enters the water and disappears. The water element is subsequently dried by the air element, which in turn absorbs into the space element and disappears. At this time the knots of the central channel loosen, the flow of wind in the right and left channels is halted, and wind enters and dissolves into the central channel. When this happens, all conceptualization of transient objects ceases. The natural clear-light mind becomes separated from all limiting conceptual elaboration and takes on the aspect of a spacelike emptiness. Within that emptiness various empty forms arise of their own volition like images in a clairvoyant’s mirror. This is known as the manifestation-of-death clear light.

de ltar yang sgrub thabs gyi le'u'i/ chu yis me ni rnam par nyams zhes sogs kyi 'grel chen las/
chu yis zhes pa la sogs pa ste mi'i 'jig rten 'dir mngal nas skyes pa rnams 'chi ba'i dus su chu yis me rnam par nyams par byed do/ / de'i phyir ting nge 'dzin de nyid kyis chu yis me ni rnam par nyams pa dang por 'dir ni lus kyi dbus su sdom brtson rnams kyis bya/ phyi nas mi med pa'i phyir 'dzin ma dag ni sra ba nyid spangs te lan tshwa bzhin du zhu bar gyur nas chur 'gyur te chu'i dbus su rab tu zhugs so/ / de nas rlung ni chu de rnams mtha' dag bskams nas nam mkha' la mi snang bar 'gyur ro/ / de ltar khams kyi tshogs myur du rnam par nyams byed nas sems ni mun pa'i mtha' yi me ste zhes pa nam mkha'i khams rnam pa thams cad pa'i gzugs yul dang rnam par bral ba dbus byis la kun gzhi rnam par shes pa gzhag par bya'o/[73] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Great Commentary, commenting in the Methods of Accomplishment chapter on the line beginning “Water weakens fire,” says:
“Water” and so forth means that in this human realm, at the time of death of those born from wombs, water weakens fire. Therefore, through the power of this meditative concentration, the process of fire is weakened by water, and this is the meditator’s first practice within the body. Then, because of there being no fire, earth loses its solidity and dissolves like salt to become liquid, dwelling within the water element. Then the element of air /34/ dries up every drop of water and disappears into space. In this way the elements quickly weaken. Then “the mind is the fire at the end of darkness,”[104] which means that the foundation consciousness is placed in the realm of space, in fully aspected forms empty of all objects, dwelling in the middle.[105]

d.div: [73] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 203_ba1

[104] As this passage is reproduced in the Great Commentary, it would appear to say that the mind is the fire at the end of darkness, with “fire” referring to the death clear light or foundation consciousness. Gyaltsap Darma Rinchen, however, in his Abbreviated Explanation of The Six Branched Yoga of Kālacakra, comments on this process using the relevant text from the Condensed Tantra, which speaks of the mind coming after the fire and the darkness, referring to the two appearances of light and darkness that arise just before the death clear light dawns.
[105] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 203b1.

f.d: de'i kun gzhi rnam shes zhes pa 'od gsal gyi sems dang / sems ni mun pa'i mtha' yi me ste zhes pa'i mun pa 'chi ba'i dus kyi nyer thob dang / me ni nyer thob de las byung ba'i 'chi ba'i 'od gsal lo/ / 'chi ba'i 'od gsal de tha mal pa rnams kyis nyams su myong yang nges par mi nus pas de las rigs drug gang yang rung ba'i bar do grub nas yang srid du rang dbang med par 'khor ba yin la/ gson po'i gnas skabs su rdzogs pa'i rim pa bsgoms te 'od gsal gyi sems mngon du byed nus pa'i rnal 'byor pas ni 'chi ba'i 'od gsal nges par byed pa'i 'phen pa drag po btang nas 'chi+i ba'i 'od gsal nges par byed cing de ltar nges pa'i tshe 'od gsal gyi sems de stong nyid dang sbyar nas bde stong gi ye shes sgom par byed/ de bzhin du bar do grub pa'i tshe'ang bsgom par byas pa'i sgo nas skye ba phyi ma rnams su yang sngags sgrub pa'i rten khyad par can bzung nas lam gyi 'phro rnams nyams su blangs te 'tshang rgya bar byed do/ /

Foundation consciousness in this quote refers to the mind of clear light, and in the line “The mind is the fire at the end of darkness,” darkness is the near attainment at the time of death, while fire is the death clear light, which arises from near attainment. This death clear light is experienced by ordinary beings but cannot be ascertained by them. Therefore, once the bardo state of one of the six kinds of existence has been formed, ordinary beings will move on powerlessly to another existence. However the yogi meditating on the completion stage during his lifetime develops the ability to manifest the mind of clear light and sets a powerful intention[106] for the ascertainment of death clear light. When he actually ascertains death clear light, he applies the clear light to emptiness and meditates on bliss and emptiness gnosis. Likewise, when the bardo existence arrives, the power of his meditation will ensure that he takes a special form of existence in his next life for the practice of tantra where the remainder of the path will be practiced and enlightenment realized.

d.div: [106] ’phen pa. To cast, throw, project.

f.d: 'on kyang sems 'grel skor gsum gzhir bzhag la bar dor 'tshang rgya ba'i rnam gzhag mi mdzad do/ / de'i rgyu mtshan ni bar dor 'tshang rgya zhes pa'i don ni 'chi ba'i 'od gsal de sems dben mthar thug pa'i 'od gsal gyi lam de'i dod thub pa'i lam gyi ngo bor bskyed nas 'od gsal de'i bzhon pa'i rlung shin tu phra ba de las bar dor ldang ba'i 'od la sgyu lus su bzhengs te rten de la lam lhag ma rnams nyams su blangs nas 'tshang rgya ba yin la/ sems 'grel skor gsum las ni de lta bu'i lam gyi bgrod tshul gyi rnam gzhag mi mdzad par sbyor ba yan lag drug gi mnyam gzhag gi gnas skabs su shar ba'i stong gzugs nyid sangs rgyas pa'i dus kyi stong gzugs yab yum zhal sbyor gyi rnam pa can gyi rigs 'dra'i rgyur bzhed cing / gzugs sku'i bsgrub gzhi gzhi la yod bzhin pa zhig la mi mdzad pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis yin gyi/ mkhas pa (ku mA ra ma ti )kha cig mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba 'byung ba la lus rags pa dgos kyi bar dor yid kyi lus la mchog tu mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba sgrub par mi nus pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis dus 'khor rtsa 'grel gyi bzhed pa la bar dor 'tshang rgya ba'i rnam gzhag med pa yin no [74] zhes gsungs pa 'di ni mi 'thad de/ de ltar yin na bar dor 'tshang rgya ba'i rnam gzhag bzhed pa dpal gsang ba 'dus pa sogs la'ang mtshungs pa'i phyir ro/ /

However, in the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries, there is no presentation of attaining enlightenment during bardo existence. There is a reason for this. Attaining enlightenment in the bardo means that death clear light is transformed into the path of the ultimate-mind isolation clear light. The clear-light mind rides upon the very subtle wind, from which arises the illusory body instead of the bardo existence. The remainder of the path is practiced in that form, and enlightenment is attained. The Three Bodhisattva Commentaries do not present such a path but assert that the empty form that appears during the meditative equipoise of the six-branched yoga is a similar-type cause of the empty-form father-and-mother union of enlightenment, and there is no basis for the accomplishment of the form body existing in the ordinary state. This is the reason why there is no such presentation. However some scholars (such as Kumāramati)[107] /35/ say that the reason there is no presentation of attaining buddhahood in the bardo within the tenets of the Kālacakratantra and its commentaries is that a coarse body is necessary for the development of unchanging bliss and, therefore, supreme unchanging bliss cannot be accomplished in the bardo mental body.[108] This is not correct. If that were the case, then similar consequences could be applied to the Guhyasamāja and other tantras that do assert the attaining of enlightenment in the bardo.

d.div: [74] 'dir mkhas pa kha cig ces pa yig chung du ku mA ra ma tir ngos 'dzin mdzad pa rje red mda' ba la go dgos shing / 'dir de'i gsung dus 'khor nges don gsal byed sgron me zhes pa zhig bzhugs pa der zhal 'phangs mdzad par mngon te gzhung 'di cha tshang ba si khron mi rigs dpe skrun khang nas dpar du btab pa'i bod kyi rtsis rig kun 'dus chen mo deb dang po skar nag rtsis kyi lo rgyus skor zhes pa shog grangs 383_nas 428_bar bzhugs shing / de'i shog grangs 395_phreng 13_la gzigs/
[107] Sanskritized form of Shönu Lodrö, or Rendawa.
[108] See Lamp Illuminating the Definitive Kālacakra, pp. 383–428, especially p. 395, line 13.

f.d: gnyis pa ting nge 'dzin gyi stobs kyis mngon du byed pa'i tshul ni/ /

d.i: Manifesting the mind of clear light by the power of meditative concentration

f.d: sor bsam gnyis kyis rlung dbu mar gzhug pa'i thabs kyis dbu ma sbyang / de nas srog rtsol gyi rlung bum pa can dang rdo rje'i bzlas pa sogs kyis ro rkyang gi rlung gi rgyu ba bcad de dbu mar zhugs par byas pa las 'od gsal gyi sems mngon du byed pa lta bu ste/ rdo rje lus kyi rtsa thig rlung gsum la gnad du bsnun pa las kun rtog gi bzhon pa'i rlung ro rkyang gi rgyu ba bcad nas rtsa dbu mar thim pa las 'od gsal gyi sems mngon du 'gyur ba yin no/ /

Withdrawal and meditative absorption are the methods by which the winds enter the central channel to purify it, while vase yoga and the vajra recitation in the branch of prāṇāyāma cause the flow of the winds in the right and left channels to be cut and so enter the central channel, where the mind of clear light is made manifest. Such a process of manifesting clear light arises from cutting the flow of the winds, or mounts of conceptuality, of the left and right channel by targeting the channels, drops, and winds of the vajra body and bringing those winds into the central channel.

de ltar yang khams le'i mdor bsdus dang po las/
ji ltar me ni shing la rtag gnas kyang / / gcad dang dbye ba'i thabs kyis mi mthong ste/ / gtsub shing gtsub stan lag pas bsrubs pa las/ / de la gnas pa yang ni mthong bar 'gyur/ / de bzhin sems kyi 'od gsal rtog pa yi/ / sgom pa'i thabs rnams dag gis mi mthong ste/ / de nyid du 'di rkyang ma dag dang ni/ / ro ma gcig tu sbyor bas mthong bar 'gyur/[75] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Great Commentary, in the Realms chapter, in the first summary says:
Although fire dwells constantly within wood, by cutting and separation it is not seen. Yet, when the fire-stick is worked with the hands, it is seen to dwell within. Similarly, by habitual conceptuality, the mind of clear light is not seen. But when the right and left channel are united as one, it will be manifest.[109]

d.div: [75] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 4_ba7
[109] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 4b7.

f.d: mdor na ji srid glo bur ba'i yul snang can gyi sems ma 'gags pa de srid du 'od gsal gyi sems mngon du byed mi nus la/ /glo bur ba'i yul snang can gyi sems 'gag pa la rlung d+hU tIr tshud dgos te/ ji srid ro rkyang gnyis su rlung rgyu ba de srid du glo bur ba'i yul snang can gyi sems 'gag pa mi srid pa'i phyir ro/ /

As long as the mind to which objects of a transient nature appear is not halted, it is not possible to manifest the mind of clear light. To halt such a mind, the winds must enter the dhūtī,[110] and as long as the winds flow within the left and right channel, it is not possible to halt such a mind.

d.div: [110] The central channel.

f.d:
'dir (ku mA ra ma ti/ ku mA Shisha)mkhas pa dag /gong du drangs pa'i rgyud 'grel pa dang bcas pa'i bstan don bshad ma thag pa gnyug ma 'od gsal gyi sems de (byams chos lnga'i nang tshan/)rgyud bla ma'i bstan don gyi de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po dri bcas de bzhin nyid dang don gcig cing / chos dbyings bstod pa dang rgyud bla'i bstan don gyi+i bde gshegs snying po de nyid/
rgyud ni rgyun zhes bya bar grags/ / rgyun de rnam pa gsum 'gyur te/ / gzhi dang de bzhin rang bzhin dang / / mi 'phrogs pa yis rab phye ba/[76] / zhes pa'i 'dus pa phyi ma'i rgyud tshig 'dis bstan pa'i rgyu'i rgyud yin zhes gsung ngo / /[77]

Some (such as Kumāramati and Kumāraśrī)[111] have said that the primordial mind of clear light that is the subject of the previous quotes from the tantras and commentaries is identical to the buddha essence, or impure suchness, as taught in the Uttaratantra, one of the five treatises of the protector Maitreya. They also claim that this buddha essence taught in the Uttaratantra and in the In Praise of Dharmadhātu is the causal tantra taught by the Later Guhyasamāja Tantra when it says:
Tantra it is known means continuum, and that continuum is of three kinds. /36/ The basis, the nature of suchness, and the invincible: is it thus divided.[112]

d.div: [76] sde dge_443_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_gsang 'dus rgyud phyi ma/ le'u/ 18_150_na1
[77] 'dir yig chung du ku mA ra ma ti zhes pa rje red mda' ba yin cing / ku mA ra Shisha zhes pa ni phal cher 'gos lo gzhon nu dpal yin nam snyam/
[111] Sanskritized form of Gö Lotsāwa Shönu Pal.
[112] Toh 443 Kangyur, rgyud, ca, chap. 18, 150a1.

f.d: de ni 'thad par ma mthong ste/ /rgyud bla ma las bstan pa'i nyams su blang bar bya ba'i lam de yang / /gzhi dang de bzhin rang bzhin dang /[78] /zhes pas bstan pa'i thabs rgyud du 'gyur dgos te/ rgyu mtshan mtshungs pas so/ /

Their assertion cannot be seen to be correct because that would mean the path of practice as taught in the Uttaratantra also would have to be the method tantra taught in the line “the basis, that of the nature of suchness” because the reasoning is the same.[113]

d.div: [78] sde dge_443_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_gsang 'dus rgyud phyi ma/ le'u/ 18_150_na2

[113] Jado Rinpoché pointed out that the three kinds of tantra are method tantra, referring to the two stages of generation and completion; causal tantra, referring to emptiness (Abhayākaragupta) or the jewellike disciple (Nāropa); and resultant tantra, referring to enlightenment. These three are indicated in the quote by “basis,” “suchness,” and “the invincible,” respectively.

f.d:
gzhan yang rgyud bla ma nas gsungs pa'i bde gshegs snying po mngon du byed pa la rtsa ro rkyang la rlung rgyu ba 'gags nas dbu mar chud pa cig dgos par 'gyur te/ rgyud 'grel ba dang bcas pa'i bstan don gyi gnyug ma lhan skyes kyi 'od gsal mngon du byed pa la ro rkyang la rgyu ba'i rlung 'gags nas rlung dbu mar chud dgos pa'i phyir te/ khams le'i mdor bsdus dang po las/
de bzhin sems kyi 'od gsal rtog pa yi/ / sgom pa'i thabs rnams dag gis mi mthong ste/ / de nyid du 'di rkyang ma dag dang ni/ / ro ma gcig tu sbyor bas mthong bar 'gyur/[79] / zhes gsungs pas so/ /

Furthermore it would also mean that to manifest buddha essence as taught in the Uttaratantra, it would be necessary to halt the flow of winds in the right and left channel and bring them to the central channel. This is because in order to make manifest the primordial inborn mind of clear light as it is taught in the tantras and commentaries, it is necessary to halt the flow of winds in the left and right channels and to have them enter the central channel. As the Great Commentary says in the Realms chapter, in the first summary:
Similarly, by habitual conceptuality, the mind of clear light is not seen. But when the right and left channel are united as one, it will be manifest.[114]

d.div: [79] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 5_na1
[114] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 5a1.

f.d: yang kha cig (jo mo nang pa rjes 'brangs dang bcas pa/)na re/ bde gshegs snying po mtshan dpes brgyan pa stobs bcu dang mi 'jigs pa la sogs pa bral ba'i yon tan mtha' dag dang ldan pa rtag pa brtan pa ther zug pa don dam par grub pa sems can thams cad kyi rgyud la gdod ma nas yod bzhin pa glo bur ba'i dri ma'i sbubs na gnas pa cig yod pa de rgyud kyi/ mkha' khyab mkha'i rdo rje zhes sogs dang / sems can rnams ni sangs rgyas yin te zhes sogs gong nyid du drangs pa'i rgyud 'grel pa dang bcas pa rnams dang / gos hrul nang na rgyal ba'i sku dang ni/[80] /zhes sogs rgyud bla ma'i gzhung rnams dang / chos dbyings bstod pa dang bcas pa rnams kyi don du 'chad par byed do/ /

Some (such as the Jonang tradition) assert the existence of a buddha essence adorned with the features and signs of enlightenment, endowed with the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, and every other excellent quality of abandonment. They assert this essence to be unchanging and permanent, of ultimate existence, and dwelling inside every sentient being since beginningless time but hidden within the temporary impurities. This they maintain is what is meant by the quotes from the tantra, such as the verses beginning “Pervading space, the vajra of space,” “Sentient beings are buddhas,” and so forth, as well as by the quotes from the commentaries quoted previously. They also maintain that this is the meaning of quotes such as that beginning “A statue of buddha wrapped in rags”[115] from the Uttaratantra and similar quotes from In Praise of Dharmadhātu.

d.div: [80] sde dge_4024_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rgyud bla ma/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka99_58_ba7
[115] Toh 4024 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, chap. 1, v. 99, 58b7.

f.d: gzhan yang bcom ldan 'das kyis chos thams cad bden pas stong par gsungs pa'i sher phyin sogs mdo ji snyed pa dag gis kyang gong du bshad ma thag pa'i bde gshegs snying po de nyid glo bur gyi dri ma gzhan gyis stong pa'i gzhan stong bstan pa yin gyi/ dgag bya'i dri mas stong pa'i bde gshegs snying po nyid bden par grub pas rang stong min no/ /zhes 'chad cing de nyid dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud 'grel pa dang bcas pa'i dgongs pa yang yin no/[81] /zhes zer ro/ /

Furthermore they claim that the Prajñāpāramitā and other sutras in which the Buddha spoke of all phenomena being empty of any true existence are actually teaching an “emptiness of other,” in which the above-mentioned buddha essence is empty of “other” transient impurities. Because this buddha essence is empty of the impurities or objects of negation and because it is truly existing, it is not an “emptiness of self.” They also claim that this is the thinking of the /37/ Kālacakra and its commentaries.[116]
