d.div: [81] 'dir yig chung du jo mo nang pa zhes pa jo nang kun mkhyen dol bu ba shes rab rgyal mtshan la go dgos pas 'dir phal cher dol bu pa'i gzhung ri chos nges don rgya mtsho'i bzhed pa bkod pa snang /
[116] Notes in the critical edition point out that this assertion refers to Dölpopa.

f.d: de la thog mar 'di brjod par bya ste/ khyi rgan rgya bo'i rgyud kyi gnas dang gnas ma yin pa mkhyen pa'i stobs des gnas dang gnas ma yin pa mkhyen nam mi mkhyen brtag drang / gal te mi mkhyen na gnas dang gnas ma yin pa mkhyen pa'i stobs yin pa 'gal/ gal te mkhyen na gnas dang gnas ma yin pa mkhyen pa la sgrib byed kyi dri mas bsgribs pa 'gal lo/ /

To this, firstly I say the following. Of the ten powers, there is the power of the wisdom that knows what is and what is not the basis.[117] Does this power know what is and what is not the basis of a hairy old dog? If it does not know, it could not be a wisdom that knows what is and what is not the basis. If it does know, it could not be a wisdom covered by the obscuring impurities.

d.div: [117] The first of the ten powers of a buddha. It is a wisdom that knows, for example, that from giving comes wealth and not poverty, and that from morality comes happiness and not suffering. According to the tenets quoted above, this wisdom would be an endowment of the buddha essence dwelling within every living being. “Basis” (gnas) is the Sanskrit sthā, which has the meaning of “correct and proper” as well as its usual connotation of “location.” See The Great Lexicon, p. 1119.

f.d: gzhan yang sher phyin gyi mdo sogs las chos thams cad stong par gsungs pa'i don bde gshegs snying po dri ma gzhan gyis stong pa yin zhing / dgag bya'i dri mas stong pa'i snying po bden grub yin na sher phyin sogs kyis bshad pa'i dgag byas stong pa'i stong nyid bden grub tu 'dod dgos shing 'dod kyang 'dod do/ /

Furthermore, if the meaning of statements that all phenomena are empty as found in the Prajñāpāramitā and other sutras was that the buddha essence was empty of “other” impurities, empty of the impurities to be negated, and was itself truly existing, then you would have to agree that the emptiness spoken of in these sutras as being empty of the objects to be negated would also be truly existing.

gal te de lta yin na mi 'thad de/ dbu ma rtsa ba shes rab las/
rgyal ba rnams kyis stong pa nyid/ / lta kun nges par 'byin par gsungs/ / gang dag stong pa nyid lta ba/ / de dag bsgrub tu med par gsungs/[82] / zhes dang / de'i 'grel pa tshig gsal las/
'di ltar gang zhig khyod la zong ci yang mi ster ro zhes smras pa dang / kye bdag la ci yang med pa zhes bya ba'i zong de nyid byin cig ces smra na de med par 'dzin du gzhug par thabs gang gis nus/ de bzhin du gang dag stong pa nyid la yang dngos por mngon par zhen pa de dag gi de la dngos por mngon par zhen pa de gang gis 'gog par 'gyur/[83] zhes dang /

Even if you do actually assert this, it could not be correct, because in Fundamental Treatise on the Middle Way it says:
The conquerors have said that emptiness uproots all views, and that those who have a view of emptiness will have no accomplishment.[118] And from its commentary, Clear Words:
Were someone to say, “I will not give you anything at all,” and if I were to reply, “Then give me that which does not exist!” how would it be possible to hold that as not existing? Likewise, for those who even cling to emptiness as a reality, how will they negate their clinging to reality?[119]

d.div: [82] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsaklu sgrub kyi dbu ma rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 13_sh+loka8_8_na6
[83] sde dge_3860_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'dabu ma tshig gsal/ rab byed/ 13_83_ba6
[118] Toh 3824 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, chap. 13, v. 8, 8a6.
[119] Toh 3860 Tengyur, dbu ma, ah, chap. 13, 83b6.

f.d:
de bzhin du 'grel pa tshig gsal gyi skabs 'dir mdo dkon brtsegs drangs pa las/
'od srung gang dag stong pa nyid du dmigs pas stong pa nyid la rtog pa de dag ni ngas gsung rab 'di las nyams rab tu nyams zhes bshad do/ / 'od srung gang zag tu lta ba ri rab tsam la gnas pa ni bla'i/ mngon pa'i nga rgyal can stong pa nyid du lta ba ni de lta ma yin no/ / de ci'i phyir zhe na/ 'od srung lta bar gyur pa thams cad las dbyung bar gyur pa ni stong pa nyid yin na/ 'od srung gang stong pa nyid kho nar lta ba de ni gsor mi rung ngo zhes ngas bshad do/[84] / zhes gsungs pa rnams kyis chos gang yang bden grub tu lta bar mi rung bar gsungs shing / khyad par du yang stong nyid bden grub tu lta ba gsor mi rung gi lta bar gsungs pa rnams kyis gnod pa yang dag par 'bab pas so/ /

Similarly the Heap of Jewels Sutra, quoted at this point in Clear Words, says:
Kāśyapa, those who focus upon emptiness and have thoughts of emptiness fall far from my words. Kāśyapa, to have views on self the size of Mount Meru is tolerable, but with strong pride to have views on emptiness is not. Why is that? Kāśyapa, if emptiness is that which uproots every view, then Kāśyapa, I say that those who have a view on emptiness alone are beyond all cure.[120] These quotes state that it is wrong to have a view on any phenomenon as truly existing, and to view emptiness as truly existing is said to be an especially incurable view. Such statements do great damage to the previous assertions. /38/

d.div: [84] sde dge_3860_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'dabu ma tshig gsal/ rab byed/ 13_84_na2
[120] Toh 3860 Tengyur, dbu ma, ah, chap. 13, 84a2.

f.d:
gzhan yang bde gshegs snying po mtshan dpes brgyan pa stobs dang mi 'jigs pa la sogs la sangs rgyas kyi yon tan thams cad dang ldan pa rtag brtan ther zug bden par grub pa sems can thams cad kyi rgyud la gdod ma nas yod par 'dod pa ni shin tu yang mi rigs te/ mdo kha cig las de ltar bshad pa ni bcom ldan 'das nyid kyis sgra ji bzhin du bzung du mi rung ba'i drang don dgongs pa can du bshad cing / de ltar bshad pa ltar du 'jug pa'i rang 'grel du yang dpal ldan zla bas bshad pa'i phyir te/ 'jug 'grel du lang kar gshegs pa'i mdo drangs pa las/
de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po gsungs pa de bcom ldan 'das kyis rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal ba rnam par dag pas thog ma nas rnam par dag pa nyid mtshan sum cu rtsa gnyis dang ldan pa sems can thams cad kyi lus kyi nang na mchis [85] par brjod de/ bcom ldan 'das kyis rin po che rin thang chen po gos dri ma can gyis yongs su dkris pa ltar phung po dang khams dang skye mched kyi gos kyis yongs su dkris pa/ 'dod chags dang zhe sdang dang gti mug gis zil gyis non pa/ yongs su rtog pa'i dri mas dri ma can du gyur pa/ rtag pa brtan pa ther zug par ni brjod na/ zhes khyed 'dod pa ltar gyi bde gshegs snying po drang don gyi mdos bshad tshul brjod nas/ de'i rjes thogs de ma thag tu/
bcom ldan 'das de bzhin gshegs pa de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po smra ba 'di ni mu stegs byed kyi bdag tu smra ba dang ji ltar 'dra ba ma lags/ bcom ldan 'das mu stegs byed rnams kyang rtag pa byed pa po ma yin pa yon tan med pa khyab pa mi 'jig pa'o zhes bdag tu smra ba ston par byed do/[86] / zhes de lta bu'i bde gshegs snying po smra ba de mu stegs byed kyis bdag rtag pa smra ba dang mtshungs pa 'dra ba cig 'dug lags te/ de mi mtshungs pa'i rgyu mtshan ci zhes pa'o/ /

Furthermore to assert that the buddha essence is adorned by the features and signs of enlightenment, is endowed with the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, and every other excellent quality of the buddha, that it is unchanging and permanent, of ultimate existence, and dwells inside every sentient being since beginningless time is completely wrong because the words of the Buddha in sutras that teach this way are not to be taken literally, and such teachings are intended for interpretation. This is explained in Candrakīrti’s commentary to his own Madhyamakāvatāra, where he quotes from the Laṅkāvatārasūtra:
“In the teachings on the buddha essence, the Conqueror spoke of that whose nature was pure and of clear light, pure since beginningless time, endowed with the thirty-two features of enlightenment, and existing within the bodies of every sentient being. The Conqueror taught that like a very precious jewel wrapped in dirty cloth, it lies permanent and unchanging, wrapped in the cloths of the aggregates, sensory spheres, and sense sources, eclipsed by anger, desire, and ignorance, tainted by the impurities of conceptuality.[121] This passage describing a buddha essence accords with your assertions as taught by a sutra requiring interpretation. The sutra continues:
“Conqueror, Tathāgata, if that is so, how is one who teaches on tathāgata essence unlike the outsiders who teach on self? Conqueror, the outsiders are also teachers of a self that is permanent, a nondoer, devoid of qualities, pervasive, and imperishable.” This passage states that a buddha essence described in this way is similar to the permanent self propounded by non-Buddhists and asks how it could be any different.

d.div: [85] ma dper 'chis zhes gsal/
[86] sde dge_3862_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_'jug pa rang 'grel/ 281_na6 gzhan yang / sde dge_107_bka'/ mdo sde/ calang kar gshegs pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 2_85_ba7
[121] Toh 3862 Tengyur, dbu ma, ah, 281a6. Or Toh 107 Kangyur, mdo sde, ca, Laṅkāvatārasūtra, chap. 2, 85b7.

f.d:
de'i lan du de ma thag pa der/
bcom ldan 'das kyis bka' stsal pa/ blo gros chen po ngas de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po bstan pa ni mu stegs can gyi bdag tu smra ba dang mtshungs pa ma yin te/ blo gros chen po de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas rnams ni stong pa nyid dang / yang dag pa'i mtha' dang / mya ngan las 'das pa dang / ma skyes pa dang / mtshan ma med pa dang / smon pa med pa la sogs pa'i tshig gi don rnams la de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying por bstan pa byas nas byis pa rnams bdag med pas 'jigs par gyur pa'i gnas rnam par spang par bya ba'i don du de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po'i sgo bstan pas rnam par mi rtog pa'i gnas snang ba med pa'i spyod yul ston te/ blo gros chen po ma 'ongs pa dang da ltar byung ba'i byang chub sems dpa' sems dpa' chen po rnams kyis bdag la mngon par zhen par mi bya'o/[87] / zhes gsungs te/

The sutra continues with the reply:
The Conqueror replied, “Mahāmati, my teaching of the buddha essence is not similar to the Tirthankara teachings on self. Mahāmati, the tathāgatas, conquerors of the enemy, perfectly complete buddhas, have taught the meanings of terms such as /39/ emptiness, perfect reality, nirvana, the unborn, the signless, the wishless, and so forth as buddha essence. Children are frightened by no-self, and as a means to remove that fear, the door of buddha essence is shown. By doing so the nonconceptual state, the nonappearing object, is taught. Mahāmati, those great beings, those bodhisattvas of the future and of the present, should not hold fast to a self.”[122]

d.div: [87] sde dge_107_bka'/ mdo sde/ ca'aphags pa lang kar gshegs pa'i mdo/ 86_na4
[122] Toh 107 Kangyur, mdo sde, ca, Laṅkāvatārasūtra, chap. 2, 86a4.

f.d: de yang blo gros chen po ngas zhes pa nas mtshungs pa ma yin te zhes pa'i bar gyis khyed 'dod pa ltar gyi bde gshegs snying po bstan pa de mu stegs kyi bdag rtag pa smra ba dang mi mtshungs pa'i dam bca' bstan/ stong pa nyid dang zhes pa nas/ tshig gi don rnams la zhes pa'i bar gyis de lta bu'i bde gshegs snying po gsungs pa'i dgongs gzhi bstan/ de bzhin gshegs pa zhes pa nas sangs rgyas rnams ni zhes pa'i bar dang / de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying por bstan pa byas nas zhes pa rnams kyis snying po gsungs tshul bstan/ byis pa rnams zhes pa nas/ spang bar bya ba'i don du zhes pa'i bar gyis rnam gcad [88] kyi dgos pa dang / de bzhin gshegs pa'i zhes pa nas/ spyod yul ston te zhes pa'i bar gyis yongs gcod kyi dgos pa bstan/ blo gros chen po ma 'ongs pa dang zhes pa nas/ mngon par zhen par mi bya'o zhes pa'i bar gyis de lta bu'i bde gshegs snying po ston pa'i mdo'i sgra ji bzhin pa'i don la mngon par zhen na bdag rtag pa la mngon par zhen par 'gyur bas/ bdag la mngon par zhen par mi bya'o zhes pas dngos la gnod byed bstan to/ /

The sentence beginning “Mahāmati, my teaching of” expresses the assertion that the teaching of the buddha essence as held by you is not similar to non-Buddhists’ teachings of a permanent self. The list of terms beginning with “emptiness” reveals the thinking behind the teachings on buddha essence. The words “Mahāmati, the tathāgatas, conquerors of the enemy, perfectly complete buddhas, have taught the meanings of terms,” and including the phrase “as buddha essence,” reveal the ways in which the essence was taught. The purpose of the sentence beginning “Children” up to “remove that fear” is to reveal what is to be excluded, and the purpose of the sentence beginning “By doing so” reveals what is to be included. The last sentence, beginning “Mahāmati, those great beings,” teaches that if the words of sutras that speak of this kind of buddha essence are held as literal, this leads to a clinging to a permanent self. Therefore the quote ends “should not hold fast to a self,” which illustrates the actual damage done to the previous assertion.

d.div: [88] ma dper rnam gcad ces gsal yang rnam bcad yin nam snyam/

f.d: de'i 'jug de ma thag tu/ blo gros chen po dper na zhes pa nas/ blo gros chen po de ltar de bzhin gshegs pa rnams kyis mu stegs byed bdag tu smra ba la mngon par zhen pa rnams drang ba'i phyir de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po bstan pas de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po ston te/[89] zhes pa'i bar du gsungs pa rnams kyis sems can thams cad kyi rgyud la bde gshegs snying po mtshan dpes brgyan pa stobs dang mi 'jigs pa sogs kyi yon tan dang ldan pa rtag brtan ther zug pa yod par gsungs pa ni sgra ji bzhin par khas blang du mi rung ba'i drang don dgongs pa can du bstan pa yin pas rgyud 'grel chen dang bcas pa ji snyed pa dag gis 'di lta bu'i de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po bstan pa'i sgo nas 'chad pa mi rigs par go ste/ 'dir cung zad tsam zhig bshad pa yin no/ /

The text immediately following the above passage beginning “Mahāmati, for example” up to “Mahāmati, in this way the tathāgatas taught and are teaching the tathāgata essence in order to guide those who hold to the outsiders’ assertion of self” explain that texts propounding a buddha essence within every sentient being, adorned with features of an enlightened being, endowed with qualities such as the ten powers and the four kinds of fearlessness, permanent and unchanging, are not to be adhered to literally but are for a particular purpose and are to be interpreted. Therefore, it can be understood that it is incorrect to explain the tantra and the Great Commentary by way of such a buddha essence. /40/ This has been just a brief explanation.

d.div: [89] sde dge_107_bka'/ mdo sde/ ca'aphags pa lang kar gsheg pa'i mdo/ 85_ba5_nas 86_ba3

f.d: gnyis pa gnyug ma'i lus bshad pa ni/

sngar bshad pa'i gnyug sems shin tu phra ba de dang ngo bo dbyer med pa'i rlung shin tu phra ba ste/ ngo bo dbyer med kyi rlung sems shin tu phra ba de la gnyug ma'i lus sems zhes bya zhing / de lta bu'i gnyug ma'i lus sems 'di 'khor ba'i gnas skabs su sems can rnams kyi phung khams skye mched sogs 'khor ba'i chos thams cad kyi rtsa ba dang / 'khor ba'i chos thams cad gnyug ma'i lus sems shin tu phra ba'i rlung sems ngo bo dbyer med de'i rnam 'phrul yin te/ bshad rgyud rdo rje 'phreng ba las/
skye dang gnas dang 'jig pa dang / / srid pa bar mar gnas pa ste/ / ji srid 'jig rten gyis btags pa/ / sems kyi rlung gi rnam 'phrul lo/[90] / zhes dang /

The very subtle primordial mind explained above is inseparable from the very subtle wind. This indivisible entity of very subtle wind and mind is known as the primordial body and mind. In the confines of samsara, this primordial body and mind is the root of the aggregates, sensory spheres, sense sources of sentient beings, and of every phenomenon of samsara. All phenomena of samsara are manifestations of the indivisible entity of primordial body and mind. In the Vajra Garland explanatory tantra it says:
Be it birth, abiding, or destruction, life or the intermediate state, as long as it is bound by the world, it is a manifestation of the winds of the mind.[123]

d.div: [90] sde dge_445_bka'/ rgyud/ carnal 'byor chen po'i rgyud dpal rdo rje phreng ba/ le'u/ 59_265_ba1
[123] Toh 445 Kangyur, rgyud, ca, chap. 59, 265b1.

f.d:
dgongs pa lung ston las kyang /
'du shes can dang 'du shes med/ / sems can du btags 'di gnas pa/ / de rnams rlung las byung ba ste/ / rlung las slar yang 'gag pa yin/ / ma rtogs pa yi sems de ni/ / 'khor ba'i rgya mtshor gnas gyur te/ / de ni phyin ci log song bas/ / khyi dang lce spyang glang po dang / / sems de rtar yang 'gro bar 'gyur/[91] / zhes rlung sems gnyis 'gro ba sna tshogs su 'gro ba dang / /mthar 'chi ba'i tshe yang phung khams skye mched rlung sems rags pa thams cad shin tu phra ba'i rlung sems 'di nyid la sdud do/ /

The Sandhivyākaraṇa Tantra says:
All that is tied to sentient beings, be it with consciousness or without, arises from the winds, is ended by the winds. The unknowing mind dwells in the ocean of samsara, where, by going wayward, it migrates into dogs, jackals, cows, and horses.[124] The winds and the mind migrate into different living forms, and at death the aggregates, sensory spheres, sense sources, and the coarse winds and minds withdraw into the very subtle wind and mind.

d.div: [91] sde dge_444_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_dgongs pa lung bstan pa'i rgyud/ le'u/ 2_168_na6
[124] Toh 444 Kangyur, rgyud, ca, chap. 2, 168a6.

f.d: de yang sdud pa'i tshul ni lus can rnams 'chi ba'i tshe sa chu me rlung gi khams rnams rim gyis thim nas snang mched thob gsum rim gyis shar te 'chi ba'i 'od gsal shar ba na shin tu phra ba'i rlung sems ma gtogs gang zag de'i rgyud kyis bsdus pa'i rlung sems sogs ci yang med kyang rlung sems shin tu phra ba de gnyug ma'i lus sems su 'jog pas gang zag de'i lus sems rgyun chad pa med cing slar yang 'chi ba'i 'od gsal gyi rlung sems shin tu phra ba'i rlung des nyer len byas pa las rang rang gi bar do'i grub par 'gyur ba'i bar do'i lus dang / 'chi ba'i 'od gsal gyi sems des nyer len byas pa las bar do'i sems phra rags rnams 'byung ba yin no/ /

In this process the elements of earth, water, fire, and air dissolve in turn, and the minds of appearance, increase, and attainment arise in succession. When death clear light appears, there are no minds or winds of that person’s continuum present except for the very subtle wind and mind. However, because this very subtle wind and mind is the primordial wind and mind, the continuum of that person’s mind and body is not broken. With the wind of the very subtle wind and mind of death clear light acting as a substantial cause,[125] the bardo body will arise, and with the mind of the death clear light as a substantial cause, the coarse and subtle bardo minds will arise. /41/

d.div: [125] nyer len. A substantial cause is one whose very entity transforms into the effect, as a seed becomes a flower, for example.

f.d: de la dgongs nas/ skye dang gnas dang zhes sogs dang / 'du shes can dang 'du shes med/ /ces sogs gsungs pa yin no/ /
This is the thinking behind the two quotes above.

lam nyams su len pa'i rnal 'byor pas ni rtsa thig rlung gsum la gnad du bsnun pa las snang mched thob gsum 'od gsal dang bcas pa rim gyis drangs te shin tu phra ba'i rlung sems mngon du gyur pa'i sems dben mthar thug gam/ de'i dod thub pa'i lam mngon du byas te de lta bu'i rlung sems shin tu phra ba las sgyu lus su langs nas sgyu lus des sangs rgyas pa'i zung 'jug gi sgyu ma'i sku'i rigs 'dra'i rgyu dang sems des chos sku'i rigs 'dra'i rgyu byed pa yin no/ / 'dir ni mtshon pa tsam ste/ tshul 'di ni rgyas par 'khrul pa'i dri ma thams cad dang bral ba rim pa lnga gsal ba'i sgron ma las shes par bya'o/ /

The yogi practicing on the path focuses on and penetrates the channels, drops, and winds and induces successively the minds of appearance, increase, attainment, and clear light. Then the final mind isolation, with its manifest subtle mind and wind, or the path of a suitable alternative, is actualized, and from this very subtle wind and mind arises the illusory body. This illusory body is a similar-type cause of the illusory body of the enlightenment union, while the subtle mind is a similar-type cause of the dharmakāya. This is just an introduction. The process can be known extensively from the peerless Lantern Illuminating the Five Stages.

de yang skabs 'dir gnyug ma'i sems dang lus gnyis rnam gzhag so sor che nas bshad pa na sems 'grel skor gsum la sogs pas 'od gsal gyi rlung sems gnyis kyi nang nas sems nyid gtso bor byas nas 'chad cing rlung gtso bor mi byed la dpal gsang ba 'dus pa sogs sbas rgyud rnams kyi dgongs pa 'grel ba'i grub chen mgon po klu sgrub la sogs pa rnams kyis 'od gsal gyi rlung sems gnyis ka gtso bor byas te 'chad pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis yin no/ / de ltar 'chad tshul so sor 'ong ba'i rgyu mtshan yang sems 'grel skor gsum gyi bzhed pas 'od gsal gyi sems nyid kyi steng nas sku gnyis ka'i rigs 'dra'i rgyu sgrub kyi rlung las gzugs sku'i rigs 'dra'i rgyu ma sgrub pa dang / 'od gsal lhan skyes kyi sems nyid 'khor 'das thams cad kyi byed pa po yin pa'i sgo nas kun la khyab pa po yin pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis yin la/ mgon po klu sgrub sogs grub chen rnams kyis sbas rgyud kyi dgongs pa bkral ba'i bzhed pas ni 'od gsal gyi sems las chos sku'i rigs 'dra'i rgyu dang rlung las gzugs sku'i rgyu sgrub pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis yin no/ / de ltar 'ong ba'i rgyu mtshan yang ched du bya ba'i gdul bya rigs tha dad pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis yin te 'og tu 'chad do/ /

On individual presentations of primordial mind and primordial body in the context of Kālacakra, the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries and other commentaries concentrate primarily on subtle mind in their explanations of the winds and mind of the clear light and do not concentrate on the winds. The protector Nāgārjuna and other mahāsiddhas who wrote commentaries on the Guhyasamāja and other hidden tantras focused on the clear-light mind and wind equally in their explanations. The reason for these differing and individual explanations is as follows. According to Three Bodhisattva Commentaries, a similar-type cause of both bodies of a buddha can be fashioned from the clear-light mind itself, and a similar-type cause of the form body of a buddha is not created from the subtle wind. Another reason is that in the sense of being the creator of all phenomena of samsara and nirvana, the innate mind of clear light pervades everything. According to commentaries on the Śrī Guhyasamājatantra and other hidden tantras composed by mahāsiddhas such as the protector Nāgārjuna, the mind of clear light is formed into a similar-type cause of the dharmakāya and the subtle wind becomes a similar-type cause of the form body. These two differing explanations have come about because of differing types of disciples. This will be explained later.
de ltar na sku gnyis kyi sgrub gzhi gnyug ma'i lus sems mdo tsam bshad zin to/ /
This has been a brief explanation of the primordial body and mind, the basis for the accomplishment of the two bodies of a buddha. /42/
gsum pa bla med kyi rgyud rnams kyi dgongs pa'i 'grel tshul bshad pa ni/

d.i: Explanations of the intentions of the highest yoga tantras

f.d: de yang sngags bla med kyi thun mong ma yin pa'i brjod don gnyug ma'i lus sems de nyid thabs mkhas kyis sku gnyis kyi rigs 'dra'i rgyur dngos su sgyur bar byed pa'i lam ni sngags bla med kyi thun mong ma yin pa'i brjod bya'i gtso bo rdzogs rim gyi lam rnams yin la/ de lta bu'i lam rnams 'chad par byed pa'i rtsa ba'i rgyud rnams kyang gnyis su nges te bskyed rdzogs kyi lam rnams sbas pa'i tshul gyis 'chad par byed pa dang ma sbas par gsal bar 'chad pa gnyis su nges so/ / de'i dang po ni kye rdor bde mchog gsang ba 'dus pa'i bsdus rgyud nyung ngu la sogs pa rnams so/ / de rnams kyi sbas pa'i don 'byin par byed pa'i tshul ni gnyis te/ rang rang gi bshad rgyud rnams kyis rtsa rgyud de dang de'i don bshad pa'i dgongs pa klu sgrub sogs 'phags yul gyi grub chen rnams kyis bkral tshul dang / dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud 'grel gyi dgongs pa dang mthun par rdo rje snying 'grel dang phyag rdor stod 'grel sogs kyis bkral tshul lo/ /

The skillful transformation of the primordial body and mind, the two special themes of highest mantra, into similar-type causes of the two bodies of a buddha is the path of the completion stage, which is the main topic of highest mantra. The root tantras that describe this path are of two types: those that explain the stages of generation and completion in a concealed way and those that do so clearly and in an unconcealed manner. Examples of hidden tantras would be the short condensed tantras of Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara, and Guhyasamāja. There are two ways in which the hidden meanings of these tantras are brought out. The first is to explain each root tantra by relying upon individual explanatory tantras. This was the method employed by Nāgārjuna and the other mahāsiddhas of India. The second way is to explain the tantra in accordance with the thinking of Kālacakra and its commentaries. This is the method used by the Vajragarbha Commentary, the Vajrapāṇi Commentary, and others.

de'i dang po ni dpal gsang ba 'dus pa'i rtsa rgyud kyi don bshad rgyud rdo rje 'phreng ba sogs drug gis bshad pa'i dgongs pa 'phags pa klu sgrub yab sras rnams kyis ngag dben sogs lam rim pa lngar bshad pa la sogs pa rnams dang / bde mchog rtsa rgyud nyung ngu'i don sdom 'byung sogs bshad rgyud drug gis bshad pa'i dgongs pa grub chen dril bu pas bdag byin brlab sogs rim pa lngar bshad pa sogs dang / kye rdor gyi rtsa rgyud nyung ngu'i don gur dang sam+puT dang kha sbyor sogs bshad rgyud rnams kyis bshad pa'i don gyi rdzogs rim dbang gsum gyi lam du bsdus pa'i lam 'bras bu dang bcas pa'i rnam gzhag rje btsun bir wa pas mdzad pa sogs so/ /

Concerning the first method, the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra is explained by six explanatory tantras, such as the Vajra Garland, and these in turn have been explained by Nāgārjuna and his disciples, who taught them as the five stages of the path, beginning with the isolation of speech. The Short Cakrasaṃvara Root Tantra is explained by six explanatory tantras, such as the Samvaraudbhava, and they in turn have been explained by mahāsiddhas such as Vajraghanta in the format of the five stages, such as blessing of self and so forth. The Short Hevajra Root Tantra is explained by its explanatory tantras, such as the Vajra Tent, Sampuṭa, Caturyogānisampuṭa, and so forth. These have been taught by the venerable Virupa in his presentation of the paths and results, which condense the actual completion stage into the paths of the three initiations.

dus 'khor rgyud 'grel gyi dgongs pa dang mthun par rdo rje snying 'grel dang phyag rdor stod 'grel sogs kyis bkral ba'i tshul ni phyi dang nang gi rnam bzhag dang sbyor ba yan lag drug gi rnam bzhag sogs dus 'khor rgyud 'grel las bshad pa ji bzhin du yod pa 'grel pa gnyis la bltas pa nyid kyis shes par 'gyur ro/ /

The way that texts such as the Vajragarbha Commentary and the Vajrapāṇi Commentary explain the tantras as conforming to the thinking of Kālacakra and its commentary can be known by looking at these two commentaries, which explain the Inner and Outer, the six-branched yoga, and so forth, in light of the Kālacakra and its commentary.

de ltar na 'dus pa sogs sbas rgyud rnams kyi dgongs pa 'phags yul gyi grub chen rnams kyis bkral ba ltar dang / sems 'grel skor gsum la sogs pas bkral ba ltar gyi mi 'dra ba gnyis gnyis su gnas par byed dgos so/ / de yang rdo rje snying 'grel las bde mchog dang gdan bzhi'i nges don 'bum lnga kye rdo rje las shes dgos pa dang / kye rdor dang bde mchog nyung ngu'i sbas rgyud 'di gnyis kyi nges don gdan bzhi las shes dgos pa dang / de thams cad kyi nges don dang po'i sangs rgyas dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsa rgyud dang bde mchog mngon brjod 'bum pa'i rgyud rnams las shes dgos par bshad de/ de nyid las/
kye yi rdo rje yis ni bde mchog dang ni gdan bzhi shes par bya/ / kye rdo rje dang bde mchog 'khor lo nyung ngu 'di ni gdan bzhis shes par bya/ / mchog gi dang po'i sangs rgyas tshig dang bde mchog chen pos nges don shes par bya/[92] / zhes bshad pa dang /

Therefore it is necessary to classify commentaries into those of the mahāsiddhas of India /43/ who explained the hidden tantras of Guhyasamāja and so forth and those such as the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries. According to the Vajragarbha Commentary, the definitive meanings of the Cakrasaṃvara and Four Seats tantras should be understood from the Five Hundred Thousand Hevajra Tantra. The definitive meanings of the hidden tantras of the Hevajra and the Short Cakrasaṃvara should be understood from the Four Seats Tantra. The definitive meanings of all of them should be understood from the root tantra of the Original Buddha Kālacakra and from the Hundred Thousand Cakrasaṃvara. The Vajragarbha Commentary says:
From Hevajra will Cakrasaṃvara and the Four Seats Tantra be understood. Hevajra and the Short Cakrasaṃvara will be understood from the Four Seats Tantra. From the words of the Supreme Original Buddha and from the Great Cakrasaṃvara will definitive meanings be understood.[126]

d.div: [92] sde dge_1180_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ka_rdo rje snying 'grel/ 5_na5
[126] Toh 1180 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ka, 5a5.

f.d: de bzhin du gsang ba 'dus pa'i rgyud phyi ma las sbyor ba yan lag drug gsungs pa'i rgyud tshig 'di rnams la yang dus 'khor nas bshad pa'i sbyor ba yan lag drug gi don re dang klu sgrub zla grags sogs kyis bkral ba'i sbyor drug gi don re ste mi 'dra ba gnyis yod de/ nA ro pas 'dus pa phyi ma'i rgyud tshig de rnams kyi don dbang mdor bstan gyi 'grel par dus 'khor gyi sbyor drug bzhin du bshad cing 'dus pa phyi ma'i 'grel par sgron gsal bzhin du bshad pas so/ /

In this way, the verses on the six-branched yoga taught in the Later Guhyasamāja has led to two different interpretations. One accords with the six-branched yoga of Kālacakra, and the other accords with the six-branched yoga as taught by Nāgārjuna, Candrakīrti, and others. In his Commentary on a Short Teaching on Initiations, Nāropa explains these passages of the Later Guhyasamāja Tantra in accord with the six-branched yoga of Kālacakra, while in his commentary on the Later Guhyasamāja Tantra he explains them in accord with Bright Lamp.

'o na dus 'khor nas bshad pa'i sbyor ba yan lag drug dang sgron gsal gyis rgyud phyi ma'i don bshad pa'i sbyor ba yan lag drug mi 'dra ba'i tshul ji lta bu snyam na/ de ni 'di ltar yin te dus kyi 'khor lo'i sor sdud kyi don dbang po rnams yul la mi 'jug par nang du sdud pa la bshad cing / sgron gsal las khral len pa la khral sdud pa zhes bshad pa ltar dbang po rnams kyis gzugs sogs rnams yul du bsdus nas so sor longs spyod pa sor sdud kyi don du bshad pa dang /

How does the six-branched yoga taught in the Kālacakra differ from the six-branched yoga as explained by the Bright Lamp, where it is explained according to the Later Guhyasamāja Tantra? The meaning of withdrawal in Kālacakra is that the sensory powers are withdrawn inward and do not engage their respective objects. According to Bright Lamp, withdrawal means that the sensory powers withdraw or gather into their objects, such as visual form, to be individually enjoyed in the manner of “taxes gathering unto a tax collector.”

gzhan yang 'grel chen gyi khams le'i mdor bsdus gnyis pa las/
bar ma'i mtshan ma ni mchog tu mi 'gyur ba'i skad cig brgya phrag bco brgyad kyis sa dang po thob pa dang /[93] zhes ting nge 'dzin gyi yan lag mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba stong dang brgyad brgya thob pa 'phags pa dang / sbyor ba yan lag drug gi rjes dran man la gnas pa thams cad so so skye bor bshad la/ sgron gsal gyis 'dzin pa'i yan lag don gyi 'od gsal dang / rjes dran don gyi 'od gsal las lugs bzlog tu langs pa'i gnas skabs dang / ting nge 'dzin gyi yan lag zung 'jug la bshad cing / don gyi 'od gsal thob nas stong nyid mngon sum tu rtogs pa'i 'phags par 'jog pas so/ /

Moreover the Great Commentary says in the Realms chapter in the second summary:
The intermediate sign is that by 1,800 supreme and unchanging instances, the first level is attained.[127] /44/ This explains that the achievement of 1,800 instances of unchanging bliss by the branch of meditative concentration is the attainment of the level of an ārya, while the branch of recollection and below is at the level of an ordinary being. Bright Lamp explains the branch of retention as being the actual clear light, the branch of recollection as the arising of the actual clear-light reversal, the branch of meditative concentration as being union, and that once the actual clear light is attained, the practitioner becomes an ārya directly cognizing emptiness.

d.div: [93] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 17_na1
[127] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 17a1.

f.d:
de yang sgron gsal las de ltar du bshad de/ 'dzin pa'i yan lag 'chad pa'i skabs kyi sgron gsal le'u bcu gnyis pa las/
nub par gyur pa'i gzung ba gang yin pa de ni 'dzin pa yin par bshad de/ de gang zhe na/ yang dag pa'i mtha' zhes bya ba'o/ / sems ni 'gog pa'i rdo rjer 'gyur/ / mtshan mar nyer 'dzin 'byung bar gyur/[94] / zhes bya ba la 'gog pa'i rdo rje ni 'od gsal ba'o/ / der gyur pa ni sems der gyur pa'o/ / zhes sogs kyis 'dzin pa'i yan lag don gyi 'od gsal la 'jog par bshad cing /

This can be understood from the twelfth chapter of Bright Lamp, where it comments on the branch of retention:
The sinking of all apprehending is explained as being retention. How is that? “It is called perfect reality. The mind becomes the cessation vajra and the signs of near attainment arise.” Here vajra cessation is clear light, and the mind becomes that clear light.[128] In this way, Bright Lamp establishes the branch of retention as being the actual clear light.

d.div: [94] sde dge_1785_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ hasgron gsal/ le'u/ 12_97_na3
[128] Toh 1785 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ha, 97a3.

f.d:
rjes dran don gyi 'od gsal las lugs bzlog tu langs pa'i gnas skabs la bshad pa ni le'u de nyid kyi rjes dran 'chad pa'i sgron gsal las/
de ltar bdag nyid 'od gsal bar song bar rnam par bsgom zhing mngon sum du byas nas gang mngon du dran pa smig sgyu 'dra ba la sogs pa'i rnam pas yang dag pa'i mtha' thob pa de dang 'dra zhing / de nyid kyi rim gyis spro bar bya zhing bskyed par bya ste/[95] bshad ma thag pa de dag ni rjes su dran pa zhes bshad pa yin par shes shing khong du chud par bya'o/ / zhes 'dzin pa'i yan lag don gyi 'od gsal mngon sum du byas nas/ de las ldang ba'i tshe gang sngon 'od gsal la 'jug pa'i skabs kyi smig sgyu 'dra ba la sogs pa'i rnam pas yang dag pa'i mtha' 'od gsal thob pa dang 'dra zhing ste 'dra bar smig sgyu la sogs sngar bshad pa de nyid lugs bzlog tu rim gyis spros shing bskyed pa de nyid rjes dran yin par khong du chud par bya'o zhes gsungs pas so/ /

The branch of recollection is established as being the time of the actual clear-light reversal, and this can be known from the same chapter in the section on the branch of recollection:
Therefore, having meditated upon and actualized that whose nature is clear light, the forms of miragelike appearances and so forth are recollected as they were in the attainment of perfect reality. These emanate and are created in sequence. This should be known and understood as recollection.[129] Therefore clear light is actualized in the branch of retention. Arising from this clear light, those previous forms of miragelike appearances that arose during the entering into clear light are here recollected, and they arise like those in the “attainment of perfect reality” clear light. “These emanate and are created in sequence” in a reverse sequence. This is to be understood as being the branch of recollection.

d.div: [95] sde dge_1785_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ hasgron gsal/ le'u/ 12_97_ba3
[129] Toh 1785 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ha, chap. 12, 97b3.

f.d: de bzhin du ting nge 'dzin gyi yan lag zung 'jug la 'jog pa yang sgron gsal las gsal bar gsungs pa rnams kyang shes par bya'o/ /
Bright Lamp also asserts the branch of /45/ meditative concentration as being the state of union.

gal te 'dzin pa'i yan lag don gyi 'od gsal la 'jog pa sgron gsal gyi dgongs pa yin na/ rjes dran dang ting nge 'dzin gyi yan lag thob pa'i gang zag 'phags par 'jog pa bden du chug na'ang / 'dzin pa'i yan lag la 'od gsal zhes bshad pa ni dpe'i 'od gsal la dgongs pa yin no zhe na/ de ni mi rigs te/ ma skyes pa rjes dran 'chad byed kyi sgron gsal las/
da ni zung du 'jug pa'i rim pa nyid kyis ldang ba'i gnas bstan par bya ba'i phyir de la [96] zhes bya ba la sogs pa gsungs te/ ma skyes pa ni 'dzin pa'i yan lag go/ / zhes pa nas/
de nas 'dzin pa'i yan lag gi 'og tu rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal ba zhes bya bar sbyar te/ rang bzhin ni kun rdzob kyi bden pa'o/ / 'od gsal ni don dam pa'i bden pa ste/ rang bzhin dang ldan pa'i 'od gsal ba ni rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal ba zhes bya'o/ / de gang yin zhe na/ gnyis su med pa'i ye shes kyi bdag nyid can rdo rje 'chang chen po'i sku'o/ / zhes 'dzin pa'i yan lag tu bshad pa'i 'od gsal de las ldang ba'i tshe zung 'jug gi skur ldang bar bshad pa'i phyir ro/ /

If it is Bright Lamp’s assertion that the branch of retention corresponds to actual clear light, then it is true that someone who has attained the stages of recollection and meditative concentration must be an ārya. However, doesn’t the clear light explained as being the branch of retention refer to the similitude clear light? This is not so. In the section explaining the recollection of the “unborn,” Bright Lamp says:
The verse beginning “Within that” and so on teaches the arising of the state of union. The unborn is the branch of retention. And so on until:
After the branch of retention comes entity clear light. “Entity” refers to conventional truth. “Clear light” is ultimate truth. Clear light possessing entity is known as entity clear light. What is that? It is the body of the great Vajradhara, whose nature is nondual gnosis.[130] Therefore, when arising from the clear light, which is explained as being the branch of retention, one arises in the body of union.

d.div: [96] sde dge_1785_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ hasgron gsal/ le'u/ 7_58_ba6
[130] Toh 1785 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ha, chap. 7, 58b6.

f.d:
de ltar na sbas rgyud rnams kyi dgongs pa 'phags yul gyi grub chen rnams kyis bkral ba dang sems 'grel skor gsum gyis bkral ba gnyis gcig rgyu mtshan du byas na cig shos 'gog pa'am/ lam gyi rnam gzhag rnams kyi ming gcig pa rnams don yang gcig tu 'khrul bar mi bya'o/ / gnyis pa bskyed rdzogs kyi lam rnams ma sbas par gsal bar 'chad pa'i rgyud ni/ dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsa rgyud dang bsdus rgyud la sogs pa'i rgyud rnams yin te/ khams le'i mdor bsdus gnyis pa las/
rdo rje theg pa 'dir sems can gyi bsam pa'i dbang gis rgyud kyi rgyal po thams cad la rdo rje'i tshig tu sbas te bzhi pa de yang de bzhin no zhes de bzhin gshegs pas gsungs pa'i phyir ro/[97] / bzhi pa ni gsum pa ma yin te bzhi pa zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / de yang de bzhin no zhes gsungs pa'i phyir shes rab ye shes de nyid bzhi par 'gyur ro/ / bcom ldan 'das kyi gsung 'di'i phyir rdo rje'i tshig tu sbas pa yin no/ / rgyud kyi rgyal po thams cad la rdo rje'i tshig rab tu gsal ba ma yin zhing bla ma brgyud pa'i rim pas rtogs par bya ba yin te rgyud ni rgyud gzhan dag gis rtogs par bya zhes de bzhin gshegs pas gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / zhes gsang ba 'dus pa sogs sbas rgyud rnams su dbang bzhi pas mtshon pa'i zab don sbas par bshad nas

The thinking of the hidden tantras has been explained by the commentaries of the mahāsiddhas of India and by the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries, and you should not use one to refute the other, nor make the mistake of thinking that similar terms in their respective presentations have similar meanings. Tantras that teach the paths of the generation and completion stages in an open and unconcealed way include the Root Kālacakra Tantra and Condensed Kālacakra Tantra. The Great Commentary says in the second summary of the Realms chapter:
The Vajra Vehicle, in accord with the mentality of sentient beings, lies hidden within the vajra words in the King of Tantras. The Tathāgata said, “The fourth also is likewise.”[131] The fourth is not the third and therefore is called the fourth. “Also is likewise” means that the wisdom-knowledge[132] itself becomes the fourth. Because of these words of the Conqueror, it lies hidden within the vajra words. In the King of Tantras the vajra words are not clear. They will be understood through the transmission of masters, and tantras will be understood from other tantras. This the Tathāgata has said.[133] /46/ This passage says that in hidden tantras such as the Guhyasamāja, profound meanings, as illustrated by the fourth initiation, are explained in a concealed fashion.

d.div: [97] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 16_na7
[131] From the Guhyasamāja.
[132] The third initiation.
[133] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 16a7.

f.d:
de'i mjug thog nyid du/
dang po'i sangs rgyas 'di la rdo rje'i tshig de dag nyid rab tu gsal bar bstan pa dang bshad pa dang rab tu bshad pa dag gis bcom ldan 'das kyis gsal bar mdzad do/ / 'di nyid sgrub pa la phyag rgya chen po sgom pa du ba la sogs pa mtshan ma'i lam rab tu gsal bar mdzad de/
stong par rtse gcig yid byas te/ / nyi ma gcig ni yongs su brtag/ces pas so/ / bcom ldan 'das kyi gsung 'di'i phyir mchog gi dang po'i sangs rgyas la rdo rje'i tshig phyag rgya chen po sgom pa'i lam du ba la sogs pa rab tu gsal ba yin gyi bla ma brgyud pa'i rim pas 'ongs pa ma yin la/ bla ma'i bkas byin gyis brlabs pa yang ma yin no/[98] / zhes sbas rgyud rnams su sbas pa'i zab don dang po'i sangs rgyas rtsa rgyud dang bsdus rgyud du rtsa bshad sbyar nas 'chad pa'i bla ma'i man ngag la ltos mi dgos par gsal bar bshad par gsungs pas so/ /

The quote continues:
Here in the Original Buddha, the Conqueror, has clarified those very vajra words by very clearly teaching, explaining, and well explaining. As proof of that, the signs of smoke and so forth on the path of mahāmudrā meditation are clarified.
“Focus single pointedly upon the emptiness, and meditate for a whole day.”[134] Because of these words of the Conqueror, vajra words within the Supreme Original Buddha, such as those which teach the signs of smoke on the path of the mahāmudrā meditation, are very clear and arise neither through the transmission of masters nor by the blessing of the masters.[135] Therefore the profound meanings concealed in the hidden tantras are explained clearly in the Original Buddha Root Tantra and Condensed Tantra, and it is not necessary to rely upon the explanations of masters that apply explanatory tantra to root tantra.

d.div: [98] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 16_ba3
[135] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 16b3.

f.d: de ltar na bla med kyi rgyud kyi dgongs pa 'grel tshul mdor bsdus pa tsam zhig brjod zin to// //
This has been just a brief chapter on how the thinking of the highest yoga tantras is explained. /47/
le'u dang po/ khams kyi le'u/
Part 1. The External World
3. The Three Themes of Kālacakra Tantra
bzhi pa skabs su bab pa dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i brjod bya phyi nang gzhan gsum bshad pa

d.i: An exposition of the Outer, Inner, and Other: The three themes of Kālacakra

f.d: ['di ]la gsum/ phyi nang gzhan gsum gyi grangs nges bshad pa dang / go rim bshad pa dang / phyi nang gzhan gsum so so'i rang bzhin bshad pa'o/ /
This has three outlines: 1. Ascertaining the number of themes 2. The order of the themes 3. The characteristics of each
dang po [phyi nang gzhan gsum gyi grangs nges dang /]ni

mdor bsdus gnyis pa'i 'grel chen las/
'dir rdul phra rab 'dus pa sngon du 'gro ba ni 'jig rten gyi khams so/ / 'jig rten gyi khams sngon du 'gro ba ni sems can rnams so/ / sems can sngon du 'gro ba ni 'jig rten dang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i mngon par dbang bskur ba'o/ / mngon par dbang bskur ba mngon du 'gro ba ni bsod nams kyi tshogs dkyil 'khor gyi 'khor lo sgom pa goms pas 'og min gyi srid pa'i mthar thug pa 'jig rten pa'i dngos grub sgrub pa'o/ / 'jig rten pa'i dngos grub sngon du 'gro ba ni bsod nams dang ye shes kyi tshogs dag ste skye ba snga ma'i stong pa nyid dang snying rje kun rdzob dang dmigs pa med pa'i bag chags kyi stobs kyis rdul phra rab 'dus pa las 'das shing dkyil 'khor la sogs pa rnam par rtog pa'i sgom pa dang bral ba phyag rgya chen po'i ye shes kyi dngos grub sgrub pa'o/[1] / zhes gsungs pa 'dis phyi nang gzhan gsum gyi grangs nges dang go rim gnyis ka bstan to/ /

The Great Commentary, in the second summary of the Realms chapter, states:
The coming together of the subtle particles is a prerequisite for the existence of a world realm. A world realm is a precondition for sentient beings. Sentient beings are preconditions for worldly and nonworldly initiations. Worldly and nonworldly initiations are preconditions for the attainment of worldly siddhi up to the ultimate existence of None Higher[1] by meditating upon the mandalas and gathering merit. With worldly siddhi as a precondition, and by wisdom, merit, and the force of predispositions of emptiness and compassion — conventional and non-apprehended — from previous lives, the collection of subtle particles is transcended and conceptual meditation upon the mandalas and so forth disappears, resulting in the siddhi of gnosis of mahāmudrā.[2] This passage ascertains both the number of themes and their order.

d.div: [1] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 9_na6
[1] ‘og min, akaniṣṭha. The highest of the four form realms.
[2] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 9a6.

f.d: de yang ji ltar bstan na/ dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsa rgyud bsdus rgyud kyi bstan bya'i gtso bo ni dus gyi 'khor lo'i ched du bya ba'i gdul bya'i gtso bos nyams su len pa'i lam gyi cha rkyen rnams yin la/ de lta bu'i lam nyams su len pa'i lam gyi cha rkyen de la gang sbyang par bya ba'i lam gyi sbyang gzhi dang / de sbyong bar byed pa'i lam dang / de ltar sbyangs pa'i 'bras bu dang gsum du grangs nges la/ lam gyi sbyang gzhi de la yang phyi snod kyi 'jig rten dang / nang bcud kyi sems can gnyis su nges shing / de sbyong bar byed pa'i lam de la yang lam de'i snod rung du byed pa'i dbang bskur ba dang / sbyang gzhi ma dag pa'i cha mngon gyur mgo gnon zhing sa bon drungs nas 'byin pa'i rdzogs rim skye ba'i rgyud smin byed bskyed rim gyi lam dang / sbyang gzhi'i ma dag pa'i cha rtsa ba nas 'byin pa'i rdzogs rim gyi lam dang gsum du nges shing / de lta bu'i dbang dang bskyed rdzogs kyi lam rnams dang de ltar nyams su blangs pa'i 'bras bu rnams phyi nang gzhan gsum gyi nang tshan gyi gzhan du 'du bas so/ /

How is this done? The main topics of the Root Tantra and Condensed Tantra are the necessary conditions for the path of practice of the primary intended disciples of Kālacakra. Three necessary conditions for the practice of such a path can be ascertained. They are: a basis for the path of practice, the actual path of practice, and the result of practice. The basis for the path to be practiced is ascertained as the external world and the sentient beings of the world. The actual path of practice is ascertained as the bestowing of initiation in order /48/ to create suitable vessels for that path, followed secondly by the generation stage, which suppresses the manifest impurity of the basis for practice and ripens the mind for the creation of the completion stage that will totally uproot this impurity. Thirdly, the completion stage eradicates forever the impurities of the basis for practice. The paths of these initiations and of the generation and completion stages along with the results of their practices fall under the heading of “other” within the three topics of Outer, Inner, and Other.

dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i ched du bya ba'i gdul bya'i gtso bo'i lam gyi cha rkyen la phyi nang gzhan gsum po der nges pa la dgongs nas rgyud kyi le'u yang rnam pa lngar nges par mdzad pa yin te/ de yang sbyang gzhi phyi snod kyi 'jig rten gtso bor gtan la 'bebs pa 'jig rten khams le dang / de bzhin du sbyang gzhi nang bcud kyi sems can gtso bor gtan la 'bebs pa nang gi le'u dang / gzhan la 'khor dang bcas na dbang bskur ba dang lam bskyed rdzogs gnyis dang 'bras bu mthar thug pa dang bzhir byas pa'i dbang bskur ba gtso bor gtan la 'bebs pa dbang gi le'u dang / bskyed rim gtso bo dang rdzogs rim gyi cha 'ga' zhig gtan la 'bebs pa sgrub thabs kyi le'u dang / rdzogs rim dang 'bras bu'i gnas skabs gtso bor gtan la 'bebs pa ye shes le'u dang lngar mdzad pa yin no/ /

The necessary conditions for the path of the intended disciples of the Śrī Kālacakra are therefore ascertained as being the Outer, Inner, and Other, and with these in mind the chapters of the tantra are set at five. The Realms chapter mainly establishes the basis for practice in its form of the external world, while the Inner chapter mainly establishes the basis for practice in its form of the individual person. The Other, alongside its ancillary topics, comprises the conferring of initiations, the two paths of generation and completion, and the final goal. Of these, the conferring of initiations is mainly taught in the Initiation chapter. The Methods of Accomplishment chapter mainly establishes the generation stage as well as some aspects of the completion stage. The Gnosis chapter mainly establishes the completion stage and the stage of the final fruits of practice.
gnyis pa phyi nang gzhan gsum gyi go rim bshad pa
['di ]la gnyis/ shes bya gshis la gnas pa'i go rim dang lam nyams su len tshul la ltos pa'i go rim mo/ /
This has two outlines: 1. A natural order 2. An order arising from the mode of practice
dang po [gshis la gnas pa'i go rim ]ni

gong du drangs pa'i 'dir rdul phra rab 'dus pa sngon du 'gro ba ni zhes sogs kyi dngos kyi bstan don te snod kyi 'jig rten ni rdul phra rab 'dus pa sngon du 'gro ba can yin te/ snod kyi 'jig rten snga ma zhig nas stong pa'i rdul gyi ming can rdul phra rab sil bur gnas pa rnams 'dus pa las rlung gi dkyil 'khor nas gling dang ri rab sogs kyi bar rim gyis chags dgos pa'i phyir ro/ / bcud kyi sems can rnams ni stong gi 'jig rten gyi khams chags pa sngon du 'gro dgos pa can yin te/ sngon du sems can gang du gnas pa'i gnas snod chags te de'i rjes su der gnas pa'i sems can grub nas gnas pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

The sentence that begins, “The coming together of the subtle particles” from the above passage says that the external world is preceded by the coming together of subtle particles. This is because the destruction of a previous world brought about these subtle particles, which are known as empty particles and which exist as isolated fragments. Their coming together creates a physical world from the air mandala up to Meru. This is the intermediate stage of creation. Sentient beings must be preceded by a previously created world realm, because a place for inhabitation is created first and is followed by the sentient beings who become its inhabitants. /49/

gzhan la dbang dang bskyed rdzogs 'bras bu dang bcas pa rnams su nges pa las 'jig rten dang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i dbang bskur ba la sems can sngon du 'gro dgos te/ dbang bskur ba la gang la dbang bskur ba'i slob ma dang gang gis dbang bskur ba'i slob dpon sogs sngon du grub dgos pa'i phyir ro/ / gtso bor gzugs sku'i rigs 'dra'i rgyur gyur pa'i gzhan bskyed rim gyi sngon du dbang bskur ba 'gro dgos te/ dkyil 'khor du 'jug nas dbang bskur ba mtshan nyid dang ldan pa ma thob na bskyed pa'i rim pa sgom pa'i snod du mi rung ba'i phyir ro/ /

The chapters that make up the Other are ascertained as those that teach initiations, the generation and completion stages, and the final result. The bestowing of worldly and nonworldly initiations must be preceded by sentient beings, because there must be disciples on whom the initiations are bestowed and masters who bestow them. The Other is primarily a similar-type cause of the form body of a buddha, and within it the generation stage is necessarily preceded by the bestowal of initiation, because those who enter the mandala without proper initiation will not become suitable vessels for the meditations of the generation stage.

rnam par rtog pa'i sgom pa dang bral ba phyag rgya chen po'i ye shes kyi dngos grub sgrub pa rdzogs pa'i rim pa ni bskyed rim mthar phyin pa sngon du 'gro ba can yin te/ bskyed rim mthar phyin pas rgyud smin par byed pa'i smin lam sngon du ma song bar grol lam rdzogs pa'i rim pa mtshan nyid tshang ba mi skye ba'i phyir ro/ / de ltar na shes bya'i gshis la de ltar du gnas pas rgyud kyi rgyal pos kyang le'u lngas phyi nang gzhan gsum rim pa de ltar du bshad pa yin no/ /

The completion stage, which results in the attainment of the siddhi of mahāmudrā gnosis freed from all conceptual meditation, has to be preceded by the accomplishment of the generation stage, because the completed generation stage ripens the mindstream, and without the path of ripening, the path of freedom — of a complete and proper completion stage — will not be developed. Therefore, as this is the natural order of things, this king of tantras in its five chapters sets out the outer, inner, and other in that order.
gnyis pa lam nyams su len tshul la ltos pa'i go rim ni/

d.i: An order arising from the mode of practice

f.d: rgyud 'di'i ched du bya ba'i gdul byas bskyed rdzogs kyi lam nyams su len pa'i sngon du lam gyi sbyang gzhi phyi nang gnyis shes dgos pas dang por gtan la 'bebs dgos/ de gnyis kyi nang phyi 'jig rten gyi khams zhib par bshad nas de shes pa sngon du btang ste de dang chos mthun pa'i sgo nas nang sems can gyi 'jig rten shes dgos pa yin te/ ji ltar phyi rol de bzhin nang /[2] /zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ / de gnyis shes pa sngon du btang ste gzhan bskyed rdzogs kyi lam nyams su len pa la yang de gnyis kyi snod rung du bsgrub pa'i don du dbang mtshan nyi+id dang ldan pa bskur ba dgos pas phyi nang gnyis kyi rjes su dbang bskur ba dang / de'i rjes su rdzogs rim skye ba'i rgyud smin byed du bskyed pa'i rim pa dang / de ltar bskyed rim gyis rgyud smin par byas pa las rdzogs rim dang / bskyed rdzogs nyams su blangs pa'i 'bras bur sku gnyis la sogs pa 'byung bas

Before practicing the paths of generation and completion, the intended disciples of this tantra must know the external and internal bases of practice. These, therefore, are ascertained first. The world external to oneself should be understood from an extensive explanation, and then the corresponding inner world of sentient beings should be understood. As the Tantra says: “As without, so within.”[3] With these two bases of practice as prerequisites, one must become a suitable vessel for the two Other paths of the generation and completion stages through the process of proper initiation. Therefore, after the Outer and the Inner comes conferral of initiation. This is followed by the generation stage to ripen the mindstream for the inception of the completion stage. After the mindstream has been suitably ripened, the completion stage is practiced. The results of practicing these stages are the two bodies of a buddha.

d.div: [2] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 60_na1
[3] Found in the Great Commentary, but probably in the Root Tantra also; Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 60a1.

f.d:
phyi nang gzhan gsum dang / gzhan gyi'ang dbang bskyed rdzogs de dag gi 'bras bu rnams kyi go rim de ltar du nges pa yin zhing de la dgongs nas khams le'i mdor bsdus gnyis pa las/
de bas na dang por 'jig rten gyi khams kyi brtag pa dang de nas nang gi brtag pa dang de nas dbang bskur ba'i brtag pa dang de nas 'jig rten pa'i dngos grub sgrub pa'i brtag pa dang de nas mchog tu mi 'gyur ba'i ye shes sgrub pa'i brtag pa ste/ de ltar na rim pa ji lta ba bzhin rgyud kyi rgyal po ni brtag pa lnga 'am le'u lnga'i bdag nyid do/[3] / zhes rgyud kyi brjod bya don gyi le'u lnga dang / de ston byed tshig gi le'u yang lngar gsungs pa yin no/ /

Therefore the order of Outer, Inner, and Other, and within Other, the order of initiation, generation stage, completion stage, and their fruits, are ascertained in this way. With this in mind the second summary in the Realms chapter states: /50/
Therefore first is the section on the realms of the world. Then comes the section on the inner, then the section on initiation, then the section on the attainment of worldly powers, then the section on the accomplishment of supreme unchanging gnosis. In this way the king of tantras is ordered in five sections or chapters.[4] Thus the topics of the tantra are in divided into five sections, and the text that teaches them is also of five sections.

d.div: [3] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 9_ba1
[4] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 9b1.

f.d: gsum pa phyi nang gzhan gsum so so'i rang bzhin bshad pa
['di ]la gsum/ phyi 'jig rten gyi khams kyi rnam gzhag bshad pa dang / nang sems can gyi 'jig rten bshad pa dang / gzhan dbang dang bskyed rdzogs 'bras bu dang bcas pa'i rnam gzhag bshad pa'o/ /

This has three outlines: 1. Presentation of the external world 2. Explanation of the inner, the world of sentient beings 3. Presentation of the other: initiations, generation stage, completion stage, and fruits.
dang po [phyi 'jig rten gyi khams kyi rnam gzhag ]

['di ]la snod 'chag pa'i rim pa tshad dang bcas pa bshad pa dang / der gnas pa'i bcud kyi sems can spyi'i rnam gzhag bshad pa dang / sa'i steng du lhun po la 'khor ba'i go la'i rnam gzhag bshad pa dang / 'dir snod bcud kyi 'jig rten gyi rnam gzhag bshad pa mngon pa'i sde snod dang 'gal ba spang ba'o/ /

This is under four headings: 1. The formation of the external world and its dimensions 2. A general presentation of the inhabitants of this world 3. The gola circling Mount Meru above the Earth 4. Resolving any contradictions between the presentation of the world in the Kālacakra and that of the Abhidharma texts
dang po [snod 'chag pa'i rim pa tshad dang bcas pa bshad pa ]ni
4. The Formation of the External World and Its Dimensions

snod kyi 'jig rten snga ma cig zhig nas stong par gnas pa'i tshe sa'i khams dri dang gzugs dang ro dang reg bya dang sgra ste yon tan lnga'i bdag nyid can dang / chu'i khams dri ma gtogs pa'i yon tan bzhi ldan dang / me'i khams dri dang gzugs ma gtogs pa'i yon tan gsum ldan dang / rlung gi khams dri dang gzugs dang ro ma gtogs pa'i yon tan gnyis ldan dang / nam mkha'i khams sgra'i yon tan gcig pu dang ldan pa ste

When a world undergoes destruction, there follows a time of emptiness. During this time the earth element is possessed of five qualities, namely smell, form, taste, tangibility, and sound. The water element has the above qualities, minus that of smell. The fire element has the above qualities, minus smell and form. The air element has the two qualities of tangibility and sound, while the space element possesses only the quality of sound. /51/

de lta bu'i khams lnga'i rdul phra rab sil bur gnas pa 'jig rten pa'i tha snyad kyi mig la sogs pa'i dbang po rnams kyi spyod yul ma yin pa stong pa'i rdul zhes ming gis bsnyad pa rnams nam mkha' stong pa la so sor gnas pa las/ 'jig rten 'chags pa'i sems can spyi mthun gyi las kyi nus pa smin pa'i dus kyi dbang gis dang por rlung gi rdul phra rab rnams phan tshun 'dabs 'byar bar gyur te/ de ltar 'byar ba las yang zhing g.yo ba'i rlung du 'gyur ro/ / 'dis sbas don gyi rlung ches phra ba yang shes nus gsung ngo / /

During this time of emptiness the subtle particles of these five elements exist as isolated fragments and are not in any conventional sense objects of the sensory powers of the eye and so forth. They are known as empty particles and remain isolated in empty space. When the potential of the collective karma of sentient beings is ripened, the subtle air particles come together to form air whose nature is light and moving. It is said that by this process we can come to know of extremely subtle and hidden airs.

de bzhin du ma'i rdul phra rab rnams 'dabs 'byar du gyur pa las rlung dang ldan pa'i glog gi rnam pa lta bu'i mer 'gyur ro/ / de bzhin du chu'i rdul phra rab rnams 'dabs 'byar du gyur pa las rlung dang me dang ldan pa'i char gyi rnam pa lta bu'i chur 'gyur ro/ / de bzhin du sa'i rdul phra rab rnams 'dabs 'byar du gyur pa las rlung dang me dang chu dang ldan pa'i dbang po'i gzhu'i rnam pa lta bu'i sar 'gyur ro/ / ro 'am nam mkha'i khams kyi rdul phra rab rnams ni 'byung ba'i khams gzhan bzhi po thams cad la khyab byed du gnas pa yin zhing / 'di'i nam mkha'i khams zhes pa ni 'dus ma byas kyi nam mkha' ma yin gyi/ gzugs can gzhan gyi go 'byed pa'i nam mkha' 'dus byas shig yin no/ /

Similarly the subtle fire particles come together to become forms of fire, such as lightning possessed of air. The subtle water particles also amass to become forms of water, such as rain possessed of air and fire. The earth particles amass to become forms of earth, such as a rainbow possessed of air, fire, and water. The particles of the “taste” or space element pervade the other four source elements. This particular element of space is not unformed space but a formed space, whose presence separates forms from one another.

de lta bu'i sa chu me rlung bzhi po rim gyis 'phel ba las 'og gzhi'i rlung me chu sa'i dkyil 'khor bzhir gyur pa'i dkyil 'khor bzhi pa'i mthug rngams kyi tshad stong phrag lnga bcu lnga bcur mnyam zhing 'og nas rim pa bzhin rlung me chu sa'i dkyil 'khor brtsegs nas gnas so/ / de yang 'og ma rnams kyi steng du steng ma rnams bre nang du bre chung ba'i tshul gyis gnas pa/ de yang dkyil 'khor bzhi ga'i steng gi cha kha da chang [4] du gnas pa'i sa'i dbus nas sa'i mtha' bar la dpag tshad stong phrag lnga bcu/ de bzhin du dkyil 'khor gzhan gsum gyi'ang rang rang gi nang mtha' nas phyi mtha'i bar gyi tshad stong phrag lnga bcu lnga bcu ste rang rang gi mthug rngams nyid do/ / yang sa'i dkyil 'khor gyi phyi mtha' gcig nas phyi mtha' cig shos kyi bar gyi tshad dpag tshad 'bum phrag gcig dang chu'i dkyil 'khor gyi phyi mtha' nas phyi mtha' cig shos kyi bar kyi tshad dpag tshad 'bum phrag gnyis dang / de bzhin du me'i phyi mtha' nas phyi mtha' cig shos kyi bar gyi tshad dpag tshad 'bum phrag gsum dang / rlung gi phyi mtha' nas phyi mtha' cig shos kyi bar gyi tshad ni dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi yin no/ /

These four elements gradually expand to form the four foundation mandalas — of air, fire, water, and earth — whose individual thicknesses are fifty thousand yojana and which are stacked as air surmounted by fire, water, and then earth. The manner in which they are stacked is akin to smaller measuring cups successively stacked into larger ones. The upper surfaces of each mandala are similar in that the distance from the center of the earth mandala to its rim is fifty thousand yojana and likewise the exposed distance from the inner rim to the outer rim of the other three is also fifty thousand yojana. The thickness of each mandala is also fifty thousand yojana. The distance from rim to rim of the earth mandala is one hundred thousand yojana. The diameter of the water mandala is two hundred thousand yojana, that of the fire mandala three hundred thousand yojana, and that of the air mandala four hundred thousand yojana. /52/

d.div: [4] da chad yin nam snyam/

f.d: de nas dkyil 'khor bzhi po chags pa'i rjes su mi ltung bar 'dzin par byed pa dang srub pa dang dbyibs su byed pa'i rlung gi mthu las lhun po la sogs pa'i ri dang gling la sogs pa rnams grub 'ong ste/ de yang sa'i dkyil 'khor gyi dbus su lhun po dpangs su dpag tshad 'bum phrag gcig pa can/ de'i steng du bar snang stong par snang ba'i yid gzugs kyi rnam pa la lhun po'i mgrin pa dang gdong dang gtsug tor gyi tha snyad byas pa'i mgrin pa la dpag tshad stong phrag nyi shu rtsa lnga/ gdong la lnga bcu/ gtsug tor la nyer lnga ste mgrin pa'i 'og gi mtha' nas gtsug tor gyi mtha'i bar la dpag tshad 'bum phrag gcig ste lhun po'i rtsa ba nas gtsug tor gyi rtse mo'i bar gyi tshad dpag tshad 'bum phrag gnyis so/ /

After the four mandalas have formed, winds that support, churn up, and shape, bring about the formation of Meru, the other mountains, and the continents. Standing in the center of the earth mandala, Meru rises to a height of one hundred thousand yojana. Above its summit, in empty space and in the aspect of “mental form,” are Meru’s so-called neck, face, and crown. The height of the neck is twenty-five thousand yojana, the face fifty thousand yojana, and the crown twenty-five thousand yojana, making a distance of one hundred thousand yojana from the base of the throat to the top of the crown. Therefore the base of Meru to the top of the crown is two hundred thousand yojana.

yang lhun po'i rtsa ba'i sa'i dkyil 'khor gyi dbus nas lhun po'i rtsa ba'i shar mtha' lta bu'i phyogs kyi mtha' rnams kyi bar la dpag tshad stong phrag brgyad brgyad de mtha' gcig nas mtha' cig shos kyi bar la dpag tshad stong phrag bcu drug dang / de nas lhun po la zlum por bskor ba'i khor yug dpag tshad stong phrag gcig/de nas bsil ri'i mtha'i steng gi bar du lhun po'i kha khyer gyis khyab pa'i khongs kyi rgyar dpag tshad stong phrag bcu drug yod pa'i 'og gi sa'i dkyil 'khor gyi stong cha mnyam pa bco brgyad du byas pa'i cha re la gling drug mtsho drug ri drug spel te gnas pa'i gling drug ni nang nas rim pa bzhin zla ba dang / 'od dkar dang / rab mchog ku sha dang / mi 'am ci dang / khrung khrung dang / drag po'i gling zhes pa'i ming gis bsnyad pa drug go/ /

The distance from the center of the earth mandala on which Meru stands to any of the four cardinal points of the base of Meru, such as the eastern edge for example, is eight thousand yojana. Therefore, at its base, Meru is sixteen thousand yojana across. Surrounding Meru is a circular area extending outward for a distance of a thousand yojana. Beyond this circular area is an area stretching out to the edge of the Śīta Mountains for a distance of sixteen thousand yojana. This distance is the limit of the overhang of the summit of Meru.[5] This particular area on the earth-mandala surface is divided into eighteen regions. Six continents, six seas, and six mountain ranges make up these regions. From the inner to the outer, the six continents are Candra, Sitābha, Kuśa, Kiṃnara, Krauñca, and Rudra.

d.div: [5] Meru widens out to a summit of fifty yojana diameter, which is the diameter of the circle formed by the Śīta Mountains.

f.d: mtsho drug ni nang nas rim pa bzhin sbrang rtsi dang / mar dang / zho dang / 'o ma dang / chu dang / chang gi rgya mtsho'i ming gis bsnyad pa drug go/ / ri drug ni nang nas rim pa bzhin 'od sngon dang / man da ra dang / niSha Ta dang / nor bu'i 'od dang / dro Na dang / bsil ri zhes bya ba'i ming gis bsnyad pa drug go/ / de yang lhun po'i 'gram stegs sam khor yug dang 'dabs chags par zla ba'i gling / de dang 'dabs chags par sbrang rtsi'i rgya mtsho/ de yang 'dabs chags par 'od sngon gyi ri ste/ de bzhin du gling dang rgya mtsho dang ri gzhan rnams kyang spel nas gnas pa yin no/ /

The six seas, from the inner to the outer, are known as Honey, Butter, Curd, Milk, Water, and Wine. The six mountain ranges, from the inner to the outer, are known as Nīlābha, Mandara, Niṣaṭha, Maṇikara, Droṇa, and Śīta. The continent of Candra borders the terraces or immediate environs of Meru. Bordering the continent is the Honey Sea, and bordering the sea are the Nīlābha Mountains. /53/ Likewise, the other continents, seas, and mountains are similarly arranged.

'od sngon sogs ri nang gi lnga po yang bsil ri dang mtho dman mnyam zhing gling drug ri drug mtsho drug po thams cad kyang zheng tshad mnyam ste/ de yang zla ba'i gling gi nang mtha' nas bsil ri'i phyi mtha'i bar la dpag tshad stong phrag bcu drug yod pa la ri gling mtsho dang bcas pa'i grangs bco brgyad kyis bgos pas dpag tshad brgyad brgya dang brgyad cu rtsa brgyad rgyang grags gsum gzhu 'dom stong dang brgya bcu gcig sor bcu lhag tsam (zhib par na sor gyi rjes su nas lnga nas kyi sum cha gcig 'thog /)re 'thob ste ri gling sogs re re'i zheng tshad do/ /

The five inner mountains are of the same height as the Śīta Mountains, and all six continents, seas, and mountains are of the same width. From the inner edge of the continent of Candra to the outer edge of the Śīta Mountains is a distance of sixteen thousand yojana. As there are six mountain ranges, six continents, and six seas, this distance is to be divided by eighteen. This gives a figure of 888 yojana, three krośa, 1111 armspans, and ten fingerwidths. (To be even more detailed, 5 1/30 barley seeds should be added.) That is the width of each mountain range, continent, and sea.

de nas bsil ri'i phyi mtha' nas chu'i dkyil 'khor gyi nang mtha'i bar la dpag tshad stong phrag nyi shu rtsa lnga yod pa'i sa'i dkyil 'khor gyi cha ni gling bdun pa 'dzam gling chen po las kyi sa zhes bya zhing / de la lhun po'i phyogs mtshams su cha bcu gnyis su phye ba ni sa dum bu bcu gnyis sam gling bcu gnyis so/ / de'i phyi rol gyi chu'i dkyil 'khor la rgya mtsho bdun pa lan tshwa'i rgya mtsho dang / de'i phyi rol gyi me'i dkyil 'khor la ri bdun pa rdo rje'i ri dang rta gdong gi me zhes bya zhing / bsil ri nas chu'i dkyil 'khor gyi bar gyi sa dum bu bcu gnyis kyi khyon la dpag tshad stong phrag nyer lnga yod pa'i phyed nang ma'i dpag tshad stong phrag phyed dang bcu gsum gyi sa'i cha la lho byang du dum bu drug tu byas pa'i cha rnams gangs ldan/ ke la shargya nagali/ bod/ 'phags yul te yul drug dang / de rnams dang khyon mtshungs kyi sa'i cha sa dum bu bcu gcig rnams su yang shes par bya'o/ /

From the outer limit of the Śīta Mountains to the inner rim of the water mandala is a distance of twenty-five thousand yojana. This area of the earth mandala is the seventh continent known as Greater Jambudvīpa, the realm of karma. Directionally from Meru it is divided into twelve parts, known as the twelve sectors or continents.[6] Outside of this, on the water mandala, is the seventh sea known as the Salt Ocean. Outside of this sea and on the fire mandala is the seventh mountain range, known as the Vajra Mountains, and the Fire of the Wild Mare’s Face.[7] The area of the twelve sectors stretches from the Śīta Mountains to the water mandala for a distance of twenty-five thousand yojana. Its 12,500-yojana inner half is divided into six regions. In Lesser Jambudvīpa these are the lands of Himālaya, Kailash, China, Khotan, Tibet, and India. Regions of similar size also exist on the other eleven sectors.

d.div: [6] The lands of Greater Jambudvīpa are called “sectors” (dum bu), as it is a land divided into twelve equal sectors, like a giant cake. Greater Jambudvīpa itself and the six lands stretching out from Meru are continents, or islands (gling).
[7] rta gdong gi me, vāḍavāgni.

f.d: de yang lhun po'i khor yug gam 'gram stegs nas rlung gi dkyil 'khor gyi bar gyi ri gling mtsho la sogs pa thams cad kyang lhun po la bskor ba'i tshul gyis zlum po'i rnam par gnas pa'i zlum skor gyi rgya khyon gyi tshad ni rang rang gi thad ka'i tshad sum 'gyur du 'ong ba rten 'brel gyi chos nyid yin pas rlung gi dkyil 'khor gyi thad ka'i tshad dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi'i sum 'gyur dpag tshad 'bum phrag bcu gnyis rlung gi dkyil 'khor gyi mtha' kun nas zlum po'i tshad dang / me'i dkyil 'khor gyi thad ka'i tshad dpag tshad 'bum phrag gsum gyi sum 'gyur dpag tshad 'bum phrag dgu dang / de bzhin du gzhan rnams la yang de'i rigs pas dpags nas shes par bya'o/ /

The mountains, continents, seas, and so forth that stretch out from the terraces or environs of Meru as far as the air mandala are in the forms of discs encircling Meru. Each is bound by a circumference that is three times its diameter.[8] Therefore, three times the 400,000-yojana diameter of the air mandala is 1,200,000 yojana. This is the circumference of the air mandala. Three times the 300,000-yojana diameter fire mandala is 900,000 yojana. By using the same calculations for the other mandalas, the circumference of each can be known. /54/

d.div: [8] An approximation of the value of pi.

f.d: de yang rlung gi dkyil 'khor nas lhun po'i gtsug tor gyi bar la srid pa sum cu rtsa gcig gi gnas yod te/ de yang rlung gi dkyil 'khor la dpag tshad stong phrag lnga bcu yod pa'i phyed 'og ma'i mtha'i cha la rdo rje'i me lce dang bcas pa'i dmyal ba dang ngu 'bod chen po'i dmyal ba'i gnas gnyis/ phyed steng ma la mun pa chen po'i dmyal ba'i gnas te rlung gi dkyil 'khor la dmyal ba'i gnas gsum dang / de bzhin du me'i dkyil 'khor gyi phyed 'og ma la me'i dmyal ba dang / phyed steng ma la du ba mi bzad pa'i dmyal ba ste tsha ba'i dmyal ba'o/ / de gnyis kyi steng 'og gi tshad kyang dpag tshad stong phrag nyer lnga nyer lnga yin no/ /

Between the air mandala and the crown of Meru are found the thirty-one existences. In the lower half of the 50,000-yojana-deep air mandala are the Vajra Flames hell and the Crying hell. In the upper half lies the Great Darkness hell. The air mandala, therefore, is home to three hell realms. Similarly, in the lower half of the fire mandala is found the Fire hell, and in the upper half is the Endless Smoke hell. These are hot hells, and they each plunge to a depth of twenty-five thousand yojana.

chu'i dkyil 'khor gyi phyed 'og ma la 'dam gyi chu'i dmyal ba dang / phyed steng ma la bye ma'i chu'i dmyal ba'i gnas te de gnyis ni grang ba'i dmyal ba'o/ / de gnyis kyi steng 'og gi tshad kyang dpag tshad stong phrag nyer lnga nyer lnga'o/ / sa'i dkyil 'khor gyi phyed 'og ma la gseg ma'i chu'i dmyal ba dang / phyed steng ma la lha ma yin dang klu'i gnas te de gnyis kyi steng 'og gi tshad kyang dpag tshad stong phrag nyer lnga nyer lnga'o/ / de rnams kyi rgya khyon gyi tshad ni sa'i dkyil 'khor dang tshad mnyam mo/ /

Within the water mandala, the lower half contains the Swamps hell while the upper makes up the Sandy Water hell. These two are cold hells and also fall to a depth of twenty-five thousand yojana. The lower half of the earth mandala contains the Gravel Water hell. The upper half is the home of the asuras and the nāgas. Both these realms are twenty-five thousand yojana from top to bottom, while their widths are coterminus with the earth mandala itself.

de nas sa dum bu bcu gnyis sam gling bcu gnyis po rnams ni mi dang dud 'gro dang yi dwags ci rigs pa'i gnas te yi dwags dang dud 'gro'i gnas kyi khyad par zur pa rgyud 'grel 'dir ma gsungs so/ / de yang sa'i dkyil 'khor 'dzam gling chen po la las kyi sa dang / nang gi gling drug la longs spyod kyi sa zhes bshad do/ /

The twelve sectors can be home for any of the realms of humans, animals, and ghosts. This tantra and its commentaries do not speak of any special abodes for animals and ghosts. Greater Jambudvīpa on the earth mandala is known as the realm of karma, while the six inner continents are known as realms of enjoyment.

gzhan yang 'grel chen las/
sa'i steng du dpag tshad stong phrag rnams ni ri dang klu dang gza' dang phyogs rnams dag tu 'gyur te dkyil 'khor bzhi po 'di rnams kyi dpag tshad kyi tshad ni grangs bzhin du sa'i steng du ri [5] zhes pa stong phrag bdun dang klu zhes pa stong phrag brgyad dang gza' zhes pa stong phrag dgu dang phyogs zhes pa stong phrag bcu ste/ zhes sogs dang /
shar du klung ni shin tu zlum po zhes pa ni shar du rlung gi dkyil 'khor gyi rang bzhin gyi shin tu zlum po ste zla ba nya ba'i rnam pa'o/[6] / zhes sogs kyi don la 'chad tshul mang bar snang yang 'thad pa'i phyogs ni 'di yin te

The Great Commentary says:
“The thousands of yojana upon the earth are of mountains, nāgas, planets, and directions.” This means that the size in yojana of these four mandalas of earth are “mountains,” meaning seven thousand, “nāgas,” meaning eight thousand, “planets,” meaning nine thousand, and “directions,” meaning ten thousand.[9] Again:
“The air in the east is very round.” This means that a characteristic of the air mandala in the east is that it is very round, having the shape of the full moon.[10] There are many ways of explaining the meaning of these and other passages, but the correct way is as follows.

d.div: [5] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 65_na1
[6] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 64_ba6
[9] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 65a1.
[10] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 65b6.

f.d: de yang shar lho byang nub rnams rim pa bzhin rlung me chu sa'i khams pa yin pa'i rten 'brel gyis grub pa shar lus 'phags po'i gling gi dbus kyi sa'i cha dpag tshad stong phrag bdun gyi rgya tshad tsam zhig gi dbyibs zla (zla ba phyed pa'ang zer )ba nya ba'i rnam pa lta bu'i zlum po dang / lho 'dzam bu gling chung ngu 'di'i dbus kyi sa'i cha dpag tshad stong phrag brgyad kyi tshad tsam gru gsum gyi rnam pa dang / byang sgra mi snyan gyi dbus kyi sa'i cha dpag tshad stong phrag dgu'i rgya tshad tsam zhig zlum (zlum po'i rnam pa can yin pa'ang zer )po phyed pa'i rnam pa dang / nub ba lang spyod kyi gling gi dbus kyi sa'i cha dpag tshad stong phrag bcu'i rgya tshad tsam zhig gru bzhi pa ste/ de rnams sa las 'bur du dod ba ma yin gyi de lta bu'i dbyibs sam rnam pa can du yod pa yin no/ /

East, south, north, and west are respectively the realms of /55/ air, fire, water, and earth. Because of this correspondence, the diameter of the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha is about seven thousand yojana, and its shape is circular like the full moon. (It is also described as having the shape of a half moon.)[11] The central mass of the southern continent of Lesser Jambudvīpa has a size of about eight thousand yojana and is triangular in shape. The central mass of the northern continent of Uttarakuru is about nine thousand yojana and is the shape of a half moon. (It is also described as being circular.) The central mass of the western continent of Aparagodānīya is about ten thousand yojana and is square-shaped. These shapes refer to their outline shapes and not to their shapes protruding from the earth.

d.div: [11] This annotation refers to the fact that some translations of the Vimalaprabhā and Condensed Tantra describe the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha as having the shape of a half moon or semicircle. The same applies to the annotation on Uttarakuru below.

f.d: 'dod pa'i lha rnams gnas pa'i gzhi ni 'grel chen las/ lhun po la ni tshig mda' tshangs pa la sogs pa rnams kyi tshogs te [7] zhes pas 'dod lha 'ga' zhig lhun po la gnas pa tsam zhig bstan kyang gnas nges pa can ma gsungs la/

Concerning the gods of the desire realm, the Great Commentary says that “On Meru the gatherings of Indra, Brahmā, and so forth,”[12] thereby merely indicating the abodes of some of the gods of the desire realm, but these are not taught definitively.

d.div: [7] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 65_ba6
[12] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 65b6.

f.d: 'on kyang lha'i dbang po brgya byin 'khor bcas lhun po'i steng na gnas par bya dgos shing / 'dod lha thams cad lhun po dang lhun po'i mgrin pa'i sum cha man chad la yod par bya dgos la/ de ltar na 'dod lha rigs drug gi nang nas gzhan 'phrul dbang byed pa 'phrul dga' ba dga' ldan pa 'thab bral ba rnams steng nas rim pa bzhin lhun po'i mgrin pa'i sum cha man chad la gnas par bya dgos so/ /

However Indra, king of the gods, and his retinue must live on Meru, and gods of the desire realm in their entirety must be posited as being spread throughout Meru and the lower third of the throat of Meru. Therefore it must be that of the six realms of the gods of desire, the four known as Using at Will Creations of Others, Magical Creations at Will, Joyful, and Free of Conflict are stacked upon the lower third of the throat of Meru.

'dod lha bzhi po 'di gnas sar dpangs su dpag tshad sogs ji ltar yod ce na/ ri rab mgrin pa stong phrag nyer lnga'i sum cha 'og ma bzhis bgos pa'i dpag tshad nyis stong gya gsum/ rgyang grags gcigagazhu 'dom drug brgya re drug khru do mtho gang sor bzhi re yod pa/

How high is each of these four realms? A third of the 25,000-yojana throat of Meru divided by four is 2,083 yojana, one krośa, 666 armspans, two cubits, one finger and thumbspan, and four fingerwidths.

'o na 'dod lha 'ga' zhig gnas pa'i rten lhun po'i dbyibs dang kha dog ji lta bu snyam na/ ye shes le'u las/
