f.d: zhes kai la shar lho'i bgrod mtha' las byang gi bgrod mtha' chu tshod drug cu'i drug cha chu tshod bcus nyin mo 'phel zhing mtshan mo 'grib pa dang / 'phags yul bod li rgya nag gi yul rnams su rim pa bzhin chu tshod drug cu'i bcu cha chu tshod drug dang / dgu cha chu tshod drug chu srang bzhi bcu dang / brgyad cha chu tshod bdun chu srang sum cu dang / bdun cha chu tshod brgyad chu srang so bzhi dbugs gcig dbugs kyi bdun cha lnga rnams kyis nyin mo 'phel zhing mtshan mo 'grib par bshad nas/ yul rnams kyi bgrod mtha' nas bgrod mtha' gzhan gyi bar gyi nyin mtshan 'phel 'grib kyi cha gangs ldan gyi chu tshod bcu gnyis dang / kai la sha'i chu tshod bcu dang / rgya nag gi chu tshod brgyad chu srang so bzhi dbugs gcig dbugs kyi bdun cha lnga rnams dang/ li'i chu tshod bdun chu srang sum cu dang / bod kyi chu tshod drug chu srang bzhi bcu dang / 'phags yul gyi chu tshod drug po rnams gnyis kyis bgos te phyed mar byas pa'i phyed phyed nyin mtshan mnyam pa'i nyin mo'i chu tshod sum cu la sbyin zhing / phyed phyed mtshan mo'i chu tshod sum cu la phri bas nyi ma byang bgrod mthar thug gi nyin zhag de'i yul drug po so so'i nyin mo dang mtshan mo'i tshad gong du bshad pa bzhin 'ong ngo / /

Thus, in Kailash, from the limit of the southward passage to the limit of the northward passage, daytime increases and nighttime decreases by a sixth of sixty hours, or ten hours. In the lands of India, Tibet, Khotan, and China, daytime increases and nighttime decreases respectively by a tenth of sixty hours, or six hours; by a ninth, or six hours and forty minutes; by an eighth, or seven hours and thirty minutes; and by a seventh, or eight hours, thirty-four minutes, one breath, and 5/7 of a breath. Therefore the increase and decrease of day and night found from one limit to the other in the six lands is twelve hours in Himālaya; ten hours in Kailash; eight hours, thirty-four minutes, one breath, and 5/7 of a breath in China; seven hours and thirty minutes in Khotan; six hours and forty minutes in Tibet; and six hours in India. These figures are halved, and one half is added to the thirty hours of equinox daytime, and one half is subtracted from the thirty hours of equinox nighttime, to arrive at the above figures for the length of daytime and nighttime on the day of the limit of the sun’s northward journey at each of the six lands.

de yang zhag gi 'phel 'grib 'di bshad ma thag pa ltar nyin zhag nyid kyi 'phel 'grib tu 'chad pa 'grel pa'i dgongs pa yin te/ so brgyad pa'i 'grel chen las/
bgrod pa'i yan lag ni phyed dang bcas pa'i brgyad cu rtsa gnyis lhag pa'i nyin zhag brgya ste bgrod pa'i yan lag nyin zhag de rnams kyi lho phyogs su mtshan mo 'phel bar 'gyur te byang du nyin mo'o/[83] / zhes bgrod mthar nyin mtshan 'phel 'grib rdzogs pa nyin zhag gi grangs kyi steng nas bzhag pa dang / 'phel 'grib kyang nyin re bzhin ngos 'dzin dgos pa'i phyir ro/ /

It is the thinking of the commentary that these increases and decreases in the length of a day as explained here refer to solar days. /107/ The Great Commentary says on the thirty-eighth verse of the Realms chapter:
The stages of the journey are 82 ½ solar days more than a hundred. In the south on these solar days, on the stages of the journey, nighttime increases, while in its north it is the daytime.[162] Therefore the final increase and decrease at the limits of the travels is counted in solar days. Moreover any decrease and increase has to be noted from day to day.

d.div: [83] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 78_na4
[162] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 78a4.

f.d:
'o na khyod kyis gangs ldan du nyin zhag re la chu srang gsum dbugs lnga de'i lnga cha gsum de'i yang sum brgya re lnga cha brgya dang sum cur bshad pa dang / 'grel chen las/
kai la sha'i byang gi cha kha ba can gyi bar du ste nyin zhag so so la dbugs bzhi dang chu srang gsum bgrod pa'i yan lag gis 'phel zhing 'grib bo/[84] / zhes gsungs pa 'gal zhing / de bzhin du khyod kyi kai la shar nyin zhag re'i 'phel 'grib la chu srang gsum dbugs gcig de'i drug cha bzhi sum brgya re lnga cha brgya sum cu dang / 'phags yul gyi nyin zhag re'i 'phel 'grib la chu srang gcig dbugs lnga de'i bcu cha brgyad sum brgya re lnga cha brgya dang sum cu rnams su bshad pa dang /

Some might say, “According to you, the change each day in Himālaya is three minutes, five breaths, 3/5 of a breath, and 130/365 of that again. This contradicts the Great Commentary where it says:
North of Kailash as far as Himālaya, each day the stages of the travel increase and decrease by four breaths and three minutes.[163] “Also for you, in Kailash the increase and decrease for each day is three minutes, one breath, 2/3 of a breath, and 130/365 of that again. In India, according to you, the increase and decrease for each day is one minute, five breaths, 4/5 of a breath, and 130/365 of that again.

d.div: [84] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 78_na4
[163] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 78a4.

f.d:
'grel chen las/
nyin zhag so so la nyin mo dang mtshan mo 'phel ba'am 'grib pa ni dbugs gnyis dang chu srang gsum mo/ / tshad 'di ni kai la sha'i dum bu la yin te [85] zhes pa dang /
'phags pa'i yul du yang nyin mtshan so so la chu srang gnyis 'phel ba'am 'grib par shes par bya ste/ zhes gsungs pa rnams 'gal lo zhe na/

In the Great Commentary it says:
Each day, daytime and nighttime increases or decreases by two breaths and three minutes. This is the measurement for Kailash.[164] “Also:
In India, it should be known that on each day and night there is an increase or decrease of two minutes. “Your assertions, therefore, contradict these quotes.”

d.div: [85] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 90_na7
[164] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 90a7.

f.d: skyon med de/ bdag cag gis bshad pa'i yul drug gi nyin zhag re'i 'phel 'grib rnams ni bgrod pa gnyis mthar thug gi dus kyi bgrod mtha' gcig nas cig shos kyi+i bar gyi nyin mtshan 'phel ba'i char gyur pa'i chu tshod sogs la bgrod mtha' gcig nas cig shos kyi bar gyi nyin zhag gi grangs phyed dang bcas pa'i brgya brgyad cu rtsa gnyis kyis bgos pa'i thob nor skyon med yin pas nyin zhag re'i 'phel 'grib tu 'thad la/ 'grel chen las/ gangs ldan gyi nyin zhag re'i 'phel 'grib la chu srang gsum dang dbugs bzhir [86] gsungs pa ni rags pa'i dbang du mdzad pa dang / kai la shar chu srang gsum dang dbugs gnyis su gsungs pa dang / 'phags yul du chu srang gnyis su gsungs pa ni de gnyis kyi bgrod mtha'i 'phel cha la bgrod mtha' gcig nas cig shos kyi bgrod mtha'i bar gyi khyim zhag gi grangs brgya brgyad cus bgos pa'i rnyed pa kai la sha la chu srang gsum dbugs gnyis dang / 'phags yul du chu srang gnyis 'ong bas bya sla ba la dgongs te gsungs pa yin no/ / de bas na gzhan dag gis 'phags yul nas gangs ldan gyi bar nyin zhag re la dbugs gnyis gnyis kyi bar khyad mdzad pa yod de cir yang mi 'gyur ro/ /

There is no contradiction. The increases and decreases of the solar days in the six lands that we have stated above are divisions of increase and decrease in daytime and nighttime between the limit of one passage and the limit of the other, whose times in hours and so forth are correct figures obtained by dividing by the 182½ solar days that exist between one limit and the other. Therefore they are correct as measurements of daily increase and decrease. The increase and decrease of three minutes and four breaths for each day in Himālaya as mentioned in the Great Commentary is an approximation. Concerning the three minutes and two breaths in Kailash and the two minutes in India, /108/ these increases have been calculated by dividing by the 180 zodiacal days[165] that exist between one limit and the other. This results in three minutes and two breaths in Kailash and two minutes in India. These were taught, therefore, with convenience in mind. Therefore the calculations of those that have led to a chart difference of two breaths each day from India to Himālaya cannot possibly be correct.

d.div: [86] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 83_nanas 90_nabar gzigs/

[165] A house or zodiacal day is the time taken for the sun to traverse a house divided by thirty. As there are twelve houses, so there are 360 house days in a house year. See chapter on the three kinds of days in Gojo, 40ff, and Shawo, chap. 6.

f.d: de ltar spyir bshad nas cir 'gyur lag len du sbyar na/ nyi bar lug khyim du sleb ma thag gi tshe yul drug gi dbus drang por nyin chu tshod sum cu mtshan chu tshod sum cu ste nyin mtshan mnyam par mtshungs pa las/ yul drug po so sor rang rang gi nyin zhag re'i nyin mo'i 'phel ba bsags pa las nyi bar glang khyim du sleb pa'i tshe 'phags yul du chu tshod so gcig /de bzhin du bod du'ang chu tshod so gcig chu srang drug dbugs bzhi/ lir chu tshod so gcig chu srang bco lnga/ rgya nag tu chu tshod so gcig chu srang nyer lnga dbugs bzhi de'i bdun chu gnyis/ kai la shar chu tshod so gcig chu srang bzhi bcu/ gangs ldan du chu tshod so gnyis rnams nyin mo'i tshad yin zhing /

That has been a general explanation. If it is explained astronomically, then at the moment of the mean sun’s arrival in Aries, the days of the six lands at their direct centers are thirty hours long, and the nights are thirty hours long. All six lands thereby share the equinox. From then on individual daytimes in each of the six lands increase in length daily until the mean sun arrives in Taurus, when in India the length of daytime is thirty-one hours. In Tibet it is thirty-one hours, six minutes, and four breaths. In Khotan it is thirty-one hours and fifteen minutes. In China it is thirty-one hours, twenty-five minutes, four breaths, and 2/7 of a breath. In Kailash daytime is thirty-one hours and forty minutes, and in Himālaya it is thirty-two hours.

de bzhin du nyi bar 'khrig pa'i khyim du sleb ma thag gi tshe 'phags yul du chu tshod so gnyis/ bod du chu tshod so gnyis chu srang bcu gsum dbugs gnyis/ lir chu tshod so gnyis chu srang sum cu/ rgya nag chu tshod so gnyis chu srang nga gcig dbugs gnyis de'i bdun cha bzhi/ kai la shar chu tshod so gsum chu srang nyi shu/ gangs ldan du chu tshod so bzhi rnams nyin mo'i tshad do/ / yang nyi ma karka Ta'i khyim du sleb ma thag pa yul drug gi dbus drang por byang bgrod mthar thug pa'i nyin mo'i tshad ni gong du bshad zin pa ltar ro/ /

Likewise, at the moment of the mean sun’s arrival in Gemini, daytime in India is thirty-two hours. In Tibet it is thirty-two hours, thirteen minutes, and two breaths; in Khotan it is thirty-two hours and thirty minutes; in China it is thirty-two hours, fifty-one minutes, two breaths, and 4/7 of a breath. In Kailash it is thirty-three hours and twenty minutes, and in Himālaya it is thirty-four hours. The arrival of the sun in Cancer is the day of its northern limit at the direct center of the six lands, and the length of daytime has been explained previously.

de ltar yul drug so sor nyin mo gcig la yang nyi ma ring thung mi mnyam par 'ong ba'i rgyu mtshan ni nyi ma byang bgrod mthar thug pa'i nyi mo la mtshon nas bstan par bya ste/ de yang yul drug ka'i dbus rnams su nyi bar lug khyim du sleb ma thag gi tshe nyi ma shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi steng thad du sleb pa'i tshe snga dro dang po 'char zhing nub gling dbus ma'i yang tshangs thig gi steng thad du sleb pa'i tshe phyi dro rdzogs par mtshungs pa las/ de nas nyi ma rim gyis byang du bgrod de byang bgrod mthar thug pa'i nyin 'phags yul gyi dbus su shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig las shar du nyi mas chu tshod gcig dang chu srang sum cu la bgrod pa'i khyon tsam du phyin par nyi ma sleb pa na snga dro dang po 'char zhing / nub gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig las nub tu nyi mas chu tshod gcig dang chu srang sum cu la bgrod pa'i khyon tsam du nyi ma sleb pa na phyi dro rdzogs pas shar gyi 'char sa nas 'phags yul gyi dbus drang por nyi ma sleb kyi bar la chu tshod bcu drug dang chu srang sum cu ste snga dro/ de nas nyi ma nub pa'i bar la yang chu tshod bcu drug dang chu srang sum cu ste phyi dro'o/ /de ltar nyin chu tshod so gsum mo/ /

The reasons why, on the same day in each of the six lands, the duration of the sun varies can be explained using the day on which the sun has reached its northern limit as an example. When the sun arrives above the meridian of the central sector of the east at the time of the mean sun arriving in Aries, it is the beginning of morning at the center of the six lands in the central southern sector, and when it arrives above the meridian of the central sector of the west, it is the end of the afternoon. This is true for all six lands. Then the sun moves steadily north until it reaches its northern limit. When the sun on that day arrives at a point one hour and thirty minutes east of the meridian of the central sector of the east, it is the beginning of morning in the center of India. /109/ When the sun arrives at a point one hour thirty minutes west of the meridian of the central sector of the west, it is the end of the afternoon in India. Therefore the time from its rising in the east until it arrives at the direct center of India is sixteen hours and thirty minutes of morning. From then until the sun sets is sixteen hours and thirty minutes of afternoon. This makes thirty-three hours total.

bod kyi dbus su shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig las shar du chu tshod gcig dang chu srang bzhi bcu la bgrod pa'i khyon tsam du nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe snga dro dang po 'char zhing / nub gling dbus ma'i yang tshangs thig las nub tu de mtshungs su sleb pa'i tshe phyi dro rdzogs pas shar gyi 'char sa nas bod kyi dbus drang por nyi ma sleb kyi bar la chu tshod bcu drug dang chu srang bzhi bcu ste snga dro dang / de nas nyi ma nub kyi bar la chu tshod bcu drug dang chu srang bzhi bcu ste phyi dro'o/ /de ltar dril bas bod kyi nyin tshad chu tshod so gsum dang chu srang nyi shu'o/ /

At the center of Tibet, when the sun arrives at a point one hour and forty minutes east of the meridian of the central sector of the east, morning begins. When it arrives at a similar point west of the central sector of the west, afternoon ends. Therefore, from the moment of its appearance until the sun reaches the direct center of Tibet, it is morning, and a total of sixteen hours and forty minutes passes. From then until sunset is afternoon, and a total of sixteen hours and forty minutes also passes. Putting these two sums together, daytime in Tibet becomes thirty-three hours and twenty minutes.

li'i yul dbus su shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig las shar du chu tshod gcig dang chu srang nga gnyis dbugs gsum la bgrod pa'i khyon tsam du nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe snga dro dang po 'char zhing / nub gling dbus ma'i yang tshangs thig las nub tu de mtshungs su nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe phyi dro rdzogs pas shar gyi 'char sa nas li'i dbus drang por nyi ma sleb gyi bar la chu tshod bcu drug chu srang nga gnyis dbugs gsum ste snga dro dang / de nas nyi ma nub pa'i bar la chu tshod sogs kyi grangs de nyid de phyi dro'o/ / snga phyi gnyis bsdoms pas chu tshod so gsum dang chu srang zhe lnga ni de'i dus kyi li'i nyin tshad do|_|

In the center of Khotan, when the sun arrives at a point one hour, fifty-two minutes, and three breaths east of the meridian of the central sector of the east, morning begins, and when the sun arrives at a similar point west of the meridian of central sector of the west, afternoon ends. Therefore, from the point of its rising until the sun reaches the direct center of Khotan, it is morning, and sixteen hours, fifty-two minutes, and three breaths will have passed. From then until sunset is afternoon, and the same number of hours will pass. Morning and afternoon added together make daytime in Khotan, at that particular time, thirty-two hours and forty-five minutes long.

yang rgya nag gi dbus su ni shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig las shar du chu tshod gnyis chu srang brgyad dbugs gsum de'i bdun cha gsum la bgrod pa'i khyon tsam du nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe snga dro dang po 'char zhing / nub gling dbus ma'i yang tshangs thig las nub tu de mtshungs su nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe phyi dro rdzogs pas shar gyi nyi ma 'char sa nas rgya nag gi dbus drang por nyi ma sleb pa'i bar la chu tshod bcu bdun chu srang brgyad dbugs gsum de'i bdun cha gsum ste snga dro dang / de nas nyi ma nub pa'i bar la yang chu tshod sogs grangs de nyid de phyi dro'o/ / snga phyi'i tshad gnyis bsdoms pas chu tshod so bzhi chu srang bcu bdun dbugs thig de'i bdun cha drug rnams ni de'i dus kyi rgya nag gi nyin tshad do/ /

In the center of China, when the sun arrives at a point two hours, eight minutes, three breaths, and 3/7 of a breath east of the meridian of the central sector of the east, morning begins, and when it arrives at a similar point west of the central sector of the west, afternoon ends. Therefore, from the moment of the sun’s rising until it reaches the direct center of China, it is morning, and seventeen hours, eight minutes, three breaths, and 3/7 of a breath will pass. From then until sunset is afternoon, and that same number of hours will pass. Adding together the times of morning and afternoon produces a total of thirty-four hours, seventeen minutes, and 6/7 of a breath. /110/ This is the length of daytime in China at that time.

yang kai la sha'i dbus su ni shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig las shar du chu tshod gnyis dang chu srang sum cu la bgrod pa'i khyon tsam du nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe snga dro dang po 'char zhing / nub gling dbus ma'i yang tshangs thig las nub tu de mtshungs su nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe phyi dro rdzogs pas shar gyi nyi ma 'char sa nas kai la sha'i dbus drang por nyi ma sleb pa'i bar la chu tshod bcu bdun chu srang sum cu ste/ snga dro dang / de nas nyi ma nub pa'i bar la yang chu tshod bcu bdun chu srang sum cu ste phyi dro'o/ / snga phyi'i tshad gnyis bsdoms pas chu tshod so lnga 'ong ba ni byang bgrod mthar thug pa'i nyin gyi kai la sha'i dbus drang po'i nyin tshad do/ /

In the center of Kailash, when the sun arrives at a point two hours and thirty minutes east of the meridian of the central sector of the east, morning begins, and its arrival at a similar point west of the meridian of the central sector of the west marks the end of afternoon. Therefore, from the moment of the sun’s rising in the east until its arrival at the direct center of Kailash, it is morning, and seventeen hours and thirty minutes will pass. From there until it sets, it is afternoon, and seventeen hours and thirty minutes will have passed. The times of morning and afternoon added together come to thirty-five hours, which is the length of daytime when the sun reaches its northern limit at the direct center of Kailash.

gangs ldan gyi dbus su ni shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig las shar du chu tshod gsum la bgrod pa'i khyon tsam du nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe snga dro dang po 'char zhing / nub gling dbus ma'i yang tshangs thig las nub tu chu tshod gsum la bgrod pa'i khyon tsam du nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe phyi dro rdzogs pa'i snga dro dang phyi dro'i tshad rdzogs pa gong bzhin sbyor ba dang / de gnyis bsdoms pas chu tshod so drug 'ong ba gangs ldan gyi dbus kyi byang bgrod mthar thug pa'i nyin gyi nyin tshad do/ /

At the center of Himālaya, when the sun arrives at a point three hours east of the meridian of the central sector of the east, morning begins, and when the sun arrives at a point three hours west of the central sector of the west, afternoon ends. Applying the same calculations as above, and totaling morning and afternoon times, produces a figure of thirty-six hours, which is the length of daytime at the center of Himālaya on the day of the sun’s northern limit.

de ltar yul drug gi dbus drang por nyi ma byang bgrod mthar thug pa'i nyin nyi ma ring thung mi 'dra ba tha dad par 'gyur ba ni bshad zin pa ltar gyi nyi ma 'char sa dang nub sa snga phyi mi mtshungs pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis yin te/ gal te nyi ma 'char sa'am 'char dus dang nub sa 'am nub dus snga phyi med par mnyam pa zhig yin na yul drug gi thad kar nyi ma la mgyogs bul yod pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis yin dgos la/ de ni mi rung ste/ gzhi yul drug gi dbus kyi thad sor dus nyin gang po gcig la 'gro ba po nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor gcig yul drug po 'di'i thad du mgyogs 'di 'dra ba'i thad du bul ba yin pa tshad mas ma dmigs pa'i phyir ro/ /

Therefore the reasons for the individual and differing lengths of daytime on the day of the sun’s northern limit at the direct centers of the six lands are the differing positions of sunrise and sunset, as explained. If the times or positions of rising and the times or positions of setting were all the same, and none were earlier or later, then the reason for the differing lengths of daytime would have to be put down to the speed of the sun over the six lands. This would not be a suitable reason, because on a single base, the centers of the six lands, for a time that is the duration of a whole day, a single sun disk cannot be validly perceived[166] as moving quickly over one land and slowly over another land.

d.div: [166] tshad mas ma dmigs pa. In other words, it cannot exist.

f.d: de bzhin du pad dkar zhal lung las/ nyi bar khyim bcu gnyis su rim pa bzhin sleb ma thag pa'i tshe kai la sha'i dbus su nyi ma ring thung sna tshogs su 'gyur ba rnams kyang nyi ma'i 'char sa dang nub sa tha dad pa'i dbang gis 'char dus dang nub dus snga phyir 'gyur ba bshad pa nyid [87] shin tu legs par bshad pa yin pas de dang bdag cag gis zur tsam bshad pa 'di la dpags nas 'phags yul sogs yul lhag ma lnga po rnams su yang nyi bar khyim lhag ma rnams su sleb ma thag pa'i tshe dang sbyor ba'i tshul rnams kyang shes par bya'o/ /

There is an excellent presentation of this in the Puṇḍarīka Transmission, where it explains that, as the mean sun arrives at /111/ each of the twelve houses in turn, the length of daytime differs at the center of Kailash because of the different positions of rising and setting, thereby producing earlier and later sunrises and sunsets. With this and our rather brief explanation, one can know how to apply it to the times of the mean sun arriving in the other houses at the remaining five lands.

d.div: [87] rtsis gzhung pad dkar zhal lung / shog grangs/ 268_nas 271_bar gzigs/

f.d: de la mkhas pa (jo zhal sogs )snga ma phal mo che dag lho gling dbus ma'i yul drug po gang gi dbus su yang (nyi bar khyim gang na gnas pa'i tshe yang )nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor shar gling dbus ma'i dbus drang po'i thad du sleb pa'i tshe snga dro dang po 'char zhing / rgyu mtshan de nyid kyis na 'phags yul sogs lho gling dbus ma'i dbus drang por snga dro dang shar gling dbus ma'i dbus drang por phyi dro don gcig cing / de bzhin du lho gling dbus ma'i dbus kyi phyi dro dang nub gling dbus ma'i dbus kyi snga dro don gcig pa sogs gling gzhan rnams la yang sbyar nas 'chad par byed cing / dus sbyor yang nyin drug mtshan drug 'char ba bzhin du dus nam yang snga dro dus sbyor gsum dang / phyi dro yang gsum re 'char bar 'dod do/

Most scholars of the past (such as those of the Jonang tradition) maintained that at any of the centers of the six lands of the central sector of the south, regardless of the mean sun’s position in any of the houses, morning begins when the disk of the sun arrives at the direct center of the central sector of the east. Therefore morning at the direct center of India, for example, on the central sector of the south corresponds exactly with noon at the direct center of the central sector of the east. Similarly noon at the center of the central sector of the south and morning at the center of the central sector of the west occur at the same time. The same processes are applied to the other sectors. Also, while they accept that six lagna[167] occur during the day and six occur at night, they assert that three will always occur in the morning and three in the afternoon.

d.div: [167] Here lagna means “ascendant”: every two hours or so a different house will rise over the eastern horizon. See appendix 10.

f.d: kha cig (don kun )de dag yin pa gzhir byas te/ de ltar byas pa na dus bzhi g.yas skor la skyon chags par mthong nas dus bzhi g.yon skor yin par 'dod na'ang / de nyid ni g.yas skor gsal sgron du bkag zin pas der shes par bya zhing / lho gling dbus ma'i dbus drang por dus nam yang shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi steng du nyi mas sleb pa'i tshe snga dro dang po 'char zhing / nub gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi steng thad du nyi ma sleb pa'i tshe phyi dro rdzogs par 'dod pa dang / shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi phyi dro dang lho gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi snga dro rnam pa kun tu yun tshad mnyam par 'dod pa rnams ni rigs pa dang 'gal bas mi 'thad do/ / ji ltar na

Others (such as Dönkün)[168] take these assertions as a basis, and by doing so come to the conclusion that a clockwise movement of the four seasons is wrong. They assert, therefore, a counterclockwise movement. However this is refuted in the Lamp Illuminating Clockwise Occurence,[169] as a study of this text will reveal. They all maintain that whenever the sun arrives at the meridian of the central sector of the east, it will always be the beginning of morning at the direct center of the central southern sector, and that whenever it arrives at the meridian of the central western sector, it will be the end of afternoon. They also assert that afternoon on the meridian of the central eastern sector and morning on the meridian of the central southern sector are at all times of the same duration. These assertions contradict logic, because

d.div: [168] Döndrup Künga, fourteenth-century Kālacakra scholar.
[169] A work by the author himself.

f.d: nyi bar lug khyim du sleb ma thag pa'i lho gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi dpyid mnyam gyi tshe kai la sha dang khyon mtshungs kyi shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig dang 'phags yul dang khyon mtshungs kyi shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gnyis phyi dro'i yun tshad mnyam par thal/ de'i tshe kai la sha dang khyon mtshungs kyi shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi phyi dro dang kai la sha'i tshangs thig gi snga dro yun tshad mnyam zhing / kai la sha'i tshangs thig gi snga dro dang 'phags yul gyi tshangs thig gi snga dro yun tshad mnyam/ 'phags yul gyi tshangs thig gi snga dro dang 'phags yul dang khyon mtshungs kyi shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi phyi dro yun tshad mnyam pa'i phyir ro/ /

it would follow that at the time of the mean sun’s arrival in the house of Aries, which corresponds to the spring equinox at the meridian of the central southern sector, afternoon on the meridian of the central eastern sector at a point corresponding to Kailash and afternoon on the meridian of the central eastern sector at a point corresponding to India would be of the same length. This is because, firstly, at that time afternoon on the meridian of the central eastern sector at a point corresponding to Kailash and morning on the meridian of Kailash would be of the same duration. Secondly, at that particular time, morning on the central meridian of /112/ Kailash and morning on the meridian of India are of the same length, and thirdly, morning on the central meridian of India and afternoon on the meridian of the central eastern sector at a point corresponding to India would also be of the same length.

rtags snga phyi gnyis dngos su khas blangs la/ bar pa ni don la gnas shing khas kyang blangs te/ lho gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi dpyid mnyam gyi tshe shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi steng thad du nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor sleb pa na kai la sha dang 'phags yul gnyis ka'i tshangs thig tu snga dro thog ma dus mnyam du shar ba dang / nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor lho gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi steng thad du sleb pa na kai la sha dang 'phags yul gnyis char gyi tshangs thig tu nyi ma phyed par khas blangs pas so/ /

The first and third of these reasons you must evidently accept.[170] The middle reason is consistent with the facts and must be accepted, because when the disk of the sun arrives above the meridian of the central eastern sector at the time of the spring equinox of the meridian of the central southern sector, it is the simultaneous beginning of morning at the meridians of Kailash and India. Moreover, when the disk of the sun arrives over the meridian of the central southern sector, you accept that it is noon at the meridians of both Kailash and India.

d.div: [170] Because they are consistent with the opponent’s own views.

f.d: rtsa bar 'dod do zhe na/ 'o na lho gling dbu ma ma'i tshangs thig gi dpyid mnyam gyi tshe shar gling dbus ma'i kai la sha dang khyon mtshungs kyi tshangs thig dang 'phags yul dang khyon mtshungs kyi tshangs thig gnyis nyin mo'i yun tshad mnyam par thal/ lho gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi dpyid mnyam gyi tshe de gnyis kyi snga dro yun tshad mnyam par khas len dgos shing / phyi dro yun tshad mnyam par yang khas blangs pa'i phyir ro/ /

If it asserted that the original consequence is correct, that these two places would indeed have afternoons of the same length, then it would further follow that at the time of the spring equinox on the meridian of the central southern sector, a point on the meridian of the central eastern sector corresponding to Kailash and a point on the meridian of the central eastern sector corresponding to India would have daytime of equal length, because at the time of the spring equinox on the meridian of the central southern sector, it must be accepted that these two points would have mornings of equal length, and it is accepted that afternoons are also of equal length.

'dod par mi nus te/ lho gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi dpyid mnyam gyi tshe shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi nyi ma byang bgrod mthar thug pas kai la sha dang khyon mtshungs kyi shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig tu nyin chu tshod so lnga dang / 'phags yul dang khyon mtshungs kyi shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig tu nyin chu tshod so gsum yin pa gong du drangs pa'i 'grel pa rnams kyi don yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de ltar na bshad zin pa ltar sa dum bu bcu gnyis po rnams kyi gangs ldan sogs yul drug dang / de dag dang khyon mtshungs rnams su nyi ma lho bgrod byang bgrod kyi dbang gis nyin mtshan ring thung sna tshogs su 'gyur ba rnams ni nyi ma'i 'char sa dang nub sa'i sa khyon tha dad pa'i dbang kho na las yin par shes par bya dgos te/ de'i yang rgyu mtshan dus sbyor rnams kyi 'char yun mi 'dra ba sna tshogs par 'gyur ba las shes dgos so/ /

This consequence cannot be correct, because at the time of the spring equinox on the meridian of the central southern sector, the sun has reached its northern limit on the meridian of the central eastern sector. Therefore, at a point on the meridian of the central eastern sector corresponding to Kailash, daytime is thirty-five hours, and at a point on the meridian of the central eastern sector corresponding to India, daytime is thirty-three hours. That was the point made by the previous explanations. Therefore it should be known that within the six lands of Himālaya and so forth, and the corresponding regions in the twelve sectors, the varying lengths of day and night throughout the sun’s northward and southward passages are due solely to the different positions of sunrise and sunset. Because of the same reason, it should be known that the appearance times of the houses also vary.

de'i tshul yang mdor bsdus pa tsam zhig brjod na 'di lta ste/ re gsum pa'i 'grel chen las/
da ni kai lA sha'i dum bu'i dbye bas dus sbyor bcu gnyis 'char ba'i dus gsungs pa lug gi dus sbyor la ni chu srang du 'gyur [88] zhes pa ste 'dir lug gi dus sbyor la dang po shar ba nas dus sbyor phyi ma 'char ba'i bar gyi dus la chu srang gi tshogs mkha' dgu lag ste zhes pa dgu bcu lhag pa'i nyis brgyar 'gyur ro/ / zhes sogs kyis dus sbyor rnams kyi 'char yun gsungs pa rnams ni lho gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi kai la sha'i dbus drang po'i dbang du mdzad pa yin la/ de'i dus sbyor rnams kyi 'char yun ni 'grel chen las dngos su gsungs pa ltar chu srang nyis brgya dgu bcu ni lug gi 'char yun dang / de bzhin du nyis brgya drug cu ni glang gi dang / nyis brgya ni 'khrig pa'i dang / sum brgya ni karka Ta'i dang / sum brgya drug cu ni seng+ge'i dang / sum brgya dgu bcu ni bu mo'i dus sbyor gyi 'char ba'i yun tshad de/ srang la sogs pa drug ni rim pa min par bzlog pa'i tshad kyis 'char ro/ /

To explain that briefly, the Great Commentary says on the sixty-third verse:
Now by dividing the continent of Kailash, the appearance times of the twelve houses are discussed: /113/ “The house of Aries is in minutes.” This means that concerning the house of Aries, from the time of its arising to the end of its arising, the number of minutes is space, nine, hands, which means ninety more than two hundred.[171] This and further quotes speak of the appearance times of the houses. Using the direct center of Kailash at the meridian of the central southern sector as a basis, the appearance times of the houses, as the Great Commentary says, are 290 minutes[172] for Aries, 260 minutes for Taurus, 200 minutes for Gemini, 300 for Cancer, 360 for Leo, and 390 for Virgo. The appearance times for the remaining six, Libra and so forth, are in reverse order,

d.div: [88] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 90_ba2
[171] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 90b2.
[172] One hour and fifty-six minutes in modern time.

f.d: de yang dpe ris su bkod pa ni 'di'o/ / lug_290_nya/ glang / 260_bum pa/ 'khrig_200_chu srin/ karka/ 300_gzhu/ seng+ge/ 360_sdig bu mo/ 390_srang /[89]
as this diagram will show:[173] Aries 290 Pisces Taurus 260 Aquarius Gemini 200 Capricorn Cancer 300 Sagittarius Leo 360 Scorpio Virgo 390 Libra

d.div: [89] ma dper glang gsal yang don la srang yin pas bcos/
[173] The column totaled and then doubled to incorporate the other six houses comes to 3,600 minutes, which equals sixty hours, or one complete day.

f.d: de ltar na khyim drug gi tshad nyin mo 'char ba dang / drug gi tshad mtshan mo 'char ba'i tshul gyis dus gang dang gang gi tshe'i nyin mtshan gyi ring thung rnams dang shin tu 'grig pa yin no/ / nyi ma khyim mtshams rnams su gnas pa'i tshe 'grig 'ong na'ang nyi ma lug khyim gyi phyed lta bu na gnas pa'i tshe ji ltar bsgrig snyam na/

The durations of six houses at night and the durations of six in daytime align perfectly with the length of day and night at any time of year. However, you might wonder, “This is true when the sun is at the cusps of the signs, but how would they align when the sun is halfway through the house of Aries, for example?”
de ni 'di ltar shes par bya ste/ nyi bar khyim gang dang gang yin pa der sleb nas khyim zhag ji tsam zhig 'das bltas la
This will be explained. First calculate how many zodiacal days have passed since the mean sun arrived in that particular house. /114/

de nas nyi bar khyim gang na gnas pa'i khyim de'i 'char yun gang yin pa de sum cus bgos te rnyed nor de nyi bar khyim der sleb nas khyim zhag du song gi grangs kyis bsgyur ba des nyi bar khyim gang na gnas pa'i khyim de'i 'char yun la 'phri ba'i lhag nas bgrangs pa'i khyim drug gi 'char yun dang nyi bar gang na gnas pa'i khyim de'i bdun pa'i khyim gang yin pa de'i yang 'char yun sum cus bgos pa'i rnyed nor gong du bshad pa bzhin nyi bar khyim der sleb nas khyim zhag du song gi grangs kyis bsgyur ba dang bcas pa ni dus de dang de'i tshe nyin mo'i tshad dang / de bzhin du nyi bar gang na gnas pa'i khyim de nas bgrangs pa'i khyim bdun pa de'i 'char yun la sum cus bgos pa'i rnyed nor gong bzhin bsgyur ba des bdun pa'i 'char yun la phri ba'i lhag nas snga ma las cig shos kyi khyim drug gi 'char yun dang nyi bar gang na gnas pa'i khyim de'i 'char yun la sum cus bgos pa'i rnyed nor gong bzhin bsgyur ba dang bcas pa bsdoms pa ni dus de dang de'i tshe'i mtshan mo'i tshad do/ /

Then divide the appearance time of that house by thirty and multiply the result by the number of zodiac days that have passed since the mean sun arrived in that house. Subtract that figure from the appearance time of the particular house the mean sun inhabits and begin the counting from the remainder. Include the appearance times of the next six houses, and add this to the result obtained by dividing by thirty the appearance time of the seventh house on from the house inhabited by the mean sun, and, as before, multiplying it by the number of zodiac days passed since the sun occupied that house. This is the length of daytime at that particular time. Similarly divide by thirty the appearance time of the seventh house on from the house occupied by the mean sun, multiply it as before, subtract that figure from the appearance time of this seventh house, and, counting from the remainder, include the appearance time of the other six houses, plus the result obtained by dividing the appearance time of the house occupied by the mean sun by thirty and multiplying it as before. This is the length of the nighttime at that particular time.

de dag ni rgyud 'grel las dngos su gsungs pa'i lho gling dbus ma'i kai la sha'i dbus drang po'i dbang du byas pa yin la/ de ltar bshad pa'i rigs pa de nyid kyi sa dum bu gzhan rnams la ji ltar mtshon pa ni/ kai la sha la bshad pa ji lta ba bzhin du dus sbyor so so'i 'chad pa'i yun tshad chu srang nyis brgya dgu bcu dang / nyis brgya drug cu dang / nyis brgya dang / sum brgya dang / sum brgya drug cu dang / sum brgya dgu bcu rnams bzhag pa la rang rang gi dpyid mnyam gyi thig ma byas nas bsgrigs pa ni lho gling dbus ma las g.yas skor gyi dum bu gnyis pa lho gling nub ma'i kai la sha dang khyon mtshungs kyi dbus drang por glang gis thog ma byas pa'i drug rim pa dang / sdig pa la sogs pa drug rim pa min par bzlog pa dang / de bzhin du nyi bar khyim gang du sleb ma thag gi tshe dpyid mnyam phog pa'i sa dum bu lhag ma bcu po de'i kai la sha dang khyon mtshungs kyi dbus dang dpyid mnyam phog pa'i khyim de thog mar byas pa'i drug rim pa dang / ston mnyam phog pa'i khyim la sogs pa drug rim pa min par bzlog ste nyin mo dang mtshan mo'i tshad du shes par bya'o/ /

In the tantra and commentary these appearance times are taught using the direct center of Kailash of the central southern sector as a basis. By the same reasoning used there, appearance times on the other sectors can also be shown. As depicted above, the appearance times of the house on Kailash are set as 290 minutes, 260, 200, 300, 360, and 390. On the basis of each sector being at the beginning of its own spring equinox, the order of the above appearance times on the second sector clockwise from the central southern sector, which is the western sector of the south, at the direct center of a region corresponding to Kailash, begins with Taurus for the first six houses, and then proceeds in reverse order for the six houses beginning with Scorpio.[174] Likewise, on the remaining ten sectors at the center of a point corresponding to Kailash, when the mean sun has just entered the house for that sector’s spring equinox, the house that heralds the spring equinox is the first of the six houses of forward order, and the house of the autumn equinox is the first of the six houses of reverse order. From the corresponding figures the lengths of day and night can be known.

de ltar na sa dum bu bcu gnyis rnams dang yul drug so so'i dus sbyor rnams 'char yun mi 'dra ba sna tshogs pa'i dbang gis nyin mtshan yang ring thung sna tshogs su gyur pa 'byung ba yin te/ de yang kai la sha'i dbus la dper mtshon pa tsam zhig bshad na/

In this way the differing appearance times for the house in each of the six lands and twelve sectors account for the lengths of day and night. /115/ This can be illustrated using the center of Kailash as an example.

d.div: [174] As in the diagram above, but placing Taurus as the first house.

f.d: lug khyim gyi 'go shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig gi steng thad nas 'char ba yin zhing / mjug kyang de nyid nas shar na lug gi dus sbyor gyi 'char yun la'ang chu srang sum brgya 'ong rgyu yin pa la/ lug khyim gyi mjug glang khyim dang 'dabs 'byar du gnas pas glang khyim gyi 'char sa shar gling dbus ma'i tshangs thig las shar du nyi mas chu srang lnga bcu'i yun la bgrod pa'i khyon tsam du phyin pa nas 'char bas lug gi dus sbyor gyi 'char yun chu srang nyis brgya dang dgu bcu byung ba dang / de bzhin du glang khyim gyi 'go lug khyim gyi mjug shar sa nas shar zhing / mjug kyang de nyid nas shar na de'i 'char yun la'ang chu srang sum brgya nyid 'ong rgyu yin pa la/ glang khyim gyi mjug sdom las kyang sa khyon che ba'i 'go shar sa nas shar gyi phyogs su song nas shar sa 'char yun yang chu srang nyis brgya drug cu byung ba yin no/ /

The beginning of Aries appears over the meridian of the central sector of the east. If the tail end of Aries appeared there also, then the Aries house would last for 300 minutes. The tail end of Aries borders Taurus, and therefore the place for Taurus to rise is from a point east of the meridian of the central eastern sector representing the time the sun would take to travel for fifty minutes.[175] This means that the appearance time of Aries’s house is 290 minutes. Similarly, the beginning of Taurus rises in the east at the place where the tail end of Aries rises. If the tail end of Taurus rose in the same place, then its appearance time would be 300 minutes. By rising east of the rising position of the beginning of Taurus, which is of a larger area than the end, its duration is 260 minutes.

d.div: [175] Totaling the six daytime appearance times from the diagram beginning with Taurus gives a daytime of 1,900 minutes. This is one hundred minutes more than daytime at the spring equinox. This increase is shared between sunrise and sunset at fifty minutes each.

f.d:
de bzhin du khyim rnams kyi 'go mjug 'char sa tha dad pa sna tshogs pa'i dbang gis dus sbyor rnams kyi 'char yun mi 'dra ba sna tshogs su gyur pa yin la/ khyim rnams kyi skar ma 'char sa gang yin pa de nas skar ma de'i steng na yod pa'i nyi ma yang 'char bas dus sbyor rnams la 'char yun mi 'dra ba sna tshogs 'byung ba'i dbang gis nyi ma la yang 'char sa dang nub sa shar nub mi 'dra ba sna tshogs 'byung ba yin te/ 'jig rten khams le'i re gsum pa'i 'grel chen las/
dus sbyor 'char ba'i dus kyi dbang gis nyin mo dang mtshan mo dman pa dang lhag par 'gyur te nyi ma yang dag par rgyu ba'i dbang gis so/[90] / zhes gsungs pas so/ /

In this way the different rising places of the beginnings and ends of the houses account for the different appearance times of the house. The sun lying within the stars of a particular house will also rise from the rising place of those stars. Therefore the different durations of the house account for the different rising and setting positions of the sun in the east and west. In the sixty-third verse of the Realms chapter of the Great Commentary it says:
The appearance times of the house lessen and lengthen day and night, due to the sun’s position.[176]
'di dag gi don zhib par bshad dgos na'ang / ha cang yi ge mangs par 'gyur bas de tsam mo/ /
This requires a more detailed explanation, but because it would entail far too much explanation, this will have to do.

d.div: [90] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 91_na3
[176] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 91a3.

f.d: gsum pa sa'i go la la dus rnams kyi 'ong tshul bshad pa ni/[91]

d.i: The gola of the earth: Emergence of the seasons

d.div: [91] ma dper sa'i go la dus rnams kyi 'khor tshul zhes gsal yang la chad pa mngon/

f.d:
khams le'i drug pa'i 'grel chen las/
lug la sogs pa'i khyim gang yang rung ba gcig la nyi ma gnas pa sa dum bu bcu gnyis su dus drug dang zla ba bcu gnyis dang phyogs nyi shu rtsa bzhi byed de khyim gyi 'khor lo 'khor ba'i dbang gis so/[92] / zhes sogs gsungs pa ltar nyi ma lug khyim na gnas pa'i tshe lho gling shar ma dang dbus ma gnyis su dpyid dang / de nas g.yon skor gyi shar gling nub ma dang dbus mar so ga dang / shar gling shar ma dang byang gling nub mar dbyar dang / byang gling dbus ma dang shar mar ston dang / nub gling nub ma dang dbus mar dgun stod dang / nub gling shar ma dang lho gling nub mar dgun smad de nyi ma lug khyim gcig nyid la gnas pa'i tshe sa dum bu bcu gnyis su dus drug tu 'gyur ba'i tshul lo/ /

The Great Commentary says in the sixth verse of the Realms chapter: /116/
The sun dwells in one of the houses, Aries and so on, and on the twelve sectors the six seasons, the twelve months, and the twenty-four sides[177] are formed from the orbiting of the wheel of houses.[178] As this and further quotations explain, when the sun dwells in the house of Aries, it is spring in both the eastern and central sectors of the south. At the same time, proceeding counterclockwise, in the western and central sectors of the east, it is the hot season. In the eastern sector of the east and in the western sector of the north, it is summer. In the central and eastern sector of the north, it is autumn. In the western and central sector of the west, it is early winter, and in the eastern sector of the west and western sector of the south, it is late winter. This is how six seasons are formed upon the twelve sectors with the sun inhabiting the house of Aries.

d.div: [92] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 88_na4
[177] Bright and dark sides of the month, i.e., twenty-four fortnights.
[178] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 88a4.

f.d: de bzhin du nyi ma glang khyim na gnas pa'i tshe lho gling nub ma dang dbus mar dpyid/ lho gling shar ma dang shar gling nub mar sos/ shar gling dbus ma dang shar mar dbyar/ byang gling nub ma dang dbus mar ston/ byang gling shar ma dang nub gling nub mar dgun stod/ nub gling dbus ma dang shar mar dgun smad do/ / de bzhin du nyi ma khyim gzhan rnams la gnas pa'i dus la'ang sbyar bar bya'o/ /

Similarly, when the sun dwells in Taurus, it is spring in the western and central southern sectors. In the eastern sector of the south and the western sector of the east, it is the hot season; in the central and eastern sectors of the east it is summer; in the western and central sectors of the north it is autumn; in the eastern sector of the north and the western sector of the west, it is early winter; and in the central and eastern sectors of the west, it is late winter. This formula should be similarly applied to the sun dwelling in the other houses.[179]

d.div: [179] Therefore, although the seasons can be counted in order counterclockwise through the continents, their movements through the continents is clockwise.

f.d: de bzhin du dus bzhi ru 'gyur tshul ni nyi ma lug na gnas pa'i tshe lho gling gsum du dpyid dang / shar gling gsum du dbyar dang / byang gling gsum du ston dang / nub gling gsum du dgun no/ / de bzhin du nyi ma glang khyim na gnas pa'i tshe nub gling shar ma dang lho gling nub ma dang lho gling dbus ma gsum na dpyid dang / de nas g.yon skor gyis rim pa bzhin gling gsum na dbyar dang / de nas gsum na ston dang / de nas gsum na dgun te de bzhin du nyi ma khyim gzhan rnams na gnas pa'i dus la'ang sbyar bar bya'o/ /

The way in which the seasons are divided into four is as follows. When the sun dwells in Aries, it is spring in the three southern sectors, summer in the three eastern sectors, autumn in the three northern sectors, and winter in the three western sectors. Similarly, when the sun dwells in Taurus, it is spring in the eastern sector of the west, in the western sector of the south, and in the central sector of the south. Then, proceeding counterclockwise, it is summer in the next three sectors, autumn in the following three, and winter in the last three. This formula should be applied to the times of the sun dwelling in the other houses.
yang nyi ma khyim gcig la gnas pa'i tshe sa dum bu bcu gnyis su dpyid 'bring sogs ra ba tha chung mi 'dra ba bcu gnyis su 'gyur ba sogs gong du bshad zin pa ltar ro/ /

Furthermore the formation, from the sun dwelling in a particular house, of the twelve smaller divisions of the seasons on the twelve sectors, such as middle spring and so forth, is as previously explained.
'dir snod bcud 'jig rten gyi rnam gzhag bshad pa dang / mngon pa'i sde snod la 'gal ba spong tshul/
7. Resolving Contradictions between Kālacakra and Abhidharma Cosmology
bzhi pa 'dir snod bcud kyi 'jig rten gyi rnam gzhag bshad pa dang / mngon pa'i sde snod 'gal ba spong ba

d.i: Refuting any contradictions between the presentation of the world in the Kālacakra and that of the Abhidharma texts

f.d: ['di ]la gsum/ dwogs pa'i gnas dgod pa dang / de la dwogs pa ji ltar skyes pa'i tshul dang / dwogs pa de dag sel byed kyi 'grel pa'i don bshad pa'o/ /
This has three headings: /117/ 1. The points of doubt 2. How such doubts are expressed 3. Commentary on the text that dispels such doubts
dang po [dwogs pa'i gnas ]ni/

chos mngon pa las gsungs pa'i snod bcud kyi rnam gzhag dang 'dir bshad pa'i snod bcud kyi rnam gzhag ches mi 'dra ba las/ 'dir snod kyi rnam gzhag mi 'dra ba'i khyad par mdo tsam zhig brjod par bya ba las/ rgyud 'grel chen dang bcas pa las byung tshul ni brjod zin pa ltar yin la/

The presentation of the world and its inhabitants found in the Abhidharma and the presentation of the world and its inhabitants as detailed here in the Kālacakra are very different. Here the differences in the presentation of the world will be briefly set out. The relevant presentations in the tantra and the Great Commentary are as previously explained.

mngon pa sogs las byung tshul ni/ mdzod las/
de la snod kyi 'jig rten gyi/ / gnas par 'dod pa'i 'og dag gi/ / rlung gi dkyil 'khor rngams su ni/ / sa ya drug 'bum grangs med do/ / chu rnams 'bum phrag bcu gcig dang / / stong phrag dag ni nyi shu'o/ / phyis ni rngams su 'bum phrag brgyad/ / lhag ma dag ni gser du 'gyur/ / chu dang gser gyi dkyil 'khor gyi/ / thad kar 'bum phrag bcu gnyis dang / / stong phrag gsum dang brgya phrag ni/ / phyed dang lnga rnams kho na'o/[93] / zhes sogs gsungs pa ltar

The way it is presented in the Abhidharma is as follows:
In the physical world below the realms of desire, the measurements of the air mandala: one million, six hundred thousand, and beyond number. The water and so forth, a hundred thousand times eleven, and a thousand times twenty. Outside the measurements are eight hundred thousand. The remainder is of gold. Across the mandalas of water and gold is a hundred thousand times twelve, three thousand, and four hundred and fifty.[180] Therefore, according to this and other quotes from the Abhidharmakośa,

d.div: [93] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuchos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka45_8_ba4
[180] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 45, 8b4.

f.d: gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten bye ba phrag brgya'i 'og gzhi'i rlung gi dkyil 'khor gcig yin pa dang / de yang rgya khyon gyi tshad dpag tshad grangs med dang / dpangs kyi tshad dpag tshad sa ya gcig dang drug 'bum yin pa dang / rlung gi dkyil 'khor de'i steng na gling bzhi po re re la 'og gzhi chu dang gser gyi dkyil 'khor tha dad pa re re dang / de dag gi tshad kyang dpangs su chu la dpag tshad 'bum phrag brgyad dang gser la 'bum phrag gsum dang stong phrag nyi shu/ rgya khyon gyi tshad la chu dang gser gnyis ka'i thad kar dpag tshad 'bum phrag bcu gnyis dang stong phrag gsum dang phyed dang lnga brgya yod cing zlum po'i khyon la de sum 'gyur du yod pas 'og gzhi rnams kyi tshad shin tu mi 'dra ba dang /

the basic foundation of the billion four-continent worlds is the air mandala. It extends to yojana “beyond number,”[181] and its depth is 1,600,000 yojana. Upon that air mandala, as foundations of each of the four-continent worlds, are individual water and gold mandalas. The water mandala is 800,000 yojana deep, and the gold mandala is 320,000 yojana deep. Both the water and the gold mandala are 1,203,450 yojana in diameter, while the circumference of each is three times that number. The measurements of the foundations, therefore, are very different from those of the Kālacakra.

d.div: [181] Asaṃkhyā, the last of the sixty numerical units, each increasing successively by ten. So called because there exists no number higher. See Lochen, chap. 1, on introductory topics of astronomy.

f.d:
de'i steng du chags pa'i ri gling sogs mi 'dra ba ni/ /
lhun po rin chen bzhi'i rang bzhin/ / chu yi nang du brgyad khri dag/ nub bo de bzhin steng du yang / / dpag tshad dag ni brgyad khri'o/[94] / zhes lhun po'i dbyibs gru bzhi rgyu rin po che bzhi'i rang bzhin te shar dngul lho baiDUR+ya nub shel dmar po byang gser yin la de dag gi kha dog can yin pa dang / de yang chu nang du dpag tshad brgyad khri nub pa dang / chu mtshams yan la dpag tshad brgyad khri yod par bshad cing / 'dir lhun po'i dbyibs zlum po/ kha dog shar nag lho dmar byang dkar nub ser por bshad pa dang / dpangs tshad dpag tshad 'bum phrag gcig par bshad pa dang /

On the differences regarding Meru and the continents upon that mandala foundation, the Abhidharmakośa states:
Meru is of four precious gems; eighty thousand under water, and as much as it is submerged, so above for eighty thousand yojana.[182] Thus Meru has four sides and is made of four precious gems. The east is of silver, the south of lapis lazuli, the west of red crystal, and the north of gold. Each side is also the color of these gems. Meru sinks eighty thousand yojana into the sea, while eighty thousand yojana are above sea level. That is the Abhidharma explanation. Here, however, /118/ Meru is taught as being circular, black in the east, red in the south, golden in the west, and white in the north, and while its height is taught as being one hundred thousand yojana.[183]

d.div: [94] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuchos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka50_8_ba6
[182] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 50, 8b6.

[183] This does not include the throat, face, and crown of the Kālacakra Meru, which rise for another hundred thousand yojana. Also, elsewhere in the text, the east face of Meru is described as being blue and of the color of indranīla (sapphire).

f.d: yang mdzod las/ gnya' shing 'dzin/ / gshol mda' 'dzin dang seng ldeng can/ / zhes sogs dang / de dag bar bdun rol mtsho yin/[95] / zhes sogs gser gyi ri bdun dang rol mtsho bdun bshad nas de dag gi bar na gling med par bshad cing / gser ri dang rol mtsho rnams kyi dbyibs kyang gru bzhir bshad la/ 'dir ri re re dang mtsho re re'i nang na gling re ste gling bdun dang / / de thams cad kyi dbyibs kyang zlum por bshad pa dang /

Again, the Abhidharmakośa says, “Yugandhara, Īṣādhāra, and Khadira ka,”[184] and so on. Also, “In between them, at each of the seven, an ocean,”[185] and so on lists the seven golden mountains and the seven bountiful lakes. Among them no continents are found. The shapes of the golden mountains and bountiful lakes are also said to be square. Here in the Kālacakra, a continent is located between each mountain range and lake to form the seven continents, whose shapes are all circular.

d.div: [95] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuchos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka48_8_ba5
[184] The first three of the seven golden mountains.
[185] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 48, 8b5.

f.d:
yang mdzod las/
lhag ma phyi yi mtsho chen yin/ / 'bum phrag gsum dang stong phrag ni/ / nyi shu gnyis so de la ni/ / 'dzam bu'i gling ste ngos gsum la/[96] / zhes sogs kyis mtha' lcags ri nag pos bskor ba'i nang na phyi'i rgya mtsho gnas pa'i nang gi phyogs bzhi mtshams brgyad na gling bzhi gling phran brgyad chu gzhong gang gi nang na 'bras phung por spungs pa'i tshul gyis gnas par bshad la/ 'dir ni bsil ri dang chu'i dkyil 'khor gyi bar na mtshams gcod byed kyi chu sogs med par sa'i dkyil 'khor zlum por 'dab chags par gnas pa la sa dum bu bcu gnyis sam gling bcu gnyis su cha 'byed pa yin pa dang /

The Abhidharmakośa continues:
The remainder is the outer ocean, of 322,000 yojana. Within that, Jambudvīpa of three sides.[186] The outer Black Iron Mountains surround the the outer ocean, which contains the four continents and the eight lesser continents located at the four cardinal directions and in the eight intermediate directions, and which are piled into the ocean depths like heaps of rice. In the Kālacakra there are no seas between the Śīta Mountains and the water mandala, and the area of the circular earth mandala is divided into twelve connecting continents or sectors.

d.div: [96] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuchos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka53_9_na1
[186] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 53, 9a1.

f.d:
yang mdzod las/
'di 'og stong phrag nyi shu na/ / mnar med pa'o de tsam mo/ / de yi steng na dmyal ba bdun/[97] / zhes dmyal ba'i ma mtha' 'dzam+bu gling 'di nas dpag tshad stong phrag nyi shu bcal ba na yod pa dang / de yang tsha ba'i dmyal ba dang grang ba'i dmyal ba dang nye 'khor gyi dmyal ba rnams lho 'dzam+bu'i gling 'di nyid kyi 'og na yod par bshad cing /
dmyal ba rnams kyi tshe'i tshad kyang / / yang sos la sogs drug rim bzhin/ / 'dod lha'i tshe dang nyin zhag mnyam/ / des na de dag rnams kyi tshe/ / 'dod pa'i lha dang 'dra ba yin/ / rab tu tshe byed mnar med ni/ / bar gyi bskal ba'o/[98] / zhes tsha dmyal ba rnams kyi tshe tshad de ltar du bshad pa dang /

Furthermore the Abhidharmakośa says:
Under this, at twenty thousand, the Hell of No Respite, and then no more, and above that, the seven hells.[187] This states that the lowest hell begins twenty thousand yojana beneath Jambudvīpa. Moreover, the hot hells, cold hells, and neighboring hells are spoken of as being directly below this continent of Jambudvīpa. The Abhidharmakośa continues:
On life span within the hells, one day in Reviving Hell, and so forth, is a lifetime of the desire gods. Life spans, therefore, mirror those of the gods. Those of Blazing and of Hell of no Respite are an intermediate eon.[188] This is the Abhidharma explanation of the life spans within the hells.

d.div: [97] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuchos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka58_9_na4
[98] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuchos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka82_10_na2
[187] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 58, 9a4.
[188] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 82, 10a2.

f.d:
yang /
til sbyang nas ni lo brgya zhing / / til gcig phyung bas zad gyur pa/ / chu bur can gyi tshe yin te/ / gzhan gyi tshe ni nyi shus bsgyur/[99] / zhes grang dmyal gyi tshe tshad kyang de ltar du bshad do/ /

Also:
From a store of sesame seeds, every hundred years one seed is taken until empty. Such time is the life span in the Hell of Blisters. The others are this times twenty.[189] /119/ That is the explanation of life span within the cold hells.

d.div: [99] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuchos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka84_10_na3
[189] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 84, 10a3.

f.d: 'dir ni dmyal ba'i ma mtha' 'dzam gling chen po 'di nas dpag tshad 'bum phrag gnyis kyi 'og na yod pa dang / de yang tsha ba'i dmyal ba dang grang dmyal rnams sa'i dkyil 'khor tshun chad kyi lhun po ri gling mtsho dang bcas pa thams cad kyi 'og na gnas pa dang / de bzhin du dmyal ba rnams kyi tshe tshad kyang dmyal ba'i gnas dang po bskal pa chung ngu'i tshe tshad dang / gnyis pa dang gsum pa bskal pa bar ma'i tshe dang / bzhi pa dang lnga pa bskal pa mchog gi tshe dang / drug pa dang bdun pa bskal pa chen po'i tshe dang / dmyal ba brgyad pa 'jig rten sdud pa'i tshe can du bshad cing / dmyal ba'i grangs kyang brgyad po de las ma bshad la/ mdzod sogs nas dmyal ba'i grangs bco brgyad du bshad pa sogs chos mngon pa dang dus 'khor gyi phyi snod kyi 'jig rten gyi rnam gzhag rnams dbyibs dang tshad dang grangs la sogs pa mi mthun pa 'ba' zhig tu byung ba dang / bcud mi'i lus kyi rtsa dang rlung dang rgyu ba sogs kyang rgyud gzhan dang mi 'dra ba ste de dag ni dogs pa skye ba'i gnas so/ /

Here in the Kālacakra, the lowest hell is at a depth of 200,000 yojana from Greater Jambudvīpa, while the hot and cold hells are beneath Meru and the mountains, continents, and oceans of the earth mandala. Similarly, concerning the life spans of those within the hell realms, the first hell has a life span of one small eon, the second and third of an intermediate eon, the fourth and fifth of a supreme eon, the sixth and seventh of a great eon, while the eighth is taught as having the life span the length of a world realm’s existence. As for the number of hells, no more than eight are mentioned, while the Abhidharmakośa and other texts talk of eighteen hells. In this way the Abhidharma and the Kālacakra presentations of the inner and outer worlds do not agree at all on shape, size, number, and so forth. Also the Kālacakra presentation of channels, winds, and their movements within the human body differ from those of other tantras. These are the points of doubt.
gnyis pa de la dwogs pa ji ltar skyes pa'i tshul ni/

rgya gar gyi mkhas pa 'ga' zhig dang bod kyi'ang mkhas pa 'ga' zhig /chos mngon pa dang / rgyud sde gzhan dang mi mthun pa rgyu mtshan du byas nas dus 'khor rgyud rnam dag ma yin zhing / de dag gi sdud pa po dang 'grel pa mdzad pa po rnams kyang 'jam dbyangs dang / spyan ras gzigs dang / rdo rje snying po dang / phyag na rdo rje sogs min zhes smra bar byed do/ / ji ltar du smra bar byed na/ man ngag snye ma las/
'o na dus kyi 'khor lo dang de'i rjes su 'brangs pa'i gzhung rnams su theg pa gsum dang 'gal ba'i rnam par gzhag pa mang po rnams byas te/ de'i gzhung byed pa grags pa dang pad+ma dkar po dang rdo rje snying po dang phyag na rdo rje'i ming can de rnams kyang byang chub sems dpa' rnams ma yin pa kho na'o/[100] / zhes mang du mkhyen pa rnams smra'o/ /zhes bshad cing mang du mkhyen pa ni slob dpon shAn+ti pa yin par grags la|_rnams zhes pa'i tshig gis rgya gar ba gzhan yang yod par bstan to/ /

Some Indian scholars and even some Tibetan scholars maintain that the Kālacakra is not a perfect tantra, citing its contradiction with the Abhidharma and other tantras as their reason, and assert that the compilers and composers of its commentaries were not manifestations of Mañjuśrī, Avalo kiteśvara, Vajragarbha, Vajrapāṇi, and so forth. In the Sheaves of Oral Transmission it says:
The knowledgeable and others have said that in the Kālacakra and those commentaries that follow it, there are many presentations in contradiction with the Three Vehicles, and that those responsible for these texts, possessing the names Yaśas, Puṇḍarīka, Vajragarbha, and Avalokiteśvara, are not bodhisattvas at all.[190] In this quote, “the knowledgeable” refers to the master Śāntipa, and “others” refers to other Indians.

d.div: [100] sde dge_1198_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ chaman ngag snye ma/ le'u/ 21_198_ba7
[190] Toh 1198 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, cha, chap. 21, 198b7.

f.d: de ltar 'dod pa'i bod ni bcom ldan chen po rigs ral pa 'dus pa ba chen po rngog dang bcas pa la sogs pa rnams yin no/ /
Tibetans who maintain this position include Chomden Rikral and Düpa Chenpo Ngok. /120/

rje btsun chen po red mda' bas ni/ kyog po'i shing la srong ba'i tshul bzhin du/ /zhes gsungs nas/ rgyud sde gzhan rnams dang 'gal ba ltar snang ba rnams la 'gal ba'i thal 'gyur dag brjod par mdzad do/ /[101] yang a b+ha ya la sogs pa 'ga' zhig ni/ dus 'khor rgyud 'grel rgyud dang 'grel pa tshad mar gyur pa yin yang snod bcud kyi rnam gzhag la sogs pa rgyud sde gzhan dang rnam gzhag mi mthun pa rnams drang don du 'chad do/ /

The venerable Rendawa said, “Like straightening a crooked tree,”[191] and produced many consequences for the apparent contradictions with other tantras. Abhayākaragupta and some others maintain that the tantra and commentaries of Kālacakra are valid texts but that their presentations on the world and its inhabitants that contradict other tantras require interpretation.

d.div: [101] tshig 'di rje red mda' bas rang nyid kyis sngar 'phrin yig nor bu'i phreng ba zhes pa dus kyi 'khor lo'i dpyad pa las brtsams te bod kyi bstan 'dzin rnams la gsol ba de'i rang lan zhig mdzad pa de'i nang du bzhugs/ rje red mda' ba'i 'phrin yig dang de'i rang lan/ de bzhin du 'gos lo tsA ba gzhon nu dpal gyi lan gdung sel ku mu da'i dga' ston dang / byang pa rnam rgyal bya bas mdzad pa'i lan dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud kyi mdzes rgyan bcas pa'i gzhung cha tshang bod kyi rtsis rig kun 'dus chen mo deb dang po shog grangs 283_nas 369_bar bzhugs/

[191] From a correspondence following on from Rendawa’s own Precious Garland of Letters on the examination of Kālacakra. These two works and replies by other masters of the time can be found in Great Compendium of Tibetan Astronomy, pp. 283–369. Also see Stearns, pp. 56–59, for a description of Rendawa’s opposition to Kālacakra and a translation of this particular passage.

f.d:
man snye las/
dus kyi 'khor lor bstan pa rgyud gzhan dang mi 'gal ba'i don gyi cha 'ga' zhig ni kho bos rang gi gzhung gi phyogs rnams rjes su 'brangs shing / gdul bya 'ga' zhig gi bsam pa'i rjes su 'jug pas 'gal ba'ang kha cig spangs so/ / de bas gzhan la ni 'gal ba ma spangs na yang 'di rnams la nyes pa ci yang med do zhes pa shin tu rgyas par brjod pas chog go[102] / zhes rgyud 'grel gyi bstan don 'dus pa sogs dang mi 'gal ba rnams sgra ji bzhin par bshad cing / don la rgyud gzhan dang mi 'gal yang gdul bya 'ga' zhig gi bsam ngo la 'gal ba ltar snang ba kha cig la 'gal spong yang byas te/ de las gzhanasno da bcud kyi rnam gzhag bstan pa sogs la ni 'gal ba ma spangs na'ang drang don du 'grel bar gong du shin tu rgyas par brjod pas chog par gsungs so/ /

Sheaves of Oral Transmission says:
Those parts taught in the Kālacakra that do not contradict other tantras, I follow as texts of our own scripture. Some, which are contradictory because they follow the inclinations of certain disciples, have been resolved. As to the rest, although the contradictions have not been resolved, there are no faults in them at all. This has been explained at great length and so they are perfectly acceptable.[192] This means that whatever is taught in the tantra and commentaries and does not contradict the Guhyasamāja and others can be taken literally. Some topics, which do not actually contradict other tantras but which may appear as contradictory to the minds of some disciples, have been resolved. The rest, such as the presentations of the world, its inhabitants, and so forth, may contain unresolved contradictions, but because they have been explained previously in great detail as topics in need of interpretation, they are perfectly acceptable.

d.div: [102] sde dge_1198_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ chaman ngag snye ma/ le'u/ 21_199_na2
[192] Toh 1189 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, cha, chap. 21, 199a2.

f.d:
'on kyang drang don du nam zhig gi tshe bshad snyam na/ de'i gong gi man snye las/
gang dus kyi 'khor lor nam mkha'i dkyil 'khor logs su bton nas gsungs pa de ni mu stegs pa'i lta ba la mngon par zhen pa'i nyi ma'i shing rta la sogs pa'i gdul bya rnams nges pa'i don la gzhug pa la ldem par dgongs pa'i drang ba'i don kho na ste/ phag la sogs pa'i 'dod pa'i rjes su 'jug pas ri rab kyi steng gi mtshams su khams gsum pa'i snod kyi 'jig rten gyi bkod pa la sogs pa bstan pa bzhin no/[103] / zhes dus kyi 'khor lor nam mkha'i khams kyi rlung srog 'dzin sogs rlung gi dkyil 'khor gzhan las logs su bton nas gzhi dus su sna bug nas rgyu bar gsungs pa drang don yin zhing / 'dis snod kyi rnam gzhag bstan pa yang drang don du mtshon nus par dgongs nas rgyas par brjod pas chog go/ /zhes gsungs pa yin no/ /

When is something explained as being in need of interpretation? Sheaves of Oral Transmission, prior to the previous quote, says:
In Kālacakra the space mandala is spoken of separately, and is there to lead disciples such as Sūryaratha and others who cling to tīrthika views to the definitive meaning. It is solely in need of interpretation and intentionally equivocal, like the teaching on the arrangement of the three world realms in the upper regions of Meru, asserted by those who follow Varāha,[193] and so forth.[194] Therefore, in the Kālacakra, the assertion that the space element wind[195] is separate from the other wind mandalas, such as the life-sustaining wind and so forth, and flows through the nostrils during normal existence requires interpretation. This indicates that the teachings on the presentation of the world also require interpretation. With this in mind they have “been explained at great length, and so they are perfectly acceptable.” /121/

d.div: [103] sde dge_1198_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ chaman ngag snye ma/ le'u/ 21_198_ba6
[193] Varāhamihira, renowned sixth-century Indian astronomer.
[194] Toh 1189 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, cha, chap. 21, 198b6.
[195] The winds that flow through the nose are divided among the five elements or mandalas. This is dealt with in the section on the Inner chapter.

f.d: bod kyi bla ma 'ga' zhig dus 'khor nas bshad pa nyid nges pa'i don dang / mngon pa nas bshad pa theg pa 'og ma'i bsam ngo dang bstun pas drang don yin pas sgra ji bzhin pa min no zhes bzhed do/ / de dag las dus 'khor rgyud tshad mar mi 'dod pa dag gis rgyud 'grel la 'gal ba brjod cing / rnam dag min pa'i sgrub byed brjod pa rnams la ni 'gal spong dang / sgrub byed la gnod byed kyi rigs pa mtha' yas pa dpag tu med pa dag dang / mdzod nas bshad pa dang 'jig rten gyi rnam gzhag mi 'dra ba'i khyad par sa sde dang mdo nas bshad tshul rnams ni rgyud 'grel gyi rgya cher 'grel pa de kho na nyid snang ba las shes par bya zhing / snod kyi 'jig rten gyi rnam gzhag dus 'khor nas bshad pa dang mngon pa nas bshad pa gnyis ka sgra ji bzhin pa yin pa ni 'gal spong gi 'grel tshig 'di dag gis gsal bar ston pa 'chad par 'gyur ba ltar yin no/ /

Some Tibetan lamas maintain that the teachings from the Kālacakra are definitive, while those from the Abhidharma tradition were taught to accord with the minds of the lower vehicles and are therefore provisional and not to be taken literally. To those who do not accept the Kālacakra as being valid at all, who talk of contradictions in the tantra and commentary and put forward proofs to dismiss it as an impure tantra, countless counterarguments dispelling their contradictions and refuting such proofs, as well as presentations that diverge from descriptions of world realms in the Abhidharma, in the Five Categories, and in the sutras, can be found in Illuminating Reality, an extensive explanation of the tantra and commentary. Moreover commentary passages clearly show that the description of a world realm in the Kālacakra and in the Abhidharma tradition can both be accepted literally. This will be explained.

'o na shAn+ti pa sogs gong du bshad pa'i dus 'khor rgyud 'grel rgyud dang 'grel ba rnam dag min zhes smra ba de dag la chos spong ba sogs sdig tu 'gyur ram zhe na/ de dag la chos spong ba sogs sdig tu mi 'gyur te/ mchog mi 'gyur gyi mdor bsdus las/
'dir gal te 'jig rten pas smad pas dmyal bar 'gro bar 'gyur na 'o na de'i tshe lta ba pa thams cad ni phan tshun smod par byed de phan tshun smod pa las lta ba pa thams cad dmyal bar 'gro bar 'gyur ro/ / gal te de lta na tshad ma'i bstan bcos rnams dang grub pa'i mtha' thams cad dang 'gal zhing brtul zhugs dang tshul khrims la sogs pa thams cad don med par 'gyur ro zhes pa 'ga' zhig gi bsam pa 'byung bar 'gyur te/[104] zhes dwogs pa bkod nas

It may be wondered if those, such as Śāntipa, who state that the tantra and commentaries of Kālacakra are flawed texts accrue the heavy nonvirtue of abandoning the dharma? They do not. In the Great Commentary, in the Supreme and Unchanging Gnosis summary of the Gnosis chapter, it says:
If the worldly go to hell through disparagement, then as all holders of views disparage each other, all holders of views will go to hell because of their disparagement. If that is so, this contradicts all valid scripture and tenets, and some might think that all ethics and all morality are meaningless.[196] This doubt is raised, and

d.div: [104] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 406_ba5
[196] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 406b5.

f.d:
de'i lan gsungs pa ni/ de'i 'phro nyid las/
da'i+e phyir brjod par bya'o/ / 'dir byis pa'i skye bo rnams kyis brjod par bya ba gang yin pa tshad ma'i bstan bcos la sogs pa thams cad dang 'gal ba de ni ma yin te/ gang gi phyir de kho na nyid yongs su brtag par sems pa'i phyir ro/ / lta ba po phan tshun smra ba po de rnams kyi lta ba la skyon yod pa ma yin te/ de kho na nyid yongs su brtag pa la brten pa'i sems kyi phyir dang / sems can thams cad la gnod pa byed pa'i sems med pa'i phyir dang / sems can thams cad la phan pa byed pa'i sems kyi phyir ro/[105] / zhes gsungs pa ltar slob dpon shAn+ti pa dang bcom ldan rigs ral la sogs pa de rnams bstan pa dang sems can la phan pa 'ba' zhig la dgongs nas gsung rab kyi don gyi de kho na nyid yongs su brtag par sems pa'i phyir ro zhes bya'o/ /

the text continues with an answer:
Therefore I will explain. The claim by the foolish that valid scripture and so forth would be contradicted is not so. Why? Because the intentions of holders of views are to examine meanings. Holders of views who express their views to one another are not at fault in their views, because these are states of mind that arise from examination of meaning, /122/ and there are no thoughts of harming sentient beings but only thoughts of helping them.[197] As this quote explains, Śāntipa, Chomden Rikral, and others are only examining the meanings of scripture, and their thoughts are totally focused on the benefit of the doctrine and sentient beings.

d.div: [105] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 406_ba7
[197] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 406b7.

f.d: gsum pa dwogs pa de dag sel byed kyi 'grel pa'i don bshad pa ni/

d.i: Commentary on the text that dispels such doubts

f.d: de la bshad bya'i 'grel pa ni/ 'dir 'jig rten kun rdzob tu zhes pa nas/ 'jig rten gyi khams kyi tshad dang lus kyi tshad dkyil 'khor gyi don du bcom ldan 'das kyis gsungs so/ /zhes ba'i bar yin la/ de yang rgyud 'grel las gling bzhi pa gcig du 'di nyid kyi tshad dbyibs bshad pa mngon pa nas kyang gling bzhi pa 'di nyid kyi rnam gzhag byas pa dang 'gal ba spong ba yin te/

The passage to be explained runs from “Here worldly convention” up to “The Conqueror spoke of the dimensions of the world and the dimensions of the body for the purpose of the mandala.” This passage dispels any notion that the teachings on the measurements and shape of this four- continent world contradict the presentation of this four-continent world as found in the Abhidharma tradition.

'grel chen las/
ji ltar bcom ldan 'das kyis 'jig rten gyi khams kyi tshad 'bum phrag sum cu so drug lhag pa dang / ji ltar 'jig rten gyi khams dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi'i tshad du gsungs/[106] 'dir bcom ldan 'das rdzun gsung ba po yin nam ci zhes pa 'ga' zhig 'dod par gyur na/ zhes gsungs pa ni mdzod las/
chu dang gser gyi dkyil 'khor gyi/ / thad kar 'bum phrag bcu gnyis dang / / stong phrag gsum dang brgya phrag ni/ / phyed dang lnga rnams kho na'o/[107] / zhes bshad pa'i gling bzhi pa gcig bu 'di nyid kyi 'og gzhi chu dang gser gyi dkyil 'khor gyi thad ka'i tshad de sum 'gyur du byas pas dpag tshad 'bum phrag so drug lhag ma khri sum brgya lnga bcu 'ong ba 'di dang / dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi par bshad pa 'di gnyis ka bcom ldan 'das kyi gsung yin na bcom ldan 'das rdzun gsung ba por 'gyur ro snyam pa'i dwogs pa bslang ba yin pas so/ /

The Great Commentary says:
The Conqueror said that the size of a world realm was more than 3,600,000 yojana and that the size of a world realm was 400,000 yojana. Some will ask, “Does the Conqueror speak the truth?”[198] In the Abhidharmakośa it says:
Across the mandalas of water and gold is a hundred thousand times twelve, three thousand, and four hundred and fifty.[199] This means that multiplying by three[200] the distance directly across the water and gold mandalas that act as the foundation of this four-continent world results in a circumference of 10,350 more than 3,600,000. If this figure and the figure of four hundred thousand yojana were both spoken by the Conqueror, a doubt could arise as to whether the Conqueror was speaking the truth.

d.div: [106] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 60_na6
[107] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuchos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka47_8_ba5
[198] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 60a6.
[199] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 47, 8b5.
[200] To arrive at the circumference.

f.d: de lta na 'grel tshig 'di rnams kyis gling bzhi pa gcig pu 'di nyid kyi tshad dbyibs mi 'dra ba'i bshad tshul gnyis 'gal ba spong ba yin no/ /
Therefore the text from this part of the commentary sets out to dispel any contradiction between these two differing descriptions of the size and shape of this one four-continent world. /123/

de ltar byas te 'grel ba'i don zhib par bshad na 'di yin te/ don dam par ste dngos po'i gnas tshod la gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams 'di la mngon pa nas bshad pa'am dus 'khor nas bshad pa lta bu'i tshad dang dbyibs de kho na'o zhes mtha' gcig tu gzhal du med de/ gling bzhi pa 'di'i rnam gzhag 'chad pa'i skabs 'dir 'jig rten kun rdzob tsam du mos pa sna tshogs pa'i sems can rnams kyi las rigs sna tshogs pa las/ gling bzhi pa 'di'i tshad dbyibs kyi cha shas kyang sna tshogs par grub cing / grub pa ltar bsam pa'i dbang gis te rang rang gi bsam pa dang mthun par 'jig rten gyi khams kyi tshad dang dbyibs bcom ldan 'das kyis sems can rnams la so sor gsungs shing / gsungs pa ltar rang rang gi las rigs dang mthun par rab tu snang ba yin pas so/ /

The text at this point can be explained in detail. “Ultimately,” or in reality, it is not possible to conclusively measure this four-continent world exclusively according to the measurements found in either the Abhidharma or the Kālacakra. The descriptions here of the four-continent world are “mere worldly conventions.”[201] The differing types of karma of sentient beings of differing dispositions have brought into existence differing shapes and sizes for this four-continent world, and as they exist, so the Conqueror taught sentient beings the measurements of this world realm in accord with their differing dispositions, and as he taught them, so they appeared in accord with their variety of karma.

d.div: [201] kun rdzob rtsam.

f.d: 'on te sems can rnams kyi las rigs mi 'dra ba sna tshogs pa las gling bzhi pa 'di nyid kyi tshad dbyibs kyi cha shas mi 'dra bar ji ltar du 'gyur snyam na/ de ltar du 'gyur ba yod de/ sems can bsod nams can rnams kyi bsod nams kyi stobs kyis gling bzhi pa gcig nyid kyi cha shas 'ga' zhig phun sum tshogs par 'gyur ba dang / sems can sdig pa can rnams kyi sdig pa'i dbang gis phun sum tshogs pa ma yin par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ /

How do the differing shapes and sizes of this four-continent world arise from the differing types of karma of sentient beings? “By the power of virtue” within virtuous sentient beings, some parts of this four-continent world are blessed with all things pleasant, and “by the power of demerit” in those of nonvirtue, other parts of the world are devoid of happiness and well-being.

gal te sems can 'ga' zhig gi bsod nams kyi las dang / 'ga' zhig gi sdig pa'i las kyi bdag 'bras snod phun sum tshogs pa dang phun sum tshogs pa ma yin pa so sor 'gyur ba yod mod/ gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gcig bu 'di nyid la mngon pa nas bshad pa ltar gyi tshad dbyibs kyi cha gcig dang dus 'khor nas bshad pa ltar gyi tshad dbyibs kyi cha gcig ste tshad dbyibs mi 'dra ba'i cha shas gnyis gnyis sems can gyi las rigs mi 'dra ba'i 'bras bur ji ltar du 'gyur zhe na/ de nyid dpe'i sgo nas 'chad pa ni/ 'dir phug khru lnga pa zhes sogs te/ 'dir chu dang zheng dang dpangs rnams la khru lnga lnga'i tshad dang ldan pa'i phug gang du 'dod chags dang bral ba dgra bcom pa'am dbang thob pa'i byang chub sems dpa' gnas pa'i phug der dgra bcom pa'am byang chub sems dpa' de dag gis bsod nams dang ye shes bsten pa de'i mthu dang rdzu 'phrul gyi stobs kyis 'khor los sgyur ba'i rgyal po dpung gi sde dang bcas pa 'ong zhing rab tu 'jug ste/ de'i tshe phug de sus kyang ma bskyed cing phug der zhugs pa'i 'khor los sgyur rgyal sde dang bcas pa yang dwogs pa nyid ma yin pa tshad mas sgrub la/ de ltar grub pa 'gal ba ltar snang yang don la mi 'gal ba ni dgra bcom pa'am dbang thob pa'i byang chub sems dpa' de dag gi bsod nams dang ye shes kyi mthu bsam gyis mi khyab pa las byung ba'o/ /
