It may be that the personal results[202] of those with meritorious karma and of those whose karma lacks such merit manifest as individual environments for the experience of happiness and suffering, but for this one four-continent world, there are two completely different presentations of shape and size. One is according to Abhidharma, and the other is according to Kālacakra. How do these two contrasting presentations arise from the differing karma of sentient beings? This is explained by an example, beginning with the words “In a cave of five cubits.” In a cave five cubits in height, length, and width lives “one without attachment,” i.e., an arhat or a powerful bodhisattva. In that cave this person is devoted to accumulating merit and wisdom, and by the power of such devotion and by the force of magical powers, a universal emperor arrives with his vast army and enters the small cave. At that time no one enlarged the cave, nor were the universal emperor and his armies squashed together in the cave. /124/ This is a phenomenon validly perceived as existing, and although such an accomplishment seems impossible, in actuality it is not, because it is brought about by the inconceivable power of the mighty bodhisattva’s or arhat’s merit and wisdom.

d.div: [202] bdag po’i ’bras bu. One the three kinds of karmic results as taught in stages of the path (lam rim) literature. It refers to the experience “owned” by the individual as opposed to the ripening karma that determines the realm of birth. Therefore environment, wealth, status, etc., are this particular kind of karmic result.

f.d: dpe de nyid ji lta ba de bzhin du gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams gcig pu 'di nyid kyi lhun po lta bu gcig la yang mngon pa nas bshad pa'i tshad dbyibs kyi cha gcig dang dus 'khor nas bshad pa'i tshad dbyibs kyi cha gcig ste tshad dbyibs mi 'dra ba'i cha gnyis gnyis kyang don dam par te dngos po'i gnas tshod la tshad mas grub par rig par bya ste/ phug khru lnga par 'khor los sgyur rgyal sde dang bcas pa zhugs pa'i tshe 'khor los sgyur rgyal sde dang bcas pa dwogs pa ma yin pa dang phug che bar ma song ba mi 'gal ba 'di dgra bcom pa'am byang chub sems dpa'i bsod nams dang ye shes kyi mthus yin pa de bzhin du gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams gcig bu 'di nyid kyi lhun po lta bu gcig la yang mngon pa nas bshad pa'i tshad dbyibs kyi cha shas gcig dang dus 'khor nas bshad pa ltar gyi tshad dbyibs kyi cha shas gcig ste gnyis 'ong ba mi 'gal ba 'di yang mngon pa dang / 'dus pa sogs rgyud gzhan gyi ched du bya ba'i gdul bya dang dus kyi 'khor lo'i ched du bya ba'i gdul bya gnyis kyi las rigs so so'i mthus byung ba yin pa'i phyir to/ /

In the same way, on the one Meru of this four-continent world realm, two completely different sets of shape and size measurements, one from the Abhidharma and one from the Kālacakra, can be validly perceived to exist. When the universal emperor and his armies entered the five-cubit cave, they were not crowded together nor did the cave grow larger. Such a noncontradictory occurrence was due to the might of the bodhisattva’s or arhat’s merit and wisdom. Similarly, on this one four-continent world, one set of measurements of shape and size as taught in the Abhidharma and a completely different set as taught in the Kālacakra can exist on the one Meru. This congruent and noncontradictory occurrence is due to the separate types of karma of the intended disciples of the Abhidharma and tantras such as Guhyasamāja on the one hand and the intended disciples of the Kālacakra on the other.

dgra bcom pa'am byang chub sems dpa' de dag gi bsod nams dang ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab pa bzhin du sems can spyi mthun gyi las kyi mthu'am nus pa yang bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i phyir te/ mngon pa kun las btus las/
phyi'i dngos po sna tshogs mngon par 'grub par byed pa'i las bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / nor bu dang / sngags dang / sman dang / mkhyud dpyad dang ldan pa'i las bsam gyis mi khyab pa'o/ / rnal 'byor pa thams cad kyi mthu'i las bsam gyis mi khyab pa'o/ / byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi dbang gi las bsam gyis mi khyab ste/[108] zhes gsungs pas so/ /

Just as the merit and wisdom of that bodhisattva or arhat are inconceivable, so too are the powers or capabilities of the common karma of sentient beings. In the Abhidharmasamuccaya it says:
The karma that produces various external phenomena is inconceivable. The karma connected with jewels, mantra, medicine, and secret lore is inconceivable. The karma of the powers of every yogi is inconceivable. The karma of the might of bodhisattvas is inconceivable.[203]

d.div: [108] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_chos mngon pa kun btus/ 90_na4
[203] Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 90a4.

f.d: 'o na mngon pa dang dus 'khor nas bshad pa'i gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gnyis ka dngos gnas la yod par 'dra na/ mngon pa nas bshad pa'i tshad dbyibs can de nyid dus 'khor 'dir yang bstan pas chog mod 'dir de dang mi mthun pa bshad pa la dgos pa lhag po ci zhig yod ce na/

However, if the world taught in the Abhidharma and the world taught in the Kālacakra are equal in the sense that they both exist, then it should be perfectly acceptable for the world with the Abhidharma measurements to be taught here in the Kālacakra. /125/ So what special reason is there for teaching a world system contradictory to the Abhidharma?

dus kyi 'khor lo 'dir mngon pa dang mi mthun pa'i gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams kyi tshad 'bum phrag bzhi par bshad pa gang yin pa de ni/ ji ltar phyi rol de bzhin lus/[109] /zhes gsungs pa'i phyir gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams 'di ni 'jig rten gyi khams 'di dang chos mthun par dkyil 'khor gyi 'khor lo bsgoms nas spyad par bya ba'i don dang / 'jig rten gyi tshad dang mthun pa'i lus kyi tshad bstan pa'ang lus kyi tshad dang chos mthun par dkyil 'khor gyi 'khor lo bsgoms nas lus rnam par sbyang ba'i don du yin pa'i phyir te/ lus ni dkyil 'khor zhes brjod do/[110] /zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ /

The purpose of the teaching of a four-continent world realm of four hundred thousand yojana as found in the Kālacakra and yet in contradiction to the Abhidharma is found in the words of the Great Commentary, “As without, so within the body.”[204] This means that this external four-continent world realm is a base to be purified by meditating upon the mandalas that correspond to this world realm. The body, whose measurements correspond to the measurements of the world, is also to be purified by meditating on the mandala circles that correspond to the measurements of the body. In the Great Commentary it says, “The body is said to be the mandala.”[205]

d.div: [109] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 60_na1
[110] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 60_na2
[204] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 60a1.
[205] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 60a2.

f.d: rgyu mtshan de ltar na phyi rol tu 'jig rten te kun rdzob tsam du yod par bzhag pa'i tshad kyis lhun po'i dpangs dpag tshad 'bum yin pa de bzhin du lus kyi sgal tshigs kyi dpangs khru gang ste khru'i tshad des lus la khru bzhi'o/ / lhun po dpag tshad 'bum gyi tshad kyis gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams 'di dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi yin pa'o/ / gal te 'dir gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten 'di dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi par bshad pa las rnam pa gzhan monang pa nas bshad pa ltar bshad na/ ji ltar phyi rol de bzhin lus su chos mthun tshul bshad ma thag pa de ltar du yod par mi 'gyur te/ mngon pa nas bshad pa'i lhun po la dpag tshad 'bum phrag gcig med pas lus kyi sgal tshigs khru gang dang chos mi mthun pa'i phyir ro/ /

Therefore external Meru, in measurements that are mere worldly convention, is one hundred thousand yojana high. The height of the human spine is one cubit. This makes the height of the body four cubits. The height of Meru is one hundred thousand yojana. This makes the height of a four-continent world realm four hundred thousand yojana. If this four-continent world were to be explained in the Kālacakra as being other than four hundred thousand yojana, as taught in the Abhidharma tradition, then the correspondence indicated by the quote, “As without, so within the body,” as previously explained, would not hold. This is because Meru as explained in the Abhidharma tradition is not a hundred thousand yojana, and this would not correspond to the one cubit height of the spine.

rgyu mtshan de ltar na dus kyi 'khor lo 'dir gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams kyi tshad bshad par bya ba ni kun rdzob tsam du dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi par bshad pa ji lta ba de bzhin du 'gyur ro/ /
Because of this, the measurements of a four-continent world realm here in the Kālacakra are taught conventionally to be four hundred thousand yojana, and as they are taught, so they exist.

de ltar yin pa 'on kyang /
bsregs bcad bdar bas gser bzhin du/ / legs par brtags la nga yis bka'/ / blang bar bya yi gus phyir min/[111] / zhes gser bzang po bsregs na dmar/ bcad na dkar/ bdar na ser ba gsum gyi sgo nas brtag dgos pa bzhin du sangs rgyas kyi gsung la dpyad pa gsum gyi sgo nas brtags pa na rnam par dag par mthong nas lung tshad mar blang bar bya yi gus pa tsam mam zhen pa tsam gyis len pa min par gsungs pa ltar tshad mas legs par dpyad cing brtags nas gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams 'di 'bum phrag bzhi pa'i tshad can kho nar nges par gzigs nas dpal dus kyi 'khor lo 'dir dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi pa'i tshad can du bcom ldan 'das kyis dam bcas shing gsungs pa ni ma yin te/ gong du bshad zin pa ltar gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten 'di nyid la yang sems can gyi khams rigs mi 'dra ba sna tshogs pa'i dbang gis byung ba'i tshad dang dbyibs mi 'dra ba'i cha shas du ma yod pa'i phyir ro/ /

However, it has been stated:
As gold is burned and rubbed, my word is to be accepted by examining well, not out of respect.[206] Good gold when burned turns red, when cut it shows white, and when rubbed it turns yellow; in these ways it should be tested. Similarly the words of the Buddha should undergo three tests, and when a teaching is seen to be pure, it should be accepted as valid, not merely out of respect or because of bias. /126/ However it is not the case here that we can say with valid and deep analysis that the Conqueror saw and ascertained this four-continent world realm to be solely four hundred thousand yojana and therefore spoke and declared this measurement in the Kālacakra. This is because, as previously explained, there are many differing measurements and shapes of this four-continent world due to the power of the various types of karma of sentient beings.

d.div: [111] sde dge_391_bka'/ rgyud/ gdapal stobs po che'i rgyud kyi rgyal po/ 216_ba6
[206] Toh 391 Kangyur, rgyud, kha, 216b6.

f.d: gling bzhi pa 'di'i tshad dbyibs dus 'khor nas bshad pa'i 'di kho na ltar med pa 'on kyang 'dir dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams bshad cing dam bcas pa ni dgos pa khyad par can bsod nams kyi tshogs bskyed pa'i rim pa dang ye shes kyi tshogs rdzogs pa'i rim pa'i yul la gzhug pa'i don du gsungs shing dam bcas pa yin no/ / de dag gis dus kyi 'khor lor dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi pa sogs kyi gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams bshad pa'i yongs gcod kyi dgos pa bstan nas rnam bcad kyi dgos pa ston pa ni/ nyi ma'i shing rta la sogs pa'i 'dod pa tshangs pa'i yul sa gcig pu 'di nyid dpag tshad bye ba'i khyon dang ldan pa 'gog pa ste/

The measurements of this four-continent world are not exclusively as taught here in the Kālacakra. However the teaching and assertion of a 400,000-yojana world here plays a special role in the creation of merit and wisdom for entering the generation stage and then the completion stage. This explains the affirming purpose for teaching a four-continent world realm of four hundred thousand yojana in the Kālacakra. The negating purpose is to refute the notion held by Sūryaratha and others that this single dominion of Brahmā covers an area of ten million yojana.

dus kyi 'khor lo 'dir gza' lnga'i 'gros dang skar rtsis dang khyim gyi 'khor lo'i rnam gzhag dang ldan pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams kyi tshad rab tu bkod pa 'di la phyi nang sbyor ba'i dgos pa yod par ma zad dgos pa gzhan yang yod de/ dgos pa gang gi phyir na gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams kyi yul 'di la chos mngon pa mdzod kyi 'dod pa dang rig byed kyi grub pa'i mtha'i bsam pas mi mthun pa sna tshogs pa yod cing / de ltar mi mthun pa de dag las rig byed pa'i 'dod pa tshangs pa'i yul sa gling bzhi pa gcig pu 'di ni dpag tshad bye ba'i khyon no zhes rdzun du smra bar byed de de lta bu'i rdzun smra ba'i don de la nyi ma'i shing rta la sogs pa mngon par zhen pa de log nas yongs su smin par bya ba'i slad du tshangs pa'i yul sa'i tshad de rnam par gzhom pa'i don nam dgos pa yod pa'i phyir ro/ /

In the Kālacakra the presentations of the measurements of a world realm together with descriptions of the movements of its five planets, its astronomy, and its zodiac of the houses and so forth, are not only for the purposes of inner and outer application, but they have another purpose. The thinking of the Abhidharmakośa and that of the Veda tenets are not in agreement on various features of this four-continent world realm. One of those disagreements is the false assertion made by followers of the Vedas that the dominion of Brahmā, this sole four-continent world, is of an area of ten million yojana. Sūryaratha and others cling to this assertion, and by reversing that, and in order to fully ripen them, this measurement of the dominion of Brahmā is destroyed.

de ltar na gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten 'bum phrag bzhi pa'i tshad la sogs pa gsungs pa 'di la sangs rgyas pa'i mdzod mthong nas dus 'khor nas bshad pa 'di 'khrul par gyur to snyam du mi bya ste/ gza' lnga'i 'gros dang skar rtsis dang khyim gyi 'khor lo la sogs pa dus kyi 'khor lo 'di nas ji ltar bshad pa ltar ri mos mngon sum du gtan la 'bebs pa de'i phyir ro/ /

Therefore, “having seen the Buddhist Abhidharma” teachings on the four-continent world, /127/ do not think that the Kālacakra explanation is mistaken, with its measurements of four hundred thousand yojana, because the movements of the planets, the astronomy, and the zodiac of the houses as they are explained here can be actually confirmed by the charts.

'o na ji ltar bcom ldan 'das kyis gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams 'di'i+i tshad mdzod las/ chu dang gser gyi dkyil 'khor gyi/ /thad kar 'bum phrag bcu gnyis dang /[112] /zhes sogs kyi don gong du bshad pa ltar gyi dpag tshad 'bum phrag so drug lhag ma dang bcas par yang gsungs shing / ji ltar dus kyi 'khor lor gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams 'di dpag tshad 'bum phrag bzhi pa'i tshad du yang gsungs na/ 'dir bcom ldan 'das rdzun gsung ba po yin nam ci zhes pa 'ga' zhig 'dod par gyur na bcom ldan 'das kyis mngon pa'i mdo dang dus kyi 'khor lor 'jig rten khams kyi tshad dbyibs mi 'dra ba so sor gsungs kyang bcom ldan 'das rdzun gsung ba po yin zhes pa de'i tshig las dang 'bras bu'i rnam gzhag khas len pa'i mkhas pa rnams kyis khas blang bar mi bya ste/ sngar bshad zin pa ltar gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams gcig bu 'di nyid la'ang mngon pa dang / 'dus pa sogs kyi ched du bya ba'i gdul bya dang / dus kyi 'khor lo'i ched du bya ba'i gdul bya so so'i las rigs mi 'dra ba'i bdag rkyen las tshad dbyibs mi 'dra ba'i cha shas so sor snang zhing / ji ltar snang ba dang mthun par sems can gyi bsam pa'i dbang gis te bsam pa dang mthun par gsungs pas so/ /

However[207] the Conqueror taught in the Abhidharmakośa that the measurements of this four-continent world realm were “across the mandalas of water and gold a hundred thousand times twelve,”[208] which, as previously explained, results in a circumference of over 3,600,00 yojana. Similarly, in the Kālacakra, he taught this four-continent world realm to have a measurement of four hundred thousand yojana. If that is so, does not the Conqueror speak falsely, as some assert? The Conqueror did teach different and individual measurements and shapes in the Abhidharma sutras and in the Kālacakra, but the wise who hold to the law of cause and effect should not believe in utterances such as “The Conqueror speaks falsely,” because, as explained previously, on this one four-continent world realm there are intended disciples of the Abhidharma, Guhyasamāja, and so forth, and intended disciples of the Kālacakra. These disciples have different kinds of karma, and with these types of karma as dominant conditions,[209] different measurements and shapes appear, and the Buddha taught in accord with such appearances as they appeared to the minds of sentient beings.

d.div: [112] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kuchos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka47_8_ba5
[207] The previous and following few paragraphs are essentially annotations to the Great Commentary that are woven into Norsang Gyatso’s text.
[208] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 47, 8b5.
[209] bdag rkyen. One of the three kinds of circumstance, condition, or cause that bring about a result.

f.d: 'o na 'di'i skabs kyi mdzod 'di ci la byed snyam na/ bla ma snga ma dag slob dpon dbyig gnyen gyis mdzod brtsams pa 'grel chen brtsams pa las lo sum brgya tsam gyis phyi bas dbyig gnyen gyis mdzad pa'i mdzod 'di mi+in zhing / 'o na gang yin snyam na/ mngon pa sde bdun la mdzod kyi bshad pa yod pa ltar ram/ yang na mngon pa sde bdun gyi don rgyas par gtan la 'bebs pa bye brag bshad mdzod chen mo la mdzod ces zer bas de la byed do gsung na'ang / 'grel chen las sangs rgyas pa'i mdzod mthong nas zhes ma 'ongs pa lung bstan pa lta bur 'dug pa dang / slob dpon dbyig gnyen gyi mdzod 'di bod la sogs pa kun la khyab che bas 'phags pa spyan ras gzigs dbang phyug gis ma 'ongs pa na slob dpon dbyig gnyen gyis mdzad pa'i mdzod ces pa'i bstan bcos 'byung ba la dgongs par byas na legs sam snyam mo/ /

It might be wondered to what particular text the Abhidharma mentioned here[210] refers? Lamas of the past say that the Abhidharma composed by the master Vasubandhu was written about three hundred years after the Great Commentary, and therefore it is not the Abhidharma referred to here. So which is it then? They maintain that it either refers to the Seven Great Texts of the Abhidharma or to the Great Abhidharma of Specific Explanation, which is an extensive and detailed exposition of the meanings of the Seven Great Texts of the Abhidharma and is also known as Abhidharma. However the phrase from the Great Commentary “having seen the Buddhist Abhidharma” looks like a prophecy. /128/ Also the Abhidharma of the master Vasubandhu is well established throughout Tibet and other lands, and I wonder if the noble Avalokiteśvara[211] was not thinking of a text known as the “Abhidharma” to be written in the future by Ācārya Vasubandhu?

d.div: [210] The Abhidharma mentioned in the Vimalaprabhā.
[211] In his manifestation as Puṇḍarīka, composer of the Great Commentary.

f.d: 'o na nyi ma'i shing rta la sogs pa gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten 'di dpag tshad bye ba'i khyon can du 'dod pa'i log rtog de ldog pa'am gzhom pa'i don du mngon pa nas bshad pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams kyi tshad dbyibs de nyid bstan pas chog mod/ dus kyi 'khor lo'i tshad dbyibs sogs nges par rjod ci dgos snyam na/ de lta bu'i log rtog de gzhom pa'i don du gza' dang rtsis dang khyim gyi 'khor lo dang ldan pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams 'di'i tshad nges par rjod dgos te/ gza' lnga'i 'gros dang skar rtsis dang khyim gyi 'khor lo 'khor tshul dang de la nyi zla sogs longs spyod tshul dus kyi 'khor lor bstan pa rnams sa ris kyis gtan la bab pa'i tshe de ltar bstan pa rnams sgra ji bzhin par khas blang du rung ba la nges shes skyes pa na 'jig rten 'di+i'i tshad dbyibs bstan pa rnams la yang nges shes skyes te snga ma'i log rtog ldog par 'gyur gyi de las gzhan du mngon pa nas bshad pa tsam gyi 'jig rten gyi rnam gzhag bstan pa de tsam gyis nyi ma'i shing rta la sogs pa'i log rtog de lta bu ldog par dka' ba'i phyir te/ rtsa rgyud las/ sems can mos pa sna tshogs pa/ rang gzhan gyi grub mtha' sna tshogs pa rig pa po/ bstan pa gzhan dang gzhan gyis bstan pa'i sna tshogs pa'i lam la rab tu gnas pa/ shes bya sna tshogs shes pa'i nga rgyal gyis khengs pa can de dag la rang gzhan gyi grub mtha' la ji srid sgrub byed dang gnod byed kyi rigs pa nges shes skyed nus pa ma bstan pa de srid du nga rgyal gyis khengs pa can de dag kun mkhyen gyi yang dbang du mi 'gyur ba ste gzhug par nus pa ma yin no/[113] /zhes gsungs pas so/ /

It might also be wondered if, in order to destroy or reverse the wrong view, held by Sūryaratha and others, that this four-continent world covers an area of ten million yojana, it would surely have been sufficient to teach the measurements as found in the Seven Great Texts of the Abhidharma. What need was there to categorically state the measurements found in the Kālacakra? In order to destroy this wrong view, it was necessary to state the measurements of this world realm together with its planets, its calculations, and its zodiac, because the movements of the five planets, their calculations, the way the circle of houses revolves, and the way the sun and moon move within it are taught in the Kālacakra and are ascertained by an earth-drawn chart. When this happens a conviction is born that these teachings can be held as being literally true, which in turn produces a conviction in the measurements of this world, and so the wrong view will be reversed. Otherwise, by just teaching the presentation of the world as explained in the Abhidharma, it would be difficult to destroy such wrong views as those held by Sūryaratha and others. The Root Tantra says[212] that “dispositions of sentient beings are varied / they know of various tenets” such as ours and others. “They follow various paths” and doctrines taught by others. “Proud of their knowledge” of phenomena, “the conceited will never come / under the might of the omniscient one / unless presented with reasons” that prove and disprove and that create conviction regarding our tenets and those of others.

d.div: [113] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 60_na7_'grel chen dri med 'od kyi nang du gsal ba'i rtsa rgyud las drangs shing de las logs su rtsa rgyud da lta mjal rgyu med/
[212] Quoted in the Great Commentary, Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 60a7.

f.d: 'o na tshad mas grub pa'i don bden pa bstan pa 'ba' zhig las gzhan tshad mas ma grub pa'i don bstan par mi rung ngam zhe na/ de ni mtha' gcig tu ma nges te/ gsod par nges pa'i mi la sogs pa'i srog chags mang po gsod byed gshed mas 'tshol ba'i tshe/ gsad bya de dag mthong ngam zhes 'dri ba la gsad bya de dag la snying brtse ba'i bsam pas mthong yang ma mthong zhes rdzun gyi tshig brjod pa na gsad bya dang gsod byed kyi gshed ma'i sems can de dag la phan pa las mi bden pa'i rdzun des bsod nams kyi tshogs kyi rgyu byed pa'i phyir dang / stong nyid zab mo'i snod du mi rung ba'i gang zag la stong nyid ston pa'i tshig bden pa brjod pa na gzhan stong nyid kyi snod du mi rung ba'i gang zag de la gnod pa las bden pa'i tshig des rgyu byas nas mnar med la sogs pa rab tu ster bar 'gyur ba'i phyir te/ blo sbyong ma byas sems can la/ /stong pa nyid ni brjod pa dang /[114] /zhes byang sems kyi rtsa ltung du gsungs pa bzhin no/ /

But surely it is wrong to teach something that does not validly exist instead of teaching the validly established truth? /129/ That is not necessarily so. A butcher searching for animals that he will definitely kill may ask someone if he has seen the animal he is going to kill. Moved by compassion for those to be killed, the person will reply that they have not seen it even though they have. By such a lie the animals he is seeking to kill and the would-be killer himself are both benefited, and this lie becomes a cause for great merit. If emptiness is truthfully taught to someone unfit for teachings on profound emptiness, such a teaching would harm that person, and those truthful words would become a cause for the Hell of No Respite and so forth. One of the root downfalls of a bodhisattva is “Teaching emptiness to those who have not prepared their minds.”[213]

d.div: [114] sde dge_3940_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_bslab btus/ le'u/ 43_na7
[213] Śikṣāsamuccaya, Toh 3940 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 43a7.

f.d: gtong ba po min yi dwags kyis/[115] /zhes sogs ni sems can rnams kyi las kyi nus pa bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i shes byed kyi lung ste/ de dag gi don ni gtong ba po min pa ser sna'i las kyis yi dwags su skyes pa rnams kyis las de'i nus pas bza' btung gis gang ba'i khyim gyi gnas su phyin pa na bza' btung gis dag pa'i ri dang mtshungs par mthong zhing / sdig pa chen po byed pa dmyal bar skyes pa rnams kyis khyim gyis gnas bzang po yang khab rtse dang shal ma li la sogs pa mtshon cha'i rnam par gyur nas bdag nyid la gnod par mthong ngo / /

The verse beginning “Miserly hungry ghosts”[214] expresses the inconceivable potential of the karma of sentient beings. By the force of their miserly nongiving, sentient beings are born as hungry ghosts. If they were to enter a house fully stocked with food and drink, by the force of that karma they would see it as a mountain totally bare of food and drink. For those wrongdoers born into hell, a beautiful house assumes the form of sharp weapons and sharp leaves and so forth.

f.d: de bzhin du/ sa 'og dngos grub thob gyur nas/[116] /zhes sogs ni rnal 'byor pa'i mthu bsam gyis mi khyab par bshad pa'i shes byed kyi lung ste/ de'i don yang rnal 'byor pas sa 'og na spyod pa'i dngos grub thob par gyur cing lha mo rnams kyi grong du 'gro ba'i dngos grub thob pa rnams kyis rab tu brtan cing mkhregs pa'i sa gzhi yang kun nas bug ba dang bcas pa ste/ mngon par skabs yod par mthong zhes rtsa rgyud las gsungs so/ /

Similarly the verse beginning “Having gained the siddhi of the world below”[215] teaches the inconceivable power of the yogis who have gained the powers to make use of the worlds below the earth. They possess the power to travel to the cities of the goddesses and clearly see this solid and firm earth as hollow. These verses are from the Root Tantra.

d.div: [116] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 60_ba3
[215] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 60b3.

f.d: de'i phyir zhes sogs ni sngar bshad pa de dag gi don bsdu ba ste/ gong du rgyu mtshan bshad zin pa de'i phyir 'jig rten gyi khams kyi tshad dbyibs bcom ldan 'das kyi gsungs ba ni sems can rnams kyis las rigs mi 'dra ba sna tshogs pa bsags pa'i las dang rjes su mthun par sems can rang rang gi sems kyi bag chags kyi dbang gis 'jig rten gyi tshad dbyibs sogs mi 'dra ba du ma rab tu snang ba de de ltar snang ba'i snang tshul dang mthun par de bzhin gshegs pas kyang 'jig rten gyi tshad dbyibs sogs gsungs pa yin gyi/ sems can gyi snang tshul la ma ltos par de bzhin gshegs pa rang nyid kyis mngon par zhen pa'i dbang gis 'jig rten gyi khams gyi tshad dang dbyibs la sogs pa gzigs nas gnyis snang 'khrul pa'i gzung ba dang 'dzin pa'i snang tshul gyi ngo bos dngos po'i tshad gsungs pa ni 'ga' yang med do/ /

The following passage beginning “Therefore the measurements of the world” gives a summary of the above explanation. “Therefore,” in keeping with the previous reasons, “the words that the Conqueror spoke on the measurements of the world” were spoken because sentient beings have gathered various types of karma, and in tune with that karma, “each sentient being has predispositions in their minds by whose power” the world appears in many differing aspects. /130/ In keeping with those appearances the Tathāgata likewise taught the measurements of the world, but “nowhere did the Tathāgata look at the measurements of the world under the power of attachment and speak on them from” a false and dual appearance of “internal subject and external object,” without regard to the way the world appears to sentient beings.

de rnams kyis 'grel pa'i don zhib par bshad nas mdor bsdu na mngon pa sogs nas bshad pa dang dus kyi 'khor lo nas bshad pa'i gling bzhi pa'i 'jig rten 'di'i tshad dbyibs sogs mi mthun pa la gcig rgyu mtshan du byas nas cig shos 'gog pa sogs byar mi rung ste/ mngon pa nas bshad pa ltar dpal gsang ba 'dus pa'i bskyed rdzogs kyi sbyang gzhi'i snod kyi 'jig rten 'chad pa'i skabs su slob dpon klu byang sogs kyis bshad la/ de ltar bshad pa ltar gyi tshad dbyibs can gyi snod kyi 'jig rten med na spyong byed kyi lam yang mi 'thad par 'ag+r+yur ro/ / de bzhin du dus 'khor nas bshad pa'i tshad dbyibs can gyi snod kyi 'jig rten med na yang / ji ltar phyi rol de bzhin lus/[117] /zhes lam gyi sbyang gzhir bshad pa mi 'thad par 'gyur ro// //

This has been a detailed explanation of this part of the commentary. To summarize: it is not right to use one set of measurements of the world found in the Abhidharma or in the Kālacakra to refute the other. The Abhidharma explanation is used by Ācārya Nāgārjuna and others when explaining the outside world as a purification base for the generation and completion stages of Guhyasamāja. If there were no outside world with no such measurements, the path of purification would also be invalid. Similarly, if there were no outside world with measurements as explained in the Kālacakra, it would not be valid as the purification base for the path, as expressed in the quote, “As without, so within the body.” /131/

d.i: The bardo of the being about to take birth

f.d: mdzod las/ sngon dus srid 'byung sha tshugs can/ /zhes dang / rigs mthun lha mig dag pas mthong / /zhes dang / dbang po kun tshang thogs med ldan/[1] /zhes bar do'i lus rdul phra rab tshogs pa'i gzugs dang / de'i byad dbyibs sogs gzugs kyi skye mched du bshad cing / mngon pa kun btus las kyang / gang du skye bar 'gyur ba de'i byad gzugs so [2] zhes bar do'i byad gzugs kyi skye mched du bshad la/

The Abhidharmakośa says: “With bodily form of the prior-state existence.”[1] Also: “Seeing with unfettered eyes those of similar kind.” And further: “Sense powers complete and unobstructed.”[2] The bardo body therefore is taught to be a body composed of subtle particles, and whose shape and form is a visual form source.[3] The Abhidharmasamuccaya also talks of “where the bodily form will be born,”[4] thereby referring to the bodily form of the bardo as a visual form source.

d.div: [1] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kumangon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka13_dang 14_7_na7_dang 7_ba1
[2] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_chos mngon pa kun las btus pa/ 78_na5

[1] Tib. sngon dus kyi srid pa. One of the four states of existence, beginning from the second moment of conception until the body is left behind. The other three are death, bardo, and birth. Here it refers to the future existence of the bardo being.
[2] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa; gnas v. 13, 7a7, v. 14, 7b7.
[3] gzugs kyi skye mched. The visual forms of shape and color that act as sources or conditions for the creation of visual consciousness.
[4] Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 78a5.

f.d:
'grel chen gyi mchog mi 'gyur gyi mdor bsdus las/
'chi ba'i dus su lnga'i bdag nyid kyi sa bon de nyid nges par 'byung ngo / / slar yang rmi lam gyi lus bzhin du bag chags kyi lus stong pa rdul phra rab kyi tshogs spangs pa ma 'gags pa ste las kyi bag chags las byung ba'i bag chags kyi lus ma 'gags pa de nyid kyis slar yang rdul phra rab tshogs pa'i bdag nyid kyi lus 'dzin no/[3] / zhes bar do'i lus rdul phra rab kyi tshogs spangs pa yin par gsungs shing / mkhas pa (ku mA ra/)chen po dag gis kyang bar do'i lus chos kyi skye mched pa'i gzugs yin par gsungs so/ /

The Great Commentary, in the Supreme and Unchanging Gnosis summary, says:
“At the time of death, the seed possessing the characteristics of the five[5] will definitely arise. Like a body of a dream, the empty body of imprints abandons the composite of subtle particles but does not cease.” The body of imprints formed from the imprints of karma does not cease. Once again it will take hold of a body composed of subtle particles.[6] /132/ Thus it is stated that the bardo body has left behind the composite of subtle particles. Great scholars (such as Kumāra) have also said that the bardo body has the form of a mental phenomena source.[7]

[7] chos kyi skye mched pa’i gzugs. Form, such as that in a dream, that is primarily the object of mental consciousness.

f.d: de ltar sgras zin la mi mthun par gsungs pa de dag lugs so so bar byed dam/ dus 'khor nas gsungs pa 'di nyid sngon dus kyi srid pa'i lus lta bu'i rdul phra rab med pa la dgongs zhes 'chad dam brtag par bya'o/ /

Taken literally, the above quotes contradict each other. Whether this is due to individual traditions[8] or whether the Kālacakra passage is referring to the absence of the kind of subtle particles of the body of the prior-state existence is something to be examined.

d.div: [8] Of the Abhidharma and Kālacakra traditions.

d.i: How consciousness enters the blood and fluid after bardo has ceased

f.d: ['di ]la gnyis/ gang 'jug pa'i 'jug pa po'i rnam shes ngos gzung ba dang / de ji ltar 'jug pa'i tshul dngos so/ /
This is under two headings: 1. Defining the entering consciousness 2. How the consciousness enters
dang po ['jug pa'i rnam shes ]ni/

bar do 'gag bzhin pa'i sems ni shin tu phra ba'i sems 'od gsal gyi sems yin la/ sems de dang mngal du nying mtshams sbyar ma thag pa'i sems de skad cig snga phyir byung ba'i sgo nas mngal du zhugs ma thag pa'i sems de yang shin tu phra ba'i 'od gsal gyi sems nyid yin no/ / de yang de 'dra ba'i sems de lhan cig skyes pa'i bde ba dang mtshungs ldan du gnas la/ sems de la kun gzhi rnam shes zhes bya zhing lhan skyes kyi sems zhes kyang bya ste/ nang le'i bco lnga pa'i 'grel chen las/
'dir re zhig mngal du rnam shes ni kun gzhi rnam par shes pa ste bde ba dam pa'i ye shes so/[4] zhes dang / yang de nyid kyi 'phro las/
ma dang pha dang kun gzhi rnam par shes pa bde ba'i gnas skabs gcig yin pa'i phyir ro/[5] / zhes gsungs pas so/ /

As the bardo is coming to an end, the mind at that time is the very subtle mind of clear light. That mind and the mind that crosses over into the womb are of preceding and succeeding instants. In this way the mind that has just entered the womb is also the very subtle mind of clear light. Such a mind exists alongside innate bliss and is known as the foundation consciousness[9] and as innate mind. The Great Commentary, on the fifteenth verse of the Inner chapter, says:
While the consciousness is in the womb, it is the foundation consciousness, a gnosis of the highest bliss.[10] And farther on:
Mother, father, and foundation consciousness are one at the time of bliss.[11]

f.d: 'o na 'dir mngal du zhugs ma thag pa'i sems la kun gzhi rnam shes zhes bshad pa 'di dang / rnam shes tshogs brgyad du bzhed pa rnams kyis kun gzhir bshad pa'i kun gzhi rnam shes la khyad par ci yod ce na/ de yang spyir mngal du zhugs ma thag pa'i sems 'di la 'dod pa mi 'dra ba mang ste/ mngon pa mdzod las/ skye ba'i srid pa nyon mongs can/[6] /zhes yid kyi shes pa nyon mongs can du bshad la/ mngon pa kun las btus la sogs par rnam shes tshogs brgyad du 'dod pa rnams kyis kun gzhi rnam shes su bshad cing / de ma bsgribs lung ma bstan du 'dod pa dang / de yang tshor ba btang snyoms nyid dang mtshungs ldan du 'dod de/

What is the difference between the foundation consciousness assigned to the mind that has just entered the womb and the foundation consciousness explained as the “foundation of all” by those who assert eight types of consciousnesses? Generally there are many differing assertions concerning the mind that has just entered the womb. The Abhidharmakośa says, “Birth existence is with delusion,”[12] thereby declaring that the mental consciousness is one of mental affliction. In the Abhidharmasamuccaya and similar texts, those who assert the collection of eight types of consciousnesses describe it as a foundation consciousness, which is an untaught,[13] unobstructed phenomenon and associated with neutral feelings.

d.div: [6] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ kumangon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka38_8_na7
[12] Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, gnas v. 38, 8a7.
[13] lung ma bstan. Not taught by the Buddha to be either virtuous or nonvirtuous.

f.d:
dus kyi 'khor lo sogs sngags bla med pa rnams dgongs pa mthun par/ sems rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal ba 'khor 'das thams cad kyi gzhir gyur ba bar do shi ba'i 'od gsal de nyid de/ de la kun gzhi zhes 'grel chen du gsungs shing / 'chi ba'i 'od gsal yang kun gzhi zhes gsungs te/ sgrub le'i bdun pa'i 'grel chen las/
de ltar khams kyi tshogs myur du rnam par nyams te de nas sems de mun pa'i mtha'i me ste zhes pa nam mkha'i khams rnam pa thams cad pa'i gzugs yul dang rnam par bral ba dbus kyi sa la kun gzhi rnam par shes pa gzhag par bya'o/[7] / zhes gsungs pas so/ /

Highest tantras, such as the Kālacakra, are in agreement that the clear-light nature of mind is the basis of all things in samsara and nirvana. /133/ This is the clear light of a bardo death, and in the Great Commentary this is referred to as “the foundation.” Death clear light is also referred to as the “foundation” in the Great Commentary on the seventh verse of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter:
Like this the elements quickly weaken. Then “the mind is the fire at the end of darkness,” which means that the foundation consciousness is placed in the realm of space, in fully aspected forms empty of all objects, dwelling in the middle.[14]

d.div: [7] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 203_ba3
[14] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 203b3.

f.d: de ltar na rgyud 'grel 'dir mngal du nying mtshams sbyar ma thag pa'i sems dang 'chi ba'i 'od gsal gyi sems la kun gzhi rnam shes su gsungs kyang yid kyi rnam shes las don gzhan pa'i rnam shes tshogs brgyad du bzhed pa rnams kyis bshad pa ltar gyi kun gzhi rnam shes ni ma yin te|_de dag gis bshad pa ltar gyi kun gzhi rnam shes yin na/ ma bsgribs lung ma bstan dang / tshor ba btang snyoms kho na dang mtshungs ldan dang / dmigs rnam mi gsal ba yin pas khyab pa sogs kyi khyad par gyi chos du ma dang ldan pa yin dgos shing / bar do 'gags ma thag pa'i rnam shes dang 'chi ba'i 'od gsal gyi sems ni dge ba'i sems su 'gyur ba yod cing / tshor ba ni bde ba dang mtshungs ldan du 'byung ba dang / dmigs rnam ni stong sang gi ngang nas nam mkha'i khams rnam pa thams cad pa'i gzugs yul dang rnam par bral ba zhes gsungs pa ltar gyi dmigs rnam gsal ba yin pas so/ / de ltar na sems de nyid la kun gzhi zhes gsungs pa ni 'khor 'das kun 'byung ba'i gzhi yin pa la dgongs nas gsungs pa yin gyi ngo bo ni yid kyi rnam shes nyid yin te/

Therefore, in this tantra and its commentary, the mind that has just crossed over to the womb and the mind of the clear light of death are spoken of as a foundation consciousness. However this is not a foundation consciousness that is distinct from the mental consciousnesses, as is taught by those who assert the eight kinds of consciousness. That type of foundation consciousness is distinguished by many characteristics, such as being at all times an untaught, unobstructed phenomenon, associated only with neutral feelings, of unclear focus and apprehension. Moreover the consciousness at the cessation of the bardo and the mind of the clear light of death can become virtuous minds, can become associated with feelings of bliss, and are consciousnesses of a clear focus and apprehension arising from a clarity[15] “in the realm of space, in fully aspected forms empty of all objects, dwelling in the middle.” Therefore the thinking behind calling this mind “the foundation” is that it is the foundation for the arising of all things in samsara and nirvana. As an entity, however, it is a mental consciousness. The Great Commentary says in the Gnosis chapter:

d.div: [15] stong sang.

f.d:
ye shes le'u'i 'grel chen las/
'dir ji ltar mngal 'dzin pa ni byang chub kyi sems kyi rten dang bcas pa'i yid kyi rnam par shes pa gcig bu [8] zhes byang sems dkar dmar gyi rten dang bcas pa'i yid kyi rnam par shes pa kho na mngal 'dzin pa'i rnam shes su gsal bar gsungs pas so/ /

How does it grasp the womb? Solely as a mental consciousness with the support of bodhicitta.[16] This clearly states that the mental consciousness alone, supported by a base of red and white bodhicitta, is the consciousness of conception. /134/

f.d: gnyis pa bar do 'gags pa'i rnam shes khu khrag gi dbus su 'jug tshul bshad pa ni

spyir sems can gyi skye gnas la mngal skyes/ drod gsher skyes/ sgong skyes/ rdzus skyes dang bzhir nges pa las rdzus skyes ni mdzod las/
dmyal ba rnams dang lha rnams dang/ / srid pa bar mardzu sa te skye/[9] / zhes dmyal ba dang lha dang bar do yin na rdzus skyes yin pas khyab pa dang /
yi dwags mngal nas skye ba'ang yin/[10] / zhes yi dwags la mngal skyes dang rdzus skyes gnyis su yod pa dang /
mi dang dud 'gro rnam pa bzhi/[11] / zhes mi dang dud 'gro la skye gnas bzhi ga yod par bshad cing /

Generally four places of conception for sentient beings can be ascertained. They are the womb, heat and moisture, the egg, and miraculous birth. On miraculous birth the Abhidharmakośa says:
Hell beings, gods, and those between existences are born miraculously.[17] Hell, god realms, and the bardo are characterized by taking miraculous birth. The text continues:
Hungry ghosts can also be born from the womb.[18] This means that hungry ghosts may be of miraculous birth or womb birth.
For humans and animals, four kinds.[19] This states that all four kinds of birth can be found within the human and animal realm.

f.d:
dud 'gro la skye gnas bzhi 'chad pa'i tshe khams le'i bzhi pa'i 'grel chen las/
dud 'gro skye gnas rnam pa bzhi dang zhes pa la sgong las skyes pa ni mkha' lding la sogs pa ste rlung gi skye gnas so/ / mngal nas skyes pa ni glang po'i dbang po la sogs pa ste me'i skye gnas so/ / drod gsher las skyes pa ni srin bu dang phye ma leb dang grog sbur la sogs pa ste chu'i skye gnas so/ / rdzus te skyes pa ni ljon shing la sogs pa ste sa'i skye gnas so/ / de bzhin du rdzus te skyes pa chen po ni ro'i skye gnas so [12] zhes gsungs so/ /

When describing the four kinds of birth found in the animal realm, the Great Commentary, on the fourth verse of the Realms chapter, says:
“Animals are of four kinds of birth.” Birth from an egg would be for the garuda hawk and others. It is an air-element birthplace. Birth from a womb includes the mighty elephant and others. It is a fire-element birthplace. Birth from heat and moisture is for some insects, butterflies, ants, and so forth. It is a water-element birthplace. Miraculous birth is for trees and is an earth-element birthplace. Similarly great miraculous birth is a taste birthplace.[20]

f.d:
de la kha cig (rje btsun ku mA ra ma ti/)na re/
ljon shing la sogs dud 'gro'i skye bar sdud/ / 'di ni gcer bu pa yi gzhung bzang yin/[13] / zhes dgag pa mdzad na'ang/ 'di ni ljon shing dang lhun po sogs dud 'gro'i skye gnas su sdud pa min gyi/ 'o na ji ltar yin snyam na/ dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i dgongs pa ni chos thams cad khams lnga'am drug tu sbyar nas 'chad pa yin la/ skabs 'dir yang skye gnas bzhi khams lnga dang sbyor ba'i ched du rdzus skyes la rdzus skyes tsam po ba cig dang rdzus skyes chen po gnyis su phye nas/ rdzus skyes tsam po ba de sa'i khams dang sbyor ba dang / yongs su grags pa'i rdzus skyes rnams la rdzus skyes chen po zhes byas te/ ro zhes pa nam mkha'i khams dang sbyar ba'i phyir du gtso bor sa las skyes pa'i ljon shing la sogs pa la rdzus skyes zhes bshad pa yin gyi/ ljon shing sogs dud 'gro'i skye bar ston pa yin no/ / mi la skye gnas bzhi yod pa'i sgong skyes ni gnas brtan grags dang nye ba'i grags lta bu'o/ / drod gsher skyes ni rgyal po spyi bo skyes lta bu'o/ / rdzus skyes ni slob dpon 'phags pa lha lta bu rnams yin no/ /

Regarding this quote the noble Kumāramati says:
Including trees as animal birth is a tenet of the Jains.[21] Although he is refuting the Great Commentary here, this passage is not actually classifying trees, mountains, and so forth as animal births. So what is the explanation? In Kālacakra all existent phenomena are assigned to the five or six elements. Here, in order to assign the four kinds of birth to five elements, miraculous birth is divided into two types, namely, mere and great. Mere miraculous birth is assigned to the earth element. “Great miraculous birth” refers to well-known miraculous births, and “taste” refers to the space element.[22] Therefore trees and so forth, which mainly grow from earth, are explained as being of miraculous birth, but this does not teach that trees are animal births. Of the four kinds of birth found in the human realm, birth from egg would be, for example, that of the Sthavirakīrti and Upakīrti. An example of birth from heat and moisture would be that of King Mūrdhāta. A miraculous birth would be that of Āryadeva. /135/

d.div: [13] 'phrin yig nor bu'i phreng ba/ bod kyi rtsis rig kun 'dus chen mo deb dang po/ shog grangs/ 288
[21] Jewel Garland of Letters, p. 288.
[22] ro. Possibly because ro is a word-numeral for six, and space is the sixth element.

f.d: de ltar na skye gnas la yang bzhi dang / nang sems can la yang rigs drug gam lnga la sogs pa yod kyang / nang gtan la 'bebs pa nang gi le'u 'dir gtso bor tshe de nyid la mchog gi dngos grub 'grub pa'i phyir du lam rim pa gnyis sgom pa'i rten gyi gang zag khams drug ldan gyi mi'i lus mngal skyes nyid gtan la 'bebs pa yin la/ de yang dgos pa gang gi phyir du gtan la 'bebs na/ bskyed pa'i rim pa dang rdzogs pa'i rim pa'i lam gyi sbyang gzhi dang / rdzogs rim gyis gang la gnad du bsnun pa'i gzhi rtogs pa'i don du gtan la 'bebs pa yin no/ /

There are four kinds of birth, and sentient beings are classified into six types, five types, etc. However here in the Inner chapter, which determines the inner world, the primary ascertainment is that of a sentient being possessed of a womb-born human body of the six elements[23] who will meditate in two stages in order to attain the supreme siddhi of enlightenment in this life. What is the purpose of such an ascertainment? It is to know and understand the bases of purification for the generation and completion stages as well as the locations for the practice of penetrative focusing in the completion stage.

d.div: [23] Earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.

f.d: de bas na mngal skyes khams drug ldan gyi mi'i lus 'grub tshul sogs bshad par bya ste/ de yang pha ma gnyis snyoms 'jug byas pa las byung ba'i khu khrag gi dbus su bar do 'gags pa'i yid kyi rnam shes shin tu phra ba'i 'od gsal gyi sems kun gzhi'i ming can de zhugs pa'i khu khrag rnam shes gsum ma'i mngal du 'dres pa las sems can gyi lus 'grub pa yin la/ de 'dra'i khu khrag rnam shes gsum 'dres pa'i gong bu de ma'i gsang ba'i pad+ma'i sa'i khams kyis 'dzin par byed/ chu'i khams kyis sdud par byed/ me'i khams kyis smin par byed/ rlung gi khams kyis 'phel bar byed/ nam mkha'i khams mngal gyi stong pa'i+i cha des 'phel ba'i go skabs 'byed par byed do/ / mngal gyi khu khrag rnam shes 'dres pa de'i khams lnga rnams kyi yang sa'i khams kyis lci zhing sra bar byed/ chus gsher ba nyid byed/ mes smin par byed/ ma 'ongs pa na 'byung bar 'gyur ba'i rlung bcu'i sa bon du gyur pa'i khu khrag rnam shes gsum 'dres pa'i rlung gi khams kyis khu khrag rnam shes gsum 'dres pa'i lus de 'phel bar byed/ de'i nam mkha'i khams des lus de 'phel ba'i go skabs 'byed par byed do/ /

Therefore the development of a womb-born human body of the six elements is explained. Amid the blood and fluid of mother and father in union arises the mental consciousness of the previous bardo being. This is a very subtle mind of clear light, known as the “foundation.” The consciousness, fluid, and blood are united within the mother’s womb, from which will develop the body of a sentient being. This agglomeration of fluid, blood, and consciousness dwelling in the mother’s secret lotus[24] is supported by the element of earth of the mother’s secret lotus, gathered together by her element of water, matured by her element of fire, made larger by her element of air, and given the room to grow by her element of space in its aspect of empty space within the womb. The five elements that make up this union of fluid, blood, and consciousness within the womb also perform individual functions. The earth element gives it weight and solidity, the water element gives it moisture, and it is matured by the fire element. The element of air agglomeration, which is the seed of the element-originated[25] ten winds that will develop in the future, enlarges this agglomeration of fluid, blood, and consciousness. The element of space provides the room for growth.

d.div: [24] Lotus refers to the womb and to the female pudenda.
[25] ’byung ’gyur. Arisen; all phenomena arise from the elements.

f.d:
skabs 'dir 'phel bar byed pa'i rlung la 'di'i 'grel chen las/
rab mchog rnam pa bcu'i rlung srog la sogs pa dag ni sa bon 'di'i lus la 'phel bar byed do/[14] / zhes gsungs pa ni bshad ma thag pa ltar gyi rlung bcu'i sa bon la byed dgos te/ skabs 'dir rlung bcu'i rten gyi rtsa yang grub pa med na rlung bcu ma grub pa lta ci smos pas so/ / yang skabs 'di'i rnam pa bcu'i rlung zhes pa nang gi phyi'i rlung ma'i lus kyi rlung la byed gsungs pa ni 'grel chen las/ sa bon rang gi khams kyi bya ba gsungs pa [15] zhes sa bon khu khrag rang gi rlung la bshad pa dang 'gal lo/ /

Concerning the developmental role of the winds, the Great Commentary says at this point:
The ten great winds, such as the life-sustaining wind, etc., enlarge the form of this seed.[26] “Wind” here must refer to the seeds of the ten winds, as mentioned above, because at this particular time the channels for the ten winds have not developed, and if that is so, then of course neither have the winds themselves. To say that “the ten winds” in the above passage refers to the internal winds of the mother’s body contradicts the Great Commentary in this section when it says, “This speaks of the activity of the seed’s own elements,”[27] thereby confirming that this passage is referring to the air element of the seed of fluid and blood itself. /136/

f.d: gsum pa de ltar zhugs pa las mngal du 'phel tshul sogs bshad pa ni/

de lta bu'i mngal bzung ba nas mthar 'chi ba'i bar ni khyab 'jug gi 'jug pa bcu dang sbyar nas gsungs te/ de yang khyab 'jug gi 'jug pa bcu ni nya la sogs pa'i lo rgyus rnams yin la de rnams ni rim pa bzhin dus kyi dbang gis sngon rig byed bzhi rgya mtsho'i nang du nub pa khyab 'jug gis nya ru sprul te bton pa dang / de bzhin du rus sbal gyi gzugs kyis 'jig rten bteg nas rgyun du gnas pa dang/ phag rgod kyi gzugs kyis tshangs pa'i 'jig rten man chad mnan pa dang / smad mi la stod seng ge'i gzugs kyis lha min gyi dbang po 'gro skyob gser can lto dral nas bsad pa dang / mi'u thung du sprul nas lha min stobs ldan gom pa gsum gyis blang zhes bslus pa dang / dza mA da ag+ni'i bu dgra sta rA mar sprul te rgyal rigs srid sgrub la sogs pa bsad nas rgyal srid med par byas pa dang / rgyal po shing rta bcu pa'i bu rA _ma Nar sprul nas rang gi chung ma srin po lang ka mgrin bcus phrogs pas spre'u ha lu many+dzu la grogs bcol te srin po btul ba dang / nag pas rtsod pa'i dus su sems can gyi don byas pa dang / sangs rgyas shAkya thub tu sprul nas sngon rgyal rigs bsad pa'i sdig pa sbyangs pa dang / rigs ldan bram ze'i bu kIrti tse zhes bya ba ma 'ongs pa na 'byung bas sems can mang po btul ba'i mthar dus log pa rtogs par 'gyur ba'o/ /

The time from conception in the womb until death is taught in correspondence with the ten avatāra, or incarnations, of Viṣṇu. These ten, beginning with the fish, are tales of Viṣṇu and can be related in chronological order. Once when the four Vedas had sunk into the ocean, Viṣṇu manifested as a fish and recited them. In the form of a turtle he hoisted up the world and held it there. In the form of a wild pig he crushed the worlds as far as the realms of Brahmā. With his lower half in the form of a man and his upper in the form of a lion, he killed Hiraṇyakaśipu, the king of the asura demons, by tearing out his stomach. Manifesting as a midget he deceived the demon Bali by taking three steps. Manifesting as Rama of the axe, the son of the Brahmin Jamādagni, he murdered those of the royal kṣatriya caste, such as Arjuna, and put an end to their rule. In his manifestation as Rāma, son of King Daśaratha, his wife was snatched by Rāvaṇa, the ten-throated rakṣās of Lanka, and so accompanied by the monkey Hanuman he defeated the rakṣās. As Kṛṣṇa he worked for sentient beings in the age of troubles.[28] He manifested as Buddha Śākyamuni and purified himself of the former murder of kings. As Kīrti,[29] the son of a Kalkī Brahmin, he will appear in the future and, having tamed many beings, a new era will begin.

d.div: [28] rtsod ldan, kaliyuga.
[29] Although sometimes rendered as Yaśas, in the text the Sanskrit is transliterated as Kīrti.

f.d:
'jug pa phyi ma gnyis la mchog mi 'gyur gyi mdor bsdus las 'di ltar du bshad de/
khyab 'jug gam nor lha'i 'jug pa dgu pa sangs rgyas ni khyab 'jug gis sangs rgyas shAkya thub tu sprul nas dgos pa sngon lha ma yin gyi phyogs su gnas pa nor lhas g.yul du ma bsnan zhing ma bsad pa sangs rgyas kyi dus su dmangs rigs la sogs par gyur ba rnams dmyal bar 'gro ba'i don du bya ba g.yo thabs kyis mchod sbyin gyi chos sun 'byin par 'gyur bas na rgyas pa'i tshig b+hAr ta dang glu'i tshig dang rig byed kyi tshig rnams sun 'byin par 'gyur ro/[16] / de rnams sun phyung ste de nas dmangs rigs la sogs pa de rnams la phyin ci log gi chos ston par 'gyur ba ni 'di lta ste sbyin pa'i pha rol tu phyin pa dang zhes pa nas/ mi dge ba bcu'i las kyi lam rnams mi bya'o zhes pa'i bar pha rol tu phyin pa bcu dang / tshad med bzhi dang / mi dge ba bcu spong ba sogs phyin ci log gi chos kyi rnam grangs 'di rnams bstan pa nyid kyis dmangs rigs la sogs pa rnams bag chags sad par byas nas skra bregs te gos ngur smrig 'dzin pa'i dge slong rnams su byed par 'gyur te/ de ltar gyur pa'i dmangs rigs la sogs pa sngon lha ma yin gyi phyogs su gnas pa nor lha khyab 'jug gis g.yul du ma smin zhing ma bsad pa de rnams kyis bram ze rnams sun 'byin pa byas nas dmangs rigs sogs de rnams dmyal bar 'gro ba na 'gyur ba gang yin pa des na khyab 'jug gis sangs rgyas su sprul pa'i dus su dmangs rigs la sogs par gyur pa sngon lha ma yin gyi phyogs na gnas pa de rnams dmyal bar 'gro ba'i don du khyab 'jug gis sangs rgyas su sprul pa'i g.yo sgyu 'di byas pa yin no/ / 'jug pa bcu pa rigs ldan ni sham b+ha la'i yul du nor lha khyab 'jug bram ze'i bu grags par gyur nas rdo'i rta la zhon te ku sha'i rang bzhin gyi mdung rnams kyis kla klo thams cad bsad nas gser mang po'i me rda'i mchod sbyin byas te/ slar yang sa gzhi bram ze'i rang bzhin du byed par 'gyur ro/[17] / zhes gsungs shing /

Concerning the last two avatāra, the Supreme and Unchanging Gnosis summary from the Gnosis chapter says the following:
The ninth avatāra of Viṣṇu, the god of wealth, is the Buddha. Viṣṇu will manifest as Buddha Śākyamuni. His purpose will be as follows. In the past, in the realms of the asura, those who were not killed or defeated by the god of wealth will be born as low castes at the time of the Buddha. In order to send them to hell, he will deceptively refute the doctrine of rituals, and by doing so the extensive words of Bhārata, the words of Gīta,[30] and the words of the Veda will be refuted. Having refuted them, he will then teach the lower castes perverted doctrine and expound the ten perfections by saying, “practice the perfection of giving,” and so forth, up to “do not practice the paths of the ten nonvirtuous deeds.” /137/ He will teach the four immeasurables, the abandonment of the ten nonvirtues, and other perverted doctrine. By such teaching, the latent dispositions of the lower castes will be awakened. They will shave their heads and put on the yellow robes to become monks. These lower castes, who in former times in the land of the asura were not defeated and killed by the wealth god Viṣṇu, will refute the Brahmins. By doing so they will go to hell. Therefore, at the time Viṣṇu manifests as the Buddha, the ordinary lower castes are formerly inhabitants of the land of the asura. In order to send them to hell, Viṣṇu enacts this deception of manifesting as the Buddha. The tenth avatāra is the lineage bearer. In the land of Shambhala the wealth god Viṣṇu will incarnate as the Brahmin Kīrti, and he will ride a stone horse and with spears of kuśa[31] will kill the barbarians and perform the fire offering of “plentiful gold.” Once again the land will become Brahmin.[32]

d.div: [16] 'dir rgyas pa'i tshig b+hA ra ta zhes pa mu stegs pa'i bstan bcos yongs su grags pa ma hA b+hA ra ta zhes pa de yin la/ glu'i tshig zhes pa ni gong gi bstan bcos de'i nang gses b+ha ba wa da gI tA zhes pa yongs grags dbang phyug nag po'i glu zhes pa de yin/
[17] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 430_ba7
[30] The Bhagavadgītā or Song of God, taken from the epic Mahābhārata.
[31] A kind of sacred grass.

[32] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 430b7. The passage is in the future tense even though the supposed events have already passed. This is because the Great Commentary is presenting the account of the “ninth avatar” as a false prophecy written by Brahmins before the time of the Buddha.

f.d:
'jug pa phyi ma 'grel chen du bkod pa 'di gnyis ni sngon gyi rig byed klag pa la med par gsungs te/ 'grel chen las/
de ltar mi 'thad pa'i tshig du ma rnams ni gdug pa'i bram ze rnams kyis sangs rgyas byung ba'i dus su bkod pa ste sngon gyi rig byed klag pa la med do/[18] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

According to the Great Commentary these last two incarnations as detailed here are not found in early Vedic texts:
In this way, many false words were written by malicious Brahmins at the time of the Buddha. These are not in early Vedic literature.[33]

f.d:
de ltar na khyab 'jug gi 'jug pa bcu ni ji skad du/
nya dang rus sbal phag pa dang / / mi yi seng ge mi'u thung dang / / rA ma gnyis dang nag pa dang / / sangs rgyas kIrti tse dang bcu/[19] / zhes 'byung ba ltar ro/ /

These ten avatāra of Viṣṇu, then, are taught as:
Fish, turtle, and pig, man-lion and midget, the two Ramas and Kṛṣṇa, the Buddha and Kīrti, to make up the ten.[34]

d.div: [19] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ khams kyi le'u/ 1_sh+loka152_38_na6
[34] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, khams v. 152, 38a6.

f.d:
de lta bu'i khyab 'jug gi 'jug pa bcu bshad pa ni nang le'i 'di nyid kyi 'grel chen las/
'dir phyi rol tu nya la sogs pa'i lo rgyus tshangs pa'i drang srong gdug pa rnams kyis byis pa rnams bslu ba'i slad du bkod pa gang yin pa de ni dmyal ba 'thob pa'i rgyu ste 'chad par 'gyur ba mchog tu mi 'gyur ba'i ye shes grub pa las rgyas par brjod par bya'o/[20] / zhes khyab 'jug gi 'jug pa bcu'i lo rgyus bshad ma thag pa rnams rdzun tshig tu gsungs so/ /

The accounts of the ten avatāra of Viṣṇu are spoken of in the Great Commentary:
On the outside, the narratives such as that of the fish and others, were written by malicious Brahmin sages to deceive the foolish. Such works are causes that result in hell. These are explained in greater detail in the later section on the supreme and unchanging gnosis.[35] /138/ Thus the accounts of the ten avatāra as related above are taught to be lies.

d.div: [20] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 119_ba5
[35] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 119b5.

f.d: de ltar phyi rol pa la grags pa'i khyab 'jug gi 'jug pa bcu'i lo rgyus rnams rdzun yin na'ang / 'jug pa bcu'i tha snyad kyis de dang chos mthun par dang po mngal du chags pa nas 'chi ba la thug pa'i bar gsungs pa yin la/ de yang rim pa bzhin bshad na thugs rdo rje 'dzin pa'am byang chub kyi sems rdo rje 'dzin pa dang / khyab 'jug gi tha snyad kyis bsnyad pa ma'i mngal gyi pad+ma'i nang du khu khrag rnam shes tshogs pa de nyid ni nya ro hi ta ltar dmar ba'i nya'i rnam par 'gyur te mngal chags pa nas zla ba gnyis kyi bar nya'i gnas skabs dang sbyar ro/ / nya'i gnas skabs kyi zla ba dang po la rtsa med pa'i khu khrag gi gong bu tsam mo/ / zla ba gnyis pa la de'i snying ga 'ong ba'i gnas su srog la sogs pa'i rlung rnams kyi rten tu 'gyur ba'i snying ga'i rtsa bcu shin tu phra ba dang / lte ba 'ong ba'i gnas su lte ba'i rtsa 'khor gyi rtsa drug cu rtsa bzhi shin tu phra ba rnams kyi rten du 'gyur ba'i rtsa shin tu phra ba bcu gnyis rnams 'chags so/ /

Although these stories, which are well known to outsiders, are fabrications, the terminology of the ten avatāra is used to explain the corresponding times from the first moment of conception to death. These are explained in order. The agglomeration of blood, fluid, and consciousness within the lotus of the mother’s womb is the bodhicitta vajradhara, or mind vajradhara.[36] Using Viṣṇu terminology the first two months in the womb are designated the time of the fish, because the form of this agglomeration is like the red rohita fish. In the first of these two months, the blood and fluid exists devoid of any channels. In the second month the heart develops, and within it the ten very subtle channels of the heart are formed. These become the supports of the winds, such as the life wind and so forth. The navel is created, and within it develops the twelve very subtle channels that become the supports for the sixty-four channels of the navel cakra.

d.div: [36] In keeping with the tantric doctrine of “result as the path,” vajradhara is used here as a cause labeled as result.

f.d: de nas zla ba gsum pa dang bzhi pa'i gnas skabs kyi mngal na gnas pa ni rus sbal gyi gnas skabs dang sbyar ro/ / de yang rus sbal la rkang lag mgo dang bcas pa'i lnga 'bur por yod pa bzhin du/ zla ba gsum pa'i thog ma nas mngal na gnas pa'i lus de 'phel ba la rkang lag dang gdong gi rnam pa mtshon pa tsam du cung zad 'bur ba nas zla ba gsum pa rdzogs pa'i tshe rkang pa lag pa mgrin pa rnams kyi mgo bo mnyam par rags par gyur pa rus sbal dang cha mtshungs par 'gyur ro/ / de nas zla ba bzhi pa'i thog ma nas brtsams te rdzogs pa'i bar la rkang pa dang lag pa dang gdong dang mgrin pa la sogs pa 'ong ba'i 'bur po lnga rim gyis 'phel te rkang lag gi tshigs chen drug dang gdong dang mgrin pa'i phyogs rnams su lhan cig skyes pa dang longs spyod rdzogs pa'i rtsa shin tu phra ba rnams 'chags so/ /

The third and fourth month of pregnancy is the time of the turtle. The turtle has four limbs and a head in the forms of protrusions. Similarly, from the beginning of the third month, the body within the womb develops, and mere indications of limbs and face start to protrude. At the end of the third month the limbs and throat are roughly formed, hence the resemblance to a turtle. From the beginning of the fourth month until its completion the protrusions of the hands, feet, face, throat, etc., develop steadily, and the very subtle innate and saṃbhoga channels are formed in the areas of the six major limb joints and of the face and throat.

de nas zla ba lnga pa nas ji srid ma btsas kyi bar phag gi gnas skabs dang sbyar ro/ / de yang zla ba lnga pa la sha la brten nas rus pa sum brgya drug cu dang / tshigs chen drug las gzhan pa'i tshigs rnams dang / skye mched rnams 'chags pa'i 'go rtsom mo/ / de nas zla ba drug pa la sha dang khrag so sor phyed par 'gyur zhing / tshor ba bde ba dang sdug bsngal yang rig go/ / zla ba bdun pa la mngal na gnas pa des sngon gyi gnas rjes su dran par yang gsungs te/

From the fifth month until birth is the time of the wild pig. The fifth month sees the beginnings of the 360 bones formed in dependence on the flesh, joints other than the six major joints, as well as the sense sources. In the sixth month blood and flesh separate, and feelings of suffering and happiness are experienced. In the seventh month it is said that the being inside the womb remembers its previous existence. /139/

'di'i thad kyi 'grel chen las/
mngon par shes pa'i stobs kyis sngon gyi gnas rjes su dran par yang 'gyur te rang gi sems kyi bag chags dang bral bar byed cing srid pa'i sdug bsngal la smod par byed la sangs rgyas kyi lam la bsngags par byed do/[21] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Concerning this the Great Commentary says:
By the power of clairvoyance the former existence is remembered. Divorced from imprints in the mind, the sufferings of existence are held in contempt, while the path of the buddhas is praised.[37]

d.div: [21] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 120_na7
[37] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 120a7.

f.d:
'o na 'di ltar gsungs pa'i dgongs pa ci/ rus pa sum brgya drug cu ji ltar zhe na/ rus pa sum brgya drug cu ni/ 'grel bshad de kho na nyid snang bar byed par dga' bo mngal gnas kyi mdo drangs pa las/
mgo thod rus pa dgu 'dus shing / / 'gram pa'i rus pa gnyis 'brel te/ / so ni sum cu rtsa gnyis ldan/ / de yi rtsa ba'ang de bzhin no/ / rna rtsa gnya' ba'i rus pa dang / / rkan dang sna yi rus pa dang / / brang dang mid pa'i rus pa ni/ / bsdus na rus pa nyi shu yod/ / mig la rus pa bzhi yod de/ / phrag pa byin pa zung gnyis yod/ / lag pa gnyis dang sor mo rnams/ / bsdus na rus pa lnga bcu yod/ / ltag rgyab rus pa brgyad yod de/ / sgal tshigs la ni sum cu gnyis/ / 'di dag kun la rtsa yod pas/ / 'di yi grangs ni cha bzhir 'gyur/ / rtsibs logs g.yas pa'i rus pa ni/ / phan tshun 'brel ba bcu gsum yod/ / rtsibs logs g.yon 'brel skye ba yi/ / rus pa dag ni bcu gsum yod/ / rus pa'i lu gu rgyud 'di dag / gsum gsum dag ni phan tshun 'brel/ / gnyis gnyis dag ni tshigs ldan te/ / lhag ma gzhan ni 'brel ba med/ / g.yas g.yon brla ni gnyis po la/ / bsdus na rus pa lnga bcu yod/ / lus nang 'brel ba'i rus pa ni/ / bsdoms na sum brgya drug cu yod/[22] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

Concerning the 360 bones, the Womb States of Nanda Sutra is quoted in the commentary Illuminating Reality:
Nine bones joined at the skull, two connected bones of the cheek, the teeth possess thirty-two, and similarly, their roots. The base of the ears, bones of the nape, palate bones, bones of the nose, those of the throat, and of the chest; in total, twenty bones. Four bones in the eyes, two pairs in the shoulders; the two hands and fingers; in total, fifty bones. The upper back has eight bones, the spine thirty-two, all of which have channels, they are therefore of four parts. The bones of the right rib cage are thirteen interconnected. Those connected of the left are also thirteen. Within this succession of bones three sets are interconnected, two sets have joints, the remainder are unconnected. The right and left thighs in short have fifty bones. The bones within the body in total number 360.[38]

d.div: [22] mkhas grub rje'i gsung 'bum/ pod/ gnang gi le'u'i 'grel bshad/ 13_na4_sde dge_57_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ gdaga' bo mngal na gnas pa bstan pa'i mdo/ 231_ba3

[38] Toh 57 Kangyur, dkon btsegs, ga, 231b3, quoted by Khedrup Jé in his Collected Works, vol. ga, Inner Chapter, 13a4. Totaling the 161 bones up to and including “The upper back has eight bones” is straightforward. The bones of the spine are 32 × 4. In the ribs five pairs are counted as single bones, leaving 26 minus 5. To this is added the 50 bones of the thighs, etc., to make 360.

f.d:
mngon par shes pa'i stobs kyis sngon gyi gnas rjes su dran pa [23] zhes sogs kyi dgongs pa ni 'chad pa po rnams kyis 'chad tshul tha dad par gyur te/ de yang mkhas grub kha cig (dpal ldan bla ma dam pa/)ni 'di ltar du 'chad do/ / nam mkha'i rgyan zhes bya ba'i mdo mkhan po dpal brtsegs kyis mdo btus su drangs pa las/
zhag bdun pa sum cu pa la yan lag thams cad dang / khrag dang / pags pa dang / ba spu'i bu ga kun rdzogs par 'gyur ro/ / de nas ma'i lto na khrag dang dri mi zhim pa'i nang na gnas so/ / gang ma'i lto na gnas pa na tshe rabs snga ma dran nas mchog tu skyo bar 'gyur te/ bdag ma'i lto 'di nas nam 'byung zhig guphyis ma'i mngal du skye bar mi 'gyur ba de lta bu'i dge ba dag la brtson 'grus dang pha rol gnon pa brtan por bya'o snyam pa las/ btsas pa dang ma'i lus kyis gzir ba dang / sa'i reg pa dang/ lag pa'i reg pa dang / dri ma bkru ba'i sdug bsngal lus dang sems la mchog tu gnas pa dag gis tshe rabs snga ma ril brjed de/[24] zhes gsungs pa drangs nas/ chos nyid kyis de lta bu'i mngal gyi dus su mngon shes 'byung ba yin zhes gsung ngo / /[25]

The meaning of the quote beginning “By the power of clairvoyance the former existence is remembered” is understood differently by different commentators. Some scholars (such as Palden Lama Dampa) explain such clairvoyance in the womb as a natural occurrence and quote the Adornment to the Sky Sutra quoted by Khenpo Paltsek[39] in his Compendium of Sutra:
In the thirtieth week the limbs, blood, skin, and pores are all completely developed. From then on it dwells in the mother’s womb amid blood and fetid smell. /140/ At that time it remembers past lives and in great despair thinks, “When I emerge from my mother, I will not take birth in another mother’s womb, and I will strive toward virtue with constant effort.” However the process of birth, being squeezed by the mother’s body, the touch of the earth, the touch of hands, the pain of being washed, all dominate the mind and body, and past lives are forgotten.[40]

d.div: [23] bu ston zhabs kyi nang le'i mchan/ gsung 'bum pod/ kha_7_na3
[24] sde dge_4357_bstan/ sna tshogs/ co_nam mkha'i rgyan zhes bya ba'i mdo/ 338_ba4
[25] 'dir yig chung du dpal ldan bla ma dam pa zhes bkod 'dug/ phal cher bu ston gyi slob mar gtogs pa zhig yin snyam zhes sngar mchan du zhus zin/
[39] Khenpo Paltsek is identified in the critical edition as an Indian master, but his Sanskrit name is not found in the Dergé index.
[40] Toh 4357 Tengyur, sna tshogs, cho, 338b4.

f.d:
bu ston thams cad mkhyen pa ni/
mngal gyi gnas skabs su rlung rtsa dbu mar dbyug pa'i rnam pa ltar 'byung 'jug mi byed par gnas pa'i stobs kyis sngon gyi gnas dran pa sogs mngon shes cha 'dra tsam 'byung ba la dgongs pa yin no/[26] / zhes gsung ngo / /

On this the omniscient Butön says:
The meaning of the quote is that during pregnancy, wind dwells within the central channel like a stick, without inhalation or exhalation, and because of this, a quasi-clairvoyance arises that remembers the past.[41]

d.div: [26] bu ston gsung 'bum/ pod/ khanang gi le'u/ 7_na3_la'ang gzigs/
[41] Notes on the Inner Chapter, Collected Works, vol. kha, 7a3.

f.d: yang mkhas pa (chos sde phyogs pa/)[27] kha cig ni mngal gyi gnas skabs de lta bu'i tshe de ltar 'ong yang rmi lam dang 'dra bas las sog pas ma khyab ces gsung ngo / /
Other scholars (such as Chöje Chok)[42] say that although such experiences may arise during the time in the womb, they are like dreams and, therefore, are not certain to accumulate karma.

d.div: [27] 'dir yig chung du chos sde phyogs pa zhes pa chos rje phyogs pa yin tshe jo nang phyogs las rnam rgyal yin nam snyam/
[42] Chöje Choklé Namgyal, fourteenth-century Jonang master.

f.d:
rnam bshad de kho na nyid snang bar byed pa las/
sngon ma rnams mngal du skye ba spyi dang sbyar zhing / 'di dag ni sngon gyi rgyu khyad par can sngon du song bas mngon shes sogs yon tan gyi chos de dag tshe rabs snga ma'i rgyu'i stobs kyi mngon du 'gyur ba'i mngal gyi chos bye brag pa la sbyor dgos pa 'dra'o zhes rje thams cad mkhyen pa'i gsung ngo / / de yang gang zag khyad par can de 'dra yin yang zla ba drug gi bar du mngal du brgyal ba dang 'dra bar dran pa mi 'byung la 'tshams de na 'di ltar dran par 'gyur ro zhes shes par bya ba'i phyir du de ltar smos par shes par bya'o [28] zhes gsungs so/ /

According to the commentary Illuminating Reality:
Those of the past have applied this to womb births in general, but these are qualities whose particular causes have preceded them. Therefore it seems that these qualities, such as clairvoyance, must be special phenomena made manifest in the womb by the power of particular causes created in previous lives. This my omniscient master has said. Even though the being in the womb possesses that particular quality, for six months it will reside in the womb in a kind of unconsciousness and with no memory. Then at this particular time it remembers in this way. It was in order to make this point that this was spoken of.[43]

d.div: [28] mkhas grub rje'i gsung 'bum/ gnang gi le'u'i 'grel bshad/ 14_na4
[43] Khedrup Jé, Collected Works, vol. ga, Inner Chapter, 14a4.

f.d: gzhan yang zla ba bdun rdzogs par gyur pa na smin ma dang skra dang / mig la sogs pa'i skye mched sngar zla ba lnga pa nas skye ba'i 'go brtsams pa rnams yongs su rdzogs par gyur ro/ / de yang mngal du zhugs pa nas brtsams te zla ba gcig gi bar la rtsa cung zad kyang med pa yin pa la zla ba gnyis pa'i thog ma nas bzung ste zla ba bcu gnyis kyi bar la zhag re la rtsa nyis brgya nyis brgya re skye bas mngal chags pa nas zla ba bcu gsum dang / rtsa thog mar chags pa nas zla ba bcu gnyis kyi bar la rtsa bdun khri nyis stong rdzogs par 'gyur ro/ /

By the end of the seventh month, the eyebrows, hair, and the five inner sense sources, which began to develop in the fifth month, are now complete. From the time of conception to the end of the first month no channels have developed. From the beginning of the second month, two hundred channels develop each day for the next twelve months. Therefore thirteen months from conception and twelve months from the growth of the first channel, 72,000 channels are complete. /141/

de yang dngos bstan la zhag gsum gang yin gyi rnam dbye mi gsal bar de tsam zhig gsungs kyang 'di'i zhag nyin zhag la byed na zla ba yang nyin zhag sum bcu la zla bar byas pa'am/ zla ba tshes zla la byed na zhag kyang tshes zhag la byed dgos te/ bcu gnyis sum cu pa bsgyur pa de nyis brgyas bsgyur bas bdun khri nyis stong 'ong bas so/ /

From the actual text it is not clear which of the three types of days is being used in these calculations.[44] However, if “day” is taken to be a solar day, then a month also must be taken to mean thirty solar days. Alternatively, if a month is taken to mean a lunar month, then a day too must be read as a lunar day. This is because thirty times twelve multiplied by two hundred gives a figure of 72,000.

d.div: [44] Solar, lunar, and zodiacal.

f.d: skye mched rnams grub pa de nas zla ba brgyad pa la rus pa rnams kyi nang du rkang chags par 'gyur zhing / ro 'dzin nus kyi ro 'dzin lce'i dbang po bskyed pa'i slad du sngar chags zin pa'i mig la sogs pa'i skye mched rnams rtas par 'gyur ro/ / de nas ro 'dzin lce'i dbang po ro 'dzin nus su skyes pa'i dus de nas gci ba dang bshang ba rnams kyang zla ba brgyad pa de la 'byung bar 'gyur ro/ /

After the inner sense sources have developed, marrow forms inside the bones in the eighth month. The eye and other inner sense sources expand to create the organ of the tongue with its ability to taste. After the sense organ of the tongue has developed its ability to taste, urine and feces are formed.

de nas ma'i mngal nas 'gyur ba ni/ 'ga' zhig zla ba dgu rdzogs ma thag 'byung ba dang / la la bcu pa la 'byung ba dang / kha cig bcu gcig pa la 'byung ba dang / gzhan dag bcu gnyis pa la 'byung ba sogs yod pa'i zla ba lnga pa nas mngal nas 'byung ba'i bar phag gi gnas skabs dang sbyor ba ni phag mi gtsang ba bshang ba sogs kyi 'tsho ba bzhin du mngal na gnas pa de yang ma'i bza' btung gi dwangs ma'i mi gtsang ba tsam gyis 'tsho ba'i rgyu mtshan gyis yin no/ /

Concerning the emergence from the mother’s womb, some beings emerge as soon as nine months are completed, some are born in the tenth month, some in the eleventh, while others may be born in the twelfth month. For all of them, the fifth month in the womb until birth is designated the time of the wild pig. The reason for this being that just as a pig lives on the filth of excrement and so forth, the being in the womb lives only on the foulness that is the essence of the mother’s digested food and drink.

ma'i mngal nas phyir 'byung ba ni mi'i seng ge'i gnas skabs dang sbyor ba ste/ khyab 'jug ro stod seng ge la ro smad mi'i rnam pa'i gnas skabs su gyur pa des 'gro skyob gser can lto dral nas bsad pa dang 'dra bar mngal na gnas pa de btsa' ba'i tshe ma'i skye gnas rnam par 'byed pa'i phyir mi'i seng ge zhes bya'o/ / mngal nas btsas nas so ma skyes bar ni mi'u thung gi dbyibs can du yod pas mi'u thung gi gnas skabs dang sbyar ro/ /

The time of emergence from the mother’s womb is designated the time of the man-lion. This is because at the time of birth the being inside its mother opens up the womb. This correlates with the time when Viṣṇu, in the form of a man-lion with his upper half a lion and his lower a man, killed Hiraṇyakaśipu by tearing out his stomach. The time from birth until the growth of teeth is known as the time of the midget, because that is the form of the child.

de yang mngal du chags pa nas zla ba bcu gsum rdzogs pa na rtsa rnams kyi 'phel ba rdzogs shing zla ba bcu bzhi pa'i thog ma nas khams dkar dmar 'phel ba'i 'go rtsom la rtsa bdun khri nyis stong gi nang nas gnyis gnyis re zhag re la chad pa'i 'go yang rtsom mo/ / de yang bud med rnams kyi rdul 'byung ba'i dus lo bcu gnyis kyi bar du khams dmar po rdul 'phel zhing / lo bcu gnyis rdzogs pa'i 'tshams nas 'phel ba gtong ngo / / de bzhin du skyes pa rnams kyi khu ba 'byung ba'i dus lo bcu drug gi bar du khams dkar po khu ba 'phel zhing 'tshams de nas khu ba 'phel ba gtong zhing 'chad do/ /

Thirteen months after conception, the expansion of the channels is complete. The beginning of the fourteenth month marks the beginning of the expansion of the red and white elements, as well as loss of two channels each day from the 72,000 channels. In girls, the red menstrual element increases until the time of menstruation at the age of twelve. /142/ After that the increase is halted. In boys, the white fluid element increases until the time of semen emission at the age of sixteen. From then on the increase is halted.

mngal nas btsas pa'i rjes su so skyes pa nas lo brgyad kyi mthar so lhung ste brje ba'i bar ni dgra sta rA ma'i gnas skabs dang sbyar ro/ / de nas so lhung ste brjes na lo bcu drug lon gyi bar ni rgyas pa rA ma Na'i gnas skabs dang sbyar ro/ / lo bcu drug lon pa nas skra dkar skyes pa'i bar ni nag pa'i gnas skabs dang sbyar ro/ / skra dkar skyes pa de nas 'chi ba'i nyin zhag gi bar ni sangs rgyas kyi gnas skabs dang sbyor ba ste/ sangs rgyas ni sems zhi ba dang brtul zhugs nges pa la gnas pa bzhin du rgas pa'i gnas skabs la yang sems zhi bar gnas pa dang / bud med la sbyor ba dang bral bas brtul zhugs nges pa'o/ /

After birth the teeth appear. Eight years later they fall out and are replaced. This is the period of Rāma of the Axe. From the time the teeth are replaced up to the age of sixteen is the time of Rāmaṇa. From sixteen until the onset of gray hair is the period of Kṛṣṇa. From the growth of gray hair until the day of death is designated as the time of the Buddha. This is because, just as the Buddha has a mind at peace and is of stable behavior, so the aged are of peaceful minds and, because they lack the sexual company of women, are of stable behavior.

'chi ba'i gnas skabs ni rigs ldan dang sbyor ba ste/ rigs ldan gyi don ni thams cad rigs gcig tu byed pa bzhin du 'chi ba'i tshe yang 'byung ba thams cad gcig tu 'dres pa'i tshul gyis 'chi ba yin pas so/ /
Death itself is designated the time of the lineage bearer. This is because the term kalkin means to make all as one caste. Similarly, at the time of death, all the elements come together as one.
de ltar lus grub pa'i tshul bstan zin to/ /
That concludes the formation of the body.
gnyis pa de ltar grub pa'i lus la brten pa'i chos bshad pa

d.i: Phenomena supported by such a body

f.d: ['di ]la gnyis/ lus la brten pa'i chos spyi'i rnam gzhag bshad pa dang/ rtsa rlung thig le'i rnam bzhag khyad par du bshad pa'o/ /
This is under two headings: 1. A general explanation of such phenomena 2. A particular explanation of channels, winds, and drops
dang po [lus la brten pa'i chos spyi'i rnam gzhag bshad pa ]ni

d.i: A general explanation of such phenomena

f.d: khams drug ldan gyi gang zag gi lus la brten pa'i chos mang ste/ nam mkha'/ rlung / me/ chu/ sa/ ye shes kyi khams te khams drug dang / rnam shes/ 'du byed/ tshor ba/ 'du shes/ gzugs/ ye shes kyi phung po ste phung po drug dang / rna ba/ sna/ mig/lce/ lus/ yid kyi dbang po ste dbang po drug dang / sgra/ dri/ gzugs/ ro/ reg bya/ chos kyi skye mched de yul drug dang / gsang gnas kyi dbang po/ ngag gi dbang po/ lag pa'i dbang po/ rkang pa'i dbang po/ bshang lam gyi dbang po/
