de ltar na lte ba'i g.yon gyi rtsa 'dab dang po la rlung thog mar rgyu ba dang dus mnyam du snying ga'i g.yon gyi rtsa 'dab dang po la thog mar rlung rgyu ba'i dbang du byas na snying ga'i g.yon gyi rtsa 'dab dang po la dbugs stong brgyad brgya pa tshan pa gcig rgyus/ de'i rjes su g.yas kyi rtsa 'dab dang po la stong brgyad brgya pa tshan pa gcig rgyus/ de nas yang g.yon gyi rtsa 'dab dang po de nyid la dgu brgya rgyus/ de'i rjes su yang g.yon gyi rtsa 'dab gnyis pa la dgu brgya rgyus te/ de'i rjes su g.yas kyi rtsa 'dab dang po de nyid la dgu brgya rgyus/ de'i rjes su g.yas kyi rtsa 'dab gnyis pa la dgu brgya rgyus/ de'i rjes su g.yon gyi rtsa 'dab gnyis pa la stong brgyad brgya rgyus/ yang de'i rjes su g.yas kyi rtsa 'dab gnyis pa de nyid la yang stong brgyad brgya rgyus/ de bzhin du gzhan rnams la rigs pas bsgre zhing / de dag kyang dbu ma la rgyu ba logs su ma phye ba'i dbang du byas pa ste/ de ltar na snying ga'i rtsa 'dab re la dbugs nyis stong bdun brgya re'i rgyu tshul de ltar du shes par bya zhing /

This process can be explained using the first flow of wind through the first navel-channel petal on the left while wind flows simultaneously through the first heart-channel petal on the left. Firstly, one set of 1,800 breaths flows through the first heart-channel petal on the left. Then one set of 1,800 breaths flow through the first channel petal on the right. After that 900 breaths flow again through the first petal on the left. Then 900 breaths flow through the second petal on the left. After that 900 breaths flow through the first petal on the right, and then 900 breaths flow through the second petal on the right. Then 1,800 breaths flow through the second petal on the left, and after that 1,800 breaths flow through the second petal on the right. This process continues in similar fashion through the other petals. This has been calculated without separating out the flow of wind from the central channel, and so the number of breaths flowing through each petal of the heart should be known in this way as being 2,700.

mgrin pa'i rtsa 'khor rtsa 'dab so gnyis yod pa'i bzhi stong pa'i rtsa yin pas rlung mi rgyu zhing nyer brgyad la rgyu ba'i tshul yang 'di nyid kyi 'grel chen las/
'dab ma nyi shu rtsa brgyad po rnams la nyin mtshan gyi srog yang dag par rgyu ste/ dbyug gu drug cu la cha yis thob pa ni 'dab ma so so la srog yang dag par rgyu ba'o/[43] / zhes chu tshod drug cu'am dbugs nyi khri chig stong drug brgya la rlung rgyu ba'i rtsa 'dab kyi grangs nyer brgyad kyis thob pa'i nor dbugs bdun brgya dang don gcig dbugs kyi bdun cha gsum 'ong ba de mgrin pa'i rtsa 'dab re la nyin zhag re re dbugs sam rlung rgyu ba'i grangs dang /

The throat cakra has thirty-two petals, of which four are empty channels through which no wind flows. The way in which wind flows through the other twenty-eight is spoken of in the Great Commentary:
In the twenty-eight petals flows the wind day and night. Through a division of sixty hours, the wind flows in each petal.[76] This means that sixty hours or 21,600 breaths is divided among the twenty-eight wind-carrying petals. /161/ This comes to 770 3/7 breaths. This is the number of breaths or winds that flow within each petal of the throat cakra each day.

d.div: [43] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 134_na5
[76] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 134a5.

f.d:
de bzhin du 'di nyid kyi 'grel chen las/
dpral ba'i pad+ma 'dab ma bcu drug pa la 'dab ma gnyis dor nas 'dab ma bcu bzhi po rnams la nyin mtshan gyi srog yang dag par rgyu ste dbyug gu drug cu las bcu bzhi'i cha thob pa 'dab ma so sor 'dor ro/[44] / zhes chu tshod drug cu'i dbugs kyi grangs nyi khri chig stong drug brgya la dpral ba'i rtsa 'dab bcu drug gi stong pa'i rtsa 'dab gnyis ma gtogs pa'i rlung rgyu ba'i rtsa 'dab bcu bzhis bgos pa'i stong lnga brgya dang zhe gnyis/ dbugs kyi bdun cha drug rnams thob pa de dpral ba'i rtsa 'dab re la zhag re'i rlung rgyu ba'i grangs so/ /

Similarly, the Great Commentary says:
Of the sixteen petals of the forehead lotus two are ignored, and in the remaining fourteen flows the wind day and night. For a fourteenth of sixty hours, it flows through each channel.[77] This means that for sixty hours, or 21,600 breaths, apart from the two empty petals, wind flows through the sixteen-petal forehead cakra. This number of breaths divided by fourteen gives a figure of 1,542 6/7 breaths, and this is the number of breaths that flow through each channel petal of the forehead each day.

d.div: [44] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 134_na7
[77] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 134a7.

f.d: de dag kyang dbu ma la rgyu ba'i rlung logs su ma phye ba'i dbang du byas pa yin gyi/ logs su phye ba gnas tshod kyi dbang du byas na zhag re la dbu mar rgyu ba'i grangs drug brgya don lngas dbugs nyi khri chig stong drug brgya la dman pa'i lhag nyi khri dgu brgya nyer lnga la bgo ba sogs gong gi rigs pas shes par bya'o/ /

These are all calculated on the basis of not separating out the flow of wind from the central channel. If they were, then the 675 breaths that flow through the central channel each day are to be subtracted from the 21,600 breaths to leave 20,925, and how this is to be divided up can be known from the above.
gnyis pa sna bug la rlung gi rgyu tshul bshad pa ni/

d.i: Movement of wind through the nostrils

f.d: ma'i mngal nas btsas ma thag gi tshe dbu ma nas rgyus pa'i rlung nga drug rkang bcas sna bug gnyis ka la mnyam rgyu byas te de nas lte ba'i g.yon gyi 'pho chen de la rlung gi grangs ji tsam rgyus pa de nyid sna bug g.yon kho na la rgyu ba dang / rtsa 'dab g.yas g.yon gyi 'pho 'tshams su dbu ma la rgyus pa'i grangs ji tsam yod pa de nyid sna bug gnyis ka la mnyam rgyu byed pa dang / de bzhin du g.yas kyi 'pho chen gyi rtsa 'dab re la rlung gi grangs ji tsam re rgyus pa de nyid sna bug g.yas kho nar rgyu ba yin no/ /

Upon birth from the mother’s womb, fifty-six and a quarter winds flow from the central channel through both nostrils equally. Then the same number of winds that are flowing in the major wind movement at the navel on the left will flow only through the left nostril. At the changeover period from left to right, the number of breaths flowing through the central channel will be the number of breaths that flow through both nostrils equally. Similarly the number of winds that flow in each major wind movement of the channel petals on the right is the number of breaths that move solely through the right nostril.

de yang 'pho chen gyi rlung re re la 'pho chung gi rlung 'byung ba chung ba lnga lnga yod pa'i nam mkha'i rlung rnams ni sna bug gi bu ga'i dbus nas rgyu ba dang / de bzhin du rlung gi rlung rnams bu ga'i steng phyogs ngos nas rgyu ba dang / me'i rlung rnams g.yas g.yon gnyis ka'i mkhur tshos ngos nas rgyu ba dang / chu'i rlung rnams ni sna bug gnyis kyi dbus kyi re kha'i phyogs gnyis nas rgyu ba dang / sa'i rlung rnams ni bu ga'i 'og ngos yam chu la bdar nas rgyu'o/ /

The wind of each major wind movement is divided into the wind of the five minor elements. The space-element wind flows through the center of the nostrils. The air-element wind flows through the upper part of the nostril. The fire-element wind flows through the sides of the nostrils that border the cheeks. The water-element wind flows through the center of the nostrils close to the bone. /162/ The earth-element wind flows through the nostrils close to the base and toward the upper lip.

yang rlung rnams sna bug gi phyi dang nang du ji tsam 'gro ba ni/ sa'i dkyil 'khor gyi rlung sna bug gi phyi rol du sor bcu gnyis kyi bar du 'gro ba nas/ chu'i dkyil 'khor sor bcu gsum dang / me'i dkyil 'khor sor bcu bzhi dang / rlung gi dkyil 'khor sor bco lnga dang / nam mkha'i dkyil 'khor sor bcu drug gi bar du 'gro zhing / de nas ldog go/ / nang du ni phyi rol du ring du rgyus pa de nang du thung ngu dang phyi rol du thung ngu rgyus pa de nang du ring bas rgyu bas nam mkha'i dkyil 'khor lte ba'i dbus dang / rlung gi dkyil 'khor lte ba nas sor gcig gi 'og dang / me'i dkyil 'khor lte ba nas sor gnyis kyi 'og dang / de bzhin du me'i dkyil 'khor sor gsum gyi 'og dang / sa'i dkyil 'khor sor bzhi'i 'og tu phyin nas yang phyir 'gro'o/ /

How far the breath travels outside the nostrils and inside is explained as follows. The earth-mandala wind travels twelve fingerwidths outside the nostrils. The water-mandala wind travels thirteen fingerwidths outside the nostril. The fire-mandala wind travels fourteen fingerwidths, the air-mandala wind travels fifteen, and the space-mandala wind travels sixteen fingerwidths. Each breath then returns, and the farther it travels outside, the shorter it travels inside, and the shorter it travels outside, the farther it travels inside. Therefore the space-mandala wind reaches the center of the navel. The air-mandala wind reaches one fingerwidth below the navel. The fire-mandala wind reaches two fingerwidths below the navel, the water-mandala wind three fingerwidths below, and the earth-mandala wind four fingerwidths below.

rlung lnga char yang lte ba'i dbus bar du 'gro dgos te/ rlung lnga ga'i 'pho 'tshams su dbu mar 'jug pa'i tshe lte ba'i rtsa 'khor gyi lte ba nas 'jug dgos shing / rlung lnga po gang gi mjug tu dbu mar zhugs pa'i ye shes kyi rlung de dang de'i sngon ma'i rlung lnga po gang yin pa de phyi rol du 'gro ba dang nang du 'gro ba tshad mnyam pa'i phyir te/ nang le'i zhe bdun pa'i 'grel chen las/
ye shes kyi dkyil 'khor gyi rlung ni sa'i dkyil 'khor gyi mthar de dag gi dbus su rab tu zhugs pa ni sna bug gnyis nas sor bcu gnyis 'bab bo/ / nam mkha'i mthar dbu mar zhugs pa ni sor bcu drug 'bab bo/[45] / zhes gsungs pas so/ /

The wind in its five parts must travel at least as far as the navel, because at the times of a wind-movement changeover, wind enters the central channel, and it has to enter from the center of the navel cakra. Moreover the gnosis wind that enters the central channel after the flow of the five winds will travel the same distance inward or outward as the particular wind that precedes the gnosis wind. The Great Commentary says:
The gnosis-mandala wind enters in the middle after the earth-mandala wind and travels twelve fingerwidths from both nostrils. The wind entering the central channel after the space-mandala wind travels sixteen fingerwidths.[78]

d.div: [45] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 135_na4
[78] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 135a4.

f.d: 'dir bshad pa'i rtsa rlung gi rnam gzhag dang rgyud sde gzhan nas bshad pa'i rnam gzhag mi mthun par byung ba'i dgongs pa dpyad pa/
10. Discrepancies between Kālacakra and Other Tantras
gnyis pa 'dir bshad pa'i rtsa rlung gi rnam gzhag dang rgyud sde gzhan nas bshad pa'i rnam gzhag mi mthun bar byung ba'i dgongs pa dpyad pa

d.i: An examination of the queries arising from the discrepancies between this presentation of channels, winds, and drops and that of other tantras

f.d: ['di ]la gnyis/ rgyud sde gzhan nas byung ba'i rtsa rlung gi rnam gzhag dang rgyud 'grel 'di nas bshad pa gnyis mi mthun pa'i tshul mdo tsam zhig bshad pa dang / 'dir bshad pa dang de dag tu bshad pa'i dgongs pa ji ltar yin pa bshad pa'o/ /

/163/ This is dealt with under two headings: 1. A brief explanation of the discrepancies between this presentation and presentations of channel, winds, and drops in other tantras 2. An explanation of the thinking behind presentations as given here and in other tantras
dang po ni

d.i: A brief explanation of the discrepancies between this presentation and presentations of channel, winds, and drops in other tantras

f.d:
brtag gnyis las/
sprul pa'i 'khoralo la pad+ma 'dab ma drug cu rtsa bzhi dang / chos kyi 'khor lo la 'dab ma brgyad dang / longs spyod rdzogs pa'i 'khor lo la 'dab ma bcu drug dang / bde ba chen po'i 'khor lo la 'dab ma sum cu rtsa gnyis so/[46] / zhes gsungs pa'i don sgra ji bzhin par mdzad de mgrin pa'i rtsa 'khor rtsa 'dab bcu drug pa dang / spyi bo'i rtsa 'dab sum cu rtsa gnyis par bshad cing de yang bde chen 'khor lor bshad do/ /

In the Hevajra Tantra it says:
At the emanation wheel is a lotus of sixty-four petals, at the dharma wheel eight petals, at the enjoyment wheel sixteen petals, and at the wheel of great bliss thirty-two petals.[79] This is to be taken literally and means that the throat cakra has sixteen petals and that the crown cakra, also explained as the wheel of great bliss, has thirty-two petals.

d.div: [46] sde dge_417_bka'/ rgyud/ nga rgyud brtag gnyis/ le'u/ 1_2_ba7
[79] Toh 417 Kangyur, rgyud, nga, part 1, 2b7.

f.d: rdo rje snying 'grel las ni 'grel chen ltar mgrin pa'i rtsa 'khor rtsa 'dab so gnyis pa dang / dpral ba'i rtsa 'khor rtsa 'dab bcu drug par bshad nas/ de yang rgyud las de gnyis bzlog nas gsungs pa bla ma'i man ngag gis so gnyis dang bcu drug de ltar du shes par bya yi/ rgyud du ni lugs las bzlog pas gsungs pas so zhes bshad pas/ bde ba chen po'i 'khor lo la/ / 'dab ma sum cu rtsa gnyis so/[47] / zhes pa des dpral pa'i rtsa 'khor bstan par yang mdzad do/ / de ltar na sbas rgyud kyi ched du bya ba'i gdul bya rnams kyi bde ba chen po'i 'khor lo spyi bo 'am gtsug tor gyi rtsa 'khor yin par dang / de rtsa 'dab kyang so gnyis pa dang / dpral ba'i rtsa 'khor ram smin mtshams kyi rtsa 'khor rtsa 'dab bcu drug pa rlung gi 'khor lo zhes bshad do/ / de dag ni rtsa'i rnam gzhag mi mthun pa'i tshul mdor bsdus pa tsam mo/ /

In keeping with the Great Commentary, the Vajragarbha Bodhisattva Commentary says that the throat cakra has thirty-two petals and that the forehead cakra has sixteen. Concerning this reversal in the Kālacakra, the oral tradition of the lamas says that these two should be known as being of thirty-two and sixteen petals as explained, but that in Kālacakra the order is reversed. Therefore the line “and at the wheel of great bliss thirty-two petals” also refers to the forehead cakra. In this way, for the intended disciples of hidden tantra, the wheel of great bliss is explained as being the cakra of the crown or uṣṇīṣa, with its thirty-two petals, and the cakra of the forehead, the cakra between the eyebrows, is known as the sixteen-petal wheel of wind. This is just a brief explanation of the inconsistencies in the presentation of the channels.

d.div: [47] sde dge_417_bka'/ rgyud/ nga rgyud brtag gnyis/ le'u/ 1_3_na1

f.d:
rlung gi rnam gzhag ni srog 'dzin sogs grangs bcur byed par ni 'dra la/ de yang srog 'dzin thur sel gyen rgyu mnyam gnas khyab byed de rtsa ba'i rlung lnga gnas gang na gnas pa dang mgon po gang gi rlung gang yin pa ni bshad rgyud rdor 'phreng las/
srog gi rlung ni snying gar gnas/ / mi bskyod bye brag rigs las skyes/ / 'doms na gnas pa'i thur sel ni/ / rin chen 'byung ldan bye brag skyes/ / steng du rgyu bar lkog mar gnas/ / 'od dpag med kyi rang bzhin no/ / mnyam gnas lte ba'i pad+mar gnas/ / don yod grub pa'i rang bzhin no/ khyab byed yan lag kun la gnas/ / rnam snang mdzad kyi ngo bo'o/[48] / zhes srog 'dzin snying gar gnas shing mi bskyod pa'i rlung dang / thur sel gsang gnas na gnas shing rin 'byung gi rlung dang / gyen rgyu mgrin pa'i rtsa 'khor la gnas shing 'od dpag med kyi rlung dang / mnyam gnas lte ba'i rtsa 'khor la gnas shing don grub kyi rlung dang / khyab byed yan lag gi tshigs la sogs pa'i tshigs kun la gnas shing rnam snang gi rlung du gsungs so/ /

The inconsistencies in the presentations of the winds are as follows. The presentations of the ten winds are similar. However, concerning the locations and the guardians of the five root winds, the Vajra Garland Explanatory Tantra says:
The life-sustaining wind abides in the heart, born from the family of Akṣobhya. The downwardly expelling, dwelling in the secret area, is born from Ratnasambhava. The upwardly moving dwells in the throat, in the nature of Amitābha. The coexisting is in the lotus of the navel, in the nature of Amoghasiddhi. The pervading dwells in every limb, in the nature of Vairocana.[80] /164/ Therefore the life-sustaining wind abides in the heart and is the wind of Akṣobhya. The downwardly expelling wind is found in the secret place and is the wind of Ratnasambhava. The upwardly moving wind dwells in the cakra of the throat and is the wind of Amitābha. The coexisting wind dwells within the navel cakra and is the wind of Amoghasiddhi. The pervading wind is found in all joints, such as those of the limbs, and is the wind of Vairocana.

d.div: [48] sde dge_445_bka'/ rgyud/ cabashad rgyud rdo rje phreng ba/ le'u/ 68_276_ba1
[80] Toh 445 Kangyur, rgyud, cha, chap. 68, 276b1.

f.d: de yang srog 'dzin snying gar gnas par bshad pa ni srog 'dzin la phra rags gnyis su yod pa'i rags pa ni gzhi dus la sna bug la 'byung 'jug byed cing snying ga'i rtsa 'khor la gnas kyang snying ga'i rtsa mdud kyi d+hU tI'i nang na gnas pa min la/ srog 'dzin phra ba ni 'od gsal gyi sems shin tu phra ba dang ngo bo dbyer med cing de'i bzhon par gyur pa mi shigs pa zhes pa snying ga'i rtsa 'khor gyi lte ba rtsa mdud kyi d+hU tI'i nang na gnas pa ste/

Furthermore the life-sustaining wind dwelling at the heart is also explained as being of two kinds — coarse and subtle. The coarse wind brings about inhalation and exhalation at the nostrils, and although this coarse wind is in the heart cakra, it does not enter the dhūtī of the heart channel knot. The subtle life-sustaining wind is inseparable from the very subtle mind of clear light and is known as its indestructible mount. It dwells within the dhūtī of the channel knot at the very center of the heart cakra.

bshad rgyud rdor 'phreng las/
snying gi pad+ma'i sbubs mkha' la/ / ye shes rdo rje rtag tu bzhugs/[49] / zhes dang /
gtso bo chen po mi bskyod pa'i/ / 'jig rten khams ni de nyid do/ / der ni rtag tu bzhugs pa'i sa/ / srog gi ye shes ming can te/[50] / zhes gsungs pa dang /

The Vajra Garland Explanatory Tantra says:
In the space within the lotus of the heart the wisdom vajra always sits.[81] And:
This is the worldly realm of powerful Akṣobhya, there his constant residence, under the name “wind of gnosis.”[82]

d.div: [49] sde dge_445_bka'/ rgyud/ cargyud rdo rje phreng ba/ le'u/ 6_216_ba1
[50] sde dge_445_bka'/ rgyud/ cargyud rdo rje phreng ba/ le'u/ 25_238_ba4
[81] Toh 445 Kangyur, rgyud, cha, chap. 6, 216b1.
[82] Toh 445 Kangyur, rgyud, cha, chap. 25, 238b4.

f.d:
bshad rgyud lhag mo bzhis zhus pa las/
phyed tshad tsam gyi phra mo mchago/ / yid kyi dngos po thig le'i gzugs/ / rtag tu snying gi dbus gnas pa/ / 'od zer chen po 'bar ba can/[51] / zhes pa yang 'od zer lnga 'bar ba'i mi shigs pa'i rlung shin tu phra ba yin pa dang /

Also the Requests of the Four Goddesses Explanatory Tantra says:
Of tiny size, the supreme and subtle, the phenomenon of mind in the form of a drop, dwelling constantly at the heart’s center, ablaze with great rays of light.[83] Thus the indestructible and very subtle wind is also described as five blazing rays of light.

d.div: [51] sde dge_446_bka'/ rgyud/ calha mo bzhis zhus pa'i mdo/ 278_na6
[83] Toh 446 Kangyur, rgyud, 278a6.

f.d:
rdo rje dkyil 'khor rgyan gyi rgyud las kyang /
snying gi dbus na mi shigs pa/ / gsal zhing mar me dag dang mtshungs/ / mi 'gyur mchog tu phra pa ste/ / a ni gtso bo dam pa'o/[52] / zhes pas kyang mi shigs pa'i rlung shin tu phra ba ston cing / de kho na nyid grub pa las rlung gzhan rnams thim nas lhan cig skyes pa'i rlung rang gnas su gnas pa na de kho na nyid rtogs par gsungs pa'i lhan cig skyes pa'i rlung zhes pa yang srog 'dzin gyi rlung shin tu phra ba 'di yin zhing / rlung shin tu phra ba 'di dang 'od gsal gyi sems shin tu phra ba 'di 'khor ba'i chos thams cad kyi gzhi dang / sku gnyis kyi thun mong ma yin pa'i bsgrub gzhi dang / khyad par du yang rlung 'di longs sku'i bsgrub gzhi thun mong ma yin pas sbas rgyud rnams kyi dgongs par de'i ched du bya ba'i gdul bya rnams kyis 'chad par byed cing /

The Vajra Mandala Ornament Tantra says:
In the center of the heart, the indestructible, clear and like a lamp, unchanging and extremely subtle, the syllable “a” supreme.[84] This, too, teaches the very subtle indestructible wind. Illuminating Reality talks of “emptiness perceived when the innate wind returns to its place after the other winds have dissolved.” This innate wind is the very subtle life-sustaining wind. This very subtle wind and its very subtle mind of clear light form the foundation of all phenomena of samsara and are the special meditative foundations of the two forms of a buddha, with this wind being the special meditative foundation of the enjoyment body of a buddha. The above is the thinking behind hidden tantras as explained by their intended disciples. /165/

d.div: [52] lung 'di brnyed son ma byung /
[84] Unable to trace quote.

f.d: 'grel chen las 'od gsal gyi sems nyid 'khor 'das thams cad kyi gzhir gsungs pa ma gtogs shin tu phra ba'i rlung gi bshad pa zur tsam yang ma byung ba dang / rlung rnams kyi gnas kyi gtso bo yang snying ga'i rtsa 'dab rnams yin par bshad pas thur sel nas khyab byed kyi bar gyi rlung bzhi'i gnas kyang mi mthun pa dang / srog 'dzin dang mnyam gnas mgon po gang gi rlung yin pa mthun na'ang / 'grel chen las gyen rgyun rin 'byung dang / thur sel rdor sems dang / khyab byed snang mthar bshad cing rnam snang gi rlung du ma bshad pas rlung de gsum mgon po gang gi rlung yin pa yang ma mthun no/ /

The Great Commentary says that the mind of clear light is the foundation of all phenomena of samsara and nirvana but does not even mention the very subtle wind. Furthermore the main seat of the winds is said to be the heart-channel petals, which is at variance with the locations of the four winds, from coexisting wind to pervading wind, as taught in the other tantras. Although the guardians of the winds coincide as far as the life- sustaining and coexisting winds are concerned, the Great Commentary mentions the upwardly moving as belonging to Ratnasambhava, the down wardly expelling as belonging to Vajrasattva, and the pervading as belonging to Amitābha and not to Vairocana. Therefore there is some discrepancy concerning the guardians of these three winds.

gzhan yang rlung rnams 'gro 'ong byed pa'i tshe sna bug gang las [53] rgyu ba dang / 'byung ba'i dkyil 'khor gang gi rlung gang yin pa dang / rlung rnams kyi kha dog ji ltar yin pa ni bshad rgyud rdor 'phreng las/
sangs rgyas lnga yi rigs gnas pa/ / sna yi bu ga las byung zhing / / rlung lnga steng du yang dag rgyu/ / lus la spyod par rtag tu 'gyur/ / kun rdzob snar ni rgyu ba yi/ / sgo nga las ni rnam par 'byung / / g.yon dang g.yas dang gnyis ka dang / / ngal bar rgyu dang rnam pa bzhi/ / g.yas pa nas ni 'byung ba'i khams/ / me yi dkyil 'khor nyid yin te/ kha dog dmar po bzang po 'di/ / pad+ma mgon po'i rgyu ba'o/ / g.yon pa nas ni 'byung ba'i khams/ / rlung gi dkyil 'khor la brten pa/ / ljang ser dag tu snang ba ste/ / las kyi mgon po'i rgyu ba'o/ / gnyis ka las ni 'byung ba'i khams/ / gser gyi mdog tu snang ba ste/ / dbang chen gyi ni dkyil 'khor nyid/ / rin chen mgon po'i rgyu ba'o/ / dal zhing rgyu ba med pa'i khams/ / dag pa'i shel ltar snang ba ni/ / 'di na chu yi dkyil 'khor te/ / rdo rje mgon po'i rgyu ba'o/ / khams kun las ni yang dag byung / / rten dang brten pa'i gzung ba ni/ / rnam par snang mdzad rang bzhin te/ / 'chi ba'i mthar ni 'byung bar 'gyur/ / dkyil 'khor bzhi po 'di dag ni/ / mnyam par gzhag pas rtag tu zlos/ / sngags pa'i zlos pa'i grangs nyid kyi/ / nyin mtshan rtag tu zlos pa yin/[54] / zhes sangs rgyas lnga'i rigs su gnas pa'i rlung lnga steng du sna'i bu ga las byung zhing yang dag par rgyu'o/ /

Moreover, concerning which nostril the winds pass through at the times of their coming and going, of which element mandala they are, and of their colors, the Vajra Garland Explanatory Tantra says:
The five buddha families arise from the nostrils, flowing upon the five winds, constantly active within the body. Flowing into the nose, emerging from the five openings, left, right, both, and gently, these are the four ways. From the right, the fire-mandala element, of the color red, the wind of the lotus protector. From the left, the air-mandala element, appearing as green and yellow, the wind of the activity protector. From both, the mighty mandala, the element of earth, the color of gold, the wind of the jewel protector. The element of the gently flowing, the color of pure crystal, the water mandala, wind of the vajra protector. That arising from all elements, supporter and supported, the nature of Vairocana, arising at death. In meditative equipoise, constant recitation on these four mandalas; as to the number of mantras, recite them constantly day and night.[85] /166/ Thus the five winds of the five buddhas flow through the nostrils.

d.div: [53] lung ma dper gang yas rgyu ba zhes gsal yang gang las zhes bcos/
[54] sde dge_445_bka'/ rgyud/ cabashad rgyud rdo rje phreng ba/ le'u/ 24_237_ba5
[85] Toh 445 Kangyur, rgyud, cha, chap. 24, 237b5.

f.d: de yang ji ltar rgyun kun rdzob kyi sna g.yon nas rang dbang du rlung mnyam gnas kho na rgyu zhing mnyam gnas kha dog ljang ser 'byung ba rlung gi khams pa dang / gyen rgyu ni rang dbang du sna bug g.yas kho na la rgyu zhing kha dog dmar po 'byung ba me'i khams pa dang / thur sel ni rang dbang du sna bug gnyis ka la drag tu mnyam rgyu kho na byed cing kha dog ser po 'byung ba sa'i khams pa dang / srog 'dzin ni rang dbang du sna bug gnyis ka la dal bus mnyam rgyu kho na byed cing kha dog dkar po 'byung ba chu'i khams pa dang / khyab byed ni 'chi kha'i dus su ma gtogs gzhi dus su rang dbang du sna bug nas rgyu ba med cing kha dog sngo bsangs 'byung ba nam mkha'i khams pa yin par gsungs shing /

The way they flow is as follows. Only the coexisting wind flows freely through the left nostril, its color is a mixture of green and yellow, and it is of the element of air. The upwardly moving wind flows freely only through the right nostril, is red in color, and is of the element of fire. The downwardly expelling wind moves freely through both nostrils, flowing forcefully through both. It is yellow and of the earth element. The life-sustaining wind flows gently and freely through both nostrils. It is white and of the water element. The pervading wind does not flow freely through the nostrils during normal existence except at the time of death. It is pale blue in color and of the element of space.

'grel chen las srog 'dzin nam mkha'i khams pa kha dog ljang gu dang / thur sel ye shes kyi khams pa kha dog sngon po dang / mnyam gnas rlung gi khams pa kha dog nag po dang / khyab byed chu'i khams pa kha dog dkar por gsungs pas rlung bzhi po de'i kha dog ma mthun zhing / mnyam gnas ma gtogs pa gsum gyi 'byung ba'i khams kyang ma mthun no/ / de bzhin du 'grel chen las 'byung ba'i khams lnga char gyi rlung rang dbang du yang sna bug g.yas g.yon gnyis ka las rim can du rgyu bar gsungs pas rlung sna bug la rgyu tshul yang ma mthun no/ /

The Great Commentary speaks of the life-sustaining wind being of the element of space and green in color. The downwardly expelling wind is of the element of gnosis and blue in color. The coexisting wind is taught as being of the element of air and black in color. The pervading wind is of the water element and white. There are, therefore, discrepancies in the colors of four winds and in the elements of three of the above winds. Similarly the Great Commentary speaks of the winds divided into the five elements flowing in sequence and of their own accord through left, right, and both nostrils. There is, therefore, disagreement in the way wind flows through the nostrils.

gzhan yang dgongs pa lung ston sogs sbas rgyud dgongs 'grel dang bcas pa rnams las gzhi dus su sna bug las rang dbang du rgyu ba'i rlung la me rlung chu'i rlung sa rlung rlung gi rlung dang bzhi po 'di las ma bshad cing / bzhi po 'di re re rgyu ba la yang rgyu thengs re la dgu brgya pa phrag re rgyus te rlung rgyu ba phyi ma'i 'go rtsom pa sogs byas pa'i sgo nas rlung bzhi re re yang zhag re la dgu brgya pa phrag drug drug rgyu zhing / dgu brgya pa phrag re re la yang lha mo bzhi'i rlung nyis brgya nyer lnga rer phye nas rgyu ba yin te/ grol ba'i thig le las/
phyag rgya bzhi 'brel re re zhing / / nyis brgya nyi shu rtsa lnga ste/ / de bzhi bsgres pas dgu brgya'o/ / de ni 'pho ba nyi shu bzhis/ / brtsis pas khri phrag gnyis dang ni/ chig stong dang ni drug brgya'o/[55] / zhes gsungs shing / lha mo bzhi'i rlung la 'byung ba chung ba'i rlung zhes tha snyad mdzad do/ /

Hidden tantras and their commentaries, including the Sandhivyākaraṇa Tantra,[86] speak only of four winds — fire, water, earth, and air — flowing of their own accord through the nostrils during normal existence, and that each flow is 900 breaths. In this way, with flows following each other, each of the four winds flows 900 times multiplied by six in a single day. Moreover each set of 900 breaths is divided into four sets of 225 winds — one for each of the four goddesses. The Drop of Freedom says:
Each of the four mudrās is of 225, which added together comes to 900. And of that, twenty-four movements makes two times 10,000 plus 1,600.[87] /167/ The winds of the four goddesses are correlated with the winds of the minor elements.

d.div: [55] sde dge_1859_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ di_grol ba'i thig le/ 49_ba5
[86] Guhyasamāja explanatory tantra.
[87] Toh 1859 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, di, 49b5.

f.d: de bzhin du 'chi ba'i dus ma gtogs gzhi dus la rtsa dbu ma la rlung rgyu ba med par yang bshad do/ / 'grel chen las sna bug la 'byung ba lnga'i rlung re re yang rgyu thengs re la nga drug bzhi chas dman pa'i stong brgyad brgya re rgyun re la rgyu bar bshad cing / lte ba'i 'pho chen gyi rtsa 'dab dang / sna bug g.yas g.yon gyi 'pho ba'i 'tshams su rlung nga drug bzhi cha re dbu ma nas rgyu bar bshad do/ /

Also, according to the hidden tantras, apart from the time of death, there is no flow of wind in the central channel during normal existence.[88] The Great Commentary, on the other hand, explains that 1,800 breaths less fifty-six and a quarter flow through the nostrils during the flow of each of the winds of the five elements, and that at the time of the changeover of the major wind movements at the navel and the changeover of the flow between left and right nostril, fifty-six and a quarter breaths of wind flow from the central channel.

d.div: [88] Ordinary existence/state is a semitechnical term used for the physical and mental condition of ordinary beings who at a particular time are not actively engaged on the tantric path. According to all tantras except the Kālacakra, winds do not flow in the central channel during this normal existence, except at the time of death.

f.d: de ltar na sbas rgyud du rang dbang ngam gtso bo byas nas sna bug nas 'byung bzhi'i rlung ma gtogs nam mkha'i rlung ma rgyu bar bshad pa dang 'grel chen las nam mkha'i rlung rgyu bar bshad pa ma mthun/ sbas rgyud las rlung bzhi po rgyun re la dgu brgya re rgyus nas dkyil 'khor gzhan du 'pho thengs drug drug ste dril bas 'pho ba nyi shu rtsa bzhir byed pa bshad pa dang 'grel chen las 'byung ba lnga'i rlung re re rgyun re la stong bdun brgya dang zhe gsum dbugs kyi bzhi cha gsum re rgyus nas dkyil 'khor bzhin du 'pho ba'i 'pho ba bcu gnyis su bshad pas rlung rgyu ba'i grangs dang 'pho ba'i grangs ma mthun/ sbas rgyud las 'chi kha dang lam dus ma gtogs gzhi dus su rlung dbu ma nas rgyu ba med par bshad pa dang 'grel chen las gzhi dus su yang rlung dbu ma nas rgyu ba yod par bshad pa ma mthun pa rnams so/ /

Furthermore the hidden tantras talk only of the winds of the four elements flowing freely or predominantly through the nostrils and do not mention the flow of the space-element wind. This is in conflict with the Great Commentary, which talks of the flow of the space-element wind. The hidden tantras talk of 900 breaths flowing during each period of the four winds, each of which moves to other element mandalas six times, making in total twenty-four wind movements. The Great Commentary talks of 1,743 3/4 breaths flowing during each period of the winds of the five elements, each period changing from element to element twelve times to form the twelve major wind movements. These, therefore, are discrepancies in the number of breaths within each flow and in the number of wind movements. The hidden tantras say that except for the moment of death and while on the path, the winds do not flow in the central channel. The Great Commentary says that even during normal existence wind flows in the central channel. These are the discrepancies.
gnyis pa 'dir bshad pa dang de dag tu bshad pa'i dgongs pa ji ltar yin pa bshad pa

d.i: An explanation of the thinking behind presentations as given here and in other tantras

f.d: ['di ]la gnyis/ a b+ha yas ji ltar bshad pa'i tshul dang / mkhas pa dag gis ji ltar gsungs pa bkod de de'i dgongs pa'i don bshad pa'o/ /
This has two outlines: 1. Abhayākaragupta’s explanation 2. A presentation of statements by other scholars and their meanings /168/
dang po [a b+ha yas ji ltar bshad pa'i tshul ]ni

sbas rgyud nas bshad pa rnams nges don dang / dus 'khor sogs sems 'grel rnams nas bshad pa rnams sgra ji bzhin par bshad du mi rung ba'i drang don du 'chad de/ snye ma nyer gcig pa las/ nam mkha'i dkyil 'khor gyi rlung rlung gzhan bzhi'i 'khor du rgyu ba tsam ma gtogs rang dbang du 'byung ba bzhi'i rlung las logs su rgyu ba spyod bsdus dang de'i shes byed du bshad rgyud rdor 'phreng dang dgongs pa lung ston dang gnyis med rnam rgyal gyi rgyud rnams drangs nas bkag cing / dus 'khor nas de ltar gsungs pa rnams nyi ma'i shing rta sogs kyi gdul bya'i bsam ngo la ltos pa'i drang don du bshad do/ /

Explanations from the hidden tantras are definitive, while those from the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries that comment on Kālacakra and others are interpretive and not to be taken literally. In the twenty-first chapter of the Sheaves of Oral Transmission, he explains that the space-mandala wind flows only as a secondary accompaniment to the other four winds, thereby rejecting that it flows of its own accord separately from the four other winds. This he does by quoting from A Lantern of Condensed Practice and backing that up with scriptural reference from the Vajra Garland Tantra, Sandhivyākaraṇa Tantra, and the Triumph of Nonduality Tantra. The teachings in the Kālacakra are interpretive, as they are based upon the views of Sūryaratha and other disciples.

de yang ji ltar bshad na/ snye ma nyer gcig pa las/
'byung ba lnga pa nam mkha'i khams ni khyab par byed pa nyid kyis gnas bzhi rnams su yang dkyil 'khor bzhi yang dag par rgyu ba'i dus kho nar yang dag par rgyu'o [56]zhes pa logs su ma gsungs so/ / de skad du yang 'phags pa lha'i zhabs kyis gsungs pa/ / rdo rje pad+ma dag gi sna dag las 'od zer byung zhing gyen du song ste rab tu grags pa'i sna'i rtse mo nas rgyu'o/ / de la sa dang chu dang me dang rlung zhes khams kyi bya ba dkyil 'khor bzhi rnams phyir 'byung zhing khyab byed ni khyab par byed pa'i rlung mi 'byung ba khyab pa'i 'od zer can te/ zhes pa nas/ khams kyi dkyil 'khor gcig gis khams bzhi rnams la khyab pa'o [57] zhes pa'i bar drangs shing /

How are they to be interpreted? The twenty-first chapter of Sheaves of Oral Transmission says:
The fifth element of space is pervasive, and so only flows at the times of the four mandalas flowing at the four places. It was therefore not taught as being separate. This was spoken of by the venerable Āryadeva: “From the openings of the vajra and lotus, rays of light rise and travel upward to flow from the tip of the nose. Within them the four mandalas of the elements of earth, water, fire, and air are exhaled. The pervading wind does not emerge, it is together with the pervading rays of light”[89] This quote of Āryadeva continues until “One element mandala pervades four elements.”[90]

d.div: [56] sde dge_1198_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ cha_man ngag snye ma/ le'u/ 21_197_na7
[57] sde dge_1803_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ngi spyod pa bsdus pa'i sgron ma/ le'u/ 3_69_ba3_'gyur cung mi mthun/
[89] Toh 1198 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, cha, chap. 21, 197a7.
[90] Toh 1803 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ngi, chap. 3, 69b3 (Caryāmelāpakapradipa by Āryadeva).

f.d:
de dag gi sgrub byed du dgongs pa lung ston gyi rgyud drangs pa ni/ dgongs pa lung ston pa'i rgyud du/
gos dkar la sogs bzlas bshad pa/ / brgya phrag gnyis dang nyi shu lnga/ / bzhi yis yang dag bsgyur ba ni/ / sbyor ba bzhi la brgya phrag dgu/[58] / zhes pa dang /
dgu brgya rnams su gang bstan pa/ / nyi shu rtsa bzhi'i rigs rnams kyis/ / de ni so sor 'byung ba las/ / nyi khri chig stong drug brgya'o/[59] / zhes 'pho ba'i dbugs kyi grangs gsungs pa ci ltar / zhes bshad pa dang /

Abhayākaragupta validates this position by quoting from the Sandhivyākaraṇa Tantra:
In the Sandhivyākaraṇa it says: “The recitations of Pāṇḍarā and so forth, 225 multiplied by four, are the four yogas — 900 in each.” Also:
“That taught as 900, by twenty-four similar kinds, totals 21,600.”[91] This speaks of the number of breaths in the wind movements.

d.div: [58] sde dge_444_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_dgongs pa lung ston/ le'u/ 2_69_ba2_171_na6_'gyur cung mi mthun/
[59] sde dge_444_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_dgongs pa lung ston/ le'u/ 2_171_na7

f.d:
yang sgrub byed du bshad rgyud rdor 'phreng drangs pa ni/
dpal rdo rje 'phreng ba'i rgyud du yang nam mkha'i nang du 'dus pa kho nas dkyil 'khor bzhi rnams kho na'i rgyu ba gsungs pa/ / sna rtse yungs dkar zhes bya ba/ / srog dang rtsol bar btags pa ste/ / srog dang rtsol ba la gnas pa/ / 'od lnga sangs rgyas rnams su bsgom/ / steng du sna las nges 'byung ba/ / zhes pa nas/ ye shes lnga yi ngo bo nyid/[60] /ces pa'i bar drangs pa rnams so/ /

Concerning the validating quote from the Vajra Garland, the text continues:
By including them in space, the Vajra Garland speaks only of the flow of four mandalas. “For the ‘mustard seed at the tip of the nose,’[92] focus on prāṇāyāma, dwell within prāṇāyāma, meditate as buddhas, the five rays of light arising through the nose.” The Vajra Garland quote is continued until “The nature of the five wisdoms.”[93] /169/

d.div: [60] sde dge_445_bka'/ rgyud/ cabashad rgyud rdo rje phreng ba/ le'u/ 18_223_ba5
[92] This does not necessarily refer to the nose on the face. This is explained later.
[93] Toh 445 Kangyur, rgyud, ca, chap. 18, 223b5.

f.d:
yang sgrub byed du gnyis med rnam rgyal gyi rgyud drangs pa ni/
de bzhin du gnyis su med pa mnyam pa nyid rnam par rgyal ba'i rgyud du/ ya yig don gyi gang ci'ang rung / / dngos grub 'dod pas bya ba'o/ / ra la sogs pa gsum gyis kyang / / 'gro ba'i don la 'jug par bya/[61] / me dang rlung dang dbang chen dang / / chu ste so so'i dkyil 'khor du/[62] / thun ni phyed phyed dus rnams su/ / las dag gnyis gnyis gnas par 'gyur/[63] / zhes pa rnams drangs te 'byung ba bzhi'i dkyil 'khor gyi rlung rgyu ba la sogs su nam mkha'i dkyil 'khor gyi rlung rang dbang ngam des gtso bo byas nas gzhi dus la rgyu ba med par bsgrubs so/ /

Concerning the validating quote from the Triumph of Nonduality, the text says:
Similarly, in the Triumph of Nonduality Tantra it says: “That which the letter ya symbolizes is practiced by those who desire siddhis. With the three letters ra and so forth, engage in the welfare of others. “In mandalas of fire, air, earth, and water, two activities in half a session at a time.”[94] These quotes establish that within the flows of wind of the four element mandalas, the space-mandala wind does not flow independently or predominantly during normal existence.

d.div: [61] sde dge_444_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_dgongs pa lung ston/ le'u/ 2_167_na6_gnyis med rnam rgyal du lung 'di mi snang /
[62] sde dge_444_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_dgongs pa lung ston/ le'u/ 3_171_na3_gnyis med rnam rgyal du lung 'di mi snang /
[63] gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/ gnyis med rnam rgyal du lung 'di mi snang /
[94] Verse not found.

f.d: de la dpags nas rtsa bshad kyi sbas rgyud rnams dang mi mthun pa'i bsdus rgyud sems 'grel skor gsum dang bcas pa las bshad pa'i rtsa dang rlung gi rnam gzhag gzhan rnams kyang sgra ji bzhin par a b+ha yas mi bzhed par go nus so/ / de ltar na dus 'khor rgyud 'grel sogs sems 'grel rnams las de ltar gsungs pa rnams ni drang don du 'chad de

It can be inferred from the above that Abhayākaragupta would also not accept as literal the presentations of the channels and winds as found in the Condensed Tantra and the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries where they disagreed with the root and explanatory hidden tantras. Presentations, therefore, found in the Bodhisattva Commentaries on the Kālacakratantra and so forth are explained as being subject to interpretation.

man snye'i de'i 'phro nyid las/
gang dus kyi 'khor lor nam mkha'i dkyil 'khor logs su bton nas gsungs pa de ni mu stegs pa'i lta ba la mngon par zhen pa'i nyi ma'i shing rta la sogs pa gdul bya rnams nges pa'i don la gzhug pa la ldem por dgongs pas drang ba'i don kho na te/ phag la sogs pa'i 'dod pa'i rjes su 'jug pas ri rab kyi steng gi mtshams su khams gsum pa'i snod kyi 'jig rten gyi bkod pa la sogs pa bstan pa bzhin no/ / 'o na dus kyi 'khor lo dang de'i rjes su 'brang ba'i gzhung rnams su theg pa gsum dang 'gal ba'i rnam par gzhag pa mang po rnams byas te/ de'i gzhung byed pa grags pa dang pad+ma dkar po dang rdo rje snying po dang phyag na rdo rje'i ming can de rnams byang chub sems dpa' rnams ma yin pa kho na'o/ /zhes mang du shes pa rnams smra'o/ / 'di'i phyir 'gal ba thams cad ma spangs pas na 'ga' zhig tu 'gal ba spong ba'i 'bad rtsol gyis ci bya zhe na dus kyi 'khor lor bstan pa rgyud gzhan dang mi 'gal ba'i don gyi cha 'ga' zhig ni kho bos rang gi gzhung gi phyogs su rjes su 'brangs shing / gdul bya 'ga' zhig gi bsam pa'i rjes su 'jug pas 'gal ba'ang kha cig spangs so/ / de las gzhan la ni 'gal ba ma spangs na yang 'di rnams la nyes pa ci yang med do zhes pa shin tu rgyas par brjod pas chog go[64] / zhes gsungs pa'i mang du shes pa zhes pa slob dpon shAn+ti pa dang/ rnams zhes pas rgya gar ba gzhan yang yod par bstan cing /

Sheaves of Oral Transmission continues:
In the Kālacakra the space mandala spoken of separately is there to lead disciples such as Sūryaratha and others who cling to Tīrthika views to the definitive meaning. It is wholly in need of interpretation and intentionally equivocal, like the teaching on the arrangement of the three world realms in the upper regions of Meru asserted by those who follow Varaha.[95] However the wise and others have said that in the Kālacakra and the commentaries that follow it, there are many presentations that contradict the three vehicles, and that those responsible for these texts, possessing the names of Yaśas, Puṇḍarīka, Vajragarbha, and Vajrapāṇi, are not bodhisattvas at all. Therefore, as all contradictions have not been resolved, you may ask what is the point in trying to resolve part of the contradictions? Those parts of the Kālacakra that do not contradict other tantras of the doctrine, I follow as I would my own. Some contradictions I have resolved because they are adapted to the minds of certain disciples. /170/ As to the rest, although the contradictions are not resolved, it has been explained at great length that there are no faults in these at all and so therefore they are acceptable.[96] “The wise” mentioned in the above quote refers to Ācārya Śāntipa, and “others” refers to other Indians.

d.div: [64] sde dge_1198_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ chadapal yang dag sbyor ba/ le'u/ 21_198_ba6
[95] Varahāmihira, renowned sixth-century Indian astronomer.
[96] Toh 1198 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, cha chap. 21, 198b–6.

f.d: 'di'i phyir zhes pa nas/ ci bya zhe na zhes pa'i bar gyis ni dus 'khor gyi rgyud dang sems 'grel du grags pa rnams shAn+ti pa sogs mkhas pa rnams kyis bkag pa 'di'i phyir 'gal ba thams cad ma spangs pa de bas na a b+ha ya khyed kyi gzhung gi cha 'ga' zhig tu 'gal ba spong ba'i 'bad rtsol gyis ci bya zhe na zhes pa'i dwogs pa bkod nas/ dwogs pa de sel ba ni dus kyi 'khor lor bstan pa zhes sogs so/ /

The questio, “Therefore, as all contradictions have not been resolved, you may ask what is the point in trying to resolve part of the contradictions” expresses the following doubt. The Kālacakra and those texts known as the Bodhisattva Commentaries have been refuted by Śāntipa and other scholars. Therefore all contradictions have not been resolved, and so what is the point in you, Abhayākaragupta, persevering in resolving contradictions in parts of the text? This doubt is cleared up by the lines that follow, beginning with “Those parts of the Kālacakra.”
gnyis pa [mkhas pa dag gis ji ltar gsungs pa bkod de de'i dgongs pa'i don bshad pa ]

d.i: A presentation of statements by other scholars and their meanings

f.d: mkhas pa (ku mAr ma ti/)dag gis ji ltar gsungs pa bkod de de'i dgongs pa'i don bshad pa ni/ snod kyi 'jig rten gyi rnam gzhag dang rtsarlu nga sogs kyi rnam gzhag /du sa 'khor nas bshad pa mngon pa'i sde snod dang sbas rgyud rnams dang ma mthun pa rnams drang don du bshad mi rung ste/ de ltar rung na 'jig rten khams le'i mdor bsdus brgyad pa dang dgu pa dang bcu pa gsum nas bstan pa phal mo che sgras zin ltar gzhi ma grub [65] pa'i dgongs pa can du 'grel dgos shing / nang le'i yang rtsa rlung gi rnam gzhag sogs mang po zhig sgra ji bzhin par khas blang du mi rung bar 'gyur la/ de lta na des shan brgyab ste le'u lhag ma gzhan rnams la yang sgra ji bzhin du khas blangs pas chog pa nyung zad tsam zhig kyang gzhag dka' bar 'gyur ro zhes gsungs nas/ dus 'khor skor nas bshad pa dang sbas rgyud rtsa bshad rnams nas bshad pa gnyis ma mthun yang gnyis ka nges don nyid du khas blang bar bya'o zhes gsungs pa ltar bshad par bya'o/ /[66]

Scholars (such as Kumāramati[97]) say that it is not right to posit as interpretive those presentations from the Kālacakra on the formation of the world realms and on channels and winds and so forth that conflict with the Abhidharma tradition and the hidden tantras. If it were, then almost everything taught in the eighth, ninth, and tenth summaries from the Realms chapter would have to be explained from the point of view that it does not exist as literally taught. In the Inner chapter also, many presentations on channels, winds, etc., would not be literal. Therefore, in the remaining chapters, it also becomes very difficult to settle almost anything as being literally true. They go on to say that although the explanations from the Kālacakra and from the hidden tantras disagree, they should both be accepted as being definitive and should be explained as such.

d.div: [65] ma dper bzhi ma grub gsal yang gzhi ma grub yin nam snyam/

[66] 'dir yig chung du mkhas pa dag ces pa red mda' ba chen por ngos 'dzin mdzad 'dug kyang red mda' bas dus 'khor bkag par grags pas 'di red mda' chen por sbyor dka' zhing / gsham du rim lnga gsal sgron gyi lung drangs bas rje tsong kha pa chen por sbyar dgos par mngon pas dpyad/
[97] The critical edition notes that Kumāramati is usually identified with Rendawa, but as he was an opponent of Kālacakra it would be difficult to match the following assertion to him.

f.d:
de yang ji ltar 'chad na/ gsal sgron las/
'o na 'dus pa'i bshad rgyud ltar na zhag gcig gi rlung gi phyed la sna bug gi 'pho ba bcu gnyis dang / sdom 'byung ltar na brgyad dang / dus 'khor ltar na drug brgya dang don lnga ma gtogs pa zhag gcig gi rlung ril po la sna bug gi 'pho ba bcu gnyis pa gsungs pa rnams 'gal mi 'gal ji ltar yin snyam na/ 'dus pa'i lugs de ni 'jam dpal zhal lung dang 'phags pa yab sras kyis bkral ba na yang sor bzhag tu mdzad cing / sdom 'byung gi de yang rgyud de'i don du snang bas lung de dag gi don gcig tu bshad du mi rung la/ sna bug tu rgyu ba la lugs 'di mngon sum gyis 'grub la gzhan mi 'grub pa'i khyad par yang gzhag dka' bar snang ba'i phyir gdul bya'i dbang gis gsungs pa mi 'gal bar bya'o/[67] / zhes gsungs pa ltar shes par bya ste/

How is that to be explained? Lantern Illuminating the Five Stages says:
However, according to the explanatory tantra of the Guhyasamāja, in half the breaths of a day there are twelve wind movements at the nostrils. According to the Saṃvaraudbhava there are eight, /171/ and according to the Kālacakra, except for 675 breaths, there are twelve wind movements at the nostrils in a whole day. Are these statements contradictory? Although the tradition of Guhyasamāja has been explained by the Oral Tradition of Mañjuśrī and by Nāgārjuna and his disciples, it has been done so in its own context. The Saṃvaraudbhava, too, exists for the purpose of its own tantra. Therefore it is inappropriate to explain the meanings of those statements together. Concerning the flow of breath through the nostrils, it seems difficult to say that one tradition can be verified and that another cannot. They are taught, therefore, according to the needs of disciples and should not be held as being contradictory.[98] This is how it should be understood.

d.div: [67] rje tsong kha pa/ gsung 'bum pod/ jarim lnga gsal sgron/ 123_ba6
[98] Jé Tsongkhapa, ja, 123b6.

f.d: de yang 'dus pa'i bshad rgyud rdor 'phreng dang lung ston nas gsungs pa ltar 'thad pa ni rim pa lnga gsal ba'i sgron mer gsungs pa ltar yin la/ dus 'khor nas gsungs pa'i tshul ni dus 'khor gyi rgyud sems 'grel skor gsum dang bcas pa tshad mar mi 'dod pa dag lta zhog /de dag tshad mar 'dod phyin chad a b+ha yA ka ra ltar rlung gi rgyu tshul sogs dus 'khor nas gsungs pa rnams sgra ji bzhin pa ma yin pa'i drang don du 'chad pa mi 'thad de/

Moreover the validity as expressed in the explanatory tantras of the Guhyasamāja, such as the Vajra Garland and Sandhivyākaraṇa is as explained in the Lantern Illuminating the Five Stages. As for the Kālacakra, put aside all assertions that the Kālacakratantra and the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries are not valid. From the perspective that they are indeed valid texts, Abhayākaragupta is not correct when he presents the winds, etc., as taught in the Kālacakra as interpretive and not to be taken literally.

khams le'i mdor bsdus gnyis pa las/
rdo rje theg pa 'dir sems can gyi bsam pa'i dbang gis rgyud kyi rgyal po thams cad la rdo rje'i tshig tu sbas te/[68] zhes sbas pa'i rtsa rgyud rnams su rgyud don rnams mi gsal bar sbas nas bstan par gsungs shing / de'i 'phro nyid las/
dang po'i sangs rgyas 'di la rdo rje'i tshig de dag nyid rab tu gsal bar bstan pa bshad pa dang rab tu bshad pa dag gis bcom ldan 'das kyis gsal bar mdzad do/ / de nyid sgrub pa la phyag rgya chen po sgom pa du ba sogs pa mtshan ma'i lam rab tu gsal bar mdzad de/[69] zhes sogs kyis sbas rgyud gzhan du sbas pa'i zab don dang po la sangs rgyas kyis rgyud du gsal bar bstan pa sgra ji bzhin pa'i don can du bshad pa 'di nyid kyis rtsa rlung la sogs pa bstan pa rnams kyang sgra ji bzhin pa'i don can du khas blang dgos par grub bo/ /

The second summary from the Realms chapter states:
The Vajra Vehicle, in accord with the mentality of sentient beings, lies hidden as vajra words in the King of Tantras.[99] Thus in the root hidden tantras, the meanings are taught in an unclear or hidden style. Further on it says:
In this the Kālacakra Original Buddha,[100] the Conqueror has clarified the vajra words by very clearly teaching, explaining, and well explaining.[101] As proof of that, the process of the signs of smoke, etc., in the mahāmudrā meditation is very clear.[102] These and further quotes establish that the profound meanings, which are obscured in other hidden tantras, are taught clearly in the Original Buddha and are to be understood literally. Therefore the teachings on the winds and so forth must also be accepted literally.

d.div: [68] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 16_na7
[69] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 16_ba4
[99] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 16a7.
[100] The Kālacakra root tantra.
[101] “Very clearly teaching, explaining, and well explaining” are the three distinct ways in which the Kālacakra was taught.
[102] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 16b4.

f.d: 'o na mi mthun pa gnyis ka sgra ji bzhin par 'chad tshul ji lta bu snyam na/ de ltar rgyud gnyis las rtsa dang rlung gi rnam gzhag sogs gzhi'i gnas tshul dang bskyed rdzogs kyi lam bgrod pa'i rim pa rnams mi 'dra bar gsungs pa ni rang rang gi ched du bya ba'i gdul bya'i gtso bo'i dbang du byas nas gsungs pa yin la/ 'di la gnyis las dang po ni dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i ched du bya ba'i gdul bya'i gtso bo rnams kyi las kyi spyi mthun gyi bdag 'bras la gling bzhi pa'i snod kyi 'jig rten 'di'i tshad dbyibs dang kha dog sogs mngon pa dang rgyud sde gzhan nas bshad pa dang mi 'dra bar byung ba'i tshul 'grel chen nyid las bshad pa'i don gong du bshad zin pa ltar yin zhing /

But how can both of these conflicting presentations be taken literally? In the two types of tantras the presentations on normal-existence channels, winds, and so forth and the practices on the paths of generation and completion are taught differently, /172/ and this is because they were taught on the basis of the primary intended disciples of each tantra. There are, therefore, two distinct presentations. Firstly, the four-continent world realm with its measurements, colors, and so forth, explained differently from the Abhidharma tradition and other tantras, arises as the dominant result[103] of the common karma of the primary intended disciples of the Śrī Kālacakratantra. How it arises is taught in the Great Commentary and was explained earlier.

d.div: [103] bdag po’i ‘bras bu.

f.d: de bzhin du de 'dra ba'i gdul bya'i gtso bo rnams kyi las kyi rnam smin gyi 'bras bu la yang snod kyi 'jig rten dang chos mthun pa'i lus kyi tshad dang lus kyi cha shas so so'i kha dog dang / lus kyi nang gi rtsa dang rlung dang rlung rnams rtsa 'khor so so dang sna'i bug pa la rgyu tshul rnams byung ba yin pas gnas tshul la grub pa yin zhing / de lta bu'i snod kyi 'jig rten dang bcud kyi sems can gyi lus ngag sems dang bcas pa sbyang gzhir byas nas de dag dang rnam pa mthun pa'i lam gyi rnam gzhag dang / de 'dra ba'i gdul bya'i gtso bo rnams kyi rtsa rlung thig le rnams rgyud 'grel las ji ltar gsungs pa bzhin grub pa gzhir bzhag ste de dag la gnad du bsnun pa'i rdzogs rim gyi lam sgom tshul byas pa las ro rkyang gi rlung dbu mar zhugs pa sogs kyis stong gzugs dang mi 'gyur ba'i bde chen 'dren pa'i tshul rnams ni dpal dus kyi 'khor lo las ji ltar gsungs pa bzhin gnas tshod la grub pa'i tshul lo/ /

Similarly the dimensions of the body and the individual colors of its constituents correlating with the outside world, plus the channels and winds within the body and the way the winds move through the individual cakras and through the nostrils, all arise as the results of the ripening karma of those same disciples. These phenomena exist, therefore, as actual situations. This external world and the inner world of sentient beings with body, speech, and mind are the bases of purification practice. The presentations of the path correlating with those phenomena, and the winds, channels, and drops of these primary disciples existing as they are taught in the tantra and its commentaries, form a basis upon which the penetrating activities of the completion stage are practiced. From such practices, the winds of the left and right channels enter the central channel, thereby inducing the empty forms and unchanging bliss. As these processes are taught in the Śrī Kālacakratantra, so they actually exist.

de ltar yang nang le'i nga dgu pa'i 'grel chen las/
de ltar na lnga bcu rtsa drug lhag pa'i brgya ni dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsa lha dang lha mo'i rang bzhin gyis gnas pa byis pa rnams la 'chi ba ster bar byed pa ste/ rigs drug gi rtsa dang lhan cig drug cu rtsa gnyis lhag pa'i brgya'i dus kyi 'khor lo 'khor lo drug gi rtsa'i bdag nyid can bsgoms par gyur ba na rnal 'byor pa rnams la bde ba ster bar byed pa'o/[70] / zhes gsang gnas kyi rtsa 'dab so gnyis/ lte ba'i re bzhi/ snying ga'i brgyad/ mgrin pa'i so gnyis/ dpral ba'i bcu drugagatsug tor gyi rtsa 'dab bzhi ste/ rtsa brgya dang lnga bcu rtsa drug po de pad+ma gdan can gyi lha dang lha mo lnga bcu rtsa drug gi ngo bor mos nas sgom pa dang /

The fifty-ninth verse of the Inner chapter says:
Therefore the 156 are channels that dwell in the nature of the Kālacakra gods and goddesses and that bring death to ordinary beings. Together with the channels of the six families, the 162 channels, in the nature of the six Kālacakra wheels, bring bliss to the yogi when meditated upon.[104] This passage teaches that the 156 channels comprise the thirty-two channel petals of the secret place, sixty-four of the navel, eight of the heart, thirty-two of the throat, sixteen of the forehead, and four of the crown. These are visualized as 156 lotus-seated gods and goddesses and meditated upon. /173/

d.div: [70] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 143_ba3
[104] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 143b3.

f.d: de bzhin du steng gi rtsa ro rkyang dbu ma gsum dang 'og gi khu ba bshang gci'i rtsa gsum ste drug po rigs drug gi ngo bor mos te sgom pa sogs kyi bskyed rim gyis rgyud smin par byas nas rtsa rlung thig le gsum la gnad du bsnun pa'i sbyor ba yan lag drug gi rdzogs rim bsgoms pa las rnal 'byor pa la mthar thug gi bde ba ste+er bar gsungs pa dang /

Likewise the three upper channels of the left, right, and middle plus the three lower channels of fluid, excrement, and urine are visualized and meditated upon as the six families. This generation-stage practice ripens the continuum and the meditations of the six-branched yoga of the completion stage, which penetrates the channels, winds, and drops and brings the yogi to ultimate happiness.

de bzhin du nga brgyad pa'i 'grel chen 'di nyidalas/
'khor lo drug la dus kyi rtsa brjod pa rnams bla ma'i man ngag gis bsgoms par gyur na 'chi ba'i 'jigs pa 'phrog ste rnal 'byor pa rnams kyis 'di la ngo mtshar med do/[71] / zhes gsungs pa'i bla ma'i man ngag ni sbyor ba yan lag drug yin te/

The Great Commentary says on the fifty-eighth verse of the Inner chapter:
The six channels are the time channels. When meditated upon in accord with the guru’s instruction, the fear of death will be destroyed. To the yogi this is nothing special.[105] The “instruction” refers to the six-branched yoga.

d.div: [71] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 140_na6
[105] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 140a6.

f.d:
nang le'i drug cu pa'i 'grel chen las/
steng du zla ba dang nyi ma dang sgra gcan te g.yon dang g.yas dang dbu ma'i lam la gnas pa dang / 'og tu zla ba dang nyi ma dang me'i dbye bas bshad pa dang gcig dang khu ba'i lam la gnas pa'o/ / des ni rnal 'byor ma'i lus la bsrung bar bya'o/ / gang gis zhe na/ bla ma'i nges pa'i dbang gis zhes pa la bla ma'i nges pa ni sbyor ba yan lag drug ste des 'chi ba las bsrung bar bya'o/ / gang zhig srog chags rnams la 'chi ba ster ba ni drug po 'di rnams la srog zhugs pa'o/ / drug po rnams la gal te srog ni rab zhugs gyur na de'i tshe mi rnams dus thams cad du 'chi bas 'dzoms par nges te mtha' gcig tu'o/ / drug po 'di rnams kyi nang nas phra mo ni dbu ma la a wa d+hU tI ste phra mo de la srog ma zhugs par gyur na rnal 'byor pa rnams kyi 'chi ba'i yul ni gang du gcod par byed de nges par 'chi ba'i yul gcod par mi byed do/[72] / zhes sbyor ba yan lag drug gi rnal 'byor gyis rlung dbu mar zhugs par ma byas na mthar thug gi 'bras bur gyur ba'i 'chi ba med pa 'thob pa'i thabs med par gsungs so/ /

Regarding the sixtieth verse the Great Commentary says:
Above, the moon, sun, and Rāhu dwell in the paths of the left, right, and center. Below, divided into moon, sun, and Agni, they dwell in the paths of excrement, urine, and fluid. These the yogi protects in the body. How? “By the precepts of the guru.” The precepts of the guru are the six-branched yoga, which will bring protection from death. “They bring death to living creatures” because these six are entered by the winds. If the winds enter the six, at that time and at all times men will definitely be destroyed by death. Among the six is “the subtle” or the central avadhūtī. If the winds do not enter “the subtle,” “how will the yogis destroy the realm of death?” Definitely they will not destroy the realm of death.[106] Therefore, if the yogi does not induce the winds into the central channel by way of the six-branched yoga, the ultimate result of deathlessness is unobtainable.

d.div: [72] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 141_na1
[106] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 141a1.

f.d: gnyis pa sbas rgyud rtsa bshad rnams las rtsa dang rlung gi rnam gzhag sogs gzhi'i gnas tshul dang / bskyed rdzogs kyi lam bgrod pa'i rim pa rnams rang gi ched du bya ba'i gdul bya'i dbang du byas pas sgra ji bzhin pa yin tshul ni sbas rgyud rtsa bshad kyi ched du bya ba'i gdul bya'i gtso bo rnams kyi spyi mthun gyi las kyi bdag 'bras la gling bzhi pa 'di nyid kyi tshad dbyibs sogs mngon pa dang sbas rgyud rtsa bshad dang de dag gi dgongs pa 'grel ba'i mkhas grub rnams kyis bshad pa ltar dngos gnas la grub pa mdo rgyud sogs de dag gi dgongs pa yin pa lta ci smos/ dus 'khor gyi dgongs pa yin par yang phug khru lnga pa zhes sogs kyi 'grel tshig de rnams kyis bstan par gong du bshad zin pa ltar yin zhing /

Secondly, the presentation of the channels and winds of normal existence, plus the stages along the paths of generation and completion, as found in the root and explanatory hidden tantras, exist on the basis of their intended disciples and therefore are to be taken literally. This is done as follows. /174/ For the primary disciples that the root and explanatory hidden tantras are intended for, the dominant result of their common karma is this four-continent world with its measurements and shape as taught in the Abhidharma tradition and in the root and explanatory hidden tantras, together with commentaries on their meanings unraveled by the great masters. That this world exists as a reality is clearly the thinking of the tantras and sutras. That it is also the thinking of the Kālacakra is taught by the words of the commentary that begin “In a cave of five cubits,” which was explained earlier.

de bzhin du sbas rgyud rtsa bshad rnams kyi ched du bya ba'i gdul bya'i gtso bo rnams kyi rang rang gi las kyi rnam smin gyi 'bras bu'i phung khams skye mched rnams dang / khyad par du rtsa dang rlung dang rlung rnams rtsa 'dab dang sna bug la rgyu tshul rnams sbas rgyud dgongs 'grel dang bcas pa las ji ltar du gsungs pa ltar dngos gnas la grub cing ji ltar grub pa ltar gyi snod kyi 'jig rten dang chos mthun par gzhal yas khang sgom pa dang / phung khams skye mched rnams lha dang lha mo'i ngo bor sgom zhing / khyad par du yang rtsa rlung thig le rnams dpa' bo dang dpa' mo'i ngo bor sgom pa sogs kyi bskyed rim gyis rgyud smin par byas te ji skad bshad pa'i rtsa rlung thig le rnams la gnad du snun pa'i rdzogs rim sgom pa mthar phyin pa las 'bras bu sku gnyis thob bar 'gyur gyi/ gzhi ma grub pa'i snod dang bcud kyi rtsa rlung sogs dang chos mthun pa dang dmigs par byas kyang 'bras bu ji lta ba bzhin 'thob par dka' 'o/ /

Likewise, as taught in the hidden tantras and commentaries, the aggregates, realms, and sensory sources, and particularly the channels and winds, together with the way the winds move through the channel petals and the nostrils, all exist in reality as the ripening results of the common karma of the primary disciples intended for the root and explanatory hidden tantras. Celestial palaces are meditated upon as correlating with the external world as it exists; the aggregates, realms, and sensory sources are meditated upon as being of the nature of gods and goddesses; and in particular, the channels, winds, and drops are meditated upon as being of the nature of male and female heroes. These generation-stage meditations ripen the continuum of the mind. The channels, winds, and drops, existing exactly as they are taught, are penetrated by the meditations of the completion stage, whose ultimate development results in the two bodies of a buddha. Conversely, if one correlates with and focuses upon an external world and an inner world of channels and so forth that do not actually exist, it will be difficult to attain any kind of result.

de ltar na ched du bya ba'i gdul bya gnyis kyi las rigs mi 'dra ba tha dad pa'i dbang gis snod kyi 'jig rten dang nang gi rtsa rlung sogs mi 'dra ba'i khyad par byung zhing de ltar byung ba nyid kyis sbas rgyud rnams kyi dgongs pa 'phags yul gyi mkhas grub rnams kyis bkral ba'i lam gyi bgrod tshul dang sems 'grel skor gsum rjes 'brang dang bcas pa rnams kyis bshad pa'i lam gyi bgrod tshul la khyad par mi 'dra ba'i tshul byung bar shes par bya'o/ /

Therefore, because of the separate and different types of karma of the two kinds of intended disciples, differences arose in the external worlds and the internal worlds of channels, winds, and so forth. Because of these differences, two ways of traveling the path arose — the method of the masters of India who explained the meanings of the hidden tantras, and the method of the followers of the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries.
de ltar nang gi rnam gzhag cung zad tsam zhig bshad zin to// //
This has been a brief explanation of the presentation of the inner world.
le'u gsum pa/ dbang gi le'u/
Part 3. Initiations
gsum pa gzhan dbang dang bskyed rdzogs 'bras bu dang bcas pa'i rnam gzhag bshad pa
11. Qualifications of Master and Disciple
['di ]la gnyis/ dbang gi rnam gzhag bshad pa dang / bskyed rdzogs 'bras bu dang bcas pa'i rnam gzhag bshad pa'o/ /
dang po [dbang gi rnam gzhag bshad pa ]

This has three outlines: 1. By whom and upon whom initiations are bestowed: The definitions of master and disciple 2. Where the initiations are bestowed: A description of the mandala 3. Presentation of the initiations to be bestowed

d.i: Definition of a guru to be relied upon

f.d:
dbang le'i gnyis pa las/
dang por yang dag bsten bya bla ma dag kyang dam tshig ldan zhing rdo rje theg la lhag par gnas/ / de nyid bsgoms shing ma chags dri ma dag dang rnam par bral zhing bzod pa'i ngang tshul lam la zhugs/ / slob ma rnams la lam ni sbyin byed dmyal ba'i 'jigs pa 'phrog cing de nyid las ni tshangs spyod ldan/ / bdud rnams la ni rdo rje dbyug pa de yang 'dzin ma'i gzhi la rdo rje sems dpar rab grags pa'o/[1] / zhes gsungs pa'i mtshan nyid dang ldan pa ste/ de yang de dag gi don cung zad cig bshad na/ dbang la sogs pa zhu ba'i don du dang por bla ma dag kyang bsten par bya'o/ /

The second verse of the Initiations chapter from the Condensed Tantra says:
Firstly, the guru to devote oneself to keeps his vows, dwells within the Vajra Vehicle, meditates upon the reality,[1] is unattached, untainted, and of a patient nature, has entered the path, shows the path to the disciples, and takes away the fear of hell. From reality he is of the brahmacarya, and for māra he is the vajra club. Such a one is known as a heroic vajra mind upon this earth.[2] This passage speaks of the qualified guru. His qualities will be briefly explained. To request an initiation, one must first rely upon a guru. /176/

d.div: [1] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ sh+loka2_58_na3
[1] De nyid, tattva.
[2] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, v. 2, 58a3.

f.d: bla ma ji lta bu snyam na/ drang nges kyi dam tshig gnyis dang ldan pa/ rdo rje theg pa gsang sngags bla med kyi lam la gnas pa ste dus kyi 'khor lo'i dbang la brten pa'i sngags kyi sdom pa dang ldan pa/ de nyid bsgoms shing ste dus kyi 'khor lo'i bskyed pa'i rim pa sngon du song ba'i rdzogs pa'i rim pa sgom pa dang ldan pa/ ma chags pa ste bu dang chung ma la sogs pa dang rang gi lus la yang ltos pa med pa'o/ / dri ma dag dang rnam par bral ba ni 'dod chags zhe sdang gti mug nga rgyal phrag dog ser sna rnams ci rigs pa dang bral ba'o/ / bzod pa'i ngang tshul ni rnyed bkur la sogs pa'i 'bras bu la ltos pa med par slob ma'i don nyid la zhugs pa'o/ / lam la zhugs pa ni spyir theg pa chen po'i lam la zhugs pa'o/ / slob ma rnams la lam ni sbyin byed dmyal ba'i 'jigs pa 'phrog cing zhes pa ni rang nyid bla mar bsten par gyur pa'i slob ma rnams la yang dag pa'i lam sbyin pa'i sgo nas dmyal ba la sogs pa'i 'jigs pa 'phrog par nus pa'o/ / de nyid las ni tshangs spyod ldan zhes pa ni de kho na nyid goms pa las ni mi 'pho ba'i tshangs spyod mchog tu mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba thob pa'o/ / bdud rnams la ni rdo rje dbyug pa zhes pa ni/ phung po dang nyon mongs pa dang 'chi bdag dang lha'i bu'i ste bdud bzhi po 'joms pa la rdo rje dbyug pa dang 'dra ba ste yon tan de rnams dang ldan pa de yang 'dzin ma ste sa'i gzhi la rdo rje sems dpar rab tu grags pa ni bsten bya rdo rje slob dpon gyi mtshan nyid do/ /

What kind of guru should one rely on? One who keeps both interpretive and definitive samaya[3] and one who dwells within the path of the Vajra Vehicle, the highest secret mantra. This means to possess the mantra vows from the initiation of Kālacakra. “Meditates upon the reality” means one who meditates upon the Kālacakra completion stage preceded by the generation stage. “Unattached” means to have no attachment for wife, children, and so forth, and no regard for his own body. “Untainted” means to be untainted by desire, anger, ignorance, pride, jealousy, and miserliness. “Of a patient nature” means to have no regard for the fruits of fame and wealth but to be occupied instead by the welfare of the disciples. “Has entered the path” means that he has entered the general Mahayana path. “Shows the path to the disciples, and takes away the fear of hell” means that by showing the perfect path to those disciples who rely upon him as a guru, it becomes possible to remove the fears of hell. “From reality he is of the brahmacarya”[4] means that from meditating upon emptiness he has attained the unmoving brahmacarya, the supreme unchanging bliss. “For māra he is the vajra club” means that in destroying the four types of māras he is like the vajra club. The four kinds of māras are the aggregates, the delusions, death, and the devaputra.[5] One who possesses these qualities is famed as a heroic vajra mind upon the earth. These are the characteristics of a vajra master to be relied upon.

d.div: [3] dam tshig. Pledge or vow. Each of the five buddhas has its own set of pledges.
[4] tshangs spyod.
[5] Or kāma, a cupidlike personification of desire who lives in the celestial realms.

f.d:
gzhan yang dbang le'i gnyis pa'i 'grel chen du lung drangs pa las/
brtan cing dul la blo gros ldan/ / bzod ldan drang la g.yo sgyu med/ / sngags dang rgyud kyi sbyor ba shes/ / snying brtser ldan zhing bstan bcos mkhas/ / de nyid bcu ni yongs su shes/ / dkyil 'khor bri ba'i las la mkhas/ / gsang sngags 'chad byed slob dpon te/ dwa/ nga ba'i bdag nyid dbang po thul/[2] / zhes gsungs pa 'di dag gis kyang bsten bya rdo rje slob dpon gyi mtshan nyid bstan to/ / de dag gi gzhan rnams go sla zhing / de nyid bcu ni yongs su shes/ / zhes pa'i de nyid bcu ni rdo rje snying po rgyan gyi rgyud kyi le'u tha ma las/

Furthermore the Great Commentary, commenting on the second verse of the Initiations chapter of the Condensed Tantra, quotes a text that says:
Stable, disciplined, and of intelligence, patient, honest, free from deception, knows mantra and the yogas of tantra, is compassionate, wise in the commentaries, knows well the ten activities, is wise in mandala drawing, a master skilled in teaching tantra, of great faith and with senses tamed.[6] This quote also teaches the characteristics of a vajra master. These are not difficult to understand. The ten activities mentioned in the line “knows well the ten activities” taught in the last chapter of An Adornment to the Vajra Essence Tantra /177/:

d.div: [2] sde dge_3721_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ tshubla ma lnga bcu pa/ 10_na6_sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 262_na7
[6] Fifty Verses on the Guru, Toh 3721 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, tshu, 10a6.

f.d: phyir bzlog gnyis kyi cho ga dang/ / gsang dang shes rab ye shes dang / kha sbyor 'byed pa'i cho ga dang / / gtor ma rdo rje'i bzlas pa dang / / drag shul sgrub pa'i cho ga dang / / rab tu gnas dang dkyil 'khor sgrub/ / gsang ba'i de nyid bcu yin no/ / dkyil 'khor ting 'dzin phyag rgya dang / / stangs stabs 'dug stangs bzlas brjod dang / / sbyin sreg mchod pa las sbyor dang / / slar sdud pa yi rnam pa ni/ / phyi yi de nyid bcu yin no/[3] / zhes gsungs pa rnams te/ de dag gi don zhib par ni rje thams cad mkhyen pas mdzad pa'i bla ma lnga bcu pa'i rnam bshad las shes par bya'o/ /

The two rituals for repelling, the secret and wisdom-knowledge, the ritual of separating, the ritual food, vajra recitation, the ritual of wrathful expression, consecration, mandala meditation, these are the ten secret activities. Mandala, meditative concentration, mudrā, standing posture, seated posture, recitation, the fire ritual, activity yoga, concluding. These are the ten outer activities.[7] The detailed meanings of these can be known from A Commentary on the Fifty Verses on the Guru, composed by the Omniscient Master.[8]

d.div: [3] sde dge_451_bka'/ rgyud/ chardo rje snying po rgyan gyi rgyud/ 57_ba7
[7] Toh 451 Kangyur, rgyud, cha, 57b7.
[8] Jé Tsongkhapa. This text has been translated by Gareth Sparham as The Fulfillment of All Hopes: Guru Devotion in Tibetan Buddhism (Boston: Wisdom Publications, 1999).

f.d: de ltar na de ltar bshad pa'i mtshan nyid de rnams dang ldan pa'i gang zag ni dbang bskur ba sogs kyi bla mar 'os pa yin no/ / de la yang nang gses kyis phye na gsum ste/ de lta bu'i mtshan nyid dang ldan pa'i dge slong dang dge tshul dang khyim pa'o/ / de gsum gyi'ang dge slong slob dpon du 'os pa mchog dang / dge tshul 'bring dang / khyim pa tha ma yin pas de gsum tshogs pa'i tshe dge slong bla mar bsten par byed dgos shing / rgyal po rnams kyis kyang dge slong nyid bla mar bsten dgos te/ de ltar ma byas par khyim pa bla mar bsten na bstan pa la gnod par 'gyur bas so/ / de yang ji ltar gnod na/ slob dpon du 'os pa'i rab tu byung ba yod bzhin du khyim pa bla mar bsten na skye bo rnams sangs rgyas dang chos dang dge 'dun la ma gus par 'gyur zhing / des rkyen byas te bstan pa bsnub pa sogs su 'gyur ba'i phyir te/

Such a person, therefore, endowed with such characteristics is suitable to be a guru and is capable of bestowing initiations and so forth. These characteristics may be further divided into those possessed by a fully ordained monk, those possessed by a novice monk, and those possessed by a layperson. Among these three types of persons worthy of being a vajra master, a fully ordained monk is the best, a novice monk is second best, and a layman the lowest of the three. Therefore, when all three are present, it is the fully ordained monk that one should rely upon as one’s guru. Moreover kings should rely upon fully ordained monks as gurus, because if they rely upon laymen, it will bring harm to the teachings. How will this happen? If a layman is taken as a guru even though a fully ordained monk worthy of being a vajra master is accessible, the people will lose respect for the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, which in turn will lead to the disappearance of the doctrine.

dbang le'i gnyis pa'i 'grel chen du lung drangs pa las/
de nyid bcu ni yongs shes pa/ / gsum las dge slong mchog yin zhing / / 'bring ni dge tshul zhes bya ste/ khyim gnas de las tha ma'o/[4] / zhes dang

The Great Commentary, on the second verse of the Initiations chapter, quotes passages that say:
“Of the three who know well the ten activities, the full monk is the best, the novice is second best, the householder the lowest.”

d.div: [4] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 262_na3

f.d:
de bzhin du/
sa thob ma gtogs khyim pa ni/ / rgyal pos bla mar mi bya ste/ / de la thos pa yongs shes pas/ / gang zhig rtags can bya ba nyid/ / sa thob ma gtogs slob dpon ni/ khyim gnas gang tshe mchod byed pa/ / de tshe sangs rgyas chos dang ni/ / dge 'dun rnams la gus med 'gyur/[5] / zhes dang /

Similarly:
“Except for those on ārya levels, kings should not take householders as gurus. Of those whose learning is complete, who perform deeds of those possessing the signs, except for those upon ārya levels, venerating vajra masters while they live as householders will bring disrespect for Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.”

d.div: [5] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 262_na4

f.d:
de bzhin du/
lha khang sogs kyi rab gnas sogs/ / rtags can gyis ni rtag tu bya/ / gnas gcig dag na gsum yod na/ khyim pa gos dkar ldan pas min/[6] / zhes pa ste|_de ltar rnam pa du mas slob dpon yongs su brtag pa las bcom ldan 'das kyis gsungs pa'i bla ma slob ma rnams kyis bsten par bya ste/ zhes gsungs pa ltar bla mar bsten du rung ba'i mtshan nyid rnams shes par byas te bla ma yang dag pa btsal bar bya'o/ /

Also:
“For consecrating temples and so forth, from among those possessing the signs, if all three are in one place, the white-clothed householder is not the one.” Therefore, by examining the master in many ways, disciples should devote themselves to a master as taught by the buddha.[9] Therefore, knowing the characteristics of a guru worthy of devotion, one should seek out the proper guru. /178/
