[21] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 395_na2
[22] rje tsong kha pa/ gsung 'bum pod/ da_sbyor ba yan lag drug gi rdzogs rim gyi gnang bsdus pa/ 6_na2
[32] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 437b4.
[33] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 395a2.
[34] Jé Tsongkhapa, Collected Works, vol. da, 6a2.

f.d:
gzhan yang ye le'i brgya nyer gcig pa'i 'grel chen las/
da ni dbu mar srog ces pa la sogs pa rnal 'byor nye bar bsdu ba gsungs te 'dir dang por rnal 'byor pas dbu mar srog ni rab tu gzhug par bya ste gang gis mtshan ma mthong bar 'gyur ba a wa ng+hU tIr ro/[23] / zhes sor sdud kyi skabs su rlung dbu mar zhugs dgos pa gsal bar gsungs so/ /

Also the Great Commentary on verse 120 of the Gnosis chapter says:
“Wind in the central channel” and so forth speaks of the yoga of withdrawal. Here initially the yogi places the winds in the central channel, by which he will see the signs within the avadhūtī.[35] These quotes clearly state that the winds must enter the central channel during the process of withdrawal.

d.div: [23] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 390_ba5
[35] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 390b5.

f.d: gal te de ltar gsungs pa de srog rtsol gyi skabs la dgongs pa yin no zhe na/ 'di ni ma yin te/ 'grel tshig snga ma'i rgyun de nyid las/ 'di ni dpal ldan bla ma zhes pa sangs rgyas kyi sku rdo rje ste/[24] zhes sku rdo rje bsnyen pa'i yan lag tu bshad cing / de'i mjug de ma thag tu/ srog rtsol ni gnyis pa gsung rdo rje'o/[25] /zhes srog rtsol gsung rdo rjer bshad pas so/ /

But one may wonder if this quote refers to the branch of prāṇāyāma. That cannot be, because the quote continues, “Glorious guru, body vajra of the Buddha,”[36] /342/ thereby placing it in the approximation and body vajra section. After this sentence the text continues, “Prāṇāyāma is the second, the speech vajra,” thereby placing prāṇā yāma within the speech vajra section.

d.div: [24] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 390_ba6
[25] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 390_07
[36] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 390b6.

f.d:
gzhan yang ye le'i brgya bco lnga pa'i 'grel chen las/
'dir dbu mar srog rab tu zhugs pas stong pa kho na las du ba la sogs pa'i mtshan ma mthong ste nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig ni mi 'dzum rdo rje'i lam du rab tu zhugs pas stong pa las ni du ba smig rgyu rab gsal dri ma med pa'i mkha' snang nyid dang mar me dang zhes pa ni mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor gyis mthong ngo /[26] / zhes sor sdud kyi mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor gyi skabs su dbu mar srog ste rlung zhugs pa las stong gzugs mthong bar gsal bar gsungs so/ /

Furthermore the Great Commentary, on verse 115 of the Gnosis chapter, says:
Here the winds enter the central channel, and from the total emptiness the signs of smoke and so forth are seen. Therefore, “with the mind fixed into space, the eyes unclosed, the vajra path is entered. From the emptiness arises smoke, mirage, a clear, uncontaminated light in the sky, a butter-lamp flame.” These are seen in the night yoga.[37] This clearly states that during the night yoga of the withdrawal process, the winds enter the central channel, causing empty forms to arise.

d.div: [26] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 388_ba2
[37] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 388b2.

f.d:
gzhan yang ye le'i brgya bco brgyad pa'i 'grel chen las/
sgyu ma'i grong khyer bzhin du dkar po la sogs pa'i kha dog dang ldan yang rdzas med pa'i phyir kha dog ma yin no/ / rnam pa kun ldan yin yang dus thams cad du byis pa rnams kyis mthong ba min no/ / de ci'i phyir zhe na/ nyon mongs bdud kyi mthu las te g.yon pa dang g.yas pa'i rtsal srog rab tu rgyu ba las sa zhes pa nges pa'o/[27] / zhes gsungs pa 'dis kyang sor sdud kyi skabs kyi stong gzugs mthong ba la rlung dbu mar zhugs dgos par go nus te/ 'dir ro rkyang la rlung rgyu ba'i dus su sor sdud sogs lam gyi ngo bor gyur pa'i stong gzugs mi mthong bar bshad pas so/ /

The Great Commentary states on verse 118 of the Gnosis chapter:
Like an illusory town they have colors, such as white and so forth, but because they are immaterial there are no colors. Although they are endowed with many features, they are never seen by ordinary beings. Why is that? “It is by the power of the māra of mental affliction,” whereby the winds flow in the left and right channels.[38] From this quote too we can understand that for the empty forms of the withdrawal yoga to appear, winds must enter the central channel, because while winds are flowing in the right and left channel, empty forms as part of the yogas of withdrawal and so forth are not seen.

d.div: [27] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 390_na2
[38] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 390a2.

f.d:
nyi ma dpal gyis yon tan gyis 'gengs pa zhes bya ba'i 'grel pa las/
'di ni ste sems kyi snang ba ni rkyang ma dang ro ma gcig tu sbyor bas mthong ste/[28] zhes du sogs kyi snang ba mthong ba la ro rkyang gi rlung dbu mar gcig tu sbyor dgos par bshad do/ /

In the commentary called Filled with Good Qualities by Sūryaśrī, it says:
These appearances to the mind are seen when the left and right channel join as one.[39] This means that seeing the appearances of smoke and so forth is due to the right and left channel joining as one in the central channel.

d.div: [28] sde dge_1388_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ pa_yon tan gyis 'gengs pa/ 8_ba7
[39] Toh 1388 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 8b7.

f.d:
dpal sha ba ri pas kyang /
mi g.yo ba ni gsum ldan gyis/ / ng+hU tIr rlung bcu chud gyur pas/ / phyi nang rtog 'gags rtags byung ba/ / so sor gcod pa'i yan lag go[29] / zhes sor sdud kyi rtags bcu 'byung ba la ng+hU tIr rlung bcu chud dgos par gsungs so/ /

Śavaripa also says:
By the three unmoving, the ten winds enter the dhūtī, outer and inner conceiving is halted, and the signs arise; this the branch of individual cutting.[40] This also means that for the ten signs of withdrawal to arise, the ten winds must move into the central channel.

d.div: [29] sde dge_1373_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ parnal 'byor yan lag drug pa/ 251_ba6
[40] Six Yogas, Toh 1375 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 251b6.

f.d:
dus zhabs snyan brgyud las kyang /
so sor sdud pa 'di ltar bsgom/ / bsgom pa stong nyid bsgoms pa yis/ / 'gag pa rlung ni 'gag par byed/[30] / ces sor sdud kyi dmigs pa bsgoms pas ro rkyang gi rlung rgyu ba 'gags nas dbu mar 'jug par bshad pa sogs rgyud 'grel dang rgya gzhung rnams nas ji snyed cig bshad pa rnams so/ / de ltar bshad pa bzhin du jo zhal sogs lugs 'di'i mkhas pa snga ma rnams kyang bzhed do/ /

The Kālacakrapāda Transmission also states:
Meditate on withdrawal this way: meditate on emptiness, the object of meditation, and halt the winds that are to be stopped.[41] Therefore, by meditating on the practices of withdrawal, the winds of the right and left channel are halted and moved to the central channel. These and other quotes are from the tantra, its commentary, and other Indian texts. Earlier scholars of the Kālacakra tradition, /343/ such as those of the Jonang, also accepted this explanation.

d.div: [30] sde dge_1372_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ pa_dus zhabs snyan rgyud/ 224_na6
[41] Toh 1372 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 251b6.

f.d:
gal te 'grel chen las/
'dir gang gi tshe so sor sdud pa la sogs pas gzugs mthong bar gyur ba la srog ma bcings pa nyid kyis 'gyur ba med pa'i skad cig ma skyes na de'i tshe nA da goms pa 'chad par 'gyur bas btsan thabs su dbu mar 'bab par byas nas/[31] zhes gsungs pa rnams kyis sor sdud kyi lam gyi stong gzugs mthong bar gyur pa yang yin rlung dbu mar ma chud pa yang min pa yod par bshad pa ma yin nam snyam na/

However the Great Commentary says:
During withdrawal and so forth, when forms are seen but instances of the unchanging have not been generated, because the winds have not been bound, at that time meditate on the nāda, which will be explained, and by wrathful means bring them to the central channel.[42] Doesn’t this teach a scenario where the empty forms of withdrawal are seen but the winds have not entered the central channel?

d.div: [31] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 238_na6
[42] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 238a6.

f.d: sor sdud kyi dmigs pa sgom pa'i gnas skabs su rlung dbu mar ma chud bar du sogs kyi mtshan ma shar ba 'ong ba 'grel tshig de dag gis bstan kyang de dag sor sdud kyi lam ma yin te/ sor sdud kyi lam gyi mtshan nyid tshang ba'i stong gzugs sngon du 'gyur ba la rlung dbu mar chud pa cig dgos pas de 'grub pa'i phyir du 'dir spogs chog byed dgos pa 'grel tshig de dag gis bstan pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

These words do teach a time during the meditations of withdrawal where the signs of smoke and so forth can be seen without the winds having entered the central channel. However such an experience is not on the actual path of withdrawal, because before the definitive empty forms on the path of withdrawal are seen, the winds must have entered the central channel, and if that is not the case, one should perform the above-mentioned enhancement ritual to accomplish it.

'o na sor sdud kyi skabs su rlung dbu mar chud dgos na/ de'i skabs kyi rlung dbu mar 'dzud pa'i thabs ji lta bu snyam na/ 'di la kha cig /dus zhabs snyan brgyud las/
'bol ba'i stan la byed pa ni/ / lus bsrang rdo rje skyil krung bca'/ / lce bzlog gsus sbyar mig gyen bzlog / gtsug tor sgyur ba'i lta ltangs so/ / lag gnyis rdo rje bsdam par bya/ / des ni rlung rnams 'ching byed pa'o/[32] / zhes gsungs pas lus kyi 'dug stangs dang mig gi lta stangs byed pa de nyid kyis rlung dbu mar 'ching ba yin no zhes gsung yang de ni mi 'thad de/

If the winds have to enter the central channel during withdrawal, how is that achieved? To this some reply by quoting the Kālacakrapāda Transmission:
On a comfortable seat, guard the body in vajra position, tongue turned back, clasped to stomach, eyes turned upward, in the manner of Uṣṇīṣacakrī,[43] hands vajra-bound. This will bind the winds.[44] Therefore, they maintain, by adopting a sitting posture and gazing in a certain way, the winds will be bound within the central channel. This cannot be correct.

d.div: [32] sde dge_1372_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ pa_dus zhabs snyan rgyud/ 224_ba1
[43] Wrathful deity found in the body mandala.
[44] Toh 1372 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 224b1.

f.d: ji ltar mi 'thad snyam na/ sor sdud sgom pa'i skabs 'dir sems kyi 'jog tshul sogs kyi sgom pa mi dgos par 'gyur te/ sor sdud sgom pa'i lag rjes kyi gtso bo ni rlung dbu mar chud pa'i stobs kyis du sogs kyi stong gzugs rnams 'char ba 'di yin la/ lus kyi 'dug stangs dang mig gi lta stangs kyi byed pa nyid kyis ro rkyang gi rlung gi rgyu ba bkag nas dbu mar 'jug nus pa gang zhig/sor sdud kyi gnas skabs su rlung dbu mar chud na de'i stobs kyis du sogs kyi stong gzugs 'char ba rten 'brel gyi chos nyid yin pa'i phyir ro/ / gang zhig khas blangs shing / 'dod par mi nus pa ni 'grel chen las sems kyi 'jog tshul bshad pa nyid kyis shes so/ /

Why? Because it would mean that the meditations of withdrawal would not involve practices of mental placement. This follows because the primary effect of the withdrawal meditations is that the power of the winds in the central channel causes the signs of smoke and so forth to appear, and, according to you, adopting a seated posture and placing the eyes in a certain way by themselves halt the winds of the right and left channel and send them into the central channel, and moreover, in the yoga of withdrawal, the process of winds entering the central channel to bring about the resultant appearance of empty-form signs is a natural cause-and-effect occurrence. You must accept the reasons for this consequence, but you cannot accept the consequence itself,[45] because there are explanations of mental placement in the Great Commentary. /344/

d.div: [45] The opponents cannot agree with the consequence that the meditations of withdrawal are not meditations that involve practices of mental placement because of scriptural authority that says otherwise.

f.d: yang jo zhal sogs bod kyi sbyor drug pa phal mo che ni smin mtshams kyi thad kyi mun khang gi gnas lus kyi phyi rol gyi nam mkha' la mig gis lta ba'i lta stangs dang / sems kyi 'jog tshul yang lta stangs gang du gtad pa'i mun khang gi nam mkha' de nyid la rtse gcig tu gtad de gzhan du cung zad kyang mi 'phro bar ci yang yid la mi byed par glod nas 'jog/de ltar bzhag pas rlung dbu mar chud nas mtshan rtags rnams 'char bar bzhed la/ 'di dag gi ltar na lus gnad dang lta stangs kyis rkyen byas pa'i sems kyi 'jog tshul nyid rlung dbu mar 'dzud pa'i thabs su 'dod dgos shing de ltar 'dod pa yang yin no/ /

The Jonang tradition and most Tibetan practitioners of the six yogas assert a positioning of the eyes that takes place in a darkened room. They say the eyes are fixed on a point in space outside the body directly in front of the point midway between the eyebrows. The mental placement involves focusing the mind one-pointedly on that very point in the space of a darkened room on which the eyes have focused. There it is held without the slightest wandering, in a relaxed manner, and without any mental activity.[46] This, they maintain, ensures that the winds enter the central channel and that the signs will appear.

d.div: [46] yid la byed pa.

f.d: de lta yin na phar phyin gyi theg pa nyid kyis lam bgrod pa'i 'phags pas lus rnam snang gi chos bdun ldan du byas te stong nyid la rtse gcig tu mnyam par bzhag pa'i gnas skabs su ro rkyang gi rlung gi rgyu ba 'gags nas dbu mar chud par khas len pa'am/ de ltar khas mi len na de lta bu'i gnas skabs su rlung dbu mar chud pa med pa dang / /lus kyi phyi rol gyi mun khang gi nam mkha' la sogs rtse gcig tu bzhag pas rlung dbu mar chud 'ong ba'i khyad par 'byed dgos na'ang de lta bu'i khyad par phyed dka' 'o/ / rang lugs nisems kyi 'jog tshul nyid rlung dbu mar 'dzud pa'i thabs yin pa shes byed dang bcas pa 'og tu 'chad do/ /

If this were the case, they must assert, and do assert, that a mental placement determined by the position of the eyes and body is sufficient to bring the winds into the central channel. If so, then it must be accepted that when an ārya traveling the path by the Perfection Vehicle is in the sevenfold position of Vairocana[47] in meditative equipoise and focused single-pointedly upon emptiness, he has necessarily halted the flow of winds in the left and right channels. Alternatively, if that is not accepted, then you would have to differentiate between this situation, where the winds have not entered the central channel, and the situation where the winds have entered the central channel through placing the mind one-pointedly on a point in space in a darkened room. However it is difficult to make a distinction between these two situations. Our position is that it is the mental placement itself that brings the winds into the central channel. This and the sources will be explained below.

d.div: [47] This refers to the seven main features of the standard meditation posture, cross-legged, hands cupped at navel, and so forth. The consequence hinges on the fact that the Perfection or Sutra Vehicle is a nontantric path and therefore does not involve manipulation of the winds.

f.d: gnyis pa sor sdud la gnyis su phye ba rgyu mtshan dang bcas pa

d.i: Division of withdrawal into two parts, plus reasons for the division

f.d: ['di ]la gnyis/ sor sdud la mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor dang nyin mo'i rnal 'byor gnyis su dbye ba dang / de ltar 'byed pa'i rgyu mtshan bshad pa'o/ /
This is under two headings: 1. Dividing withdrawal into night yoga and day yoga 2. Reasons for this division
dang po [sor sdud la mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor dang nyin mo'i rnal 'byor gnyis su dbye ba ]ni

d.i: Dividing withdrawal into night yoga and day yoga

f.d:
ye le'i brgya bco lnga pa'i 'grel chen las/
'dir sngags kyi theg pa dang pha rol tu phyin pa'i theg pa la rnal 'byor goms pa rnam pa gnyis te nam mkha' dang bla gab med pa la rnal 'byor goms pa'o/[33] / zhes nam mkha' la rnal 'byor goms pa mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor dang bla gab med pa la rnal 'byor goms pa nyin mo'i rnal 'byor gnyis su 'byed par gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

The Great Commentary, on verse 115 of the Gnosis chapter, says: /345/
Yoga meditations of the Perfection Vehicle and the Mantra Vehicle are of two kinds, namely those in space and those without cover.[48] Yoga meditations are of two kinds: those “in space” are night yogas, and those “without cover” are day yogas.

d.div: [33] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 388_ba1
[48] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 388b1.

f.d:
pha rol tu phyin pa'i theg pa las rnal 'byor goms pa rnam pa gnyis gsungs tshul ni bde mchog stod 'grel las/
de'i phyir so sor sdud pa'i sgom pa la rnam par rtog pa'i sgom pa dmigs par mi 'gyur ro zhes bcom ldan 'das kyis gsungs so/ / sgom pa 'di ni bcom ldan 'das kyis shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin par yang gsungs pa 'di lta ste/ de nas lha rnams kyi dbang po brgya byin gyis tshe dang ldan pa rab 'byor la 'di skad ces smras so/ / 'phags pa rab 'byor 'dir shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa la rnal 'byor du byed pa des ji ltar bslab par bya/ rab 'byor gyis smras pa/ kau shi ka gang nam mkha' la rnal 'byor du byed pa de shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa la rnal 'byor du byed pa'o/ / ko shi ka gang bla gab med pa la rnal 'byor du byed pa de shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa la rnal 'byor du byed pa'o zhes phyag rgya chen po sgom pa pra phab pa dang sgyu ma dang mtshungs pa sprin med pa'i nam mkha' la snang ba bcom ldan 'das kyis gsungs so/[34] / zhes gsungs pa'i de nas zhes pa nas/ rnal 'byor du byed do zhes pa yan gyis sher phyin gyi mdo las nam mkha' dang bla gab med pa la rnal 'byor du byed par bstan pa rnams drangs nas de dag dang cha 'dra bar bla med kyi rgyud rnams las mtshan mo dang nyin mo'i rnal 'byor gyis pra phab pa dang / sgyu ma dang mtshungs pa'i stong gzugs sna tshogs mthong ba'i sor sdud bcom ldan 'das kyis gsungs so zhes ston pa la/ phyag rgya chen po zhes pa nas/ gsungs so zhes pa'i bar gsungs pa yin gyi/ 'grel pa 'di dag gi don nyin mo dang mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor gyi sor sdud sher phyin gyi mdos bstan par ni gzung bar mi bya ste/ gal te de ltar yin na sher phyin gyi mdo nyan pa'i snod rung du dbang bzhi rdzogs par thob dgos pa la sogs par 'gyur ro/ /

The way yoga meditations of the Perfection Vehicle are divided in two is found in the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary:
Therefore, in the meditations of withdrawal, the Buddha has said that conceptual meditation is not seen. This meditation the Buddha has taught in the perfection of wisdom scriptures:
“Then Indra, Lord of the gods, said to Subhūti, ‘Noble Subhūti, how does one practice yoga in the perfection of wisdom?’ Subhūti replied, ‘Kauśika, one who practices yoga in space practices yoga in the perfection of wisdom. Kauśika, one who practices yoga without cover practices yoga in the perfection of wisdom.’”
Therefore the Buddha taught the mahāmudrā meditation by which the prognostic imagelike and the illusionlike appear in the cloudless sky.[49] The passage quoted from a perfection of wisdom sutra teaching the yoga practices “in space” and “without cover” shows similarities with the Buddha’s teachings from the highest yoga tantras that explain the night yogas and day yogas of the withdrawal practice, wherein various illusionlike and prognostic imagelike empty forms are seen. This is indicated by the sentence of the commentary beginning, “Therefore the Buddha.” However do not take this commentary to mean that the day and night yogas of withdrawal are taught in the perfection of wisdom sutras. If that were the case, it would mean that becoming a suitable vessel for receiving the perfection of wisdom sutras would entail receiving all four initiations.

d.div: [34] sde dge_1402_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ba_bde mchog stod 'grel/ 132_ba5_tshig sna cung mi mthun/
[49] Toh 1402 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 132b5.

f.d: gnyis pa de ltar 'byed pa'i rgyu mtshan bshad pa ni/

bla ma snga ma rnams lo la lho bgrod byang bgrod/ zla ba la yar ngo mar ngo / zhag la nyin mtshan gnyis rnams yod pas mtshan mo dang nyin mo'i rnal 'byor gnyis su 'byed pa yin zhes gsung / rang lugs ni snang ba dang mun pa gang la bsgoms kyang rtags rnams 'dod dgur 'char thub pa'i phyir du mtshan mo dang nyin mo'i rnal 'byor gnyis ka sgom dgos pa yin la/ de yang mun pa la sgom pa snang ba la sgom pa bas stong gzugs rnams 'char ba dang nges sla bas go rim yang mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor dang por bsgom zhing nyin mo'i rnal 'byor phyis bsgom par gsungs pa yin no/ / rtags 'char ba la dka' sla 'ong ba'i rgyu mtshan ni lta stangs byas te dmigs pa bzung dus su mig gi rlung ma rengs par la skya bo sogs snang ba log mi nus pas stong gzugs 'char dka'/ mun pa la skya bo sogs mi 'char pas stong gzugs 'char sla ba yin zhes gsung ba ltar ro/ /

Previous lamas have said that a year consists of the sun’s northward and southward passages, /346/ a month consists of two periods of waxing and waning, and a day consists of daytime and nighttime, and that those are reasons for the division into day and night yogas. Our own position is that both day and night yogas are necessary to ensure that whenever the meditation is performed, in daytime or in darkness, all desired signs are made manifest. In nighttime meditation the empty-form signs are easier to manifest and to ascertain than in daytime meditation. Therefore it is taught that the night yoga is performed first and followed by the day yoga. The reason for the difference in the degree of difficulty in manifesting the signs is explained as follows. When the eyes are positioned and the meditation object is held during the day, the winds of the eyes are not rigid, and it is not possible to banish an everpresent grayish appearance. This makes it difficult for empty forms to arise. In darkness this grayish appearance is not there, and this makes it easier for empty forms to appear.
mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor sgom tshul bshad pa/
27. Withdrawal: Night Yoga
gsum pa phye ba so so'i sgom tshul bshad pa
The meditations of the two sections
['di ]la gnyis/ mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor sgom tshul bshad pa dang / nyin mo'i rnal 'byor sgom tshul bshad pa'o/ /
This has two outlines: 1. Nighttime yoga meditations 2. Daytime yoga meditations
dang po mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor sgom tshul bshad pa

['di ]la lnga/ gang du bsgom pa gnas kyi nges pa dang / lus kyi 'dug stangs byed bcings kyi nges pa dang / lta stangs kyi nges pa dang / sems kyi 'jog tshul gyi nges pa dang / de ltar bsgoms pas nyams rtags 'char tshul gyi nges pa'o/ /
This is under five headings: 1. The place of meditation 2. Posture and binding 3. Positioning the eyes 4. Mental placement 5. The signs of meditative accomplishment and their appearance
dang po [gang du bsgom pa gnas kyi nges pa ]ni

ye le'i brgya bco lnga pa'i 'grel chen las/
gang zhig nam mkha' la rnal 'byor goms par byed pa des mtshan mo bug pa med pa'i khyim du mun pa la/[35] zhes gsungs pa dang / 'jam dpal gyi sprul pa 'jam dbyangs grags pas rnal 'byor gsum gyi snying po las/
mtshan mo gseng med khyim du ni/[36] / zhes dang / tsi lu pa'i sbyor drug las/
dang po so sor sdud pa ni/ / mtshan mo sngon la nyin mo phyis/ / bu ga med la thog mtho'i nang /[37] / zhes sogs kyis mun khang bstan pa ltar mun khang mtshan nyid dang ldan par sgom dgos so/ /

The Great Commentary, on verse 115 of the Gnosis chapter, says:
Those who practice the yoga in space are in the night, in the darkness of a room with no holes.[50] /347/ Mañjuśrīkīrti, a manifestation of Mañjuśrī, states in the Essence of the Three Yogas:
In a house with no break in the darkness.[51] In Cilupa’s Six Yogas Also:
First is withdrawal; begin at night then in the day in a tall house with no holes.[52] The meditations should be performed in the kind of darkened room that matches the description taught in these and other quotes.

f.d: de la mun khang ji ltar bya ba ni/ 'byor pa dang ldan pas ni khang pa thog sum rim pa'i bar khang du bya ste de'i dgos pa ni 'og nas sa rlangs dang steng nas thigs pa sogs kyis gnod pa mi 'byung ba'o/ / de tsam mi 'byor ba yin na skam sar brtsigs te 'og nas sa rlan mi 'byung ba dang thog mtho ba/ dkar khung phyi rub la nang yangs pa/ 'bol tho lta bus dgag sla ba/ de las gzhan pa'i bu ga skra rtse shong ba tsam yang med pa/ phyogs thams cad zhal bas bstar ba/ sgo 'khyo gsum rim pa mun pa shin tu nag pa bya'o/ / de lta bu yang ma 'byor na/ sgogs pa sogs med pa bcad pa'i steng du yol ba sogs btang ste mun pa shin tu nag pa bya dgos te/ de'i rgyu mtshan snang ba cung zad shor na'ang mig la gnod/ rnam rtog 'phro/ mthong snang phyin ci log 'char ba sogs kyi skyon 'ong ba yin no/ /

What should that room be like? Those who have the means should meditate in the middle story of a three-story house. The reason is that such a room avoids the harms of vapors from the earth below and the dripping of water from above. If that is not possible, the room should be built on dry ground, not damp underfoot, with a high ceiling. The windows should be narrow on the outside and wide on the inside and be easy to cover, with a blanket, for example. Apart from those openings, there should not even be a hole the size of a hair tip in the room. Everywhere should be smoothly plastered, and the entrance should have three turns in it to cut out all light. If that is not possible, hang a curtain over any cracks or openings in the door, and make the room very dark. The reason for this is that if any light enters the room, it will damage the eyes, thoughts will appear, and deluding appearances will be seen.
gnyis pa lus kyi 'dug stangs byed pa cings kyi nges pa ni

rnal 'byor gsum gyi snying po las/
mtshan mo gseng med khyim du ni/ / shin tu mnyam bzhag sgrub pa pos/ / byed pa lnga la bcing ba gnyis/ / bla ma'i zhal las shes par bya/[38] / zhes gsungs pa'i byed pa lnga ni lus gnad kyi byed pa lnga dang / bcing ba gnyis ni rlung sems gnyis dbu mar bcing ba yin zhing / de bla ma'i zhal las shes tshul ni bla mas lus gnad 'cha' tshul dag gis brda sprad nas shes dgos pa yin te/

Essence of the Three Yogas says:
In a house with no break in the darkness, the practitioner in deep equipoise performs the five actions and the two bindings, which can be known from the guru.[53] The five actions are the actions of parts of the body. The two bindings refer to the holding of mind and winds within the central channel. The way these can be known is by the guru’s demonstration.

f.d:
'di dag gi don 'grel ba'i dus zhabs snyan brgyud las/
'bol pa'i stan la [39] byed pa ni/ / lus bsrang rdo rje skyil krung bca'/ / lce bzlog gsus sbyar mig gyen bzlog / gtsug tor sgyur ba'i lta stangs so/ / lag gnyis rdo rje bsdam par bya/ / des ni rlung rnams 'ching byed pa'o/[40] / zhes dang /

They are described in the Kālacakrapāda Transmission:
On a comfortable seat, the body straight, in vajra position, tongue turned back, clasped to stomach, eyes turned upward, in the manner of Uṣṇīṣacakrī, hands vajra-bound. This will bind the winds.[54]

f.d:
tsi lu bas/
ri rab bsrang la gling bzhi bsdu/ / gyen la nyi zla dar lce bskyod/ / rdo rje bsdams pas rgya mtsho gzhom/ / snying gi rlung chen thur la brdig / lus kyi byed pa zhes bya ste/ / des ni rlung rnams nang du 'ching / / gtsug tor chen po'i lta stangs bya/[41] / zhes gsungs pa rnams kyis lus kyi 'dug stangs lnga byed par bshad cing / des rlung sems gnyis 'ching ba'i rkyen byed par bstan to/ / don ni/

Cilupa says:
Mount Meru is straight, four continents gathered in, sun and moon spread above, the tongue is moved, vajra binding subdues the oceans, the great winds of the heart flow: these are the actions of the body; they will hold the winds inside. /348/ Look with the look of great Uṣṇīṣa.[55] The two passages teach five postures as the actions and also that these actions are instrumental in binding the winds and mind. The explanation of these two passages is as follows.

d.div: [41] sde dge_1374_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ payan lag drug gi sbyor ba'i man ngag250_ba2
[55] Toh 1374 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 250b2.

f.d: lus bsrang zhes pa dang ri rab bsrang la zhes pa gnyis kyis lus sgal tshigs pa drang por bsrang ba bstan/ rdo rje skyil krung bcas zhes pa dang gling bzhi bsdu zhes pa gnyis kyi snga mas rdo rje skyil krung nyid bca' zhing / phyi mas yan lag bzhi bsdu ba bstan pas rdo rje skyil krung dang / rdo rje bsdams pas rgya mtsho gzhom/[42] /zhes pa dang sbyar bas lag pa gnyis rdo rje khu tshur bsdams pa phan tshun bsnol nas brang la sbyar ba bstan cing / gzhung snga ma'i gsus sbyar zhes pa dang / lag gnyis rdo rje bsdam par bya/ /zhes pa sbyar bas kyang de nyid bstan to/ /

“The body straight” and “Mount Meru is straight” mean that the spine is straight and erect. Of the two phrases “in vajra position” and “four continents gathered in,” the former teaches the vajra position itself[56] and the latter that the four limbs are gathered in. Therefore the feet are in the vajra position. The line “vajra binding subdues the oceans” teaches that the two hands are bound as overlapping vajra fists and clasped to the abdomen. The phrases “clasped to stomach” and “hands vajra-bound” from the first passage teach the same.

d.div: [42] sde dge_1371_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ parnal 'byor gsum gyi snying po gsal ba/ 250_ba2
[56] The cross-legged full-lotus position.

f.d: lce bzlog ces pa dang / mig gyen bzlog ces pa sbyar ba dang / gyen la nyi zla dar lce bskyod/ /ces pa gnyis kyis lce rkan la sbyar ba dang / mig gnyis gyen la blta ba gnyis bstan cing / gyen la lta tshul gsal bar ston pa lta stangs ni/ gtsug tor sgyur ba'i lta stangs so/ /zhes pa dang / gtsug tor chen po'i lta stangs bya/ /zhes pa gnyis kyis bstan to/ /

The phrases “tongue turned back” and “eyes turned upward” from the first passage and “the sun and moon spread above, the tongue is moved” from the second teach that the tongue is touching the palette and that both eyes look upward. How they gaze upward is also clearly taught by the lines “in the manner of Uṣṇīṣacakrī” and “Look with the look of great Uṣṇīṣa.”

mdor bsdu na sgal tshigs drang por bsrang ba dang / rkang pa rdo rje skyil krung dang / lag pa gnyis rdo rje khu tshur bsdams te phan tshun bsnol ba gsus pa la sbyar ba'am yang na lag pa g.yon pa gan rkyal du byas pa'i steng du g.yas pa bzhag nas mthe bong lto sprad pa mnyam gzhag gi phyag rgya 'am/ yang na rdo rje khu tshur bsdams pa brla'i steng du bzhag pa rdo rje sems dpa'i phyag rgya rnams gang rung bya ste/ 'grel chen las/
'dir lag pa gnyi gas rdo rje khu tshur bcings nas khu tshur gyis mthe bong bsdams pa dag brla g.yas dang g.yon pa'i steng du rdo rje'i gdan la gnas pa ni rdo rje'i phyag rgyar 'gyur ro/[43] / zhes sogs gsungs so/ /

To summarize, the spine is straight and erect, the feet are in the vajra position, and the hands are bound as vajra fists crossed over the abdomen. Alternatively the right hand is placed upon the upturned left with the thumbs touching in the equipoise mudrā, or both hands bound as vajra fists are placed upon the thighs in the Vajrasattva mudrā.[57] Any of these positions is acceptable. The Great Commentary states:
Hands are bound as vajra fists, thumbs held by fists, on the right and left thighs, resting on the vajra seat to become the vajra mudrā.[58]

d.div: [43] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 344_ba3
[57] Here mudrā refers to a symbolic positioning of the hands, in this case clenched fists on the sides of the thighs. Elsewhere in the book it is predominantly used to mean consort.
[58] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 344b3.

f.d: lce rkan la sbyar ba dang / mig gnyis gyen la bzlog pa'i lus kyi 'dug stangs lnga ni byed pa lnga yin la/ des rlung sems gnyis dbu mar bcing ba ni bcing ba gnyis yin pa ni/ byed pa lnga la bcing ba gnyis/[44] /zhes gsungs pa'i don yin no/ /

Together with the tongue against the palette and the eyes looking upward, this five-part posture constitutes the five actions. The winds and the mind held in the central channel by these five constitute the two bindings. This is the explanation of the line “performs the five actions and the two bindings.”

d.div: [44] sde dge_1371_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ parnal 'byor gsum gyi snying po gsal ba/ 223_na6

f.d: gal te lus kyi 'dug stangs dang mig gi lta stangs kyi byed pa 'di nyid kyis rlung dbu mar 'ching bar 'dod pa bkag pa ma yin nam zhe na/ de ltar bkag pa ni de kho nas rlung dbu mar 'ching nus pa bkag pa yin zhing / 'dir bshad pa'i rgya gzhung de dag gi don ni gtso bor dmigs pa yid la byed tshul gyis rlung dbu mar 'dzud pa yin la/ de'i mthun rkyen nam cha rkyen byas pa'i sgo nas lus gnad dang lta stangs kyang rlung dbu mar 'ching byed du bshad pas skyon med do/ /

But wasn’t the assertion that the winds could be bound into the central channel by positioning the body and the eyes refuted? /349/ That was a refutation of the assertion that positioning alone could bring the winds into the central channel. The intention of the passages quoted from these Indian texts is that it is primarily the placement of the mind that brings the winds into the central channel. However here they are describing the positioning of the body and the eyes as conducive conditions for the binding of the winds into the central channel. Therefore there is no contradiction.
gsum pa lta stangs kyi nges pa ni/

sgrub le'i brgya nyi shu pa'i 'grel chen las/
gtsug tor gyi khro bo'i lta bas zhes pa mig mi 'dzums par steng du lta bas mtshan mar 'gyur te mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor gyis rnam pa bzhi dang /[45] zhes mig mi 'dzums par gtsug tor gyi khro bo'i lta stangs byed par gsungs pa ni steng du lta bas zhes gyen la lta ba dang / de yang mig mi 'dzums par zhes 'byed 'dzums dang sgul skyod med pa dang / mig gi 'jog tshul yang ri gi a ra li'i rgyud las/ phyed mig gyen du log nas ni/[46] /zhes pa ltar mas lcibs kyis mig gi phyed tsam bkab nas sems kyis gang la dmigs pa'i gzhi de nyid la lta ba'i tshul du 'jog pa'o/ /

The Great Commentary, on verse 120 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter, states:
“With the wrathful look of Uṣṇīṣa,” with eyes not closed and looking above, the signs will appear.[59] This quote speaks of the eyes not being closed and looking with the wrathful look of Uṣṇīṣa. “Looking above” means looking upward. “Eyes not closed” means half shut and not moving. The position of the eyes is also taught in the Rigi Ārāli Tantra when it states, “Half eyes turned upward.”[60] Therefore the eyes are half covered by the eyelids and look toward the object of the mind’s focus.

f.d: de yang ye le'i brgya bco lnga pa'i 'grel chen las/ nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig ni mi 'dzums/[47] zhes sems kyis gang du zhen sa der mig gis kyang lta ba'i tshul du byed pa dang / mig cung zad kyang mi 'dzums shing sgul skyod mi byed par gsungs so/ / de ltar bshad pa rnams ni dus zhabs snyan brgyud las/ mig gyen bzlog/ gtsug tor chen po'i lta stangs so/[48] /zhes dang / tsi lu pas/ gtsug tor chen po'i lta stangs bya/[49] /zhes gsungs pa rnams kyi yang don yin no/ /

The Great Commentary, on verse 115 of the Gnosis chapter, says, “With the mind fixed into space, the eyes unclosed,”[61] which teaches that wherever the mind is fixed, there the eyes are positioned also, and that the eyes are slightly open and unmoving. These explanations are mirrored by the Kālacakrapāda Transmission, when it says “eyes turned upward, in the manner of Uṣṇīṣacakrī”[62] and by Cilupa, “Look with the look of great Uṣṇīṣa.”[63]

f.d: 'o na lta stangs kyang sems kyis gang la dmigs pa de nyid la lta ba'i tshul du byed na sems kyi dmigs pa ji ltar bya snyam na/
If the eyes are positioned wherever the mind is placed, then what is the placement of the mind?
bzhi pa sems kyi 'jog tshul gyi nges pa
['di ]la gnyis/ ci yang mi bsam pa sems kyi 'jog tshul yin pa dgag pa dang / dmigs pa yid la byed pa'i sgo nas sems kyi 'jog tshul 'thad par bstan pa'o/ /
This topic is under two headings: 1. Refuting that mental placement is a state of no thought 2. The validity of mental placement by mental application to an object
dang po [ci yang mi bsam pa sems kyi 'jog tshul yin pa dgag pa ]ni/

d.i: Refuting that mental placement is a state of no thought

f.d:
kha cig/
bsam pa thams cad yongs spangs te/ / nyi ma gcig ni yongs su brtag[50] / ces sogs dang / sgrub le'i brgya bcu bzhi pa'i 'grel chen las/
'dir dang po stong nyid byang chub ces pa ni mun pa la cung zad kyang bsam par mi bya ba'o/[51] / zhes sogs gsungs pa rnams kyi don du bsams te/ dmigs pa yid la byed pa'i bsam pa thams cad bkag nas ci la yang mi sems par sems 'jog pa nyid sor sdud kyi skabs kyi sems kyi 'jog tshul du 'dod pa ni mchog mi 'gyur gyi mdor bsdus las gsal bar bkag ste/ mdor bsdus de nyid las/
de ltar shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa las de bzhin gshegs pa'i ye shes rnam par bsam pa med pa ni yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas nyid thob pa'i slad du bcom ldan 'das kyis gsungs so/ /bsam pa ni ma yin te/ zhes pa nas/
bsam pa med pa ni de bzhin gshegs pa'i ye shes yin gyi gzhan rnam par rtog pa'i ting nge 'dzin ni ma yin no/[52] / zhes pa'i bar gyis phyogs snga smra ba bo'i 'dod pa bkod nas/

The Hevajra Tantra says:
Abandon all thoughts, meditate thoroughly for a day.[64] Also the Great Commentary begins, on verse 114 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter:
“First the emptiness enlightenment” means that in the darkness, do not think at all.[65] /350/ Some think that the meaning of these and other quotes is that the mental placement for the yoga of withdrawal is to halt all mental activity and to place the mind in a state of no thought. This is clearly refuted by the Great Commentary in the Supreme and Unchanging Gnosis summary. It begins with a presentation of the above assertion:
In the perfection of wisdom sutras, the Buddha has taught the no-thought gnosis of the tathāgatas to be the way to the attainment of the perfect and complete enlightenment of a buddha. The passage continues up to:
The accomplishment of enlightenment is by the no-thought gnosis of the tathāgatas and not by conceptual meditative concentration.[66] This is the assertion.

[51] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 236_ba3
[52] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 411_na6

[65] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 236b3.

f.d:
de 'gog pa ni de'i 'phro nyid las/
de ltar rab tu mi mkhas pa bsam pa med pa ye shes su 'dod pa chad pa chen por lhung ba 'ga' zhig smra bar 'gyur te/ de'i phyir brjod par bya'o/[53] / zhes pa nas/
'dir gal te rin chen sgron ma bsam pa'am rab tu snang ba med pa yin na de'i tshe rin chen sgron ma zhes bya ba'i ting nge 'dzin du ji ltar 'gyur/ de bzhin du ting nge 'dzin gzhan rnams kyang bsam pa med par mi 'gyur te rang rig pa'i mtshan nyid kyi phyir dang bems po'i stong pa nyid ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ / zhes pa'i bar gyis gnyid mthug po log pa'i gnas skabs na yang ci yang mi sems ci yang yid la mi byed pa rang gi ngang gis 'jug pas sems can thams cad sangs rgyas par 'gyur zhes ha cang thal bas bkag pa rnams las shes par bya'o/ /

The text continues with the refutation:
In this way the ignorant assert no thought to be gnosis. They are falling to a great extreme. Some assert this, and therefore it is discussed.[67] This passage continues up to:
If at such a time there was no thought or appearance of a precious lamp, how could it come to be known as the meditative concentration of the precious lamp?[68] It is the same with other meditative concentrations: they are not without thought because they possess the characteristics of self-perception and are not examples of inanimate emptiness.[69] This passage also includes a refutation by logical consequence, which states that in a deep sleep, a state of no thought and no mental activity naturally occurs, and therefore all living beings must be buddhas.

d.div: [53] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 411_ba2
[67] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 411b2.
[68] In Great Exposition of Secret Mantra, p. 564, Tsongkhapa suggests that this refers to a sutra of the same name, possibly Ratnapradīpa, (Rin po che’i sgron ma), Toh 2318.

[69] bems po’i stong pa nyid. This phrase occurs a few times in Kālacakra literature. It is often used as a description of Rangtong phenomena in the sense of their being nihilistic and without essence. See Rendawa in Stearns, p. 59. This passage as it appears in the Great Exposition of Secret Mantra, p. 564, and in the translator’s copy of the Vimalaprabhā, has “inanimate and empty” (bems po dang stong pa nyid). Bem(s) po can also mean “composed of atoms.”

f.d: 'o na 'grel tshig 'di dag gis phyogs 'di na yang bla ma'i man ngag las 'byung ba phyag rgya chen po zhes grags pa'i sgom tshul bkag par 'gyur ba ma yin nam zhe na/ sgom tshul 'di yang ci yang yid la mi byed pa ha shang lta bu'i sgom tshul du song na bkag go zhes brjod par bya zhing / kho bo ni phyag rgya chen po'i sgom tshul mkhas pa chen po dag gi gsung las/ phyag rgya chen po'i rnal 'byor gyi tshul ni sems nyid la lta bar byed do zhes grags la/ sems de yang glo bur ba'i sems sna tshogs pa la mi rjod kyi gnyug ma 'od gsal ba'i sems te zhes 'byung ba ltar 'dod do/ /

Wouldn’t the above passage also refute the meditation tradition of mahāmudrā handed down through the oral transmission? If this system of meditation has become a tradition not unlike that of Hoshang[70] in which nothing is brought to mind, then we must say that it does. I concur with the words of the great masters who say that the yoga of the mahāmudrā is well known to involve looking at the mind, but that ”mind” refers not to the various transient states of mind but to the primordial mind of clear light.

d.div: [70] Hoshang, or Hvashang, Mahāyāna: Chinese abbot defeated in debate on Tibetan soil by the Indian pandit Kamalaśīla during the reign of the Tibetan king Trisong Detsen in the ninth century. See Great Lexicon, p. 3,074, and Hopkins, p. 533.

f.d:
'o na/ bsam pa thams cad yongs spangs te/ zhes pa dang / mun pa la cung zad kyang bsam par mi bya'o/[54] /zhes sogs kyi don ji ltar yin snyam na/ de dag gi don ni sor sdud kyi skabs kyi dmigs pa yid la byed pa las gzhan pa'i bsam pa thams cad spang / zhes pa dang / sor sdud kyi dmigs pa las gzhan cung zad kyang mi bsam zhes pa yin te/ brtag gnyis kyi brtag pa phyi ma'i le'u gnyis pa'i/ bsam gtan nyon mongs 'jig byed pa/[55] /zhes sogs kyi snga 'grel du rdo rje snying pos/
yan lag drug gi dang po so sor sdud pas bsdus te goms par byed pa na mtshan ma 'di dag 'byung bar 'gyur la/ gal te yang dag pa'i lam mi 'dod de 'on kyang ltad mo'i phyir yang na zla ba phyed dam yang na nyin mtshan gcig tu dmigs pa rtse gcig tu zhog la ltos/[56] zhes yang dag pa'i lam mi 'dod pa ste don gnyer med pa 'on kyang du sogs kyi stong gzugs la ltad mo blta ba'i phyir du yang na zla ba phyed dam/ de yang mi nus na yang na nyin mtshan gcig tu zhog la ltos/ zhes gsungs te sor sdud skabs kyi dmigs pa rtse gcig tu bsam par gsungs pa dang /

So what are the meanings of lines such as “abandon all thoughts” and /351/ “in the darkness do not think at all?”[71] They mean that during withdrawal, “abandon all thoughts” apart from mental application to the objects of meditation, and “do not think at all.” In his commentary on the lines beginning “meditative absorption destroys the afflictions”[72] from the second chapter of the second part of the Hevajra Tantra, Vajragarbha says:
The first of the six yogas is withdrawal, and by withdrawing and meditating, these signs will appear. Even if there is no wish to enter the perfect path, simply for the sake of a spectacle, focus your mind one-pointedly on the objects for half a month or even for a day and a night.[73] Even those who have no wish to enter the perfect path, meaning those who do not strive for such a path, should apply their minds to the objects of meditation for half a month or, if that is not possible, for a day and a night, in order to see the spectacles of empty forms, such as smoke and so forth. This passage talks of a single-pointed mental application to objects during the withdrawal yoga.

f.d:
yang tshigs su bcad pa snga ma'i 'phro nyid las/
bsam pa thams cad yongs spangs nas/ / lha yi gzugs su sems pa yis/ / nyi ma gcig tu ma chad par/ / sgom pas yongs su brtag par bgyi/[57] / zhes gsungs pa'i rdo rje snying 'grel las/
bdag med pa'i rnal 'byor 'di zla ba phyed du 'bad pa'i skal ba med pa rnams kyis nyin mtshan gcig tsam du yang dmigs pa gzhan la rtsol ba yongs su btang ste stong pa nyid gang la sems rtse gcig par bzhag na yid ches pa'i lam gyi rtags 'byung bar 'gyur te so sor sdud pas sdud pa rnams la yin gyi gzhan du na de bzhin gshegs pa'i bka' la byis pa shes rab 'chal ba dag brnyas par 'gyur ro/[58] / zhes sor sdud kyi dmigs pa sems rtse gcig tu bsams nas bzhag na yid ches pa'i lam gyi rtags du sogs kyi stong gzugs 'byung bar 'gyur bar gsungs pa dang / bsam pa thams cad yongs spangs te/ /zhes pa'i don 'chad byed ni/ dmigs pa gzhan la rtsol ba yongs su btang ste zhes gsungs pa 'di yin la|_'dis kyang sor sdud kyi dmigs pa las gzhan pa la dmigs pa'i bsam pa spang zhing rtsol ba gtang ngo / /zhes bstan pa dang gzhan yang rdo rje snying 'grel gyi de'i 'phro nyid las/
de bas na so sor sdud pa'i ting nge 'dzin las gzhan pas bsam pa thams cad spangs pas nyin mtshan gcig bsgoms pas yid ches pa 'byung ba med do/[59] / zhes bsam pa gzhan thams cad spangs nas sor sdud kyi ting nge 'dzin nyid nyin mtshan gcig bsgoms pas yid ches pa'i rtags 'byung gi/ de las gzhan pa las ma yin par gsal bar gsungs pas so/ /

The next verse of the Hevajra Tantra says:
Having abandoned all thoughts, the mind in deity form unceasingly for a day, complete the meditation.[74] On this verse Vajragarbha says:
If those who lack the fortune to be able to strive in this yoga of no-self for half a month can place their minds one-pointedly on emptiness for even a day, abandoning all other objects of mind, trustworthy signs of the path will appear. These are signs of the withdrawal achieved by withdrawal yoga. Anything other than that is the foolish, in their deluded wisdom, slandering the teaching of the Tathāgata.[75] Therefore this passage states that if the mind is placed one-pointedly on the meditation objects of withdrawal, trustworthy signs of the path, such as the empty forms of smoke and so forth, will arise. “Abandon all thoughts” is explained by the line “abandoning all other objects of mind,” which means to abandon meditation objects other than those of withdrawal yoga. The Vajragarbha Commentary continues: /352/
Therefore abandoning all thoughts by using meditative concentrations other than those of the concentrations of withdrawal yoga and meditating for a day and night will not produce the trustworthy signs.[76] This clearly teaches that abandoning all other thoughts and meditating on the concentrations of withdrawal yoga for a day and a night will produce trustworthy signs. Other meditations will not.

f.d: gnyis pa dmigs pa yid la byed pa'i sgo nas sems kyi 'jog tshul 'thad par bstan pa

d.i: The validity of mental placement by mental application to an object

f.d: ['di ]la gnyis/ de ltar 'thad pa'i shes byed dgod pa dang / sems kyi 'jog tshul dngos bshad pa'o/ /
This has two outlines: 1. Presenting sources to show its validity 2. The actual placement of mind
dang po [de ltar 'thad pa'i shes byed dgod pa ]ni/

d.i: Presenting sources to show its validity

f.d:
ye le'i brgya bco lnga pa rtsa 'grel las gsungs pa ni/
nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig ni mi 'dzums rdo rje'i lam du rab tu zhugs pa yis/ / stong pa las ni du ba smig rgyu rab gsal dri ma med pa'i mkha' snang nyid dang mar me dang /[60] / zhes pa'i 'grel chen las/
gang zhig nam mkha' la rnal 'byor goms par byed pa des mtshan mo bug pa med pa'i khyim du mun pa la nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig mi 'dzums shing rdo rje'i lam du rab tu zhugs pa [61] zhes pa 'dir dbu mar srog rab tu zhugs pas stong pa kho na las du ba la sogs pa'i mtshan ma mthong ste nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig ni mi 'dzums rdo rje'i lam du rab tu zhugs pas stong pa las ni du ba smig rgyu rab gsal dri ma med pa'i mkha' snang nyid dang mar me dang zhes pa ni mtshan mo'i rnal 'byor gyis mthong ngo / / zhes pa rnams so/ /

Verse 115 of the Gnosis chapter, quoted in the Great Commentary, says:
With mind fixed into space, eyes unclosed, the vajra path is entered. From the emptiness arises smoke, mirage, a clear, uncontaminated light in the sky, and a butter-lamp flame.[77] The commentary to this says:
Those who practice the yoga in space are in the night, in the darkness of a room with no holes. “With mind fixed into space, eyes unclosed, the vajra path is entered.” Here the winds enter the central channel, and from the total emptiness, the signs of smoke and so forth are seen. Therefore: “With mind fixed into space, eyes unclosed, the vajra path is entered. From the emptiness arises smoke, mirage, a clear, uncontaminated light in the sky, and a butter-lamp flame.” These are seen by the night yoga.[78]

d.div: [60] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ ye shes le'u/ sh+loka115_113_na2 sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ ye shes le'u/ 388_ba2
[61] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 388_ba2_dpyad dgos/
[77] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, ka, v. 115.
[78] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 388b2.

f.d: 'di dag gis ni sor sdud kyi dmigs pa dang / dmigs pa de la sems 'jog tshul mig gi lta stangs dang bcas pa dang / sems kyi 'jog tshul mig gi lta stangs de ltar byas pa las rlung dbu mar 'jug tshul dang / de ltar rlung dbu mar zhugs pa las du sogs kyi rtags rnams 'char tshul rnams nges can du bstan to/ /

This passage clearly teaches the objects of meditation during withdrawal yoga, as well as the placement of the mind on those objects in conjunction with the positioning of the eyes. It also teaches that the winds enter the central channel from that placement of mind and eye position, and that from the winds /353/ entering the central channel, the signs of smoke and so forth appear.

'o na tshul ji ltar du bstan snyam na/ de yang / rdo rje'i lam du rab tu zhugs pa yis/ /stong pa las ni du ba zhes sogs dang /[62] de'i 'grel pa/ 'dir dbu mar srog rab tu zhugs pas stong pa kho na las du ba la sogs pa'i mtshan ma mthong ste/[63] zhes pa rnams kyis rdo rje'i las rtsa dbu mar srog ste rlung zhugs pa las sor sdud kyi mtshan nyid tshang ba'i du sogs kyi mtshan ma mthong gi dbu mar rlung ma zhugs par de mi mthong bar bstan to/ /

How are these taught? The lines beginning “the vajra path is entered. From the emptiness arises smoke” and the ensuing commentary, “Here the winds enter the central channel, and from the total emptiness, the signs of smoke and so forth are seen,” teach that as a result of the vajra activity of the winds entering the central channel, the definitive signs of withdrawal yoga, smoke and so forth, will be seen. However they will not be seen without the winds entering the central channel.

d.div: [62] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 388_ba2
[63] sde dge_1351_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ na_dbang mdor bstan pa'i 'grel bshad/ 251_na1

f.d: 'o na skabs 'dir rlung dbu mar 'jug pa'i thabs ji ltar snyam na/ nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig ni mi 'dzum/ /zhes pa dang /de'i 'grel pa nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig ni mi 'dzums rdo rje'i lam du rab tu zhugs pa/ /zhes pa 'di rnams kyis nam mkha'i dmigs pa yin pa dang / dmigs pa de la zhen pa'i rnam pa'i sems rtse gcig tu 'jog pa'i 'jog tshul dang / sems gang la bzhag pa der mig kyang mi 'dzums par lta ba'i tshul dang / de ltar byas pas las rlung dbu mar 'jug par bstan pa yin no/ /

What is the method for bringing the winds into the central channel in this meditation? The lines from the Condensed Tantra and the Great Commentary, “With mind fixed into space, eyes unclosed, the vajra path is entered” teach the object of meditation to be “space” and that a single-pointed placement of the mind onto that object is the mental placement. Wherever the mind is placed, there the unclosed eyes are focused. From this the winds will enter the central channel.

gzhan yang dbang mdor bstan gyi nA ro pa'i 'grel pa las/
gang zhig nam mkha' la rnal 'byor goms par byed pa des mtshan ma bug pa med pa'i khyim du mun pa la nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems bsam pa thams cad yongs su spangs pa yis stong par rtse gcig pa'i yid du byas nas nyi ma gcig yongs su brtag par bya'o/ / mig ni mi 'dzums rdo rje'i lam du rab tu zhugs pa zhes pa 'dir dbu mar srog rab tu zhugs pa ste stong pa kho na las du ba la sogs pa'i mtshan ma mthong ngo /[64] / zhes gsungs pa dang /

Furthermore Nāropa in his Commentary to a Short Teaching on Initiations says:
Those who practice the yoga in space are in the night, in the darkness of a room with no holes, with the mind fixed into space, and all thoughts abandoned. There with the mind one-pointedly on emptiness, meditate for a day. “The eyes unclosed, the vajra path is entered. Here the winds enter the central channel, and from the total emptiness, the signs of smoke and so forth are seen.”[79]

tsi lu pas kyang /
nam mkhar zhen pas nam mkhar blta/ / du ba la sogs rtags lnga 'byung /[65] / zhes dang /

d.div: [65] sde dge_1374_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ payan lag drug gi sbyor ba'i man ngag251_ba3
[80] Toh 1374 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 251b3.

f.d:
dus zhabs snyan brgyud las kyang
mtshan mo bla gab med pa ru/ / nam mkha' la dmigs stong nyid bsgom/[66] / zhes gsungs pa ltar phyogs 'di'i rgya gzhung dang 'grel pa rnams kyis/ nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i zhes sogs kyi rgyud rtsa 'grel gyi dgongs par bsams nas nam mkha' stong pa sor sdud kyi dmigs par bshad de/ de yang stong pa bshad tshul ni khams le'i mdor bsdus gnyis pa las/ 'di nyid sgrub pa la phyag rgya chen po sgom pa du ba la sogs pa mtshan ma'i lam rab tu gsal bar mdzad de/
stong par rtse gcig [67] yid byas te/ / nyi ma gcig ni yongs su brtag[68] / ces stong pa dmigs par gsungs so/ /

The Kālacakrapāda Transmission states:
At night and without cover, focus on space, meditate on the emptiness.[81] These and other Indian texts on the same topic and their commentaries have explained the object of withdrawal meditation as taught in the phrase “the mind fixed into space” from the tantra and commentary as being an “empty space.” This emptiness is mentioned in the second summary of the Realms chapter of the Great Commentary: To accomplish this, the meditation on mahāmudrā, the path of the signs of smoke and so forth are clearly taught:
“The mind one-pointedly into emptiness, meditate thoroughly for a day.”[82] This explains that an emptiness is the object of meditation.

d.div: [66] sde dge_1372_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ pa_dus zhabs snyan rgyud/ 224_ba2
[67] ma dper stong par rtsa gcig zhes gsal yang rtse gcig ces bcos/ sde dge_418_bka'/ rgyud/
[68] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 16_ba4
[81] Toh 1372 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 224b2.
[82] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 16b4.

f.d:
de bzhin du bde mchog stod 'grel las/
de'i phyir yod pa dang med pa'i blo yongs su spangs te zhen pa med par byas nas zab mo stong pa dang dmigs pa med pa bsgom par bya ste rnal 'byor pas du ba la sogs pa'i rtags 'byung ba mthong bar 'gyur ro/[69] / zhes gsungs pa dang /

Similarly, in the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary, it says:
Therefore, abandoning thoughts of existence and nonexistence, with no grasping, meditate on the deep nonapprehended emptiness. /354/ The yogi will then see the arising of the signs of smoke and so forth.[83]

d.div: [69] sde dge_1402_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ba_bde mchog stod 'grel/ 131_na7
[83] Toh 1402 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, 131a7.

f.d:
'di dang mthun par slob dpon dpe med 'tshos kyang /
des na yod pa dang med pa'i blo yongs su spangs te rten med par byas nas zab mo stong pa dmigs pa med pa bsgom par bya ste/[70] zhes bshad cing 'di dag gi don 'og tu 'chad pa las shes par bya'o/ /

Ācārya Anupamarakṣita’s commentary is similar to this:
Therefore, abandoning thoughts of existence and nonexistence, with no support, meditate on the deep nonapprehended emptiness.[84] The meaning of these quotes on emptiness will be explained later.

d.div: [70] sde dge_1387_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ pasbyor ba yan lag drug pa/ 297_ba5
[84] Toh 1387 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 297b5.

f.d:
yang nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i zhes sogs kyi don 'chad pa'i tshe dpe med srung ba'i sbyor drug rtsa 'grel las/
mtshan mo zhes pa mun pa nye bar mtshon pa'o/ / nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems ni gang rnams kyi sems nam mkha' la chags pa ste de dang ro mnyam par gyur pa gang yin pa de rnams kyi'o/ / rdo rje'i lam du zhugs pa ni srog a wa ng+hU tIr son pa nyid kyi phyir ro/[71] / zhes nam mkha' la dmigs dgos par bshad do/ /

When explaining the meaning of the lines beginning “the mind fixed into space,” the commentary on Anupamarakṣita’s six yogas says:
“Night” means darkness. “The mind fixed into space” means that the mind draws toward space and becomes of one taste with it. Entering into the vajra path, the winds reach the avadhūtī.[85] This explains that space is the object of meditation.

d.div: [71] sde dge_1388_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ pa_yon tan gyis 'gengs pa/ 325_ba5_nas 329_na5
[85] Filled with Good Qualities, Toh 1388 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 325b5.

f.d: de ltar na sor sdud kyi skabs kyi dmigs par bshad pa'i nam mkha' dang stong pa don gcig tu byed dgos pas sgrib thogs kyi bya ba bcad tsam gyi nam mkha' rdos bcas kyi dmigs rten med pa'i stong pa 'di sor sdud kyi dmigs par bya'o/ / 'o na nam mkha' stong pa de la gnas gang du sems ji ltar du gzhag par bya snyam na/

In that case, space and emptiness, both explained as being the objects of meditation during withdrawal yoga, must be synonymous. Therefore a space that is the mere lack of any obstruction and obscuration, an emptiness with no material support, is the meditation object of withdrawal yoga. How is the mind to be placed in such a state?
gnyis pa sems kyi 'jog tshul dngos bshad pa
['di ]la/ bod kyi mkhas pa snga ma rnams kyi dgongs pa dgod pa dang / rje btsun tsong kha pa'i dgongs pa sgrub byed dang bcas pa bshad pa'o/ /
This is under two headings: 1. The assertions of previous Tibetan masters 2. The assertion of Jé Tsongkhapa and the proof of its validity
dang po [bod kyi mkhas pa snga ma rnams kyi dgongs pa dgod pa ]ni/

d.i: The assertions of previous Tibetan masters

f.d: thams cad mkhyen pa chos rje bu'i bzhed pa ni/ mig gi lta stangs smin mtshams kyi thad kyi mun khang gi nam mkha' la lta zhing lta stangs gang du gtad pa'i mun khang gi nam mkha' stong pa de nyid la sems kyang rtse gcig tu gtad nas gzhan gang la yang mi 'phro bar ci yang yid la mi byed par glod nas 'jog par bzhed do/[72] / jo nang pa rjes 'brang dang bcas pa ni mi g.yo ba gsum ldan gyis sems mi g.yo bar byed tshul mang du gsung yang / thams cad dril ba'i 'gag bsdus na lus kyi phyi mun khang gi nam mkha'i lta stangs gtad sar sems rtse gcig tu bsgrims nas yul gzhan ci yang yid la mi byed par 'dzin med du glod nas 'jog par bzhed do/ / bzhed tshul 'di gnyis kas rgyud dgongs 'grel dang bcas pa rnams kyi nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i zhes sogs kyis gsungs pa'i nam mkha' stong pa'i don lus kyi phyi'i mun khang gi nam mkha'i bar stong la bzhed par mngon no/ /

The omniscient Butön asserts that the eyes are focused into the space of a darkened room directly in front of the point midway between the eyebrows. The mind also is one-pointedly focused on the emptiness that is the space of the darkened room upon which the eyes are positioned. Without wandering to anything else, and without any other thoughts whatsoever, the mind is released into this state.[86] The Jonang and their followers mention many ways in which the mind is held still by the “three nonmovements.” However, in each method, the mind is one-pointedly focused onto the external place where the eyes have been positioned in the space of a darkened room. These two assertions seem to take the meaning of “empty space” as taught by the phrase “the mind fixed into space,” /355/ and other phrases from the tantra and its commentaries, to refer to an external emptiness within a darkened room.

d.div: [72] bu ston rin chen grub/ gsung 'bum pod/ gasrog 'dzin 'khrid yig3_ba7_sor bsam 'khrid yig_10_na5
[86] Instructions on Praṇāyāmā and Retention, 3b7; and Instructions on Withdrawal and Meditative Absorption, 10a5.

f.d: de ltar bzhed pa rnams kyis ni 'di'i skabs kyi lus gnad sems kyi 'jog tshul dang bcas pas rlung dbu mar 'jug nus pa dang / phar phyin theg pa dang rgyud sde 'og ma gsum gyi lam gyi skabs su sems kyi 'jog tshul ji ltar byas kyang rlung dbu mar 'jug mi nus pa'i khyad par 'byed dgos so zhes bya'o/ /

Those who hold these positions must differentiate between the practices here in Kālacakra, with their ability to bring the winds into the central channel by mental placement on various points of the body, and the practices in the Perfection Vehicle and three lower tantras, where no amount of mental placement will bring the winds into the central channel.
gnyis pa rje btsun tsong kha pa'i dgongs pa sgrub byed dang bcas te bshad pa ni/

d.i: The assertion of Jé Tsongkhapa and the proof of its validity

f.d: gong du bshad pa ltar sor sdud kyi skabs 'dir rlung dbu mar chud pa zhig dgos so/ / de la yang las dang po pas rlung dbu mar 'dzud pa'i thabs ni phyi'i phyag rgya srog rtsol du sad pa dang / bla med pa'i rlung gi rnal 'byor dang / lus la gnad du bsnun pa'i thabs dang gsum du nges la/ lus la gnad du bsnun pa la ni rtsa 'khor drug gi dbu ma'i lte ba dang rtsa dbu ma'i yar sna mar sna gnyis te de rnams na rlung ng+hU tIr 'jug pa'i sgo re yod pas de dag tu gnad du bsnun dgos so/ / gnad du bsnun tshul yang de dag tu sems rtse gcig tu gtad nas ma yengs par 'jog pa yin te/ sems der bzhag na rlung sems 'jug pa gcig pa'i gnad kyis rlung yang der 'du'o/ /

As explained previously, withdrawal yoga is a practice in which the winds must enter the central channel. For beginners there are three methods of bringing the winds into the central channel: using an external mudrā consort to awaken the practice of prāṇāyāma, the wind yoga practices of highest tantra, and thirdly, penetrative focusing upon the points of the vajra body. The last method involves the centers of the six cakras and the upper and lower openings of the central channel, which are entrances through which the winds enter the dhūtī and are therefore locations of penetrative focusing. This practice is accomplished by the mind being placed single-pointedly on those places and held there without distraction. With the mind placed on these points, the winds will also gather there, because mind and wind engage similarly.

'o na skabs 'dir thabs gang gis rlung dbu mar 'dzud snyam na/ rgyud dang sems 'grel skor gsum dang gong du drangs pa'i rgya gzhung 'grel pa dang bcas pa rnams kyis sems gtod sa'i dmigs par bshad pa'i nam mkha' dang stong pa ni smin mtshams kyi thad kyi nang na dbu ma'i yar sna yod pa de'i sbubs stong gi nam mkha' stong pa de la mdzad nas de nyid la sems rtse gcig tu gtad nas yul gzhan la sems pa'i bsam pa thams cad yongs su spangs te 'jog pa ni/ bsam pa thams cad yongs spangs nas/ /zhes pa dang / stong par rtse gcig yid byas te/ / nyi ma gcig ni yongs su brtag[73] / ces sogs gsungs pa rnams kyi don no/ /

Which method is used here to bring the winds into the central channel? The emptiness and space explained as being the object of mental focus by the tantra, the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries, and the above Indian texts and commentaries refers to the empty space of the cylindrical hole that is the upper opening of the central channel located internally between the eyebrows. The mind is placed one-pointedly on this space, and all other thoughts on all other objects are abandoned. This placement of mind is what the lines “Having abandoned all thoughts” and “the mind one-pointedly into emptiness, meditate totally for a day” are referring to.

d.div: [73] sde dge_1180_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ka_rdo rje snying 'grel/ dngos grub kyi le'u gnyis pa/ 80_ba6

f.d: 'o na rgyud 'grel sogs nas 'di'i skabs su bshad pa'i nam mkha' dang stong pa dbu ma'i yar sna'i sbubs stong gi nam mkha' la byed pa'i shes par byed pa ji lta bu snyam na/ de yang brjod par bya ste/

How can we know that the emptiness and space spoken of in the tantra and commentaries in this section refer to the space that is the cylindrical hole of the upper opening of the central channel? I will explain. /356/

'grel chen las/ rgyud ni rgyud gzhan dag gis rtogs par bya/[74] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ri gi a ra li las/
mig gnyis ma phye ma btsums par/ / smin ma'i bar du sems byas na/ / mun pa mi bzad pa yi tshul/ / dang por rnal 'byor pas mthong 'gyur/[75] / zhes pa'i rkang pa dang pos mig gi lta stangs bstan la/ gnyis pas sems yul la gtod tshul dang / tha ma gnyis kyis rtags 'char tshul gsungs pa'i sems yul la gtod tshul ni smin ma'i bar ram dbus na dbu ma'i yar sna yod pas der sems gzung bar bya ba'i don yin no/ /

In keeping with the Great Commentary statement “Tantras will be understood from other tantras,”[87] the Rigi Ārāli Tantra says:
The eyes are not open, not closed, mind is placed between the eyebrows; in the medium of total darkness, initially the yogi sees.[88] The first line describes the position of the eyes. The second teaches how the mind is placed upon an object, and the last two lines explain how the signs will arise. Between the eyebrows, or in the center of the eyebrows, is where the upper opening of the central channel is found, and the placement of the mind described in this verse means that the mind is held there.

d.div: [74] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 16_ba2
[75] sde dge_427_bka'/ rgyud/ nga ri gi A ra li'i rgyud kyi rgyal po/ 178_ba3
[87] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 16b2.
[88] Toh 427 Kangyur, rgyud, nga, 178b3.

f.d:
gzhan yang sgrub le'i brgya bcu pa'i 'grel chen du rtsa rgyud drangs pa las/
so sor sdud pa phyag rgya che/ / nam mkha' stong pa'i mtshan nyid do/ / sna de yi ni phyogs su yang / / gang zhig kho nar yid bkod pa/ / mtshan ma'i mthar ni re khA gang / / de la sna tshogs rgyu ma rgyu/ / ma lus bsgom par bya de la/[76] / zhes pa 'dis dbu ma'i sbubs stong gi nam mkha' la sems 'jog pa gsal por bstan te/ de yang ji ltar bstan na|

Furthermore the Root Tantra, quoted in the Great Commentary on verse 110 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter, says:
The great mudrā of withdrawal has the characteristics of empty space. At that tip the mind is solely placed. In the black line, last of the signs, meditate on inanimate and animate in all their variety.[89] This clearly teaches that the mind is to be placed in the space of the empty interior of the central channel. How?

d.div: [76] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 234_na1
[89] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 234a1.

f.d:
nam mkha' stong pa la sems rtse gcig tu 'jog pa'i mtshan nyid can gyi so sor sdud pa sgom pa'i sems ni sna de'i phyogs su yang nam mkha' stong pa gang zhig kho nar yid rtse gcig tu bkod de bsgoms pas du sogs kyi mtshan ma bcu'i mthar re khA nag po skra'i tshad tsam gang yin pa de la sna tshogs rgyu mi rgyu pra phab ba lta bu ma lus pa shin tu gsal bar bsgom par bya zhes sna'i phyogs kyi nam mkha' stong pa la sems 'jog par bshad cing / sna de yang de nyid las/
dung can ma 'di phyag rgya che/ / de ni gtum mor rab tu brjod/ / lte ba'i steng du g.yung mo gang / / a wa ng+hU tI mi yi sna/[77] / zhes a wa ng+hU tI la skabs 'di'i snar bshad pa de'o/ /

The mind meditating on withdrawal yoga, which is characterized by the mind being single-pointedly placed into empty space, is single-pointedly and exclusively placed in the empty space “at that tip.” This produces the signs of smoke and so forth, the last of which is a hair-sized black line, in which the yogi meditates vividly on all the various prognostic mirrorlike animate and inanimate phenomena. The verse says that the mind is to be placed in the empty space at a “tip.”[90] On that tip the Root Tantra says:
This śaṅkhinī is the great mudrā, spoken of as caṇḍālī. Above the navel Lakṣmī, the avadhūtī, the human tip.[91] Here the avadhūtī is referred to as a “tip.”

d.div: [77] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 233_ba6
[90] sna. Tip, end, peak, etc.
[91] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 233b6.

f.d: des na lung snga mas sor sdud kyi skabs su sems sam yid sna'i phyogs su gtod par byed par bshad cing lung phyi mas sna de ni ng+hU tI la byed par bshad pas ng+hU tI'i phyogs su sems gtod par gsal por bshad pas so/ / de yang dbu ma'i yar sna yin par ni 'chad par 'gyur ro/ /

Therefore the first quote teaches that during withdrawal yoga, the mind is to be focused upon a tip, and the second quote explains that tip to be the dhūtī. This clearly indicates that the mind is to be focused on the dhūtī. That this tip refers to the upper tip will be explained later.

gzhan yang
nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig ni mi 'dzums rdo rje'i lam du rab tu zhugs pa[78] zhes pa'i 'grel par/
'dir dbu mar srog rab tu zhugs pas stong pa kho na las du ba la sogs pa'i mtshan ma mthong ste [79] zhes pas du sogs kyi mtshan ma mthong ba'i nye rgyu dbu mar srog rlung zhugs pa dgos par bstan cing /

Furthermore the Condensed Tantra says:
With the mind fixed into space, the eyes unclosed, the vajra path is entered And the commentary on this says:
Here the winds enter the central channel, and from the total emptiness, the signs of smoke and so forth are seen. /357/ This teaches the necessity of the winds entering the central channel as the immediate cause of seeing the signs of smoke and so forth.

d.div: [78] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ ye shes le'u/ sh+loka115_233_ba6
[79] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 388_ba2

f.d:
'grel par de'i 'phro nyid las/
nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig ni mi 'dzums rdo rje'i lam du rab tu zhugs pas stong pa las ni du ba smig rgyu/[80] / zhes sogs gsungs pa 'dis/ nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i sems dang mig ma 'dzums pa gnyi gas rdo rje'i lam a wang+hU tIr rab tu zhugs pas stong pa las du sogs kyi mtshan ma mthong bar yang gsal bar bstan pas/ nam mkhar kun nas zhen pa'i nam mkha' dbu ma'i sbubs stong gi nam mkha' dang / der sems rtse gcig tu 'jog pa yang gsal bar bstan pa yin no/ /

The commentary continues:
Therefore, with the mind fixed into space, the eyes unclosed, the vajra path is entered. From the emptiness arises smoke, mirage…[92] This clearly teaches that both the mind fixed into space and the unclosed eyes bring the winds into the avadhūtī, or vajra path, through which the signs of smoke and so forth will arise from the emptiness. Therefore it also explains that “space” in the phrase “the mind fixed into space” is the space of the emptiness that is the inside of the central channel and that the mind is placed one-pointedly in it.

d.div: [80] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 388_ba2
[92] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 388b2.

f.d: 'o na sor sdud kyi skabs kyi sems 'jog pa'i nam mkha' dang stong pa zhes gsungs pa rnams dbu ma'i sbubs stong gi nam mkha' stong pa de yin du chug mod/ dbu ma'i yar sna yin pa cis grub snyam na/ gong du drangs pa'i/ mig gnyis ma phye ma btsums bar/ / smin ma'i bar du sems byas na/[81] / zhes pa 'dis smin ma gnyis kyi dbus kyi nang thad na dbu ma'i yar sna yod pa de'i sbubs stong gi nam mkha' la dgongs pa dang /

Assuming that the space and emptiness spoken of in this section on mental placement in withdrawal yoga do refer to the emptiness that is the inside of the central channel, how is it proven that this refers to the upper opening of the central channel? The verse quoted above that runs “The eyes are not open, not closed, / mind is placed between the eyebrows”[93] refers to the space that is the emptiness of the central channel’s inner hollow, whose upper opening lies directly at the point midway between the eyebrows.

d.div: [81] sde dge_427_bka'/ rgyud/ nga ri gi A ra li'i rgyud kyi rgyal po/ 178_ba3
[93] Toh 427 Kangyur, rgyud, nga, 178b3.

f.d:
gzhan yang sgrub le'i brgya nyi shu pa'i 'grel chen las/
bgegs mthar byed pa'i lta ba zhes pa la bgegs mthar byed ni bdud rtsi 'khyil ba'o/ / de'i lta ba ni bdud rtsi'i gnas su son pa ste dpral bar son pa'o/ / bgegs mthar byed pa'i lta ba bdud rtsi'i gnas su son pa de yis nye ba'i sgrub pa la yan lag drug go/ / kyang yig gis srog rtsol dang 'dzin pa bya ste srog gzugs mthong nas so zhes pa nye ba'i sgrub pa'o/[82] / zhes gsungs pa 'dis dbu ma'i yar sna la byed pa gsal por bstan to/ /

Moreover the Great Commentary says on verse 120 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter:
In the phrase “The look of Vighnantaka,”[94] Vighnantaka means amṛtavarta.[95] His look “reaches the place of nectar,” which means reaching the brow. The look of Vighnantaka reaches the place of nectar, and by this, near accomplishment of the six branches will be achieved. The word “also” refers to prāṇāyāma and retention. “Having seen the forms of the winds” refers to near accomplishment.[96] This passage clearly refers to the upper opening of the central channel.

d.div: [82] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 238_ba4
[94] bgegs mthar byed. “He who puts an end to obstruction.” Also a wrathful protector of the Kālacakra mind mandala.
[95] bdud rtsi ‘khyil ba. Coil of nectar.
[96] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 238b4.

f.d: de yang ji ltar bstan na/ rtsa bar bgegs mthar byed pa'i lta ba zhes gsungs pa'i bgegs mthar byed ni 'grel pas bdud rtsi 'khyil bar bshad la/ de yang bdud rtsi'i gnas dpral ba la bshad cing / de'i lta ba'i don ni son pa la bshad pas mdor na bgegs mthar byed pa'i lta ba ni bdud rtsi'i gnas dpral bar son pa'o/ / de yis zhes pa gong du sor bsam gnyis bsnyen pa'i yan lag tu bshad pas bdud rtsi'i gnas dpral ba'i nang gi ng+hU tI'i yar snar son pa ste sems bzhag pa'i bsnyen pa'i yan lag thob pa de yis kyang yan lag gi nye bar sgrub pa la srog rtsol dang 'dzin pa bsgom par bya ste/ srog gi gzugs brnyan mthong bar gyur pa na nye ba'i sgrub pa'o zhes pa'i don yin no/ /

How? The commentary says that the Vighnantaka of the root text quote, “The look of Vighnantaka,” refers to amṛtavarta, and that “the place of nectar” refers to the brow. “His look” means “his reach.” In other words the look of Vighnantaka reaches the brow or place of nectar. Withdrawal and meditative absorption have already been explained as being the branch of approximation, and the words “by this” mean that by the accomplishment of the branch of approximation, which involves the mind being placed at or reaching the upper opening of the dhūtī within the brow, or place of nectar, meditate “also” upon the /358/ practices of prāṇāyāma and retention in the branch of near accomplishment. Seeing the images of the winds refers to near accomplishment.

de ltar na 'grel tshig de dag gis bdud rtsi'i gnas dpral bar son pa'i sems kyi 'jog tshul zhig bshad la srog 'dzin gnyis min pas sor bsam gyi skabs las 'os med cing / bsam gtan ni sor sdud brtan byed yin pas sor sdud kyi sems 'jog tshul du grub bo/ / des na bsnyen pa la ni dang po'i rnal 'byor rnam bcu 'khor lo can gyi khro bo'i lta bas so/ /zhes pa rtsa 'grel gyis sor sdud kyi skabs kyi mig gi lta stangs bstan nas/ bgegs mthar byed pa'i lta ba bdud rtsi'i lam du son pa yis/ /zhes pa rtsa 'grel gyis sor sdud kyi skabs kyi mig gi lta stangs byas dang / sems kyi gtod sa bstan cing kyang yig gis sor bsam bsnyen pa'i yan lag thob pa de yis yan lag drug gi nang gi nye sgrub srog 'dzin kyang bya'o zhes bstan pa yin no/ /

This passage from the Great Commentary talks of a mental placement, which involves the place of nectar, or the brow. This particular mental placement is not that of prāṇāyāma and retention, which means it can be none other than that of withdrawal and absorption. The yoga of meditative absorption is a stabilizing of withdrawal, and therefore this passage is an establishment of withdrawal mental placement. Therefore the line from the root text and commentary, “Approximation is the first yoga, of ten aspects, with the look of wrathful Cakrī,” describes the positioning of the eyes during the yoga of withdrawal. The line “The look of Vighnantaka reaches the path of nectar” refers to the positioning of the eyes during withdrawal yoga as well as the focus of the mind. The word “also” indicates that with the attainment of the withdrawal and absorption branch of approximation, the near-accomplishment branch of the six yogas, prāṇāyāma and retention, is also to be practiced.

gzhan dag na re/ skabs 'di'i bdud rtsi 'khyil ba'o zhes pa bsnyen pa'i yan lag la sbyor ba mi 'thad de/ bde mchog stod 'grel las/ nA ro pa'i dbang mdor bstan gyi 'grel par 'dus pa phyi ma'i lung drangs par/
nye ba'i sgrub pa'i dus su ni/ / bdud rtsi 'khyil ba'i gzugs brnyan no/[83] / zhes bdud rtsi 'khyil ba zhes 'byung ba nye sgrub la sbyar ba'i phyir ro zhe na/

Some say that the term amṛtavarta as mentioned here does not refer to the branch of approximation, because a verse from the Later Guhyasamāja in the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary and in Nāropa’s Commentary on a Short Teaching on Initiations links the appearance of amṛtavarta with the practice of near accomplishment:
During near accomplishment, the image of amṛtavarta.[97]

d.div: [83] sde dge_1402_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ba_bde mchog stod 'grel/ 133_na6
[97] Toh 443 Kangyur, rgyud, cha (Guhyasamāja), 154b2.

f.d: skyon med de/ bgegs mthar byed pa'i lta ba zhes sogs kyis bstan pa'i bdud rtsi 'khyil ba dpral ba la bshad pa dang / gsang 'dus rgyud phyi ma'i/ nye ba'i sgrub pa'i dus su ni/ /bdud rtsi 'khyil ba'i gzugs brnyan no/[84] /zhes pa bde mchog stod 'grel dang nA ro pas drangs pa'i bdud rtsi 'khyil ba'i don dgongs pa'i skad gzhan gyi sgo nas rlung la byed par 'grel pa de gnyis kas bshad pas nye sgrub kyi yan lag srog 'dzin gyi dmigs pa rlung yin pa la dgongs pa yin te/

There is no contradiction here. The amṛtavarta that has been described as “The look of Vighnantaka” and so forth has been explained as referring to the brow. The amṛtavarta mentioned in the Later Guhyasamāja verse, “During near accomplishment, the image of amṛtavarta,“[98] which appears in the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary and is quoted by Nāropa, is explained by both these commentaries as provisional language referring to the winds. Therefore this verse is referring to the winds as being the meditative object during the prāṇāyāma and retention yogas, the near-accomplishment branch of the six yogas.

d.div: [84] sde dge_443_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_gsang 'dus rgyud phyi ma/ 155_ba2
[98] Toh 1402 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, 133a1.

f.d:
bde mchog stod 'grel las/ nye ba'i sgrub pa'i dus su ni/ /zhes sogs kyi don 'chad pa na/
de nas bdud rtsi 'khyil ba'i gzugs brnyan gyi ming can dgongs pa'i skad gzhan gyis rlung gsungs so/ / de yang rnam pa lnga ste de bzhin du 'dus pa phyi mar bcom ldan 'das kyis gsungs pa/ rin cen lnga yi rang bzhin dbugs/[85] / zhes sogs drangs nas gsungs pa dang /

The Cakrasaṃvara Commentary, when explaining the lines “during near accomplishment,” says:
“The image of amṛtavarta“ refers to the winds by way of provisional language. Furthermore the Buddha spoke similarly of the “five aspects” in the Later Guhyasamāja, where he says, “Breath, the nature of the five jewels.” /359/

d.div: [85] sde dge_443_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_gsang 'dus rgyud phyi ma/ 154_ba2

f.d:
nA ro pas kyang 'di'i skabs su stod 'grel gyi tshig 'di nyid kho na bkod cing / bgegs mthar byed pa'i lta ba zhes sogs kyi don 'chad pa na nA ro pa'i dbang mdor bstan gyi 'grel pa las/
bgegs mthar byed pa'i lta ba zhes pa la bgegs mthar byed ni bdud rtsi 'khyil ba'o/ / de'i lta ba ni bdud rtsi'i gnas su son pa ste dpral bar son pa'o/ / de'i yang nye bar sgrub pa la yan lag drug go/ / kyang yig gis srog rtsol dang 'dzin pa bya ste [86] zhes sogs 'grel chen ji lta ba bzhin du gsungs pas so/ /

Nāropa also reproduces these words from the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary, and when explaining the line “The look of Vighnantaka” in his Commentary on a Short Teaching on Initiations, he mirrors the words of the Great Commentary:
