[210] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 388b6.

f.d:
gzhan yang de lta bu'i bzhed pa rje nyid kyi dgongs pa'ang min te/ zin bris las/
sor sdud ni gzugs ma grub pa bsgrub pa'i phyir sgom pa yin la/ bsam gtan ni grub zin brtan par bya ba'i phyir sgom pa yin no/ / 'o na dmigs pa gang bsgoms nas brtan par byed pa yin zhe na/ dmigs pa de nyid kyi rgyun goms pas brtan par byed pa yin no/[212] / zhes sor sdud kyi gnas skabs su gang shar ba'i stong gzugs rnams la dmigs nas ji ltar shar ba ltar la rtse gcig tu 'jog par gsungs pas so/ / yang kha cig yan lag so so la sgom tshul de byed pa ni mi 'thad de/ yan lag 'di dag ni bsam gtan gyi sems kyi 'jog tshul gcig pu de nyid byas pa las rtogs pa skye ba'i rim pa yin par de lta nyid du 'chad pa las shes so/ /

Furthermore the previous assertion is not that of Jé Tsongkhapa. His Notes on Kālacakra says:
Withdrawal is meditation for the creation of form not yet created. Meditative absorption is meditation for the stabilization of form already created. What is the object to be stabilized after the meditation? The continuity of the object of meditation itself is to be stabilized.[211] Therefore the empty forms are single-pointedly concentrated upon as they appear in the meditations of withdrawal. Some apply this particular way of meditating to each branch. This is not correct, because this branch is at a level of insight that only comes from the mental placement of meditative absorption, which will now be explained.

d.div: [212] rje tsong kha pa/ gsung 'bum pod/ da_sbyor ba yan lag drug gi rdzogs rim gyi gnad bsdus pa/ 11_na3

f.d: gnyis pa rang lugs kyi sgom tshul dngos bshad pa ni/

sor sdud kyi mtshan mo dang nyin mo'i rnal 'byor gyi gnas gang yang rung bar lus gnad lta stangs sems kyi 'jog tshul rnams sor sdud kyi skabs ltar byas te bsgoms pas stong gzugs sna tshogs shar ba na de nyid la rtse gcig tu bzhag nas sgom pa nyid yin te/ dbang mdor bstan las/
rmi lam bzhin du gzugs mthong 'gyur/ / gzugs de rtag tu bsgom par bya/[213] / zhes stong gzugs de gnyis ka bsam gtan gyis rtag tu bsgom par gsungs pa dang / dus zhabs snyan brgyud las kyang /
de yi [214] yul ni stong gzugs te/ / bsgom pa sngar gyi stong gzugs la/ / sems bzhag nam mkha' lta ba yin/ / stong nyid sems 'jug shes rab ste/[215] / zhes gsungs pa ltar rje nyid kyi'ang dgongs pa yin pa ni zin bris drangs zin pa ltar ro/ /

The meditation is performed in the place of day or night withdrawal yoga with eye and body positions and mental placements held as in withdrawal. When the empty forms arise, it is these forms that are single-pointedly concentrated upon. A Short Teaching on Initiations says that meditative absorption focuses constantly upon the empty forms themselves:
Like dreams, forms are seen. Meditate constantly on these forms.[212] The Kālacakrapāda Transmission also says:
The objects of mind are empty forms. On empty forms of previous meditation, mind is placed looking into space. Mind placed in emptiness is wisdom.[213] This is also Jé Tsongkhapa’s position, as can be understood from the above quote from Notes on Kālacakra.

f.d: gsum pa yan lag gi dbye ba ni/

sgrub le'i brgya bcu drug pa las/
bsam gtan dag kyang shes rab rtog dang dpyod pa dga' dang g.yo med bde ba rtse gcig sems pa'o/[216] / zhes gsungs pa'i 'grel chen las/
de bzhin du gzugs de nyid la shes rab ces pa ni lta ba'o/ / rtog pa zhes pa ni dngos po 'dzin pa'o/ / dpyod pa zhes pa ni de'i don nges par byed pa'o/ / dga' ba zhes pa ni gzugs la chags pa'o/ / g.yo med bde ba zhes pa ni gzugs dang lhan cig sems gcig tu byed pa'o/[217] / zhes dang /

Verse 116 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter states:
Meditative absorption also is wisdom, conception, discernment, joy, and unmoving bliss of a single-pointed mind.[214] On this the Great Commentary says: /396/
Similarly, within this form, there is “wisdom,” which means the view, “conception,“ meaning apprehending phenomena, “discernment,” meaning ascertainment, “joy,” meaning attraction to form, and “unmoving bliss,” meaning the mind and form together as one.[215]

f.d:
de dag gi don nA ro pas bshad pa ni/ 'dus pa phyi ma las/
bsam gtan rnam pa lnga ru 'gyur/ / rtog pa dang ni dpyod pa dang / / dga' dang de bzhin bde ba nyid/ / sems rtse gcig pa nyid dang lnga/ / de rnams bsam gtan bsdus pa'o/[218] / zhes yan lag lnga mdor bstan nas de dag gi don 'chad pa ni yang de nyid las/
gsang ba gsum 'byung rtog pa ste/ / de la rab sbyor dpyod pa'o/ / dga' ba rab gsal gsum pa ste/ / bde ba bsdus pa bzhi pa'o/ / shes dang shes bya byung zad pa'i/ / rang sems lnga par shes par bya/ / sangs rgyas thams cad rang bzhin zhi/ / 'dod pa thams cad rab tu gnas/[219] / zhes gsungs pa rnams kyi don dbang mdor bstan gyi 'grel par nA ro pas bshad pa ste/

Nāropa explains these by commenting on them as they appear in the Later Guhyasamāja, which says:
Meditative absorption is in five forms: conception, discernment, joy, bliss, and single-pointed mind. This is meditative absorption in brief.[216] These are the five divisions in brief. The tantra continues with their explanation:
Three secrets arising is conception; its application is discernment; vivid joy the third; gathered bliss the fourth; self-mind, the cessation of arising consciousness and objects of consciousness, is the fifth; it is of the nature of all buddhas, it is pacification, all desire abides this way.[217] The meaning of these verses Nāropa has explained in his Commentary on a Short Teaching on Initiations:

f.d:
'grel pa de nyid las/
gsang ba gsum zhes pa la sogs pa la sku dang gsung dang thugs kyi bdag nyid [220] dus gsum khams gsum ni gsang ba gsum mo/ / de rigs pa'i rnam pas khams gsum par rab tu gsal ba tsam nyid kyis lan cig sems dpa' ni 'byung ba yin la/ de rtogs shing khong du chud pa ni gsang ba gsum 'byung ste de nyid rtogs pa'o/ / de la rab sbyor dpyod pa'o zhes pa rtogs pa'i yul de la rab sbyor dpyod pa ste/ brtan pa dang g.yo ba bum pa dang snam bu la sogs pa'i khyad par gyi dngos po 'dzin pa ni dpyod pa'o/ / dga' ba rab gsal na dpyod pa'i yul dngos po thams cad la sems gnas pa'i rgyur gyur pa'i yid bde ba'o/ / bde ba bsdus pa zhes pa sems gnas pa'i dngos po thams cad las bde ba yang dag par rtogs pa lus shin tu sbyangs pa'i rgyu can bde ba ni bde ba bsdus pa'o/ / shes dang zhes bya ba la sogs pa la shes pa mig la sogs pa'i rnam par shes pa drug shes bya gzugs la sogs pa chos kyi khams kyi mthar thug pa la rab tu 'jug pa ni 'byung ba ste shes pa dang shes bya 'byung ba'o/ / de'i zad pa ni sems kyi gzung ba dang 'dzin pa stong pa nyid kyi mtshan nyid sems rtse gcig pa nyid ni rang sems zhes brjod do/ / rnam pa de lta bu'i rang sems de sangs rgyas thams cad kyi rang bzhin te gzugs la sogs pa'i rnam par rtog pa zhi ba'i phyir zhi ba khams gsum par rab tu gsal ba tsam nyid kyis stong pa nyid gcig pu'i mthar thug pa'o/ / 'dod pa thams cad rab tu gnas zhes pa la 'dod pa thams cad ni dngos po thams cad de rang las dbyer med pa rab tu gsal ba gcig pu'i gzugs kyis rab tu gnas pa ni 'dir gnas pa'o/ / zhes pa 'dod pa thams cad rab tu gnas/[221] zhes gsungs pa rnams so/ /

d.div: Concerning “three secrets” and so forth, the three times and three realms, whose nature is the enlightened body, speech, and mind, are the three secrets. The one-time mind, holding just their rough forms vividly illuminated as the three realms, is the “arising.” Experiencing and understanding this is the “three secrets arising.” That is “conception.” “Its application is discernment” means discernment applied to the objects of conception. The apprehending of phenomena possessed of animate and inanimate characteristics, such as the vase and the friezes and so forth, is “discernment.” “Vivid joy” means joy that is the blissful state keeping the mind on all objects held by discernment. “Gathered bliss” means that the experience of the blissful state coming from the mind dwelling in all phenomena becomes a cause of great pliancy within the body. Concerning “self-mind, the cessation of arising consciousness,” etc., “consciousness” refers to the six consciousnesses of sight and so forth that engage the “objects of consciousness,” which in turn refers to the finality of the six spheres of phenomena. “Arising” means the arising of these consciousnesses and objects of consciousnesses. Their “cessation” is the single-pointed mind /397/ in which the apprehending and the apprehended are possessed of the characteristics of emptiness. This is “self-mind.” Self-mind in such a form is in the nature of all buddhas. Because concepts of form and so forth have been pacified, there is “pacification” appearing vividly as the three realms. This is the sole and ultimate emptiness. Concerning “all desire abides,” “all desire” means all phenomena, and these phenomena abide in a form vivid and indivisible from one’s mind.[218]
[220] ma dper sku gsung thugs kyi bar gnyid ces byung yang bdag nyid ces bcos/
[221] sde dge_1351_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ na_dbang mdor bstan gyi 'grel bshad/ 246_na5
[218] Toh 1351 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, 246a5.

f.d: de rnams kyi don cung zad cig bshad par bya ste/ de la gsang ba gsum 'byung ni rtogs pa'o/ / 'o na gsang ba gsum ni gang / 'byung ba'i don ji lta bu snyam na/ sku gsung thugs kyi bdag nyid kyi stong gzugs dus gsum dang khams gsum pa'i rnam par snang ba ni gsang ba gsum mo/ / 'byung ba'i don ni rags pa'am rtsing ba'i rnam pas khams gsum pa'i rnam par snang ba'i stong gzugs rab tu gsal ba tsam lan cig sems ni 'byung ba'o/ / mdor na sku gsung thugs kyi bdag nyid dus gsum dang khams gsum gyi brtan g.yo'i rnam par snang ba'i stong gzugs rags pa'i rnam pas rab tu gsal bar rtogs shing khong du chud pa ni gsang ba gsum 'byung ste de nyid rtog pa yin no/ /

This passage should be explained a little. “Three secrets arising” is the meaning of conception. What are the three secrets and what does “arising” mean? Empty forms appearing in the aspects of the three times and the three realms and whose natures are the enlightened body, speech, and mind are the three secrets. “Arising” refers to the “one-time” mind holding the rough or coarse aspects of the vivid empty forms appearing as the three realms. In short, experiencing and perceiving in a rough but vivid form, the empty forms, whose nature is the enlightened body, speech, and mind, and which appear in the forms of the animate and inanimate phenomena of the three times and three realms, is what is meant by “three secrets arising.” That is the first branch, called conception.

yang rtog pa de'i yul la rab tu sbyor ba ni dpyod pa'o/ / de yang sbyor tshul ji lta bu snyam na/ rtog pa'i yul brtan g.yo'i rnam par snang ba'i stong gzugs de la bum pa dang snam bu la sogs pa'i stong gzugs kyi khyad par gyi dngos po zhib tu phye nas 'dzin cing gsal bar snang ba ni dpyod pa'o/ /

Application to the objects of conception is the division of discernment. How is this application carried out? The objects of conception are the empty forms of animate and inanimate phenomena, and the details of these empty-form phenomena, such as those of the vases, friezes, and so forth, are discerned and clearly appear. This is discernment.

yang dga' ba ni dpyod pa'i yul gyi dngos po stong gzugs zhib mor phye ba thams cad la sems rang gi ngang gis gnas pa'i rgyu sems shin sbyangs yin la de 'dren pa'i sems kyi dga' ba yid bde ba yin no/ / yang bde ba ni stong gzugs kyi dngos po thams cad zhib par dpyad pa la sems rtse gcig tu gnas pa las byung ba'i lus shin tu sbyangs pa'i bde ba yin no/ /

Although mental pliancy is the actual cause of the mind being naturally settled on the detailed empty forms that make up the objects of discernment, joy is a blissful or joyful mind that induces such a state. Bliss is the bliss of the physical pliancy that arises from the mind being single-pointedly held on the discerned empty forms.

yang rgyud 'grel las shes rab ces gsungs pa ni 'dus par sems rtse gcig pa [222] zhes gsungs pa 'di dang khyad par med pas sems rtse gcig pa 'di ni shes dang shes bya byung zad ces pa 'dis bstan pa'i shes pa ni mig gi rnam par shes pa nas yid kyi rnam par shes pa'i bar gyi yul can drug go/ / shes bya ni gzugs nas chos kyi khams kyi bar yul drug go/ / byung ba ni yul drug la rnam par shes pa drug rab tu 'jug pa'o/ /

The “single-pointed mind” spoken of in the Later Guhyasamāja is the same as the “wisdom” taught in the tantra and commentary and is explained by lines beginning “self-mind, the cessation of arising consciousness.” /398/ Consciousness here refers to the six consciousnesses from sight to mental consciousness. “Objects of consciousness” refers to the six objects from visual form to mental phenomena. “Arising” refers to the six consciousnesses engaging with the six objects.

d.div: [222] sde dge_443_bka'/ rgyud/ ca_gsang 'dus rgyud phyi ma/ 154_na7

f.d: de zad pa ni sems rnam par shes pa drug dang yul gzugs sogs drug gi gzung ba dang 'dzin pa'i yul yul can gyi 'brel pa chad pa yin la/ de lta bu'i 'brel ba chad pa'i stong pa nyid kyi mtshan nyid ni sems rtse gcig pa ste rang sems zhes brjod do/ / sor sdud kyi skabs nas dbang shes lnga'i yul yul can gyi 'brel ba chad kyang yid shes kyi yul yul can gyi 'brel pa ma chad pas bsam gtan gyi bde ba'i yan lag gi bar du stong gzugs dang de la rtse gcig tu gnas pa'i yid kyi rnam shes gzung 'dzin tha dad kyi rnam par gnas kyang / yul stong gzugs dang yul can 'od gsal gyi sems gnyis gzung 'dzin tha dad pa'i 'brel ba chad de yul dang yul can ro gcig tu zhugs pa rnam pa de lta bu'i rang sems te sems rtse gcig pa de ni sangs rgyas thams cad de stong gzugs kyi rnam pa thams cad dang khyad par du yang dus kyi 'khor lo yab yum gyi rnam pa can gyi stong gzugs dang rang bzhin dbyer med pa'i sgo nas gzung ba dang la sogs pa 'dzin pa'i rnam par rtog pa zhi ba'i phyir ram rgyu mtshan gyis zhi ba stong pa nyid kyi gzugs khams gsum par rab tu gsal ba tsam nyid kyi stong pa nyid kyi gzugs dang khyad par du yang dus kyi 'khor lo yab yum zhal sbyor gyi rnam pa can gyi stong gzugs dang dbyer med gcig bu'i mthar thug pa'i sems so/ /

“Cessation” refers to severing the connection of the apprehending subject and the apprehended object, which lies between the mind with its six consciousnesses and the six objects themselves. The main characteristic of the “emptiness” that is the severing of this connection is the “single-pointed mind,” spoken of as “self-mind.” Although connections between the five sensory consciousnesses and their objects are severed from withdrawal yoga onward, the same is not true of the connection between mental consciousness and its objects. Therefore, up to the division of bliss in meditative absorption, the empty forms and the mental consciousness that abides single-pointedly within them exist in separate aspects as apprehended and apprehender. However the empty-form objects and clear-light–mind subject do not exist in separate aspects as apprehended and apprehender. Subject and object are as one. This “self-mind” is a single-pointed mind, indivisible from all buddhas in the aspect of empty forms. In particular it is indivisible from the empty-form Kālacakra in the aspect of mother-father embrace. In this way “concepts of apprehended form,” or objects, “and so forth,” referring to the apprehending consciousness, “have been pacified.” “Therefore this pacification” is the “sole and ultimate” mind, indivisible from the “emptiness” form “appearing vividly as the three realms,” and especially indivisible from the empty form that is Kālacakra in mother-and-father union.
bzhi pa bsam gtan grub pa'i tshad bstan pa ni/

sor sdud kyi skabs kyi lus la gnad du bsnun pa'i dmigs pa de nyid bsgoms pas stong gzugs shar ba'i tshe stong gzugs de nyid la rtse gcig tu mnyam par bzhag pas rtog dpyod kyi yan lag gnyis kyis stong gzugs phra rags mthong nas de'i rgyun la rtse gcig tu bzhag pas ting nge 'dzin gyi thun 'khyongs pa'i mthar phan yon gyi yan lag lus sems shin sbyangs 'dren pa'i dga' bde skyes te rang gi sems kyi snang ba tsam gyi stong gzugs dus 'khor yab yum gyi sku shar ba dang rang gi sems gnyis dbyer med du 'dres nas sku de sems la sogs su mi snang zhing sku de la rang nyid kyi nga rgyal 'bad med du 'pho nus pa de'i tshe bsam gtan grub pa yin pas 'tshams 'di nas srog rtsol sgom pa la 'jug pa yin no/ /

During withdrawal, meditation is directed upon the sites of penetrative focusing within the body. When empty forms arise, these are meditated upon with constant single-pointed equipoise. In the branches of conception and discernment, rough empty forms followed by detailed empty forms are seen. The continuity of these empty forms is single-pointedly focused upon and, at the end of a continuous session of meditative concentration, joy and bliss, induce the twin benefits of mental and physical pliancy. The empty-form apparition of Kālacakra mother and father, as a mere appearance within one’s mind, /399/ is indivisibly mixed with one’s own mind. That enlightened form no longer appears as mind, and one is able to move self-pride effortlessly to that enlightened form. At that time meditative absorption has been accomplished. From then onward one moves into prāṇāyāma yoga.

mdor na bsam gtan sgom pa'i skabs 'dir lus gnad lta stangs sems kyi 'jog tshul rnams sor sdud kyi skabs su bshad pa ltar byas te bsgoms pas ng+hU tIr rlung tshud pa phul du byung ba las kun rtog g.yo ba'i rlung ro rkyang la rgyu ba rnam par rtog pa dang bcas pa yang dag par 'gags te mi rtog pa'i sems 'od gsal shar ba dang mnyam du stong gzugs rnams 'char la/ stong gzugs de rnams rnal 'byor pa rang gi sha'i mig gi rnam par shes pas gsal bar mthong zhing / de ltar mthong ba'i stong gzugs rnams dang khyad par du yang smin mtshams kyi ng+hU tI'i nang gI rA+e khA'i nang du shar ba'i dus 'khor yab yum gyi rnam pa'i stong gzugs de la 'od gsal gyi sems des dmigs nas rtse gcig tu bzhag ste bsgoms pa las yul stong gzugs de dang yul can 'od gsal gyi sems gnyis dbyer med gcig tu 'dres nas gzung 'dzin tha dad pa'i snang ba log ste dus 'khor yab yum gyi rnam par snang ba der rnal 'byor pa rang nyid nga rgyal 'pho nus pa yin no/ / de ltar nga rgyal 'phos pa'i dus 'khor yab yum gyi rnam par snang ba'i stong gzugs ni rjes dran gyi skabs dang 'bras dus kyi longs spyod rdzogs pa'i sku dus 'khor yab yum dngos gnas la grub pa de'i bsgrub gzhi dang rigs 'dra'i rgyur gyur pa yin no/ /

To summarize: In the branch of meditative absorption, the body and eye positioning and the mental placement are the same as in withdrawal. Meditation brings about a special entry of the winds into the dhūtī, from which the winds of the indicative conceptual states of mind are stopped from flowing through the right and left channels, and the conceptions themselves are halted. The nonconceptual mind of clear light arises together with empty forms, which are vividly seen by the meditator with a fleshly eye consciousness. These forms, and especially the empty-form Kālacakra mother and father that appears within the black line inside the dhūtī at the midway point between the eyebrows, are single-pointedly focused on by the clear-light mind. From the ensuing meditation the empty-form objects and clear-light–mind subject merge indivisibly until all appearance of a separate apprehender and apprehended is lost, and the yogi is able to transfer self-pride to the form of Kālacakra mother and father. The empty form in its appearance as Kālacakra mother and father, to which self-pride has been transferred, is the basis and similar-type cause for the actual realization of the saṃbhogakāya Kālacakra mother and father during the branch of recollection and the resultant state.
lta ba nyams rtags 'charatshu la ni

sngar bshad pa'i rtags rnams gong nas gong du khyad par du gyur pa las dwangs pa gsal ba rgya che ba 'byung ba dang / gzhan yang sangs rgyas kyi zhing khams dang 'gro drug gi snang ba la sogs pa tshad med pa 'byung ba dang / snyan pa dang mi snyan pa la sogs pa sgra brnyan/ sngar tshor ma myong ba'i dri brnyan/ ro zhim mi zhim sna tshogs kyi ro brnyan/ tsha grang la sogs pa reg brnyan sna tshogs 'char ba de'ang dang po phyi rol tu 'char/ de nas nang du re khA nag po'i nang du 'char te de rnams dag nas mngon shes 'char bar 'gyur zhes chos rje bu ston gyis gsungs so/ /[223]

The previously described signs become more and more distinct until they are of a brilliant clarity. Moreover appearances of limitless buddha fields and limitless beings of the six realms arise. Empty-form images of pleasant and unpleasant sounds, smells never before experienced, pleasant and unpleasant tastes, and sensations, such as heat and cold, all appear. At first they appear externally, and then they appear inside the black line. When they are purified, clairvoyance will arise. This description is according to the dharma master Butön.[219] /400/

f.d: bzhi pa tshad ma gang yin pa ni/

d.div: mig gi mngon shes kyis stong gzugs gsal bar mthong zhing mi slu bas dbang po'i mngon sum tshad ma'o/ /
Because the empty forms are clearly seen by clairvoyant eyes and such seeing is nondeceptive, the cognition is a sensory and direct valid cognition.

f.d: lnga pa dag dbye ni/

bsam gtan ni mi bskyod pa nyid do zhes pa rnam par shes pa'i phung po ste rnam pa bcu ni yul dang yul can bcu po rnams gcig nyid du sna tshogs gzugs la bsam gtan pa'o/ / zhes gsungs pa ltar rnam par shes pa'i phung po la sogs pa'i chos drug tshan gcig sgrib bral du dag par byed pa ste/ dbye na rtog pa sogs yan lag lnga la yul dang yul can gyis phye bas rnam pa bcu'o/ /

The Great Commentary says:
“Meditative absorption is Akṣobhya” refers to the consciousness aggregate. Its ten forms are the five object types and five consciousnesses. These are as one in various forms in meditative absorption.[220] The consciousness-aggregate group of six is to be purified until it becomes nonobscured. Meditative absorption is divided into the five branches of conception and so forth, each of which is divided into consciousness subject and object to make ten.

d.div: [220] P2064 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ka, 143b2. Not sourced in the critical edition; sourced from translator’s Peking edition of the Vimalaprabhā.

f.d: drug pa 'bras bu
['di ]la gnyis las/
These are of two types: immediate and final.
gnas skabs kyi 'bras bu ni/

sgrub le'i brgya bco brgyad pa/
mngon par shes pa lnga ni thob par 'gyur te mi yi bdag po bsam gtan sbyar bas dag pa'o/[224] / zhes pa'i 'grel chen las/
'dir gang gi tshe mig mi 'dzum par gyur pa de'i tshe lha'i mig tu 'gyur ro/ / de bzhin du lha'i rna ba la sogs pa ste bsam gtan gyis dag par 'gyur ro [225] zhes gsungs pa dang / de bzhin du gsang ba 'dus pa las/
bsam gtan ye shes snyoms 'jug pas/ / mngon shes lnga ni thob par 'gyur/[226] / zhes gsungs pa ltar bsam gtan gyi yan lag mthar phyin pa'i gnas skabs su mngon shes lnga 'thob cing sangs rgyas la chos nyan pa dang sems can gyi don rgya chen po byed nus pa la sogs pa phan yon dpag tu med pa 'thob pa'o/ /

Verse 118 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter says:
Lord of men, five kinds of clairvoyance are achieved, purified by the yoga of meditative absorption.[221] On this the Great Commentary says:
When the eyes are not closed, they become celestial eyes. Similarly the celestial ear and so forth are purified by meditative absorption.[222] Likewise the Later Guhyasamāja says:
By the meditative equipoise of meditative-absorption gnosis, five types of clairvoyance are achieved.[223] The immediate result of completing the meditative absorption branch is the attainment of the five kinds of clairvoyance as well as countless other benefits, such as being able to listen to the buddhas and to work extensively for living beings.

f.d: gnyis pa mthar thug gi 'bras bu ni

rnam shes kyi phung po dang / nam mkha'i khams dang / rna ba'i dbang po dang / chos kyi khams dang / gsang ba'i dbang po dang / khu ba 'phen 'dzin te chos drug tshan gcig sgrib bral du dag pa rgyal ba mi bskyod pa la sogs pa drug tshan gcig 'grub pa'o/ / 'dir bsam gtan la yang thams cad mkhyen pa bus sbogs chog mdzad de/ khong rang gi 'khrid yig las/
bsam gtan stong gzugs drag tu bsgom/ /zhes pas byed bcing dang lus gnad dam du byas la sngar gyi man ngag gis rig pa gzhur la bsgom [227] zhes gsungs pa'i lus gnad sogs slar 'chos pa sbogs chog tu mi rung ba sor sdud kyi skabs ltar shes par bya'o/ /

The consciousness aggregate, the element of space, the organ of hearing, the element of mental phenomena, the secret organ, and the control of seminal fluid, are all purified to become six unobscured phenomena, beginning with Buddha Akṣobhya. The omniscient Butön posits an enhancement ritual for the yoga of meditative absorption. In his writings it says:
“Meditate forcefully on the empty forms of meditative absorption” means in order to make firm the activities, bindings, and body positions, centralize the mind by way of the previous instructions.[224] As in withdrawal yoga the practice of correcting the body positions and so forth /401/ cannot be an enhancement ritual.

f.d:
yang 'khrid yig tu/ sgrub le'i mjug gi tshigs bcad bzhi bcu go slar bzhag pa'i brgya go lnga pa/
nyi ma las ni gzhan du phyogs te nyi 'od la gnas rang gi grib ma brtan pa'i mig gis blta/ / phyi nas nam mkha' dag la mngon par brtags na ro mnyam skyes bu du ba'i mdog can mthong bar 'gyur/ / zla ba drug tu goms pa'i sbyor ba dag las sa la gnas pa'i gter ni sa yi bu gar mthong / / yang na shing gi grib mar rab tu zhugs te nam mkha'i mthil du thig le'i phreng bar gyur lags so/ / zhes pa drangs nas de'i dgongs par bsams te/
khyad par du gnas dben par nyi ma la rgyab bstan te/ mdun du rang gi grib ma la bsam gtan gyi 'jog tshul gyis blta/ de nas sprin med pa'i nam mkha' la bltas pas grib gzugs skye bo mthong ba la bsam gtan gyi ting nge 'dzin gyi tshul gyis blta'o/ / de ltar zla ba drug tu bsgoms na bsam gtan dag ste sa 'og na gnas pa'i gter mthong bar 'gyur ro/ / yang na shing gi grib ma la 'dug nas mdun gyi shing gi grib ma la bsam gtan bsgom/ de nas nam mkha' la bltas te bsam gtan gyi yan lag gis brten par bsgoms pas zla ba drug gis gter mthong ngo /[228] / zhes bshad nas/ rgyud tshig de dag gis bsam gtan gyi sbogs chog bstan par mdzad do/ /

Also in his writings he quotes verse 195 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter, the first of the last forty verses left by the Great Commentary as “easy to understand” verses, which says:
Turn from the sun, stand in its rays, and stare at your shadow, externally examine the pure sky, and a person that is the color of smoke and one with the sky will be seen. With six months meditative yoga becomes pure, earth’s treasures will be seen through earth’s openings. Or move to the shadow of a tree, and in the heart of space, garlands of drops will form. On the meaning of this verse he comments:
In an isolated place, turn your back to the sun. In front of you look at your shadow with meditative-absorption placement. Then look into the cloudless sky, and a shadow person will be seen. Look at this with the samādhi of meditative absorption. If you meditate in this way for six months, the meditative absorption will become pure, and you will see the treasures beneath the earth. Alternatively, sitting in the shadow of a tree with the shadow in front, meditate on meditative absorption. Then look into space, stabilize with meditative-absorption meditation, and in six months you will see the treasures.[225] He maintains that this passage from the tantra teaches an enhancement ritual.

d.div: [228] bu ston rin chen grub/ gsung 'bum pod/ ka_dus kyi 'khor lo'i mchan/ 96_na3
[225] Collected Works, vol. ka, Notes on Kālacakra, 96a3.

f.d:
de'i mjug gi brgya go drug pa/ nus ma gang zhig ces sogs kyis srog rtsol gyi sbogs chog bstan pa bzhin du nyi ma las ni [229] zhes sogs kyis kyang bsam gtan gyi sbogs chog bstan par byed dgos snyam du bsams pa 'dra na 'ang de gnyis mi mtshungs te/ nus ma gang zhig ces sogs kyis sor sdud dang / srog rtsol gyi sbogs chog bstan pa ni sgrub le'i brgya bcu dgu pa'i 'grel pa las/ nA da goms pa 'chad par 'gyur bas zhes 'og tu kha 'phangs pa'i nA da goms pa 'chad byed ni nus ma gang zhig ces sogs yin pas nus pa [230] zhes sogs kyis sor sdud dang srog rtsol gyi sbogs chog bstan pa la bsnyon du med la/ nyi ma las ni zhes sogs sa 'og gi gter mthong ba'i las tshogs sgrub byed ston byed du gsal lo/ / zin bris las/
bsam gtan ni sor sdud brtan byed tsam yin pas sor sdud grub na ni de nas bsam gtan bsgoms pas mi 'grub pa mi srid la/ sor sdud ma grub na ni bsam gtan sgom pa yang med do/ / des na sogs khongs nas gtso bor srog rtsol gzung ngo /[231] / zhes gsungs nas bsam gtan la sbogs chog mi dgos par bzhed do/ /

Because the very next verse, 196, beginning “The śakti,”[226] teaches the prāṇāyāma enhancement ritual, it may seem that the previous verse quoted above, beginning “Turn from the sun,” must similarly teach a meditative absorption enhancement ritual. However these two verses are not similar. The verse beginning “The śakti” describes the enhancement rituals of both withdrawal and prāṇāyāma, because it says in the Great Commentary, on verse 119 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter, “Nāda meditation will be explained,”[227] and the later verse that this line refers to is the one beginning “The śakti.” Therefore there is no question that the verse beginning “The śakti” describes the enhancement ritual for withdrawal and prāṇāyāma. The verse beginning “Turn from the sun” is clearly a verse that describes the accomplishing of various feats, such as seeing the treasures beneath the earth. Notes on Kālacakra says:
Meditative absorption is just the stabilizing of withdrawal. Therefore, if withdrawal /402/ has been accomplished and meditative absorption meditation is performed, it is impossible not to achieve it. However, if withdrawal has not been attained, there is no meditative-absorption meditation. Therefore “and so forth” mainly refers to prāṇāyāma.[228] This is an assertion that meditative absorption does not require an enhancement ritual.

f.d: gsum pa srog rtsol gyi yan lag bshad pa/
30. Prāṇāyāma: The Yoga of the Winds
gnyis pa srog sgrub byed kyi yan lag
['di ]la gnyis/ srog ro rkyang la rgyu ba bkag nas ng+hU tIr 'jug par byed pa'i yan lag srog rtsol dang / ng+hU tIr zhugs pa gnas pa 'am brtan par byed pa'i yan lag 'dzin pa'o/ /

This has two main outlines: 1. Prāṇāyāma: The branch of bringing the winds into the dhūtī, having halted their flow in the left and right channels 2. Retention: The branch of stabilizing the winds in the dhūtī
dang po [srog ro rkyang la rgyu ba bkag nas ng+hU tIr 'jug par byed pa'i yan lag srog rtsol ]

d.i: Prāṇāyāma: The branch of bringing the winds into the dhūtī, having halted their flow in the left and right channels

f.d: ['di ]la drug /srog rtsol gyi mtshan don/ dang por bsgom [232] pa'i dus 'tshams/ gang bsgom pa'i yan lag gi nges pa/ tshad ma gang yin dpyad pa/ dag dbye/ 'bras bu'o/ /
This is under six headings: 1. Meaning of the term prāṇāyāma 2. The time for the first meditation 3. Branches of the meditation 4. Valid cognition 5. Purification divisions 6. Results

d.div: [232] ma dper bsdom pa'i dus 'tshams gsal yang bsgom pa'i dus mtshams zhes bcos/

f.d: dang po [srog rtsol gyi mtshan don ]ni

srog rtsol gyi skad dod prA Na A yA maHzhes pa yin la/ de'i prA Na zhes pa srog la 'jug cing / A yA ma zhes pa 'bad pa dang 'gog pa dang ring du byed pa gsum la 'jug pa las/ prA Na dang sbyar bas rim pa bzhin srog rtsol srog 'gog srog ring du byed pa zhes par 'gyur ba las phyi ma gnyis kyi don skabs su bab pa yin pa las 'dir srog 'gog pa dang / 'dus pa las srog ni tshe dang rtsol ba ring du mched pa'i don du bshad pas 'dir bshad pa'i dbang du byas na srog ni srog thur sogs kyi rlung dang / rtsol ba 'gog pa'i don du byas te srog thur sogs kyi rlung ro rkyang la rgyu ba bkag nas ng+hU tIr 'dzud pas na srog rtsol zhes bya'o/ /

Of the Sanskrit terms prāṇa and āyāma, prāṇa refers to the winds and āyāma can be rendered as “effort,” “stopping,” and “lengthening.” Affixing these three meanings to the term prāṇa results in the Tibetan translations, “wind exertion,” “wind stopping,” and “wind lengthening.” Here we are concerned with the second and third meanings. In the Kālacakra, prāṇāyāma is taken to mean “wind stopping.” In the Guhyasamāja, prāṇa means “life” and āyāma means “to lengthen.” Therefore, in terms of the Kālacakra explanation, prāṇa refers to the winds such as the downward wind and so forth, and āyāma has the meaning of “stopping.” These winds are stopped from flowing in the left and right channels and brought into the dhūtī.

de yang srog rtsol gyi sgra sgrub pa byas na nges pa rnyed pas de brjod par bya ste/ prA Na srog 'dzin pa la'o zhes pa'i byings la a tsa rkyen du sbyin/ tsa khyad par gyi don yin pas dbyi/ yang ya mu 'gog pa la'o zhes pa'i byings la g+hanya rkyen du sbyin/ ya mu'i ya'i sngon du nyer sgyur Ang gzhag/byings kyi mu'i srog gi u brjod don dang / nyer sgyur gyi Ang gi nga dang rkyen gyi g+hanya rnams khyad par gyi don yin pas dbyi'o/ / de nas grub pa nya Na rjes su 'brel pa la a tsa bzhin du'o zhes pa dang / iN i tsa aT rnams las a'i u sang+hA ring po'o zhes pa ltar byas pas ya'i srog gi a ring por byas te 'tshams sbyar bas pra Na.A ma zhes pa'i ming du grub/ de'i mthar rnam dbye dang po'i gcig tshig si sbyin/ si'i srog gi i brjod don yin pas dbyi/ sa rnam gcad du byas pas prA NA yA maHzhes pa'i tshig tu grub pa yin no/ / 'di dag ni rje nA ro pas/
rtsol ba ni zhes pa ya mu nye bar 'gog pa la'o zhes pa'i khams 'di'i a kun nas zhen pa 'gog pa ni A yA maH ste srog dang thur sel gyi rlung dag gnyis ka'i bgrod pa 'gog pa las dbu ma'i rtsar rab tu zhugs pa'o/[233] / zhes gsungs pa'i don yin no/ /

Moreover this can be confirmed if the grammatical formation of this term is explained.[229] Concerning the Dhātusūtra passage “Prāṇa means life-holding,” the affix[230] ac is added to the root. The consonant c is a marker[231] and therefore is dropped. Concerning the Dhātusūtra line “Yamu means stopping,” the affix ghañ is added to the root. Before the letter ya of the word yamu, the prefix[232] āng is added. The life letter u of the root mu is there for reasons of articulation,[233] the ng of the prefix āng and the affix ghañ are markers and are therefore omitted. Concerning the formation of the term, “Those joined to ñ and ṇ follow a and c” and “From aṇ, ac, aṭ, the nearby[234] a is lengthened,” meaning that the life vowel a of the letter ya is lengthened. This results in the amalgamation, prāṇāyāma. Added to that is the singular particle letter si from the first case. The life vowel i of si is for articulation and is therefore dropped. The s becomes a visarga, and the resulting term is prāṇāyāmaṃ. On this Nāropa says;
Concerning āyāma, “yamu means stopping.” Here the letter a of the root stops all conception. This is āyāmaṃ, which means that the paths of the life air and downward air are stopped and brought into the central channel.[235]

d.div: [233] sde dge_1351_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ na_dbang mdor bstan gyi 'grel bshad/ 252_na3

[229] This whole paragraph appears to be corrupt, particularly with regard to the Sanskrit spellings. With the generous help of Ven. Losang Norbu Shastri of the Tibetan Institute in Saranath, India, and Prof. Gareth Sparham from the University of Michigan in the U.S., I have reconstructed and translated it the best I could.
[230] rkyen, pratyaya. Affix or suffix added to Sanskrit roots.
[231] khyad par gyi don. In other words, it marks out other vowels and consonants for particular grammatical functions.
[232] nyer sgyur, uparsarga. Prefix.
[233] brjod don. Without the vowel the consonant would remain unarticulated.
[234] Transliterated Sanskrit: upadhā. Penultimate, or “placed near to.”
[235] Toh 1351 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, na, 252a3.

f.d: gnyis pa dang por bsgom pa'i dus 'tshams ni/

d.i: The time for the first meditation

f.d:
rje'i dgongs par bsams pa'i 'khrid yig kha cig las/
rlung dbu mar zhugs pa dang thim pa'i rtags bcu rjogs/ de bsam gtan gyis brtan par byas nas srog rtsol sgom pa la 'jug par bya [234] zhes gsung yang rlung thim pa'i rtags bcu sor bsam gyi gnas skabs su mi 'ong ba lta zhog srog rtsol gyi skabs su 'ong ba yang rje'i dgongs pa min te/ zin bris las/
srog rtsol gyi byed las ni srog dbu mar tshud pa nyid yin gyi/ srog dbu mar gnas pa ni 'dzin pa'i byed las yin pas srog rtsol gyis de sgrub par 'dod pa mi 'thad de/ srog rtsol gyis dbu mar gnas pa'ang sgrub na ni 'dzin pa'i yan lag bsgom pa la dgos pa ci zhig yod/ des na srog rtsol gyi byed las ni srog dbu mar zhugs pa'i rtags nyid yin pas srog dbu mar zhugs pa'i rtags 'khrul med rnams shar na srog rtsol gyi byed las des rdzogs so/[235] / zhes srog rtsol gyis rlung dbu mar gnas par yang mi byed par gsungs na thim pa lta ci smos pa'i phyir ro/ /

Some texts, thinking it to be the position of Jé Tsongkhapa, assert:
After the ten signs indicating that the winds have entered and dissolved within the central channel are complete and have been stabilized by meditative absorption, prāṇāyāma meditation is begun.[236] However, not only do the ten signs of the winds dissolving not arise during withdrawal and meditative absorption, it is not even the position of Jé Tsongkhapa that such signs arise during prāṇāyāma. His Notes on Kālacakra states:
The function of prāṇāyāma is to bring the winds into the central channel. However keeping the winds in the central channel is the function of retention. Therefore asserting that this task is performed by prāṇāyāma is incorrect, because if prāṇāyāma also accomplished the keeping of winds in the central channel, what would be the purpose of meditating on the branch of retention? Therefore the function of prāṇāyāma is to bring the winds into the central channel, and when the signs of winds having entered the central channel clearly and unmistakably arise, that function is complete.[237] Therefore, if it is not the function of prāṇāyāma to even hold the winds in the central channel, how could it possibly dissolve them?

d.div: [234] rje'i dgongs par bsams pa'i khrid yig kha cig ces pa 'di gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[235] rje tsong kha pa/ gsung 'bum pod/ da_sbyor ba yan lag drug gi rdzogs rim gyi gnad bsdus pa/ 17_ba4
[236] Text untraced.
[237] Collected Works, vol. da, 17b4.

f.d:
gzhan yang 'khrid yig de nyid las/
de nas yun bsrings te bsgoms pas sdod pa je ring la 'gro zhing de tsam du 'byung 'jug gnyis je thung du 'gro la/ mthar 'byung 'jug gnyis chad nas gnas pa 'ba' zhig par 'gyur ro/ / de yang 'dus pa sogs kyi skabs su rdor bzlas byas pas 'byung 'jug chad pa'i gnas pa dang thim pas lhan skyes kyi bde ba 'dren pa 'byung bar gsungs la/ skabs de'i rdor bzlas kyis de ltar nus shing 'dis mi nus pa'i khyad par mi 'thadces [236] gsungs pa yang zin bris kyi gsung des bkag par shes par bya'o/ /

Furthermore the previous text says:
Then one meditates for an extended period, and for however long one sits, inhalation and exhalation of breath become progressively shorter. When inhalation and exhalation have stopped, the winds abide completely. In the Guhyasamāja and other tantras, it is taught that vajra recitation brings about the abiding that is the severing of inhalation and exhalation as well as the dissolving, and that this in turn induces the innate bliss. It would be incorrect to say that vajra recitation is able to bring about such a result in the context of Guhyasamāja but is not able to here. However this passage is also refuted by the above quote from Notes on Kālacakra.

d.div: [236] 'di gong du drangs pa'i rje'i dgongs par bsam pa'i 'khrid yig ces pa la sbyor dgos/ bu ston rin chen grub/ gsung 'bum pod/ ga20_na5

f.d:
'o na 'di dang 'dus pa sogs nas bshad pa mi 'dra ba'i tshul ji lta bu snyam na/ de yang zin bris las/
spyir bla med kyi rgyud rnams nas rlung ng+hU tIr zhugs pa dang ng+hU tIr gnas pa dang ng+hU tIr thim pa gsum bshad la/ 'dir ni ng+hU tIr thim pa ni rlung bcings pa dang / bsres pa dang / bsad pa zhes bshad pa rnams yin la/ zhugs gnas gnyis yan lag re rer bshad pas 'di la gnyis/ srog ro rkyang la rgyu ba bkag nas d+hU tIr 'jug par byed pa'i yan lag srog rtsol/ ng+hU tIr zhugs pa gnas par byed pa'i yan lag 'dzin pa [237] zhes 'dus pa sogs nas lus dben ngag dben lta bu'i skabs su yang lus la gnad du bsnun pa'i thabs gcig nyid kyis kyang rlung dbu mar zhugs gnas thim gsum rgyun gcig la 'ong bar gsungs shing / 'dir d+hU tIr rlung 'jug par byed pa srog rtsol gyi yan lag dang / gnas par byed pa 'dzin pa'i yan lag ces rlung dbu mar 'jug pa'i thabs dang gnas pa'i thabs gnyis sbyor ba yan lag drug gi yan lag so sor bshad pa dang / gzhan du rlung dbu mar thim pa'i dod rlung bsad pa zhes pa ting nge 'dzin nas 'ong bar gsungs shing / zin bris kyi shes byed kyang rgyud 'grel dang tshad ldan gyi dgongs 'grel rnams las srog rtsol man chad du rlung dbu mar gnas pa dang thim pa zur tsam yang ma gsungs pa nyid yin no/ /

How do those explanations from the Kālacakra tradition and those from the Guhyasamāja and others /404/ differ on this topic? Notes on Kālacakra states:
In general the highest yoga tantras talk of the winds entering the dhūtī, dwelling in the dhūtī, and dissolving in the dhūtī. Here dissolving in the dhūtī is referred to as “binding,” “mixing,” and “killing” the winds, whereas entering and abiding are spoken of as being separate branches. These are the branch of prāṇāyāma, which halts the flow of winds in the left and right channels and brings them into the dhūtī, and the branch of retention, which keeps the winds in the dhūtī.[238] This passage is saying that in the Guhyasamāja and other tantras, during the practices of body isolation and speech isolation, for example, penetrative focusing on the points of the body will bring about the entering, abiding, and the dissolving of the winds in the dhūtī during one continuous practice. However here the branch of prāṇāyāma that brings the winds into the dhūtī and the branch of retention that keeps them there are two separate methods and, moreover, are two separate branches within the six-branched yoga. The above passage also says that dissolving the winds in the dhūtī, referred to here as “killing the winds,” occurs in the sixth branch, meditative concentration. Moreover the tantra, the Great Commentary, and other authoritative commentaries, which act as sources for the Notes on Kālacakra, do not even mention the abiding and dissolving of the winds in the central channel in any of the chapters up to the branch of prāṇāyāma.

d.div: [237] rje tsong kha pa/ gsung 'bum pod/ da_sbyor ba yan lag drug gi rdzogs rim gyi gnad bsdus pa/ 12_na6
[238] Collected Works, vol. da, 12a6.

f.d:
rang lugs ni ye le'i brgya bcu bdun pa'i 'grel chen las/
de nas gzugs ni mthong bar gyur na nyin zhag so so'i dus su srog gi rlung ni 'gog pa zhes pa bum pa can rab tu bya ste/[238] zhes sor bsam gyi stong gzugs mthong zhing brtan par gyur pa na rlung sbyor bum pa can gyis mtshon pa'i srog rtsol bya bar gsungs pa dang / de bzhin du nA ro pa'i dbang mdor bstan gyi 'grel pa las kyang /
srog rtsol gsungs pa gzugs brnyan mthong na zhes bya ba la sogs pa'o/ / rmi lam dang sgyu ma ci 'dra ba de 'dra ba'i gzugs brnyan rnam pa thams cad pa'i gzugs mthong bar gyur na de nas de'i bar ma chad bar srog rtsol srog dang thur sel gyi rlung dag dgang ba dang bum pa can dang dbyung pa'i sbyor bas 'gog pa bar ma chad par te rgyun ma chad bar bya'o/[239] / zhes bsam gtan grub pa'i de ma thag srog rtsol bsgom bar gsungs pa ltar bya'o/ / 'grel tshig de rnams kyis sor bsam sngon du ma song bar yang srog rtsol bsgoms pas lam ji lta ba bzhin skye bar 'dod pa yang bkag par shes par bya'o/ /

Our own position is that when the empty forms of withdrawal and meditative absorption have been seen and stabilized, the branch of prāṇāyāma, as illustrated by the vase yoga, should begin. The Great Commentary, on verse 117 of the Gnosis chapter, says:
Then, “when form is seen, each day the winds are to be halted” refers to the vase yoga.[239] Similarly Nāropa, in his Commentary on a Short Teaching on Initiations, teaches that prāṇāyāma meditation begins immediately after the completion of meditative absorption:
The lines on prāṇāyāma begin, “When images of form are seen.” When miragelike and dreamlike images of fully aspected form are seen, “meditate constantly on prāṇāyāma” and halt the life and downward winds with filling, vase, and expelling yogas.[240] These words refute the suggestion /405/ that meditation on prāṇāyāma not preceded by the practices of withdrawal and meditative absorption will develop into the correct path.

d.div: [238] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 389_na5
[239] sde dge_1351_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ na_dbang mdor bstan pa'i 'grel bshad/ 263_ba1

[240] Toh 1351 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, 263b1.

f.d: gsum pa gang bsgom ba'i yan lag gi nges pa
['di ]la bzhi/ srog rtsol gyi lam gyi ngo bo ngos gzung ba/ srog rtsol gyi dbye ba/ ji ltar sgom pa'i tshul/ ma grub pa sbogs pa'i cho ga'o/ /
This is under four outlines: 1. Identifying the path of prāṇāyāma 2. Divisions 3. The meditation 4. Enhancement ritual
dang po [srog rtsol gyi lam gyi ngo bo ngos gzung ba ]ni

rdor bzlas dang bum pa can gyi srog rtsol gyis rlung dbu mar tshud pa phul du byung ba las byung ba'i 'od gsal gyi sems dang / de dang ngo bo dbyer med pa'i stong gzugs dus kyi 'khor lo yab yum zhal sbyor gyi rnam pa can lte ba'i rtsa 'khor gyi dbus su snang ba ni srog rtsol gyi lam gyi ngo bo'o/ / de ltar yin pa yang sgrub le'i brgya nyi shu pa'i 'grel chen las/
srog rtsol gyis ni dag pa zhes pa ni 'dir gang gi tshe rnal 'byor pa nyi ma dang ri bong can gyi lam dang bral te rtag tu dbu mar 'bab par gyur pa de'i tshe srog rtsol gyis dag par gyur pas na [240] zhes gsungs pa 'dis bstan te/ 'di dag gi don ni/ gang dag pa ni 'od gsal gyi sems dang de dang ngo bo gcig pa'i stong gzugs yin la/ gang gis dag pa ni nyi zla ro rkyang gi rlung rgyu ba dang bral te rtag tu rlung dbu mar 'bab pa ste dbu mar tshud pa phul du byung ba'i srog rtsol gyis dag par gyur pas na ste dag par gyur pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyis mchod pa ste bsngags par byed do/ /zhes pa'o/ / de yang srog rtsol gyi lam gyi ngo bor gyur pa'i stong gzugs dus 'khor yab yum gyi rnam pa can ni sgrub le'i brgya nyer gnyis pa las/
dbus su srog ni rab tu zhugs pa yul dang rnam par bral ba sna tshogs yum la 'khyud pa ste/[241] zhes gsungs pa 'dis bstan to/ /

The appearance of the empty-form Kālacakra in mother-and-father embrace within the center of the navel cakra, indivisible from the clear-light mind that has arisen from a very special entry of winds into the central channel brought on by the prāṇāyāma practices of vajra recitation and vase yoga, is the path of prāṇāyāma. This is taught by the Great Commentary on verse 120 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter:
“Purified by prāṇāyāma” means that when the yogi is “divorced from the paths of the sun and moon” and is constantly within the central channel, he will be purified by the prāṇāyāma and therefore will be “praised by the bodhisattvas.”[241] What is to be purified? The clear-light mind and the empty forms that are of the same nature as this mind are the phenomena to be purified. What is the purifier? It is prāṇāyāma practice, which induces the special entry of the winds into the central channel. This occurs when the sun and moon right and left channels are divorced from their flows of wind. “Therefore,” which means because of this purification, the yogi will be “praised by the bodhisattvas.” The empty-form Kālacakra in mother-and-father embrace as the actual path of prāṇāyāma is taught by verse 122 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter:
The winds enter the center, divorced of objects, embracing Viśvamātā.[242]

d.div: [240] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 238_na1
[241] sde dge_362_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_bsdus rgyud/ sh+loka122_90_na4
[241] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 238a1.
[242] Toh 362 Kangyur, rgyud, ka, v. 122, 90a4.

f.d:
de yang lte ba'i rtsa 'khor gyi dbus su shar ba dgos pa ni ye le'i brgya nyi shu pa'i 'grel chen las/
rlung gnyis yang dag phrad pa'i dbus su zhes pa lte bar srog dang thur sel gyi rlung dag yang dag par phrad pa'i dbus su yul zhes pa rnam dbye med pa'i tshig ste yul rnams la yul can mig la sogs pa rnams 'byung ba dang rab tu 'jug pa ni lte bar te de nyid ni sngar brjod zin to/ / du ba la sogs pa rnams kyi mtshan ma 'dzin pa na a ba d+hU tI'i sgo nas te kyang gi sgras lte ba de nyid la'o/[242] / zhes pa 'dis bstan to/ /

That this phenomenon appears in the center of the navel cakra is taught by the Great Commentary on verse 120 of the Gnosis chapter: /406/
“In the center of the two winds meeting” means in the center at the navel, where the life wind and downward wind meet. “The arising and engaging in the objects by object-engagers,” such as eyes and so forth, at the navel is a topic that has been discussed previously. The word “objects” is without a grammatical case. “Apprehending the signs of smoke and so forth also” is by way of the avadhūtī. The word “also” refers again to the navel.[243]

d.div: [242] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_'grel chen dri med 'od/ 390_ba3
[243] Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 390b3.

f.d: 'o na ji ltar du bstan snyam na/ de yang 'di ltar du bstan te/ srog rtsol bum pa can bsgoms pas lte ba'i rtsa 'khor gyi dbus der srog 'dzin dang thur sel gyi rlung gnyis yang dag par phrad pa'i dbus su gzugs sogs yul rnams la mig sogs yul can rnams 'byung ba dang 'jug pa lte bar te lte ba'i rtsa 'khor gyi dbus su bkag pa'i sgo nas du ba la sogs pa rnams kyi mtshan ma'i stong gzugs dang/ khyad par du yang dus 'khor yab yum gyi rnam pa can gyi stong gzugs 'dzin no/ / gnas gang du 'dzin cing 'char na/ a ba d+hU tI'i sgo nas te a ba d+hU tI+i'i nang du'o/ / de yang kyang gis sgras lte ba'i rtsa 'khor gyi dbus kyi d+hU tI'i nang du'o/ / yul can mig sogs rnams yul gzugs sogs rnams la 'jug pa 'gog tshul de nyi+id na sngar sor sdud kyi skabs su brjod zin pa ltar ro/ /zhes pa'o/ /

How does this passage teach that the empty form appears in the center of the navel cakra? It does so like this. By meditating on the vase yoga of prāṇāyāma, the life-sustaining wind and the downwardly expelling wind meet at “at the navel,” meaning at the center of the navel cakra, where the arising and engaging of object-engagers such as eyes focusing on objects such as forms and so forth has been halted. Because of this, the empty-form signs of smoke and so forth, and especially the empty-form Kālacakra in mother-father embrace, are perceived. Where are they seen? “By way of the avadhūtī” means inside the avadhūtī. The word “also” means inside the dhūtī in the center of the navel cakra. The way that the process of object-engagers such as eyes engaging in objects such as forms and so forth has been halted “is a topic that has been discussed previously” in the section on withdrawal.

de ltar na srog rtsol gyi skabs 'di lta bur yang d+hU tI'i gnas gang du dmigs pa gtad sa der rlung 'du zhing rlung 'dus sa der stong gzugs dus 'khor yab yum gyi rnam pa can yang ma btags ma bcos par rang dbang du 'char bar nges pas rdor bzlas byed pa'i tshe d+hU tI'i yar snar shar ba'i stong gzugs de rlung nang 'jug pa dang bsres nas lte bar 'bebs pa'i dmigs pa zur du mi dgos te/ bum pa can gyi srog rtsol gyis lte bar srog thur phrad par byas pa'i dbus lte ba'i d+hU tI'i nang du rlung gnyis kha sbyor du 'dzin pa'i dmigs pa de nyid kyis stong gzugs lte ba'i rtsa 'khor gyi dbus kyi d+hU tI'i nang du ma bcos ma btags par rang dbang du 'char bar 'grel chen las bshad ma thag pa ltar yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

Therefore, in this section on prāṇāyāma also, wherever one focuses within the dhūtī, there the winds will gather, and at that particular place an empty-form Kālacakra in mother-father embrace will definitely arise of its own accord, unconceived and unimputed by the mind. Therefore, during vajra recitation, when the empty form at the upper end of the dhūtī enters and mixes with winds, there is no need for a separate visualization of it arriving at the navel. This is because the power of vase yoga will bring the life and downward winds to meet at the navel, and the union of these two winds is meditatively focused on inside the dhūtī at the center of the navel. There empty forms will appear by their own volition, unimputed and unconceived by the mind, as taught by the above passage from the Great Commentary. /407/
gnyis pa dbye ba ni

chos rje bu la sogs pa bla ma snga ma rnams rdo rje'i bzlas pa/ rngub pa/ dgang ba/ gzhil ba/ bum pa can/ ra tsa ka 'am rdul mtha' can dang drug tu mdzad pa la/ zin bris las/
rgyud 'grel nas rdor bzlas dang bum pa can gnyis las ma bshad la de gnyis kyis dgos pa yang 'grub pas rgyud nas ma bshad kyang kha 'gengs dgos pa yang ma yin no/[243] / zhes gsungs pa ltar bya zhing / rlung sbyor gzhan de rnams la rtsa dbu mar dmigs pa gtod tshul gang yang med pa 'dra bas rlung dbu mar 'jug pa'i srog rtsol tu 'gro dka' bar snang ngo / / des na dbye ba la rdo rje bzlas pa dang bum pa can gnyis so/ /

The dharma master Butön and other masters of the past talk of six divisions, namely, vajra recitation, inhalation, filling, expelling, vase yoga, and racaka,[244] or “particle limit.” However Notes on Kālacakra says:
The tantra and commentary mention only vajra recitation and vase yoga, and these two will accomplish the purpose. Although the tantra teaches no more than these two, they do not need supplementing.[245] This position should be accepted, and because the other wind yogas mentioned above are similar in not having any focus upon the central channel, it is difficult to see how they could be prāṇāyāma practices for bringing the winds into the central channel. Therefore vajra recitation and vase yoga are the two divisions of prāṇāyāma.

d.div: [243] rje tsong kha pa/ gsung 'bum pod/ da_sbyor ba yan lag drug gi rdzogs rim gyi gnad bsdus pa/ 13_na3
[244] As transliterated in Tibetan. It is normally spelled recaka and refers to the prāṇāyāma practice of expelling wind.
[245] Jé Tsongkhapa, Collected Works, vol. da, 13a3.

f.d: srog rtsol ji ltar sgom pa'i tshul/
31. Vajra Recitation
gsum pa ji ltar sgom pa'i tshul
['di ]la gnyis/ rdo rje bzlas pa'i sgom tshul dang / bum pa can gyi sgom tshul lo/ /
This has two main outlines: 1. Vajra recitation 2. Vase yoga
dang po [rdo rje bzlas pa'i sgom tshul ]
['di ]la gnyis/ rdor bzlas kyi byed las sam dngos kyi dgos pa dang / sgom tshul dngos so/ /
This is under two headings: 1. The function or actual purpose of vajra recitation 2. The meditation
dang po [rdor bzlas kyi byed las sam dngos kyi dgos pa ]ni

d.i: The function or actual purpose of vajra recitation

f.d:
sgrub le'i brgya bcu drug pa'i 'grel chen las/ /
'dir srog rtsol dag kyang lam ni gnyis po zhes pa g.yon dang g.yas pa'i lam bsgyel ba ste 'gog cing dbu ma'i lam du rab tu zhugs pa'o/[244] / zhes dang / bde mchog stod 'grel las kyang /
de nas srog rtsol zhes bya ba ni la la nA dang ra sA nA g.yon pa dang g.yas pa'i lam 'gags pa las dbu ma a ba d+hU tI'i nang du srog gi rlung rtag tu 'jug ste/[245] zhes gsungs pa ltar rdor bzlas dang bum pa can bsgoms pas ro rkyang la rlung rgyu ba chad de dbu ma 'ba' zhig tu rlung 'jug pa ni srog rtsol gnyis bsgoms pa'i byed las yin no/ / de yang rgyud rtsa bar/ srog rtsol dag kyang [246] zhes gnyis tshig smos pa 'dis srog rtsol gnyis ka'i byed las bstan cing rdor bzlas byed tshul dngos su ma bstan kyang bum pa can dngos su bstan la/ stod 'grel du rdor bzlas byed tshul dang bum pa can gnyis ka dngos su bstan pa ni 'grel ba'i don de lta nyid du 'chad pa las shes par 'gyur ro/ /

The Great Commentary, on verse 116 of the Methods of Accomplishment chapter, says:
“In the prāṇāyāma meditations also the two pathways,” referring to the left and right pathway, “collapse,” meaning are blocked, and winds enter the central pathway.[246] Similarly the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary says:
Prāṇāyāma means blocking the left and right paths of lalanā and rasanā so that the winds are constantly in the avadhūtī.[247] As these quotes say, by the meditations of vajra recitation and vase yoga, /408/ the flow of winds in the right and left channels is stopped and directed to enter only the central channel. This is the function of both types of prāṇāyāma. The tantra’s use of the plural “meditations” indicates that it is referring to the functions of both prāṇāyāma practices, and although it does not describe vajra recitation directly, it does teach vase yoga. In the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary, vajra recitation and vase yoga meditations are both described, as will be understood from the following presentations.

f.d: gnyis pa sgom tshul dngos
['di ]la gang du bsgom pa'i gnas dang / lus gnad dang / lta stangs dang / gang la dmigs nas bsgom pa'i tshul dang bsgom pas nyams rtags ji ltar skye ba'i tshul dang lnga las/
This is under five headings: 1. Place of meditation 2. Body posture 3. Eye position 4. The focus and method of the meditation 5. Signs of accomplishment
dang po [gang du bsgom pa'i gnas ]ni
sor sdud kyi skabs su bshad pa'i gnas gnyis so/ /
The place of meditation is the same as described in the section on withdrawal.
gnyis pa lus gnad ni
sor bsam gyi skabs su bshad pa dang 'dra ba las khyad par ni rkang pa g.yas pa'i rting pas bshang lam ma bkag par rdo rje'i rtsa ba mnan pa'o/ /
This is the same as described in withdrawal and meditative absorption, the only difference being that the heel of the right foot does not block the anus but presses against the base of the vajra.
gsum pa lta stangs ni

bdud rtsi'i khyil ba'i lta stangs byed par bshad pa'i bdud rtsi 'khyil ba 'di la drang nges kyi bshad tshul gnyis byung ba'i drang don ni sor sdud kyi skabs su bshad par ltar mig gnyis gyen du log ste smin mtshams kyi dbus kyi d+hU tI'i nang gi bdud rtsi byang sems dkar po'i gnas der lta ba'o/ / nges don ni 'dus pa phyi ma'i/
nye bar sgrub pa'i dus su ni/ / bdud rtsi 'khyil ba'i gzugs brnyan no/[247] / zhes pa'i don 'chad byed kyi stod 'grel las/
de nas bdud rtsi 'khyil ba'i gzugs brnyan gyi ming can dgongs pa'i skad gzhan gyis rlung gsungs so/[248] / zhes bshad pas rlung la mig gis lta bar mi nus pas yid shes kyis lta ba yin la/ de yang rdor bzlas kyi rlung 'jug gnas ldang gsum la dmigs shing / bum pa can gyi srog thur lte bar kha sbyor du byas pa la dmigs nas lta ba yin no/ /

The eye position is explained as being the “look of amṛtavarta.” Amṛtavarta has an interpretive and definitive description. In the interpretive, as described in withdrawal, the eyes are turned upward and look toward the location of the white bodhicitta nectar in the dhūtī between the eyebrows. The definitive description is found in the Later Guhyasamāja:
During near accomplishment the image of amṛtavarta.[248] Explaining this verse, the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary says:
Using provisional language, “the image of amṛtavarta” refers to the winds.[249] The eyes themselves cannot look at the winds, and so it is the mental consciousness that actually looks, and this refers to focusing upon the entering, abiding, and leaving of the winds during vajra recitation and upon the life and downward winds joining at the navel during vase yoga.

f.d: bzhi pa gang la dmigs nas bsgom pa'i tshul ni

d.i: The focus and method of the meditation

f.d:
stod 'grel las/
de nas srog rtsol zhes bya ba ni la la nA dang ra sa nA g.yon pa dang g.yas ba'i lam 'gags pa las dbu ma a ba d+hU tI'i nang du srog gi rlung rtag tu 'jug ste dgang ba dang bum pa can dang 'byung ba'i sbyor bas a ba d+hu tI'i oM yig gis 'jug pa dang hUM [249] yig gis 'gog pa dang A yig gis 'byung ba dang zla ba dang sgra gcan dang nyi ma'i rang bzhin gyis rnal 'byor pas bsgom par bya'o zhes srog rtsol gyi yan lag brjod do/[250] / zhes gsungs pa 'dis gsal bar bstan to/ /

This is clearly taught in the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary:
Prāṇāyāma means blocking the left and right paths of lalanā and rasanā so that the winds are constantly in the avadhūtī central channel. In the yogas of filling, vase, and arising, the syllable oṃ in the avadhūtī brings about the entering, /409/ the syllable hūḥ brings about the halting, and the syllable āḥ creates the arising. The yogi meditates on these, whose natures are the moon, Rāhu, and sun. This is prāṇāyāma.[250]

d.div: [249] dus 'khor nang hUM yig cha tshang la byung na nA da dgos pa dang / de yang nyung thar rjes su nga ro'am sna ldan nges par dgos pa yang bshad/ hU~M yig 'dis nyi zla dang sgra gcan mtshon zhes sngon gyi mkhas pa du ma'i gzhung du mar yod pa bshad kyang 'dir ma dpe ltar ma bcos par rang gnas su bzhag
[250] sde dge_1402_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ba_bde mchog stod 'grel/ 130_ba4
[250] Toh 1402 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ba, 130b4.

f.d: ji ltar du bstan snyam na/ de yang de nas zhes pa nas rtag du 'jug ste zhes pa'i bar gyis rlung ro rkyang la rgyu ba bzhag nas dbu mar rtag tu 'jug pa ste rdor bzlas kyi dngos kyi dgos pa'am byed las su bstan nas/ de yang thabs ji lta bus bya snyam na/ a wa d+hU tIr rlung dgang ba dang bum pa can dang dbyung ba'i sbyor bas bya'o/ / de bya ba'i tshul ji ltar bya snyam na/ dbugs nang du 'jug pa'i rang gdangs zla ba sku rdo rje oM yig gi gdangs su shar ba d+hU tI'i nang du 'jug par mos pa dang / dbugs nang du gnas pa'i rang gdangs sgra gcan thugs rdo rje hUM yig gi gdangs su shar ba d+hU tI'i nang du bum pa can dang 'gog pa ste gnas par mos pa dang / dbugs phyir dbyung ba'i rang gdangs nyi ma gsung rdo rje'i rang bzhin a yig gi gdangs su shar ba d+hU tI'i nang nas phyir dbyung ba ste 'byung bar mos pa'i rdo rje bzlas pa rnal 'byor pas bsgom par bya'o zhes pa'o/ /

How does this passage teach the focus of meditation? The first sentence shows the purpose or function of vajra recitation by stating that the winds are stopped from flowing in the left and right channels and are made to flow constantly in the central channel. How is this achieved? By filling the dhūtī with wind, by vase yoga, and by arising yoga. How are these performed? The innate tone of the breath entering arises as the sound of oṃ, the moon body-vajra syllable, and is visualized as entering the dhūtī. The innate tone possessed by the breath abiding internally arises as the sound of hūḥ, the Rāhu mind-vajra syllable. It is visualized as abiding in the dhūtī, which is the meaning of “vase” and “halting.” The innate tone of the breath being expelled arises as the sound of the syllable āḥ, whose nature is the sun speech vajra and is visualized as being expelled from the dhūtī. This is “arising.” This is vajra recitation meditation.

stod 'grel las 'di ltar gsungs pa'i dgongs pa 'grel par nA ro pas dbang mdor bstan gyi 'grel par yang /
de nas srog rtsol zhes bya ba ni la la nA dang ra sa nA g.yon pa dang g.yas ba'i lam 'gog pa las srog gi rlung rtag tu dbu ma a wa d+hU tI'i lam du rab tu 'jug pa ste a wa d+hU tIr dgang ba dang bum pa can dang dbyung ba'i sbyor bas oM yig gis 'jug pa dang hUM yig gis 'gog pa dang / AH yig gis 'byung ba zla ba dang sgra gcan dang nyi ma'i rang bzhin gyis rnal 'byor pas phyed pa ni srog rtsol gyi yan lag go[251] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Nāropa in his Commentary on a Short Teaching on Initiations cites this explanation from the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary:
Prāṇāyāma means blocking the left and right paths of lalanā and rasanā, from which the winds constantly enter the avadhūtī. In the avadhūtī, by the yogas of filling, vase, and expelling, the syllable oṃ brings about the entering, the syllable hūḥ brings about the halting, and the syllable āḥ creates the arising. The yogi accomplishes those whose natures are the moon, Rāhu, and sun. This is the branch of prāṇāyāma.

d.div: [251] sde dge_1402_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ba_bde mchog stod 'grel/ 130_ba4

f.d: bla ma kha cig rlung ro rkyang nas 'byung 'jug byed pa la dmigs pa sogs byas nas rlung dbu ma'i nang nas 'byung 'jug byed par mos mi dgos pa'i rdor bzlas byed tshul ni 'grel pa gnyis kyis a wa d+hU tIr oM yig gis 'jug pa dang zhes sogs dang / a wa d+hU tIr dgang ba dang bum pa can dang dbyung ba dang zhes sogs kyis legs par bkag par shes par bya'o/ /

Some lamas focus on the winds coming and going from the right and left channels and so forth and then consider it unnecessary to visualize the winds entering and leaving the central channel. This method of vajra recitation is well refuted by the two passages above, which talk of “the syllable oṃ in the avadhūtī brings about the entering,” etc., and “In the avadhūtī, by the yogas of filling, vase, and expelling,” etc.

yang kha cig /ye le'i sdom chen gyi skabs las/
'dir nges pa'i don ni dus thams cad du brtan par gyur pa dang bum pa can gyi gnas skabs su gyur pa ji srid bar dus thams cad du rnal 'byor bas 'jug pa dang 'byung ba nyid kyis srog dbu mar bsgom par bya'o/[252] / zhes gsungs pa'i bum pa can ni rdor bzlas kyi stobs kyis 'byung 'jug gnyis 'gags nas gnas pa 'ba' zhig tu gyur pa yin zhes gsung ba ni mi 'thad de/ rje rin po che'i dgongs pa ma yin pa ni gong du bshad zin cing / 'grel chen las kyang / dbu ma'i lam du rab tu zhugs pa'o/[253] /zhes pa dang / stod 'grel las/ dbu ma a wa d+hU tI'i nang du srog gi rlung rtag tu 'jug ste/[254] zhes rlung dbu ma nas rtag tu 'byung 'jug byed pas rdor bzlas kyi byed las rdzogs par bshad cing gnas par byed par ma bshad pa'i phyir ro/ / 'o na ye le'i 'grel pa de'i don ci yin snyam na/ de'i don ni 'og tu bshad par bya'o/ /

In the great vow[251] section of the Gnosis chapter it says: /410/
The definitive meaning is that at all times it is stabilized, and at all times during the vase yoga, the yogi meditates on the winds that enter and arise as being in the central channel.[252] Some lamas say that the “vase yoga” mentioned here refers only to the stage of abiding, the inhalation and exhalation having been stopped by the power of vajra recitation. This is incorrect, because it is not the position of Jé Tsongkhapa as explained previously. Moreover the Great Commentary talks of “winds entering the central pathway.”[253] The Cakrasaṃvara Commentary talks of “the winds constantly entering the avadhūtī.”[254] These quotes point out that it is the constant flow of wind in and out of the central channel and not the stage of abiding that accomplishes the function of vajra recitation. So what does the above passage from the Gnosis chapter mean? That will be explained below.

f.d: de yang sems 'grel skor gsum las rlung nang du 'jug pa oM dang / gnas pa hUM dang / phyir 'byung ba A: dang sbyar zhing / ma hA mA yar rlung phyir 'byung ba oM dang / gnas pa hUM du gsungs so/ / 'dus par rlung nang du 'jug pa oM dang / gnas pa A: dang / phyir 'byung ba hUM dang sbyor bar gsungs pas yi ge dang sbyor tshul mi mthun pa byung yang / de thams cad kyis rlung ro rkyang la rgyu ba bkag nas dbu mar 'jug pa'i srog rtsol du gyur pa la khyad par med do/ / de ltar na dbugs kyi 'jug gnas ldang gsum gyi rang gdangs yi ge gsum gyi gdangs su ji ltar rigs par mos par byed pa yin gyi dbugs gsum gyi rang gdangs yi ge gsum gyi gdangs su dngos po'i gnas tshod la gzhi la gnas par byas na rgyud kyi dgongs pa mi mthun pa rnams 'khrugs par 'gyur bas dpyad par bya dgos so/ /

Three Bodhisattva Commentaries speaks of the entering wind being assigned to the syllable oṃ, the abiding wind as assigned to hūḥ, and the wind being expelled as assigned to āḥ. In the Great Illusion Tantra the expelling is assigned to oṃ and the abiding to hūḥ. The Guhyasamāja speaks of the entering wind as oṃ, the abiding wind as āṃ, and the wind being expelled as hūḥ. Although there are differences in the way the syllables are assigned, there are no differences insofar as they are all prāṇāyāma yogas that block the flow of wind in the right and left channels and bring it into the central channel. Therefore the innate tone of the breath entering, abiding, and leaving is visualized as the appropriate sound of the three syllables. However the disagreement that arises on the tantra’s position when trying to establish which of the innate tones of the three breath stages are assigned to which sounds of the three syllables is confusing and should be examined.

thams cad mkhyen pa bu ston rin po ches/ 'grel chen las/
'dir bgrang 'phreng med cing sngags rjod pa med de dbugs 'jug pa dang 'byung ba dag dang lhan cig sngags kyi yi ge rnams rab tu 'jug pa dang 'byung ba me tog gi phreng ba bzhin du zla ba dang nyi ma'i rang bzhin lugs dang mthun pa dang lugs dang mi mthun pas blta bar bya'o/ / de ltar nang du nyin zhag lngas stong phrag brgyad lhag pa'i 'bum phrag gi bzlas pa rnal 'byor pas bya'o/ / nyin zhag lnga brgya rnams kyis dbugs 'bum phrag brgyad lhag pa'i bye ba bzlas pa'o/ / de nas lus dag pa ste de bzhin du ngag dag pa dang de bzhin du sems rnam par dag pa'o/ / de ltar nyin zhag brgya phrag bco lnga rnams kyi dbugs g.yo ba med par 'gyur te srog gi bum pa can gyi gnas skabs thob par 'gyur ro/ / de nas rnal 'byor pa rnams la mngon par shes pa lnga skye bar 'gyur te g.yon dang g.yas dang dbu ma'i srog yang dag par rgyu bas rdo rje'i bzlas pa'i rim pa dang ma ning gi bzlas pa'i rim pa'o zhes pa ni bcom ldan 'das kyi nges pa'o/[255] / zhes dang /
'dir nges pa'i don ni/ dus thams cad du brtan par gyur pa dang bum pa can gyi gnas skabs su gyur pa ji srid bar dus thams cad du rnal 'byor pas 'jug pa dang 'byung ba nyid kyi srog dbu mar bsgom par bya'o/[256] / zhes gsungs pa rnams kyi don du mdzad nas sdom chen gyi mkha' 'gro'i sngags dang rkang pa bdun cu rtsa gnyis pa spel ba'i yi ge rnams 'pho ba bcu gnyis po re re la dkyil 'khor lnga lnga'i rlung rgyu ba drug cu dang / 'pho 'tshams bcu gnyis su ye shes kyi rlung bcu gnyis rgyu ba dang bcas pa'i bdun bcu rtsa gnyis la me tog gi 'phreng ba brgyus pa bzhin du lugs 'byung du 'jug pa zla ba'i rang bzhin/ gnas pa sgra gcan gyi rang bzhin/ phyir lugs bzlog tu 'byung ba nyi ma'i rang bzhin du dmigs nas yid ma yengs shing bya ba gzhan gyis bar ma chod na zhag gcig la bzlas pa nyi khri chig stong drug brgya 'gro zhing / de lta bu lnga brgya pa rim pa gsum gyis rim pa bzhin lus ngag yid gsum dag nas bum pa can gyi gnas skabs thob par 'gyur ro zhes bshad nas/ 'dir rgyud 'grel nas dngos su gsungs pa'i rdzogs rim gyi srog rtsol rdo rje bzlas par mdzad do/ / rje yab sras kyi dgongs 'grel du bzhed pa'i 'khrid yig kha cig las kyang 'grel tshig de rnams kyis sbyor ba yan lag drug gi srog rtsol rdo rje bzlas par bstan par 'chad do/ /[257]

The Great Commentary says:
Here there is no counting or saying of mantra, but together with the breath entering and leaving, concentrate on the letters of the mantra entering and leaving like a garland of flowers, in the nature of moon and sun, and in forward and reverse order. In this way, inwardly the yogi performs 108,000 recitations in five days.[255] In five hundred days the yogi recites on 10.8 million breaths. Then the body becomes pure. Likewise the speech is purified and similarly the mind. /411/ In this way the breath of fifteen hundred days remains unmoving, and the state of the vase wind is achieved. The yogis will develop the five kinds of clairvoyance, and with the perfect flow of winds in the left, right, and central channels, this is the vajra recitation and neutral recitation. This has been determined by the Buddha. Also:
The definitive meaning is that at all times it is stabilized, and at all times during the vase yoga, the yogi meditates on the winds that enter and arise as being in the central channel. Using these passages as a basis, Butön Rinpoché[256] explains that the letters of the great-vow ḍāka and ḍākinī mantras intertwined with the seventy-two-line mantra are recited like a threaded flower garland upon the twelve major movements of wind,[257] each of which is divided into five elemental mandalas to make sixty, to which is added the twelve flows of gnosis wind that occur between each of the twelve movements, to make seventy-two in total. These letters are recited in forward order for the entering and the abiding, which are in the nature of the moon and Rāhu respectively, and in reverse order for the arising, which is in the nature of the sun. If this is done with no distraction and no interruption, then in one day 21,600 recitations are performed. In three blocks of five hundred days each, the body, speech, and mind are purified, and one has reached the time for vase yoga. Therefore he posits the above passages as being the tantra and commentary description of the completion-stage vajra recitation of the branch of prāṇāyāma. Other texts that claim to be commentaries in keeping with the position of Jé Tsongkhapa and his disciples also explain this passage from the commentary as a description of the vajra recitation of prāṇāyāma from the six-branched yoga.
